I used to hate this game with a vengenance due to the absolutely horrible multiplayer experience that existed for the first 2 years after the steam launch.
However, within the year of 2015, I have notice the multiplayer experience improve bit by bit over the array of updates this game has gotten since the start of the year.
I can now say that multiplayer performs very well, both in early game and late game, 1v1 up to 4v4, and the response times of units are now so much faster that it feel like I'm playing age of empires 3 multiplayer (this is good).
They have fixed bugs regarding terribly inaccurate movement of units when moved together in large group.
There is still room to improve however. Finding a multiplayer game is a tedious task at times and there are an array of bugs within the multiplayer lobby client. But from the progress I've seen this year I can totally recommend this game to anyone who likes RTS games.

Honestly, the game can be fun...
When you're not dying to a Heavy Assault's pistol from across a large settlement, and realising that tampons for men are, and would, be more effective than your rockets.
PlanetSide 2 is a large scale, F2P FPS where three teams fight over a giant map when they're not walking about trying to get to said battle, and when they do get there, die to an Infiltrator that spent the time walking out of their base to come stab you in the♥♥♥♥♥when they could've shot you.
DeathScreen 2 has the potential to be a better game.
If you spent less time looking at the death screen, and the guy with a female character with clothes tighter than David Bowies' pants in Labyrinth, you might be able to get the points to buy the better weapons that can actually fill someone with bullets and kill them.
Which brings us to the next point.
PlanetoidAngle 2 has a currency called Cercs, which you use to buy weapons for each class. From what I know, you get 1 Cerc for every 100xp (?), which honestly, you can get a few depending on your luck in 1-3 lives.
However, it's hard to get said Cercs when you have the starting Nerf guns, and everyone else has the Pay2Win nuclear bomb pistols that can kill you from anywhere on the map with any button.
With the concept this game has, it could be extremely fun if it wasn't as frustrating and featured more of a friendly weapon-obtaining system so you're not constantly getting mowed down by shotguns with the accuracy of a sniper rifle.
If I could, I would give the game a neutral recommendation.

Been a QA tester since early development, originally coming from the Project Reality scene I already had good hopes from these developers. A lot of you might not have these expectations so this is why I'd like to stress. A lot of these developers already have spent 10 years on a mod that is still running today (Project Reality). The fact that they put up something like this in EA with quality like this should be enough to back this immediatly.
It's running very well for an early acces game, it has huge potential and it has the true Project Reality feel to it already. If you're looking for a game that combines Realism and Fun and finds a way between shooters like BF/COD and milsim like ARMA then you're on the right track.
With in the future combined warfare there's lots to look out to. The VOIP system assures you of good communication on squadlevel and teamlevel. It's a long way, but they've already came a long way so far.

A beautiful puzzle game with a breathtaking, deeply philosophical story about life. Thinking of it now (about two weeks after finishing the game), it made me question and rethink some of my own views on what is life...
Now to speak more about the game: you control a robot, either from 3rd or 1st person view and you have to solve puzzles to get sigils. The core idea of the puzzles is similar to Portal: each puzzle is within an enclosed "chamber", and you have couple tools available to you to move things around, connect light beams or jam a force-field, etc. Once you collect enough sigils, you have to solve a simple (ehm, ehm) puzzle: assemble the tetris-shaped sigils so that they form a rectangle. It's sounds like a toy for 3-year-old kids, but trust me, it gets pretty frustrating sometimes :-D
The overall story-arc is about you being a child of God, who allows you to play in his Garden, as long as you don't enter the forbidden Tower. As you go through the game, you will get in touch with an AI, which will made you doubt yourself, will try to lead you off the path and will influence you on your journey through the game. The great think here is that you always have a wide variety of answers that allow you to express your actualy views on some...let's say philosophical questions :)
All in all, a marvelous game with beautiful graphics, great background music, and an atmosphere and story I've never seen in a game before. The 10/10 reviews are no joke, this game has rightfully earned it.

Comparing The Talos Principle to a game like Portal is unfair, but immediate. The first time I manipulated a gadget to set off a part of a puzzle, I muttered how much it reminded me of the amazing and witty Portal 1 and 2, and that trying to replicate it was unwise. However, I removed my premature opinions and discovered a whole new world of puzzle and story, placed perfectly in what is called The Talos Principle.
The game starts out in ruins, immediately piquing interest and curiosity. This first person interaction makes it impossible to know who you are, or what you are doing in the deserted grounds of what seems like Rome. The land is littered with broken pillars and faulty statues, most of which are missing their heads.
Very shortly after running around, an all powerful voice beams from the skies, introducing himself and welcoming you to his garden. The puzzles ahead are a test to see if you are worthy (of what is unclear) and to strengthen your faith in him, "ELOHIM."
Without going into spoilers, I must say that the story is my favorite part of this game. Despite everything right about The Talos Principle, I’m a sucker for a great story, and very few games have the tone that this one carries beautifully and makes one question the nature of humanity. Almost every word spoken or typed holds a deeper meaning. Nothing is there without reason, and everything is set up in such a way that I didn’t feel left out of anything. There will be no regrets to finishing this game and seeing everything tie together.
Gameplay is very simple, which is nice, because the puzzles are not. Having the option, I opted for controller, assuming I could sit back, relax, and enjoy a nice, scenic mind game. I was wrong. Despite the scenery being beautiful and the music peaceful, my anxiety levels were high, attempting to freeze the laser gun that will shoot you down and sneak past the bots that will blow you up. And that’s within the first puzzles. You can’t do much on your own, only using what is provided to pass each task. It makes learning controls easy, which is nice when you have to take most of your focus into the puzzle.
There are only a handful of gadgets as well, each with a specific task that they do. Don’t be fooled though, because sometimes they are good for more than what they are intended. The puzzles themselves are short, only getting a little longer with time. Difficulty levels vary, but progress nicely with you, rather than slamming you with something impossible. There are also several puzzles per section, which gives you some options in case you get stuck. This attribute is great as the story is a heavy part that everyone should be able to complete.
What the game lacks in wit and comic relief, it replaces with promise and charm as that nagging curiosity presses you forward. There is a lot of content, which can be overwhelming if you want to follow the story, but luckily the audio tracks and journal entries are logged and easy to access at any time.
Another nice feature is the hunt for stars, which can be within the puzzle or just randomly hidden on the selected map. It had a lingering feel of Mario 64 about it. It also gives you a break from some frustrating enigmas and allows you to enjoy the landscapes. The signs are helpful to look at as well, so use them. They even mark off what you have completed, though who does it for you is unknown. Kind of spooky, right?
The Talos Principle doesn’t let down on graphics, either. Each stage and each little world is beautifully done, with sounds and music to match. Voice acting was very well done, allowing you to stay immersed in the game. The settings are almost too good to be real, which makes the game ever more creepy. Keep a look out when just walking around. There are some questionable sights on the rocks, in the water. You are clearly the only one around which raises the question, “where is everyone else?” Though questions like this will be answered, the theories I came up with thanks to the surrounding areas wwere a little unsettling.
With all of the story, the background, creepy settings, and subtle hints, I’d say this game is very replayable, especially if you are like me and forget how to do the puzzles. I know I’m one to miss things the first time around, so going back is always good.
Despite the eerie feeling I got every time I turned the game on, I was so compelled to read the QR codes on the walls, left by others before me. I wanted to understand the notes in the computer library and I wanted to know who ELOHIM really was, and what he wanted with me. All of this and more is explained if you are strong enough to pass over 120 puzzles in The Talos Principle.

Everyone's favorite prescription-painkiller-popping alcoholic returns in his third installment. While some groups have complained that this installment features a departure from the game mechanics of the prior titles, Max Payne 3 features polished controls that feel rather responsive. As someone who purchased this game coming from a background in first-person shooters, I was rather skeptical of the responsiveness while aiming or moving; however, Rockstar was capable of accomplishing this while managing to include quality animations to bring Max to life.

As with previous Rockstar titles such as the Grand Theft Auto series and L.A. Noire, Rockstar has a history of producing titles that have an engrossing story. Where Grand Theft Auto features quite a great deal of campy elements and tongue-in-cheek humor, Max Payne features a rather dark storyline where Max is, unsurprisingly, subject to shortcomings and loss. In this installment, he struggles to protect key members of a well-to-do Brazilian family, but struggles navigating the various politics regarding wealth where it is evident that there is a large gap between the social classes.
Despite the responsive controls and engaging story, there are some flaws with this work. As with many on-rails shooters, Max Payne's gameplay begins to feel more like a chore instead of feeling enjoyable, which necessitates taking breaks while progressing through the campaign. Breaks become more important as the graphics include bright colors to signal to the player that they are in a tropical locale and various filters/effects during cutscenes, and may affect some of the players who are prone to migraines. While these flaws can be overlooked by gamers, Max Payne does have the annoying habit of hanging on the loading screen prior to reaching the menu while the player is supposed to be signed into the Social Club. This constitutes a game-breaking bug, however there are simple solutions that can be consulted on the Support Forum.
Nevertheless, this is yet another quality release from Rockstar featuring beautiful graphics, responsive controls, and an engrossing plot.

I don't see what the hate is about. After trying it out (Free by the way, no premium at all) I found it to be a fun little game.
--- What is Robocraft ? ---
You can build your own robot that can hover, drive, fly or walk and in many different ways. Battle them on 1 map (as I'm writing this) and use a variety of weapons that remind me of the British show "Robot Wars".
After each game, whether you win or lose, you'll get a free part box of 3 (6 for premium) that randomly give common to super rare parts such as looks, weapons or blocks.
I enjoyed it. Sure there's a premium feature but it doesn't take too much from the game and surprisingly they give you the option to buy it perminantly for the low price of £30 (roughly $55) and the only fault I can find is the limited colours and maps.
-- Bad Points --
1 map is kind of boring after a while and as good of a map it is, more variety would help. However there are other modes unlocked at level 5 so maybe there's more I don't know of.
As for painting your robot, you get 4 colours: orange, blue, grey and white: which im glad they chose because those are the most wanted robot colours to start with.
However there are about 10 other colours you can use and they're locked off to premium. It would be nice to have the paint craftable at some point.
--- Good Points ---
Fun game that you can build a war machine, Walker and anything thanks to the "minecraft" style building that's fun and easy to use. The weapons are varied and balanced; usually having a weapon that will always beat another.
While the premium is still there, it's not in your face (excluding the reward boxes) and even logging in will give you a gift box each day.
Crafting: It's very basic but useful. Got any parts you don't want? You can sell them for points that you can then use to buy other, better parts from the store.
You can also share your robot designs with friends and see its stats and such. There is a community here and the "spore"-like sharing really helps show it off.

The Talos Principle is a 1st Person 3D puzzle game. The puzzles are very good. That honestly should be enough for a review for this type of game, but let's continue.
The Talos Principle is fairly long as puzzle games go, with around 100 puzzles total of various difficulties. The length is about 20 hours if you solve everything, so don't be put off by the higher price compared to other 1st person 3d puzzlers from smaller studios.
The namesake of The Talos Principle is explained in-game as a term used in philosophy. That specific fact isn't as important as the fact that the theme of the game is very much based in questions of philosophy- what is life, what is conciousness, what is free will, what is reality, what is purpose, etc. These are weaved very well with the plot and narrative that you discover off text and audio snippets you discover while playing the game. These are obviously very common exposition devices, but they are all written or voiced acted very convincingly.
Lastly, I want to note that the game feels very polished. The movement and mechanics all feel 'right'. The graphics, while nothing amazing, are still well done and look like a good amount of time was spent on them. I did not run into any bugs in my entire playthrough.
Overall, I highly recommend TTP.

So, Wolfenstein does some things right. The setup for the game is neat, the environments are really cool with pretty graphics to follow, the guns feel nice, some of the soundtrack is great, and the story/characters, while nothing special, are at the very least tolerable and gave the ending a satisfaction in its own right.
Now, that's what all the other reviews say, and the other reviews are right on that. But those aspects might as well describe a CGI movie, we're talking about a game here. And the thing that sets a game apart is the gameplay, and Wolfenstein has some bad gameplay.
It's a cover based shooter. Now that can be fine if it's done well, but Wolfenstein didn't do it well. It's so strange how the old aspect they chose to keep is the lack of regenerating health and the new aspect they decided to take was to take cover at every moment possible. [On the Hard difficulty] If you step outside of cover for 10 seconds you're dead, and if an enemy comes up to you at point blank range then you're dead in 2 seconds. Blazkowicz is a tank according to what the cutscenes have him go through, but he's incredibly weak during actual gameplay?
You can also dual wield the 3 guns you have, but of course because you're hiding behind cover you can't sacrifice accuracy and therefore dual wielding is primarily useless. For the record, there is a heavy armored enemy that has a shotgun. If you dual wield shotguns with full health and try to take him on, you're dying first. That's just ridiculous.
And there's this one mechanic that lets you cut some things in the environment to pass as "puzzles"... but it's incredibly straightforward and you're just doing the same exploring (where you find nothing) that you do for a sadly large portion of the game.
Wolfenstein has all the parts but it doesn't have the adhesive of gameplay to put it all together. And that's why I can't recommend it.

tl;dr : like Portal? buy it.
I can hardly find any cons to this game.
Let's start with the pros :
First of all, it's a visual showcase of the new Serious Engine, which works like a charm, even on my kind of outdated GTX 680. The graphics are not the best around, but they're nice and polished. Everything blends neatly, there are no hysterical specular lights, ambient occlusion or lighting effects (other than the lens flares, maybe... but hey, you're supposed to be a robot). FPS are not capped to 60, FOV can be changed...
Also, there are TONS of options.
In a word, it's a tweakers' paradise.
The puzzles are a treat. If you want to go the easy way, they're all pretty easy.
But the game is much mor rewarding if you do go through the hard parts. I won't tell you more since I don't want to spoil anything.
But I can tell you the hardest puzzles are _really_ hard. Still not FEZ-kind-of-hard, but close.
This is not Portal, guise.
Finally, I had a little apprehension about the "philosophical" aspect, but it turned out to pretty sensible (as far as I can tell).
The plot unravels slowly, and gives all it's meaning to the various quotes and bits of text you will find throughout the game. I would really recommend to go through all of the texts and dialogs in order to really appreciate its depth.
A few things could have been better. The game design is a bit weird. These inclusions of technology among antique ruins are not really justified by the story. It could have been anything, really, so mines, lasers, gatling turrets, "Material Emancipation Grills" (kinda)? not very original.
Also, the game mechanics prime over the actual physics. Unlike in Portal games, items tend to stick to their prepared places, you can't crouch, and you cant jump wherever you wan't. So you can forget fancy object stacking and pixel-precise jumps to circumvent the logic of the puzzles. (although there actually are a few fancy thins you can do and a lot of secret stuff to be found).
But well, I guess not everyone can have Digipen students work on their first person puzzler ;)
An actual level editor and some multiplayer options would have been nice, too. I would gladly pay more for that.
I have yet to check the modding features, so these things might be possible to achieve.
Anyway, I had a wonderful time playing this, and I highly recommend it to anyone who likes first person puzzle games.

I enjoyed pretty much everything in this game, and the Wolfenstein series is thoroughly reinvigorated with this solid entry. I am totally hoping for a sequel by the same team.
I had barely seen any trailers or any information for this game before playing it, and felt strangely rewarded for it, being gradually introduced to its compelling setting. (If you are similarly oblivious, stop reading now and just go play it.)
This game succeeds at transforming player stand-in B.J. Blazkowicz into an actual character this time around, with an actual story involving other well-written characters. The character models are very detailed and well-animated, and while some of the rest of the graphics are technically not quite top-notch, the atmosphere is rich and believable. The soundtrack enhances select scenes but generally stays subtle and never bothers the player.
The gameplay is satisfyingly and gratifyingly simple; SHOOT THE NAZIS. At easier difficulties, the game is mostly a pleasant frustration-free shooting gallery, but there are enough higher difficulties to challenge even hardcore gamers. There's also a good amount of meaningful choice; story choice with distinct effects, stealth vs assault, multiple routes etc., and the developers have done a good job at making all alternatives viable and balanced.
Still reading? Just go pick it up, especially if it's on sale for 20 usd or less (like now). Those Nazis aren't going to kill themselves.

Trying to itch that real world infantry combat on a large scale itch? Tired of glitching around in Arma 3, not knowing if your FPS will plummet the next moment? Then this game is for you. I streamed this game for about 4 hours yesterday and had a blast. Being Early Access, there are a few rough edges here and there but with the quality of AAA games now-a-days this is on par with their full release quality.
Gameplay:
- Until today I had not truly felt what it was like to leave a man behind.
"I was playing a medic, and we had advanced to a small hill with some buildings on it. The enemy force started an organized counter attack and started pushing up the hill. Our squad leader yelled frantically to PULL BACK NOW! And while I worked away trying to revive my friend, I had to eventually stand up and run."
This game has a lot of flavor for such a tried, and tried again style of game (Arma 3, Insurgency, etc...). I can easily say I'd rather play this. It's not quite as large scale as Arma 3 (multiple maps, not one large island) but it makes up for it in much more intense fighting, a large community at the time of this writing, and the fact that nearly everyone I played with was using a microphone.
That being said I had a couple issues. One problem was the icons on the map are pretty hard to see, especially when trying to find a spawn point. They are so small and no doubt realistic feeling that it was a chore to figure out for a bit. Additionally it's really hard to get the names of points to pop up when mousing over them. These were really the only issues I found. There seem to be some discussions of FPS issues floating around, I can say I averaged 40 FPS which is pretty low considering my system, but it was playable and I still had a blast.
I'd highly recommend it, even as a "just launched" early access game. I can't wait until vehicles are added, (confirmed) such as HMMWV's and helicopters. See you all on the battlefield!

So, Wolfenstein does some things right. The setup for the game is neat, the environments are really cool with pretty graphics to follow, the guns feel nice, some of the soundtrack is great, and the story/characters, while nothing special, are at the very least tolerable and gave the ending a satisfaction in its own right.
Now, that's what all the other reviews say, and the other reviews are right on that. But those aspects might as well describe a CGI movie, we're talking about a game here. And the thing that sets a game apart is the gameplay, and Wolfenstein has some bad gameplay.
It's a cover based shooter. Now that can be fine if it's done well, but Wolfenstein didn't do it well. It's so strange how the old aspect they chose to keep is the lack of regenerating health and the new aspect they decided to take was to take cover at every moment possible. [On the Hard difficulty] If you step outside of cover for 10 seconds you're dead, and if an enemy comes up to you at point blank range then you're dead in 2 seconds. Blazkowicz is a tank according to what the cutscenes have him go through, but he's incredibly weak during actual gameplay?
You can also dual wield the 3 guns you have, but of course because you're hiding behind cover you can't sacrifice accuracy and therefore dual wielding is primarily useless. For the record, there is a heavy armored enemy that has a shotgun. If you dual wield shotguns with full health and try to take him on, you're dying first. That's just ridiculous.
And there's this one mechanic that lets you cut some things in the environment to pass as "puzzles"... but it's incredibly straightforward and you're just doing the same exploring (where you find nothing) that you do for a sadly large portion of the game.
Wolfenstein has all the parts but it doesn't have the adhesive of gameplay to put it all together. And that's why I can't recommend it.

This game is beautifully crafted so far.
You play as Solid Snake, a retired FOXHOUND unit member turned Alaskan Dog Musher called in for one last job against your own unit. FOXHOUND have taken over a black ops site called "Shadow Moses" in the Alaskan penninsula and have to defeat memorable bosses such as Liquid Snake, Revolver Ocelot (Troy Baker), Skullface and the biggest enemy of them all; Raiden.
However, after suffering an explosion due to an uterus bomb hidden inside a 14 year old, Solidus Snake is knocked out for 9 years and wakes up in the year 2015 in which he has to find his friend Kazuhira Miller in Afghanistan.
It is in this part of the game where stuff REALLY starts to get interesting, as you have to find your friend Kazuhira and find out the truth behind Metal Gear during an online match of 2 teams fighting eachother in Afghanistan and in Chechnya.
However, due to it being only in an alpha state, many of the features you would see in your typical SQUAD game are not implemented into the game yet, such as the sneaking suit, Metal Gears, Psycho Mantis and Motherbase.
This is truly one of the great games of our generation, thank you so much Offworld Studios.

As an avid Serious Sam player and overall fan of Croteam and Devolver, I was pretty shocked when they made a puzzle game. Even more so at the fact that it causes you to ponder philosophical quesions. Serious Sam is a 3D doom shootemup, not so big on story and philosophy. But, since they haven't failed me since they started making games nearly 15 years ago, i bought it.
I'm not even finished yet and its probably in my top 5 games of all time. Since its an adventure puzzler, I'll do a quick comparison to Portal 2:
Pros:
- Best damn responsive mechanics/controls in any game ever. Perfectly simple.
- Higher difficulty end-game content (at least in my opinion)
- Classic Croteam secrets. Plenty of em and ranging from easy to impossibly hidden.
- Nostalgic Serious Sam feel. Same engine, tons of documents that make it feel like Netrisca, and even a visit to Egypt!
Cons:
- Witty, but not nearly as humorous as Portal 2.
- Price is scary. A lot of games in the genre flop, and most dont cost as much.
All in all, I like it better than Portal 2, Qube, or any other game like it. Get it!

At first it appears to be a simple puzzle game...and then the world opens up to you and you realize this game is definitely something special.
Like Portal, the Talos principle has a gentle difficulty curve.  It teaches you a concept and builds on it until you are an expert, and then really challenges you to think outside the box using what you've learned.  Each puzzle requires you to figure out how to get to a piece of a tangram (or what the game refers to as Sigils).  Once you have enough pieces, you use the pieces to open doors by solving tangrams.  These doors often lead to more worlds and puzzles.  There are also special stars to try to get which really requires some creative thinking.  The puzzle design reminds me a little of the game Riven.  There are individual puzzles, but sometimes the individual puzzles need to be put together to solve larger problems.
Along with the puzzles is a philosophical narrative about the nature of consciousness and artificial intelligence.
The Talos Principle is one of the most addictive games I've ever played.  You will promise yourself to go to bed after on more puzzle, and before you know it, you're up until 4am hoping to see what the next puzzle/world or whatever is behind the next door.
The graphics are gorgeous and the sound effects and music are excellent.  Finally, this game has a ton of easter eggs.  My advice is take your time and make sure you explore every nook and cranny of every world.  You never know what you will find.
Highly recommended.

Talos Principle, on the surface is a puzzle game that plays similar to your traditional fps puzzler like Portal... but if you take your time to smell the roses, enjoy the view, and read all the terminals... you will experience some philosophy to your gaming experience.
I'd say more, but essentially this is a puzzle game where you unlock, learn, and master a series of elements as simple as blocks and beam connectors... all the way up to recording and replaying actions to duplicate and combine elements in a sense of timing. Starts simple, nudges you learning new things, then stretches your education. Its not challenging, sometimes the game requries you to look at things a particular way over and over.
The story... I'm gonna try not to spoil so much... but you play a robot that is essentially a test subject in which you solve puzzles. I'm seriously trying not to spoil the end because the more I say, the more I'm implying when I reveal what happens to you. Just read all the text, listen to all the audio recordings, and check QR codes in game that expand the game. Most of the bulk is philsophical commentary surrounding culture, history, religion... etc
Graphics remind me of Serious Sam, they aren't taxing on systems but you do have to be able to run the engine.
Audio isn't too bad, the music MAY be memorable... but you get like 3-5 songs per world on random loop. I bought the OST, its 50/50 good/bad
Replayability: IF you want 100% sure, if you don't... once you learn solutions you will peak at all the endings, but then probably never touch it again.
Did the developer justify me paying $35.99 (10% during xmas steam sale of 14): As someone who actually was a fan of what the game told me sure... but straight up puzzle experience you may way for a bigger cut. You need to appreciate the story telling and open your mind a bit to pick up the nuances that make this worth its standard price.

Like ARMA? Like Red Orchestra? Like Insurgency? If you answered yes to any of those, there is a good chance you will enjoy this game. It might feel a bit overwheming at first, but once you get in with a squad and everyone is working together it really is a joy. You might spend a bunch of time just moving around and getting position and scouting, without killing anyone for awhile. It really gets atmospheric when alot of action is going on, bullets flying, teammates talking,♥♥♥♥♥♥can get pretty intense! Once you get a hang of things it really is a blast.
We had one game today where one squad did supression fire at one angle and the rest of us ran around and came at the enemy from another angle. Worked to perfection as 80% of the enemy was busy with the gun fire from the other squad, that we where able to sneak around and get a great view and angle on the enemy and base we had to take over.
This is a game where you can help out alot by being smart and playing as a team. Don't expect to be running and gunnign in this game and don't expect to be shooting at enemies every second of this game, it takes patience, teamwork and communication. It feels very rewarding when a team has you're number but you are able to get past it eventually.
The game doesn't look the best and the optimization needs work, the loading takes awhile, but the good far outweigh the bad in this game and I can't wait to see how it improves with more content, optimization and polish. If you like a more tactical shooter, check this one out! As a big fan of tactical and more realistic shooters, this is a wonderful addition to my collection of ARMA, Operation Flashpoint, Project Reality (Which some of the devs of this game worked on previously) and Red Orchestra.
It has the gunplay of Insurgency to me, but with the wonderful maps of ARMA and ghost recon, along with the teamwork of Red Orchestra, Rainbow Six and ARMA. This game won't be for everyone and a big learning curve for people who are not experienced with those games I mentioned above, but I have had a blast on it with my little time on the game previous to its release on steam and now a few hours on the Steam early access version.
Get some friends or hop in on you're own and start working as a team and communicating with you're squad! This is a game where a good squad leader and good teammates who communicate and work as a team can really be rewarding.
Finishing off the attack and defend mode as the attackers, after they had you for awhile on a few sections = dem feels!

I've played all of the games with the Wolfenstein moniker and this game shattered my expectations in every way.
Gameplay is engaging and satisfying whether you want to go stealth or guns blazing. Veterans to stealth may find the skulking about to be a bit easy though. Veterans to this brand of shooters will find a fair challenge. I say this after playing the first time on the "I am Death Incarnate" difficulty and I make a habit of slaughtering UT2K4 godlike bots.
The story was leaps and bounds above standard. BJ is a complex and dynamic character as are many of his co-stars.  Blew my mind! And while it keeps the traditional Wolfenstein wackiness, the writing makes an incredible amount of sense.
The only bad thing I have to say about the game is that the context-based cover system can be finicky. It's nothing game breaking, just a bit annoying at times when you might be trying to peek out in a certain direction and not others.
Still, this is one of the few times I can say triple-A did a genuinely good job. Great stuff and I hope they keep this level of quality at id Software.

After a 5 year absence, B.J. Blazkowicz is back in Wolfenstien: The New Order, the first title from Swedish Devs - Machine Games.
Set in alternate reality 1960s Europe, Nazi Germany has won the 2nd World War, the Allied nations are in ruins and all resistance has been crushed. Or so it seems.
Mixing surrealistic humour with dark themes, WTNO treads a fine line between serious and kitsch. I personally found the story entertaining, even though plot holes abound.
Along your journey to save the world, you'll be fighting hordes of Nazi stormtroopers and robots (robo-dogs included) in open levels that are pretty unique and well desgined. (don't be put off by the 1st level's linearity, it gets better, trust me.)
Gunplay is excellent. Guns sound powerful and bullets have real impact. Enemy a.i. seems decent (played on medium diff)
Sound design is great as well, with support for up to 7.1 surround sound. Did I mention that the soundtrack is great? No? Well, it's freakin' awesome :)
Graphics aren't the best even @ high settings due to the crappy id5 engine used. However, in certain areas, the visuals look pretty damn good.
The story does drag about 3/4 to the end, but I found the ending worth pushing through it. (My 1st playthrough lasted around 15 hours give or take.)
There is no MP component, which may be a pro/con depending on your personal preference, so bear that in mind.
tldr: Highly recommended, best SP shooter I've played in quite a while.

It's very easy to find teamwork in this game, almost everyone I encountered knows what they are doing and interested in winning the game, not getting the most kills, unlike people in ego-shooters of today.
Unfortunate part is, this engine is incapable of pulling all this off. An i7-5930K with 980ti gets you 40 - 45 frames with 72 players online. You can go into the forums and hear people saying they get over 60 frames, that game plays well, that it's going to be optimized. Yes, I am sure over 60 frames with 50 players with an i7-5960X will eventually be possible. But is that really a good thing? A rig that runs BF4 over 200 FPS at 1080p runs this at 60? What does that tell you about rest of the CPUs on the market?
I never thought I'd say this but, why bother with this, if ArmA 3 gives you the same performance with much better graphics and LOD with plenty of content? Just like ARK devs have done, they will find their hands tied behind their backs since Unreal Engine is not capable of providing performance for this scale on a multiplayer game.

In some ways The Talos Principle is quite similar to Portal 2, and I would say that it is just as good if not better.
The puzzles are very logical, and they get more challenging as new mechanics are introduced, and you move forward through all the different levels. They never got frustrating, and I was never contempt to look up the solution on the Internet, and that is not to say, that I never had hard time with them, but it was very satisfying to figure them out on my own. For people who want even more challenge, there are additional puzzles, which are not required to complete the game.
For me, the strongest part of this game was its story and setting. While Portal 2 goes for the humoristic look on the artificial intelligence, this game takes a very serious look on these matters, and without a doubt succeeds in doing so.  The narrative revealed through many text and audio logs is very compelling, and can get very philosophical at times, but that is what I liked about this game. The game likes to ask some hard questions, and in quite few cases I was doubting if the answer I gave, was the right one.
I was always in a hurry to finish my puzzles, just so I could get a new piece of information about the world and its history. The closer I got to the ending, the more I found myself wanting to find out what lies at the end of this game.
Another strong part of this game was its sound and music that always was very fitting and calming. All the audio logs were beautiful and very well acted.
When I started the game, I never expected that i would get so immersed in it. I enjoyed it all the way through, and I recommend it to anyone who have any interest in puzzle games. You will definitely enjoy this game, if you played and liked either one of the following games: Portal 2, The Swapper and Braid.
The Talos Principle would be my game of the year, if not for Dark Souls 2.

Unlike a lot of other people who play this, I did not grow up with this. For years, I was hesitant to play an RTS because I thought they would be too daunting. Then, only yesterday, did I decide that I needed a game to hold me over for a few days while I waited for Fallout 4 to be released, and I saw this on sale for $4. Okay, I suppose I could give it a try.
So, I play the tutorial, and am pleasantly surprised to see there's a bit of history included, and I love history, so it was already on my good side. I learned the basics, and decide to jump into a game, Japan vs. Vikings. Without the tutorial holding my hand, I got my♥♥♥♥♥♥wrecked. I rushed into battle too fast, before I had upgraded enough of my units.
Okay, new strategy. I start a new game, Britons vs. Franks, and decide that patience is the name of the game. I spend generations expanding my kingdom, upgrading my units, and only holding an army only for the rare occasion that the Franks decide they want to fight. It wasn't until I was well into the Imperial Age, and relative peace between our two nations had been held for generations, did I attack. I attacked from the south with my oldest, largest settlement, and from the north with my newer, smaller village. Some 125 men in total. When a few soldiers died, I replenished them quickly, and sent them off into battle, fresh from training.
The Franks were wiped from existance. I was victorious. It took me three hours to prepare for my battle, and it was over within minutes. I felt great satisfaction in seeing large numbers of troops swarm my enemy's city, and leave nothing but rubble.
10/10 would spend hours preparing for a fifteen minute fight, again.
One problem, though: The launcher only works, like, 40% of the time. I have tried every suggestion, and it still decides it's going to be a spoiled ♥♥♥♥♥, and work when it wants to.

I tried it again for the past few days after not playing for a year, only to find out that, quite literally, the exact same issues are present
Firstly, the servers are attrocious. Youll get kicked out of battles midgame, no warning, no lag. And then they slap you with a quitter penalty for leaving. Rejoin option? Doesnt have technology that sophisticated.
May i also point out that the most helpful reviews all seem negative, and most of the positive reviews are from people who have not logged a ton of hours. If those players knew what robocraft used to be, theyd probably rate it negatively too. Quite honestly i half feel like some are fake reviews to make the game look good. Because i hate to say this, but its not that great. Aside from the fact that its virtually unplayable because the servers are so bad, ALL your progress and item unlocks are locked behind loot boxes. Yes, loot boxes.
Also, they basically threw out any sense of progression and bascally entirely randomized every item you get, then inputted a lotto pay system which is notorious for being supremely hated in gaming communities. You cant earn money at a reasonable rate, so theres essentially no way to save up for a specific item you want. Youll have to luck out on the lotto. And you can play games for that, but with only 4 chances per 20min match without premium, you tell me how soon youll lose your sanity before you finally get what you want. The games loot model is designed to push players into paying.
And thats really sad, because the old system they had was great. when the game first came out everything about it was fantastic, the only problem presented was the snowball effect (It was ridiculously hard for a losing team to pull out of losing and end up winning, still kindav is). Bot design was highly creative and there was motivation to create something that functioned in a unique way. Tiers existed and evenly matched players. Thanks to Tiers even being a thing, you were likely to play against players who played as much as you did and were probably around the same skill level. And best of all, the only buyable thing was premium, and all it did was double exp earned. Exp back then dictated max CPU, but the fact that you could buy a way to earn cpu at twice the rate didnt matter because no matter how much cpu you had, you still had to be within a certain tech bracket to fight certain people. Im not saying there wasnt ways to "seal club" as it was called, there definately was. But its much more prevalent now
Now, everything is unlocked from the start. You can get anything, anytime. You can work with 2000 cpu right from the start. Regardless of your cpu or skill level, youre matched with literally anyone. Tech tiers dont exist. Everything about the old game that made it good is gone
Including the veteren players. Freejam continued to ignore us, they favored the largest possible audience instead of the most dedicated. As you can imagine, that doesnt work well. The solution was likely the birth of the loot box system which, as stated, basically makes the game pay to win
It saddens me that a game i once thought was one of the best concepts and best games of its time, is now this. It had so much potential

I think no one expected a game like this from Croteam, but here it is. A philosophical puzzle game from the human beings responsible for the Serious Sam franchise. This game essentially learns from all the mistakes great puzzle and story driven games make, and churns out an extremely unforgettable gameplay and story experience as a result. As a story driven game I was wary of two common mistakes, sacrificing gameplay for a story you watch instead of take part in, and not fleshing out its gameplay elements completely (something even Portal 2, a great game is guilty of). Fortunately The Talos Principle avoids both sins.
Be advised however, The Talos Principle has puzzles that you could spend 40 minutes trying to solve, worse case scenario they can last even an hour, they range pretty wildly in difficulty, but tend to be harder towards the end (as it should be), and you can only gain the maximum of around 4 hints (not freebies, hints) through the entire game, unless you're a baby and look up guides. Although any persistent person with a brain should be able to finish this game. For those of you not wanting what the story offers, (philosophical ponderings on human existence and what not) do not be afraid, the story is entirely avoidable here, you don't even have to skip cutscenes, because the story is told mostly through the environment, or datalogs and audiologs you can avoid if you care not to hear them and just want puzzle gameplay. Either way, The Talos Principle offers top notch puzzle gameplay.
The Serious Engine is on full display here, and it is as impressive as ever. If you've played Serious Sam 3 however, expect to see some familar assets. Asset reusage asside, The Talos Principle is a damn gorgeous game. Luckily for toaster users out there, the settings can be turned down to even PS2 graphics levels, so most everyone should be able to run it.
Overall, The Talos Principle is one of the better, and more overlooked titles of 2014, and maybe the current decade. I can definitely say it is worth your money, and even the asking price with its lengthy runtime. Avoid looking into this game too mush, the less you know about it going in the better, the story is a hot topic so spoilers are everywhere. I cant recommend this game more enthusiastcally, it's worth your time.

Where to start? I read a few reviews today and a lot of them cited Arma and this alpha game's similarity to Arma. Seeing as I've bought every ARMA game and never really found that it was (a) accessible, or (b) actually ran well on any rig I've ever owned, I thought I would invest in this alpha and spend 10 minutes on it, before coming back in 6 months (as per almost every other alpha I've backed).
Well, it's now 11:44pm and this game's taken enough of my attention that it stopped me playing Fallout 4. 2 hours flew by... There was some really intense gameplay that doesn't go anywhere towards showing the real horror of serving in a war, but which conveyed the sense of panic when being surrounded and isolated in an outpost as enemies closed in. More than once I was hidden behind a tree stump or on an exposed roof not knowing where to look or shoot.... So, this gets a tick for suspense and tactical play.
Basically, if you love military sims like Arma, but have always found them overwhelming and inaccessible, then definitely try Squad.
It's the best looking alpha I have ever played. It puts other higher profile alphas to shame... (Hello, Star Citizen!). You definitely need a mic, and you need to be a team player to play this game. It's no run and gun. You will die and won't know why. Join a squad, follow your squad leader, participate in radio comms, and you'll have a good time. Even getting a single kill is satisfying when you have worked as a team to outflank a well entrenched enemy force and taken the compound.
Cannot recommend this enough to military sim fans, and I'm hopeful of the directions it will go in the future.
My one negative comment is that there were some really snotty and stuck up players who wanted only their friends in squads and would boot you out, but that's entirely server and squad dependent and not a direct criticism of the alpha.

This is a game that has made me genuinely sad. I have just over 300 hours invested in this game and all of that time was within the course of about a year. This game was one of the most promising games I'd seen in a long time and it got me back into gaming. Sometimes, I'm not the kind of person who likes to spend money to get things in-game so I went into this game as a free to play player and I sometimes spent over 5 hours at a time just simply playing the game with my friends or on my own. I managed to get myself to max level, I had my end game bots and I saw the game's community grow. But being a good free to play game has to have a balance of playability with and without money. Before the Epic Loot update, which ruined the game, there was a currency system known as RP which was the main currency in game. You got it for winning and losing matches, buying and selling items etc. And it was a great system because for people like me who chose to put a lot of time into a game that we really enjoy, we felt like nothing was out of reach and anything was affordable while people who wished to play money wouldn't recieve an advantage anymore that what a few days of light grinding wouldn't have given. This was a near perfect balance because it appealed to both parts of the market. The money payers and the free players, giving neither one much of an advantage over the other. But the Epic Loot update literally threw that system out the window and implemented the pathetic excuse for currency known as robits. Before, we were able to focus on saving up for certain parts that we wanted and build our bots as we liked. But now the system is heavily relied on random number generation and we have to be limited and forced to adapt. You could sell you parts for robits but the selling prices for any part were essentially penalties. You would get a minuscule amount of robits for even the rares and legendary items. Normally recieving a couple hundred robits while the better weapons costed close to a hundred thousand. Обзор на игру "The Talos Principle"
The Talos Principle - это игра от Хорватской студии Croteam, которая прославилась серией игр "Serious Sam". Эта компания всегда занималась мясными шутерами, с кишками, оторванными конечностями, кровью и т.д. Вдруг выходит игра "The Talos Principle" Сразу задается вопрос, что это? Это филосовская игра, с необычным сюжетом и атмосферой. Компания, которая всегда занималась мясными и зубодробительными шутерами, вдруг выпускает спокойную и миролюбивую игру? Этот факт навел на меня ооочень большое любопытство. Я начал активно следить за игрой, смотреть трейлеры и т.д. И вот настал момент, когда я её купил. Как только я появился в этом мире, меня охватило чувство таинственности. Кто я? Робот? Какого черта я робот?! Что за голос говорит со мной с небес? Что мне нужно делать? Именна эта особенность, делает атмосферу этой игры незабываемой! Всю игру нам предстоит не только тупо решать головоломки, но и следовать филосовскому сюжету и смыслу. А филосовские тексты в данной игре, могут даже дать пару жизненных уроков и поводов для размышления. Даже головоломки несут в себе смысл в этой игре. Играя в неё, вы одновременно думаете и наслаждаетесь этой игрой. Даже если вы не особый любитель философии, здесь вы все равно найдете потрясающе интересные головоломки, красочные и живописные виды (я их заскриншотил и поставил на рабочий стол), великолепное музыкальное сопровождение и удовольствие от прохождения! Это нечто больше чем игра...

#Campaign videos (Narrated Stories)#

To be honest, I was expecting that for a long time and it seems no chance for AoFE no longer.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

The Talos Principle (TTP) stands on the shoulders of giants. Among those being Portal, Myst, and Antichamber. That's not to say TTP does not bring its own stock of new ideas to the table. Discovery in TTP plays a major role so the less details you know in advance, the better. Enter the world of impeccable visuals, music, and voice acting; the world full of ingenious 2D and 3D puzzles; the world with a mysterious story only revealed to you in glimpses if you care to follow them; the world of thought-provoking philosophical undertones so rare in video games; the world with tons of secrets, extra content, and Easter eggs; and finally, the world when you don't need guns and weapons to make progress. Even if you are not a completionist, TTP will provide you with around 20 hours of gameplay. The game is extremely polished, well-tested, and rewarding and satisfying to play. I would not expect such a gem coming from the creators of Serious Frikkin' Sam :-) This is a complete paradigm shift and I'm very glad Croteam took this turn to expand their horizons - and everyone else's. I rate 10/10.

First and foremost: this is an opinion from the early access, so by the time you are reading this all that I said might be old news or invalid so take it with a grain of salt.
I met this game quite a while ago but did not give it any attention because of my police to stay away from early access games, but since it got featured in one of the videos from the Mighty Jingles I decided to give it a try.
And boy didn’t I get surprised! This game features a lot of small nice things that make from a great experience. You can go around building vehicles with small blocks in a very lego-esque way that feels very, very nice. It makes you think this is one of these games you will spend more time in the editor room than actually fighting and there’s nothing wrong with that.
First impressions are important and this game managed to leave a very good one with its dynamic battles and an immense quantity of pieces to build your machine of utter annihilation and destruction, but enough of my impressions! Let’s get on the nice things(pros):
+Fast paced, dynamic combat. Go in fast and pew-pew things like an action movie and feel good about it. It’s simple and feels AWESOME.
+Hundreds of pieces to make you little toy move. From wheels, spider legs, horse legs, floating motors, turbines to tank threads. Whatever it makes your ideal machine moves, they have it (unless you want something very specific, but we can always make compromises when building).
+Lots of pieces to make things interesting. You have radars, reflector shields, flags and a lot of weapons to fit in your machine and make it go pew-pew with style.
+Very easy to use controls. The controls are very simple and easy to get hang on but how you actually get around will vary greatly depending on what your machine do. Wheeled creations will turn better and have better handling than tanks, while things that float or fly around will require a bit more of finesse on your part to make then go the direction you want. This leads to…
+Test Drive room. While building your machine you can always press “T” and go take it for a spin to see how it handles, moves and fires at stuff. Very useful since you don’t have to change menus or exit the editor to do that. Bonus points for keeping it simple and easy.
The game has a nice feel to it. With everything having names on with in a way you can understand what each menu does, so it’s very easy to get around.
Now onto the not so good stuff… (cons):
-The editor makes me feel lost. For example, let’s say you got a big chunk of blocks that make the “main body” of your vehicle but you want to raise it a bit to add parts to its underside.  It’s pretty damn hard to lift the whole thing, and if there’s a tool/hotkey that can do it it’s not on the screen or any menu.
-Still talking about User Interface, the lack of hotkeys on the screen to open the menus in the editor is a bit annoying. It took me a while to learn that “Z” opens weapon fire binding menu. This kind of thing is minor, but it is annoying.
-You can only fire one type of weapon at once. Even weapons of the same category are treated as different weapons and must be selected before firing. This makes sense if you have some Rapid Firing Lasers and one Sniper Rifle, not so much if you have Rapid Firing Lasers of the different sizes.
- Still on weapons, the lack of a “fire everything” makes me feel a bit restricted. Since each type of weapon requires a binding to fire, having multiple different weapons equals have a lot of keys bound and having to switch that in during combat might cost you precious seconds.
One thing I want to note is that there are a few things that currently the game lacks but I would not classify it as minor points or problems at all, just something they should add to make the experience feel a bit better. Such points are:
I might be asking for too much here, but this game has SO MUCH potential that it would be a shame not to push this concept to the limit. Even with the cons, this game is still worth checking out.
8/10 (for the current stage and because it seems to be moving towards).

+Hundreds of pieces to make you little toy move. From wheels, spider legs, horse legs, floating motors, turbines to tank threads. Whatever it makes your ideal machine moves, they have it (unless you want something very specific, but we can always make compromises when building).
+Lots of pieces to make things interesting. You have radars, reflector shields, flags and a lot of weapons to fit in your machine and make it go pew-pew with style.
+Very easy to use controls. The controls are very simple and easy to get hang on but how you actually get around will vary greatly depending on what your machine do. Wheeled creations will turn better and have better handling than tanks, while things that float or fly around will require a bit more of finesse on your part to make then go the direction you want. This leads to…
+Test Drive room. While building your machine you can always press “T” and go take it for a spin to see how it handles, moves and fires at stuff. Very useful since you don’t have to change menus or exit the editor to do that. Bonus points for keeping it simple and easy.
The game has a nice feel to it. With everything having names on with in a way you can understand what each menu does, so it’s very easy to get around.
Now onto the not so good stuff… (cons):
-The editor makes me feel lost. For example, let’s say you got a big chunk of blocks that make the “main body” of your vehicle but you want to raise it a bit to add parts to its underside.  It’s pretty damn hard to lift the whole thing, and if there’s a tool/hotkey that can do it it’s not on the screen or any menu.
-Still talking about User Interface, the lack of hotkeys on the screen to open the menus in the editor is a bit annoying. It took me a while to learn that “Z” opens weapon fire binding menu. This kind of thing is minor, but it is annoying.
-You can only fire one type of weapon at once. Even weapons of the same category are treated as different weapons and must be selected before firing. This makes sense if you have some Rapid Firing Lasers and one Sniper Rifle, not so much if you have Rapid Firing Lasers of the different sizes.
- Still on weapons, the lack of a “fire everything” makes me feel a bit restricted. Since each type of weapon requires a binding to fire, having multiple different weapons equals have a lot of keys bound and having to switch that in during combat might cost you precious seconds.
One thing I want to note is that there are a few things that currently the game lacks but I would not classify it as minor points or problems at all, just something they should add to make the experience feel a bit better. Such points are:
I might be asking for too much here, but this game has SO MUCH potential that it would be a shame not to push this concept to the limit. Even with the cons, this game is still worth checking out.
8/10 (for the current stage and because it seems to be moving towards).

This game had me intrigued and invested throughout the whole experience. First and foremost, it's a fun puzzle game - the challenges range from simple to very difficult, and some extra challenges require good abstract thinking. It is incredibly satisfying when you complete a puzzle.
The graphics and visual style are very appealing. From lush Greek ruins to mystical castles in forests, it had me exploring every bit of the surprisingly open worlds, as you can find bits of narrative hidden throughout, along with additional stars to collect.
The story is fed to you through a mysterious godly voice from the sky, through computer terminals scattered around, and through collectible voice recordings. Every piece you discover adds to a greater understanding of this strange world, and leads to several "Aha!" moments as you realize what the heck is happening.
The undertone of this game is philosophy and consciousness itself. An entity within the aforementioned computer terminals sometimes decides to chat with you about these things. I found these sessions really interesting, and I actually gained some insight from playing.
I could spout on for a long time about how much of a great experience this was for me, but I won't. All I'll say is that this game is a 10/10 for me, but depending on if you like to read or really think when you play games, it may not be for everyone.

The Talos Principle is a puzzle within a puzzle. In short, you solve puzzles by connecting lasers and push plates on your way to sigils, but that's only on the face of it. There's a deeper puzzle within, one that makes you question your own beliefs. Who is this voice in the sky? Should I trust him? Who's this person in the computer? Should I trust him? He certainly seems to have an answer against everything I believe in. Should I continue believing in the things I do?
It certainly is a unique experience that touches you on an intellectual level that is so rarely seen in gaming. The puzzles, while pretty easy in the first third to half of the game, grow increasingly more difficult, especially if you seek out all the star sigils as well. This game kind of came out of left field and I didn't even hear about it until it was already released. I bought it on a whim after enjoying the demo and am not disappointed at all. This is game of the year quality and I worry that it will slip through the cracks and become a hidden gem. It certainly deserves a lot of praise.

As a relatively new player I thought I'd put my opinion out there to counter all the veterans comparing it to older builds - I've played quite a few construction games, Scrap Mechanic, Crossout, Besiege, that kind of thing, and I found the building system to be fairly easy to get along with. If you've played games of this kind, you won't be confused.
So far I've had relative success with walkers, tanks, helecopters (my favourite) and I've even managed a few kills with jets, though I'm not sure the flight mechanics are quite built for constant movement... Could just be me being useless though! Either way it seems like however you want to play, you can be successful.
A lot of the other reviews were complaining of limited creativity, but this just isn't true from what I've seen. I've not unlocked league play yet so maybe it's different in there, but team deathmatch and all the other game modes always have a variety of builds, and so far it's never felt like the same match twice, other than those grim matches where a poor design means almost instant death...
At the moment the game feels pretty limited in terms of maps and game modes, but that's all stuff that's relatively easy to add in once the core mechanics of the game are set, so hopefully that'll be coming with the full release.
All in all, I'm enjoying my time with Robocraft, and would definitely recommend it if you like this kind of thing - and if you've never tried a builder game before, it's probably not a bad place to start, as it's all fairly simple geometric shapes and a forgiving (unless you have wings) physics engine.

T game is fantastic in a couple of different ways but instead of that (since you can figure out what I'm talking about by actually playing it) I will tell you about my first game as a Squad Leader. For once in my entire gaming history, 8 other people took orders from me and did so without complaint. They gave me info, ran me about where choke points were, and I ran it back to all the other Squad Leaders. As it came to the climax of the round, I decided it was time for Delta Squad to all come together. We all spawned on the original base, and made our way down. As we moved, I had my sniper set up on the hill and start overwatch. Two men set up with LAW on each side of the crossroads in the streets, and the rest of us went into two groups, one that followed me and the other with a smaller squad that had been ambushed not more than 15 minutes before and was left with 3 men in the city at the time. It was one of the best feeling I had ever had. The overwatch called out enemies and sniped while we picked off anyone running into cover. The two soldiers with LAWS fires up the street and split the two oncoming forces in half. We only had 1 casualty and critical down the entire time. I had successfully controlled my squad and we topped the scoreboard. Literally the most fun I have had in a FPS game in a long time. If you're looking for a fun puzzle game, pick this title up.
If you're looking for a good successor to portal, pick this game up.
If you're looking for a sci-fi allegorical exploration of existentialism, faith, and doubt that utilizes the common tropes of game design to explore the fuzzy borders of free will... that's very specific of you, but yeah pick this game up.
Though it has been flying under most of the game playing public's radar, I'm fairly sure the Talos Principle will be remembered as an important step in the evolution of this medium. It's not just a fun game, it's video game literature. With all of the humor, humility, and self doubt of Kurt Vonnegut, the Talos Principle manages to be quite literally a soul-searching exercise without ever veering into the pretentious.

After playing this game for 66 hours I've decided to give this a negative review.
This game simply isn't the best I've played for a F2P game.
Pros:
- Game is fast-paced
- Game is optimized
Cons:
- Weapons aren't logical at all (4-5 shots to kill with a Deagle, 6+ to kill with a M4, etc)
- Sensitivity options aren't fitting
- Poor map randomization (no randomized map selections pre-game)
- Poor character balance (proxy getting 2 mines instantly, as well as other explosives)
- Hit detection is rubbish (tested with 40-60ms)
- It takes 3-5 bullets to finish someone off whereas 1 melee hit finishes them instantly (not logical at all)
- Poor gun balance (such as recoil, damage, rate of fire etc)
- Very limited amount of objectives
- Getting credits/coins takes way too long to get them
- No customizable loadouts
- Some characters move so fast to the point where you don't even know where they ran to
I could go on and on about how bad this game is but I wouldn't want to spend hours writing it all.

Do I enjoy playing Planetside 2? Yeah, when I'm with my friends. Do I recommend other people play it? Only under certain circumstances.
I just started playing this game again after nearly a two year break, and a lot of the problems it had when I left are still here. This game is still a giant zerg vs. zerg simulator, and while that CAN lead to big, fun fights, it's more common that enemies will simply bypass one another to try and capture bases, or a small force getting completely obliterated by a vastly numerically superior enemy force. On top of that, the game takes every opportunity it can to try and convince you to spend your hard-earned money on minor upgrades and cosmetic fluff.
But beneath all that, Planetside 2 is a fun shooter with lots of toys to play with. As long as you're running with friends, you can get a lot of enjoyment out of this game. It's not P2W, and you can do just fine without spending a dime.
TL;DR: If you want to try this game, don't play alone. Don't stress about winning. Just grab some friends and go shoot some bad guys.

Mixed feelings on this title. Good in some ways, but I would err on the side of caution for those looking to get it.
First off, it's a Wolfenstein game, but the story is surprisingly done quite well. Hell, the fact there's a story at all is impressive given what origins the game has. I won't spoil it, but it has an interesting revisionist history approach with WW2 and all that goes along with it. Voice acting is top notch and the computer cut scenes simply rock.
Combat is reasonably entertaining. You can stealth a number of enemies in this title, although the mechanics for it are a little wonky; both for and against the player. Primarily, Wolfenstein works with the fighting and that's the big draw of this franchise.
The downside has less to do with the game and more the technical issues. This is one of those ported games to Steam that's not well optimized for the PC particularly well. There's a thread in the forums with various suggestions about tweaks you can make in the config, but honestly, this is stuff the developer should be doing. The playerbase should not be responsible for trying to get the game to play smoother. The game is resource intensive and there are numerous threads indicating a LOT of people are having trouble running this thing. While combat runs okay on mine, the ingame cut scenes (not the computer animated ones) run hilariously slow. Characters can literally be doing talk and gesture animations some 20 seconds after their dialogue is done. This breaks the immersion of an otherwise good story and these scenes can't be skipped.
There is fun to be had but unless you're going to spend time tweaking the configuration or you've got a stronger than not comp (mine is pretty good, but not when it comes to this title), I'd recommend playing this one on console instead. It's just not well optimized at this time and I don't know when it will be, if ever.

By far the best F2P shooter out there.  A lot of you reading this may be thinking it's "pay 2 win" because it's a free game, but that's not the case.  Yes, weapons and attachments can be purchased with real money, but there are no weapons that are a direct upgrade to other weapons.  When you use a different weapon in the same class (assault rifle, LMG, carbine, etc) you will sacrifice in one area to be better in another - close vs long range, large mag/slow reload vs small mag/fast reload, etc.  Also, other items CANNOT be purchased with cash - ability upgrades, suit slot items, etc.
Graphically it looks pretty good, especially for DX9, but it's a bit unoptimized which really sucks for a free game.  I have an FX-6300 and R9-270 and I can get a steady 45-60fps with my settings in all fights except 96v96 zergfests.
The core shooting mechanics are very solid - the game rewards good aim and trigger discipline.  That being said, you will still die to "WTF was that crap?" because this is an MMO and enemies will always be there.  Usually it's a Stalker Infiltrator camping your vehicle terminal with the Blackhand sniper pistol, other times it could be a Lockdown Prowler up on a ridge shelling the crap out of your armor column.
Overall 9/10.

Max Payne 3 is a very different beast compared to the first two games. They told gritty, hard-boiled noir stories interweaved with conspiracies and mythological themes, and the intense combat was mixed up with quiet moments of exploration and... those damn nightmares. The series' third installment is bigger and louder, packed to the brim with intense action scenes which are a lot more challenging this time around, thanks to the scarcity of ammo, your ability to carry only 3 guns at once, and the very crafty, dangerous AI. If you stick behind a piece of cover too long, they'll either shoot it away, exposing you or circle around and flank you. Bullet time is much less plentiful too, which makes careful use of it essential to surviving.
I'd call MP3 the best third-person shooter I've played. Its story doesn't grip me in the same way as previous installments, but it sure gets depressing and with all that said, I feel it does bring closure to the series in a nice way.

No AAA release (at least not recently) has hooked me like Wolfestein: The New Order did, however the $49 price tag I got it at and 40gb file size (including the 10gb download I had to do following installing the game FROM A DISC) might have inclined me to push through it. Nevertheless, it is a wonderful slightly over-the-top run-and-gun styled FPS that harkens back to the days of DOOM, Quake and even the original Wolfenstein 3D itself.
The story was interesting but it quickly becomes mediocre, in my opinion, by the end of it so the latter half of the game was mostly driven by the excellent and satisfying combat. It was also very short; Steam has me logged in at 8 hours of playtime, two of those hours are possibly AFK, replaying due to death or finding collectibles. There is no other form of gamemode other than playing the story mode.
All the weapons feel unique and, as said before, satisfying to fire and the stealthy approach that includes using a knife is also effective, however not relied on extremely. It did confuse me that there was a stealth 'skill tree' when at some points in the game, you really could not use stealth at all.
TL;DR: Wolfenstein: The New Order is an amazing reboot to the old series and a great breath of fresh hair towards better next-generation games. The story is unfortunately short but the time you spend playing it is amazing. If suitable DLC releases for this, I would be glad to purchase it.

After playing Shadow Warrior and being left wanting, I decided to give this game a shot after hearing that it was very arcadey and action packed. I was a bit apprehensive because I was afraid there would be too many Halo or Call of Duty style elements introduced to the old formula to make it more palatable for modern gamers, but after playing the game through I can say that my fears were unfounded.
Although Wolfentstein: The New Order has some modern elements, such as the perks system and weapon upgrades, it eschews the systems popularised by CoD and Halo, such as limited weapon loadouts (you can carry all at once, and dual wield almost everything), and reduces the importance of others; I didn't use the cover system at all, and although your health regenerates at very low levels, you will definitely be hunting for health and ammo. On top of that, the combat encourages you to run around a lot, bringing enemies on thick and fast and giving you few places to hide.
The level design is great, with environments that feel like real places but that are both interestingly laid out and packed with multiple layers, air ducts and hidey holes so that you are given some freedom in how you tackle the combat situations you are thrown into. Most of the time you can choose to play stealthily, or run in guns blazing, although the stealth system is not especially fleshed out, and the AI is extremely forgiving, so it just feels like a way to give the player some more options, and also make some tougher situations easier since you can just sneak round and take out key squad captains to prevent them from setting off the alarms.
The weapons in this game are mostly the standard fare, but they all feel very good to use and are all useful in different situations. There is one weapon that is used throughout the game to great effect, which allows you to cut through fences, break chains, or switch modes and use it like a railgun. The heavy cannons in the game also cut holes in some walls, sometimes revealing secrets or ammo caches in crates scattered around the battleground. All weapons can be upgraded by finding modules around the levels, or by getting perks, which are given if you achieve some specific goal, such as performing 5 silent takedowns to get a silenced pistol.
The story actually added to the game for once. There are fairly few action FPS games where the story adds a lot to the game, but here it provides a great setting (alternative WW2 where Nazi Germany took over the world), and is well written and compelling enough that you do care what happens, regardless of how cliched the whole resistance fighter thing has become. Having said that, I did feel a bit cheated by the ending.
If you were holding out on Wolfenstein: TNO like I was, definitely consider grabbing it, as it straddles the lines between modern and retro FPS brilliantly, providing satisfyingly creative combat with a compelling and immersive story and uses some modern smarts to round out the corners and make a more forgiving game than those you might remember playing 15 years ago.

Max Payne 3 is a noir journey to the heart of the protagonist. The story is unfold upon the player's eye with convoluted and deep story telling by the protagonist, which is getting older and struggles with addiction and the ghost of loved ones. Max Payne 3 proves its audience that there can be noir settings other than snow and night.
In Max Payne 3, you can see and feel not only story-wise but gameplay-wise that Max is getting old, he no longer can dodge bullets and get up as quickly he used to do. Getting up takes time, Max dives awkwardly and stays down on the ground and ocasionally would hit walls. These are all story details that are blended into the gameplay masterfully. It doesn't breaks the frantic shooting action in any way, but also gives you a new way to play Max Payne and makes you be careful about making mistakes.
The action is pretty well paced as far the story and the gameplay goes. There are a good set of quiet segments and frantic bullet spraying all over the place as well.
But the star of the show of this game is Rockstar's SUPERB physics. Shooting guns never felt this good before. The impact physics is amazing and fun at the same time. Each gun has a different impact and power depending on the direction and range you shoot. I'm astounished by the physics which along the story is the selling point of this game.
Multiplayer is dead, which is a shame, I'd like to know how it feels like to use bullet time on a multiplayer game.
I really like the setting. Rockstar's R&D dept. did a pretty damn good job on researching Brazil's favelas, police forces and street gangs in a way that felt realistic and made sense even for a Brazilian. The voice acting plays a major role in the Brazil's impersonation aspect; The brazilian accent is perfect and the english doesn't seem awkward at all. They did a pretty good job on voice acting.
My only complaints goes to the railshooter sections. Railshoot doesn't fit in a Max Payne game. At all. It doesn't feel clunky, but it's boring when you'd rather be jumping and shooting bad guys.
Overall, Max Payne 3 is IMO the best game in the series. Major overhauls at gameplay elements, daring settings and deep story will suck you into this noir journey in Brazil and New Jersey.
