The New Order is a well done game. No doubt the fans of RTCW and old RTCW3D will love the New Order. The core idea and story of the game is very attractive. Playing a WWII game is great, but playing the game in artificial "what if NAZI's won the war" world is much better. The mechanical robots, wardogs, devices and weaponry provides the player with unique atmosphere and the experience from the shooter is unlikely other RTCW I played before.
I also enjoyed the no scripts waves of enemies. You need to shoot all the enemies in the area, you do not need to keep shooting until you reach a certain point in the game. On the other hand you can choose whether you approach your enemies with brutal force and fire power (where you usually do not run out of ammo as there are too many places with equip and ammunition) or if you choose a stealth way to clear the path. I am the stealth guy, so using throwing knives and silenced handgun is my way.
What I disliked are the secrets. Enigma codes to collect, all the extras that you may come across, but you do not need to finish the game. I left too many behind and I do not feel like playing the game again just to collect them all. Thus I will not be able to open the extra modes etc. Also I lack the secret pathways like in the very old RTCW3D. There are no real hidden paths, no puzzles to solve. Everything is pretty simple as long as you crawl behined every corner. With enough time invested into exploration, you should not have a problem in discovery of all the secrets.
All in all it is a great game, I played it 'til I completed it and I rate it 7.5/10

Mixed feelings on this title. Good in some ways, but I would err on the side of caution for those looking to get it.
First off, it's a Wolfenstein game, but the story is surprisingly done quite well. Hell, the fact there's a story at all is impressive given what origins the game has. I won't spoil it, but it has an interesting revisionist history approach with WW2 and all that goes along with it. Voice acting is top notch and the computer cut scenes simply rock.
Combat is reasonably entertaining. You can stealth a number of enemies in this title, although the mechanics for it are a little wonky; both for and against the player. Primarily, Wolfenstein works with the fighting and that's the big draw of this franchise.
The downside has less to do with the game and more the technical issues. This is one of those ported games to Steam that's not well optimized for the PC particularly well. There's a thread in the forums with various suggestions about tweaks you can make in the config, but honestly, this is stuff the developer should be doing. The playerbase should not be responsible for trying to get the game to play smoother. The game is resource intensive and there are numerous threads indicating a LOT of people are having trouble running this thing. While combat runs okay on mine, the ingame cut scenes (not the computer animated ones) run hilariously slow. Characters can literally be doing talk and gesture animations some 20 seconds after their dialogue is done. This breaks the immersion of an otherwise good story and these scenes can't be skipped.
There is fun to be had but unless you're going to spend time tweaking the configuration or you've got a stronger than not comp (mine is pretty good, but not when it comes to this title), I'd recommend playing this one on console instead. It's just not well optimized at this time and I don't know when it will be, if ever.

One of the best games of 2014, and one of the best puzzle games ever.
A mix of very good puzzle design and an intriguing story place it easily in the pinnacle of the genre, right with Portal 1/2 and The Swapper.
The puzzle design manages the precarious balance between too hard and too easy. Quite often you have to think for a bit about the puzzle, but after a while you get the trick and feel quite intelligent about it. Furthermore, most puzzle do not rely on trial and error, or dexterity, but have a simple trick to them. This makes puzzle solving a very pleasant activity. I found myself wondering over particularly difficult puzzle while I was away from the game, only to find the solution a few moments later, wondering hoe I could have overlooked something so simple.
The story goes a long way in making the game truly exceptional. I found myself drawn into the game world, wanting to know more about it. I also enjoyed the philosophical discourse quite a lot, especially the interactivity. I was reminded of reading Sophie's World as a child.
Overall I would highly recommend this game, it is easily worth he full price

The game is set in beautifully nuanced, digitally simulated world with a bittersweet backstory told through found texts and voice recordings. It presents a compelling commentary on faith, technology, philosophy, and transhumanism while not taking a galvanizing stance on any of them.  There's a few pop-culture references and computing jokes sprinkled throughout the narrative, and I also found a hilarious easter egg.
The voice actors for Elohim and the girl in the recordings deliver a spectacular performance. I found myself very strongly emphasizing with the latter, to the point where by the end I just wanted to be able to find her and give her a hug and tell her everything is going to be okay.
It has a surprising amount of content for a (pseudo) indie game, very open-ended and for the most part, totally nonlinear. The gameplay is addicting, and rewards clever, creative solutions and a keen eye.
However, some puzzles have entirely counterintuitive solutions while others are stupidly simple but horribly tedious. But this isn't entirely unexpected in a puzzle game, so I can't fault the devs for that. However, they seemed to rely a bit too heavily on red herrings and excess complexity to make some puzzles seem harder than they should be.
The
-like 2D puzzles required to unlock new areas and tools were novel and enjoyable... the first few times. Then they started to become tedious. I think the devs could have come up with at least one or two more puzzle types for these parts to add some variety.
The "hints" the messengers give are usually painfully obvious and not really helpful. I found that often by the time I resorted to getting a hint, I had already figured out the part the messenger was hinting about and was stuck on something else entirely. The hint system could have been made more intelligent so it didn't tell you something you already knew. And since you only get a few of them throughout the game, the hints could have been a lot more useful than a vague sentence or two.
Failure, such as dying or getting stuck and needing to reset, is extremely inconvenient as it resets you to the very beginning of the puzzle, making you lose all your progress, inside and outside the puzzle. This is especially frustrating on long puzzles with many intricate steps. But some might argue that failure
be inconvenient, as it incentivizes the player to put more thought and time into their solutions. So I guess this should be more of an FYI to potential players than a criticism.
I like reading as much as the next guy, but I found that there was
too much to read for a video game. I think there's more written text in this game than all the
titles put together (hyperbole). By the end of the game, I didn't really bother to read anything unless it seemed important. I would have liked to have the story told more in voice recordings from more characters and maybe even video logs, essentially more stuff that I can have playing while I'm running around or solving puzzles, and less stuff I have to stop and read.
If you're still reading after all that, I hope you understand that the disproportionate amount of time I spent on the game's flaws doesn't mean I didn't like it. In fact, I loved the hell out of it. It was an extremely enjoyable yet thought-provoking experience. Just as good as, if not better than,
and
put together.
My only
complaint is that it had to end.

One (small) issue. I suppose this is common of any video game involving guns: In your pursuit to save a person's life, you kill about 600 people.  You uncover some bad guys doing bad things. But still, you kill over 600 people to uncover those bad things. There's one level where you kill about a hundred New Jersey mobsters in an evening. If anything remotely close to that happened in the real world, that man wouldn't be allowed to quietly become a body guard. He would become part of American legend. He would be public enemy number 1. He would be hounded by every law enforcement agency even remotely allied with the United States. But in Max Payneland, that's just another night on the town.

EDITED REVIEW!
Months ago I reviewed this game and took a serious stab because of it's lack of optmization and a serious problem with the engine involving VOIP. Which would cause unbearable lag anytime someone spoke over Squad channel. At the time it made the game totally unplayable.
I have been playing quite a bit the past couple of days upon seeing that the vehicle update is coming soon. So I gave Squad, hoping it has been updated and optimized during the course of the past few months, a second chance.
I'm glad I did!
I had promised to return when the game has been updated and I have fulfilled it. The game runs a whole lot better now. Squad VOIP still offers SOME lag at times when someone speaks but has largely been fixed and it seems to only be a more rare issue and occurs in brief moments. Largely however the problem is fixed and I have been able to play without problem.
The gunplay mechanics are pretty good. My only gripe is how slow some of the animations area. I think they could afford to be slightly sped up. No to the point of COD style animations but just a little more sense of urgence. Especially shouldering the weapon to fire from the sights. But this is just a minor issue I have and does not put a big dent in my overall gameplay.
Maps are large and expansive as well as detailed. You never know when you will run into an enemy squad constructing a FOB or on patrol in the countryside. Making combat truly dynamic. No map is ever played the same.
Right now until the vehicle update is released be ready to do a whole lotta walkin'.
Every squad I have joined in Squad has been communicative and extremely teamwork oriented. This makes the tactical game portion of myself giggle with glee. My first FPS's were tactical shooters - so I have a soft spot for them and heavily prefer them over the arcade ones. This whole package warms my heart when it comes to this style of gameplay.
Right now, yes, I would recommend the game. It's worth checking out if you enjoy the tactical shooter premise. The vehicle update is due sometime this summer (I believe by the end of the month?) and will only add to this game! I look forward to it!

This game may have just surpassed Portal as my favorite game of all time. The comparison between the two is common, and I still have a certain favoritism toward Portal's core mechanics (the portals, which just feel cooler to play with than many of the mechanics in The Talos Principle), but the fact is that the two games have wildly different atmospheres. I still love Portal for its wonderful characters, voices, and its general feel, but The Talos Principle is thought-provoking, somber, and genuinely brought me to the brink of tears.
Portal's main conflict revolves around the player and GLaDOS -- a very concrete adversary. The conflict is still resolved as a direct confrontation.
The Talos Principle's main conflict exists within the player's own mind, and while characters may attempt to sway the player's opinion, the player is given full control over their progression and the outcome.
From a world design point of view, The Talos Principle feels wonderfully open. The player can choose to go anywhere they wish, but it's clearly defined when something impedes your progress.
To summarize, Portal still wins in my heart for humor, presentation of its characters, and some in-game mechanics. The Talos Principle has atmosphere, world design, and far more food for thought, which makes it far more up my alley. Even if most of my friends don't really enjoy puzzle games, I'll be recommending this to everyone I know.

This game is still a giant zerg vs. zerg simulator, and while that CAN lead to big, fun fights, it's more common that enemies will simply bypass one another to try and capture bases, or a small force getting completely obliterated by a vastly numerically superior enemy force. On top of that, the game takes every opportunity it can to try and convince you to spend your hard-earned money on minor upgrades and cosmetic fluff.

This is a puzzle game, much like
, where you will be using boxes to keep buttons pressed, manipulate lasers and fans, and even duplicate yourself in order to finish the game.
Gameplay is kept very simple: You can run, jump, and interact with objects.
The real fun lies in solving the puzzles, which often require thinking outside the box.
Unlike Portal, there are very few opportunities to die in this game and they are easily avoidable by paying attention - there are no crazy turrets that will snipe you from across the room.
The story is very philosophical and requires some involvement on the player's part. If you ignore the various computers spread across the world and instead focus on solving only the puzzles, you'll have a hard time understanding what's going on, or what happened when you reach the true ending.
Also, some of the questions asked in the game are very interesting, such as: "Are machines conscious beings, or do they only pretend to be?", "If they aren't conscious, what makes you think humans are?" and similar.
Graphically speaking, this game is absolutely stunning, especially in 4k. The textures are very sharp (assuming your GPU is powerful enough to handle it) and it provides the player with a vast variety of graphical options to choose from.
The only downside is that the game looks so good, that the lack of tesselation on walls becomes slightly distracting (if you're not busy solving the puzzles, that is).
If you're looking for an action game, this isn't it.
If instead you are looking for an intellectually challenging and stimulating game, this is a must-buy.

What is it about rockstar creating games that really leaves you with a bad taste in your mouth. I mean, the game is really well done, but man it is violent and nasty.
But, yes, I think it still one of the better games they have made, if you have the stomach for it.
The good:
Amazing production value. Rockstar has made lots of money and can afford a game that just looks and sounds absolutely fantastic. They could afford good writers too, thank God. The story is clever, witty and sometimes sort of funny. There are also some hits of deeper self relfection and meta-gaming. (I do wonder the purpose behind these games sometimes...) It is well optimized for PC, but you are still gonna need a fairly powerful computer to truly enjoy it. Ports from rockstar are usually crap, but this one is good. Gameplay is solid.
The bad: SOCIAL CLUB! what a pain, really. A service no one wants, but that you have to sign up for in order to play. If social club does not work, forget playing. I had constant problems connecting, and almost every time it actually worked, I had to reestablish my account and game again, making the game start over. I never lost my save though, but at times I had to see the non-skippable intro again before I could play. Very frustrating indeed. You'll find a few forums about it on steam for sure.
The game is really gruesome and violent. I know it is what the game is about, but still, it really relishes in it, and has slow cams for final killing shots. It kind of scares me that people find that amusing. It does fit the game, just a lot of gore for my taste.
The controls are good. Mouse and keyboard is your better experience.
I think this game is a great example of what huge amounts of cash can do. Sometimes, a lot of money can convert a fairly simple game, to a great experience. Because if you look at the mechanics, they are fairly simple. This game is basically a shooting gallery, and quite often on rails. And also a corridor cover shooter from time to time. Then there are som "collecting stuff" thrown in there, but it just feels contrived. Perhaps they felt the actual gameplay was too short?
Too short? Well, the campaign will take you about 10 hours, but most of it is cutscenes. Well made, well acted, sometimes epic cutsenes with great sound and music, but nevertheless a lot of cutsecenes. It really is an interactive movie. Thankfully, this is all so well done, that you don't mind. It is an interesting, albeit crazy story, and the main characters are well developed. This game oozes of tense and intese moments. You really feel the characters pain and frustration, and the horror of the situation. Locations are greatly realized. You feel involved. I kind of feel that the simple game mechanics get played out quite quickly, I did not feel I wanted more when the game was done. So, perhaps the whole "movie with some game play thrown in" was a smart move?
Reckommended.

As a long time fan of series like Battlefield and ARMA I was more than excited to hop into the long awaited and anticipated Squad.
An intense first person shooter that combines the realism of ARMA 3 and the playability of Battlefield my first impressions are great. Right off the bat I hopped into the training area of the game to get a feel for the mechanics and other key aspects. Immediately impressive was the sounds, absolutely spectacular, with dynamic sounds inside buildings and around objects it adds to the immersion of the game.
As I continued my exploration I came across the range and decided to give my AK74 a try. Again I was impressed with how well the developers had engineered the sounds for the weapons in the game. Not only was the sound of the bullet firing great, but so was the actual sounds of the gun itself. The shooting mechanics are similar to Insurgency but with a little more punishment for spraying especially with the AK’s. Hipfire was surprisingly accurate compared to other games but a better model on real life.
From a graphics standpoint the game looks quite beautiful but I found a lot of the in-game community complaining about optimization. Personally I was able to run the game in  1080p on the “epic” setting. I am not sure what my FPS was exactly because the game seems to not let any overlays on the screen but I would estimate it at being 50-70. My only complaint was that the sun rays that come through the trees and around buildings are too bright and form a wall of light.
One of the biggest aspect of an online game is the community it fosters. This game, unlike several other games such as Battlefield and ARMA 3, actually requires not only teamwork but real leadership to come out on top. This makes the game very interesting to play and will really make certain people shine when they lead their squad to victory.
Building to the community aspect of the game is one of my personal favourite additions, local and team chat. With the added radio sounds it creates an even more immersive environment for the player. Something the ARMA series has repeatedly left out and modders have had to add in. When you’re in the fray and the bullets are flying,  it sucks you that much further in as a teammate screams for a medic.
Overall I think Squad has started out as a great game full of potential for the future. I will continue to keep a close eye on development and also hope it doesn’t suffer the same fate as Insurgency did. I can’t wait to see vehicles released and how that changes both the balance of the teams and the way people play the game.
Final ratings:
Mechanics: 8/10
Graphics: 7.5/10
Sounds: 10/10
Community: 8/10 (subject to change in the future)
Total: 8.3/10

It would seem that today’s gaming market would be full and there would be no space for a new FPS shooter game at all. Assumption is surprisingly faulty, the market have been out of product at least a decade that is focusing on realistic yet smoothly rolling tactics, strategy and teamwork over pedantically modelled simulator mentality or overly simplified score hunting block busters. That void is filled today when SQUAD did hit to the Steamstore as Early Access product.
The game is realistically unforgiving, but at the same time you can concentrate to the actual doing of things as the game is built in mentality of "easily accessible, but hard to master", so no need to spend first hours reading manuals of how interact with game world or hunting down a game mods to get access to online server to get your daily dose of online fragging.
As game is unforgiving it will mean that basic Battlefield games tactic of sprinting to point A taking some damage while shooting enemies popping around the corners along the way there and to just sit top of the medic box afterward that someone dropped randomly on the ground, will not work in this game. The harsh damage model combined with the fact that there is just not any kind of visual spotting system hovering above enemies makes the headless running around a one way ticket to under the soil. The game needs one to hook up with the team and think before actions, it is a thinking man’s battlefield.
The size of the Squad is stunning, maps are just huge compared most of anything. This is increased by the fact that the spawn system makes you at times to walk from the main base back to the action, if your team’s strategy of building the respawns were faulty, although when the vehicles are implemented later on the development of the Early Access your time is more used in battle zone than traveling around. Once again after long time of zwarms of restricted world military FPS games the flanking of the enemies are just as valid tactic as breaching the defences with the force and actually the flanking is working even better. Success in Squad comes from finding the weak spots of the enemy defence and not just throwing all forces to the grinder, similar philosophy is found from many traditional martial arts.
"The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy." - Sun Tzu

Collect all the Sigils, disregard
orders, and let yourself be tempted by the Snake, but
take the lift to the 6th and last floor of the forbidden Tower, for there you shall find only Death!
This is a puzzle game, much like
, where you will be using boxes to keep buttons pressed, manipulate lasers and fans, and even duplicate yourself in order to finish the game.
Gameplay is kept very simple: You can run, jump, and interact with objects.
The real fun lies in solving the puzzles, which often require thinking outside the box.
Unlike Portal, there are very few opportunities to die in this game and they are easily avoidable by paying attention - there are no crazy turrets that will snipe you from across the room.
The story is very philosophical and requires some involvement on the player's part. If you ignore the various computers spread across the world and instead focus on solving only the puzzles, you'll have a hard time understanding what's going on, or what happened when you reach the true ending.
Also, some of the questions asked in the game are very interesting, such as: "Are machines conscious beings, or do they only pretend to be?", "If they aren't conscious, what makes you think humans are?" and similar.
Graphically speaking, this game is absolutely stunning, especially in 4k. The textures are very sharp (assuming your GPU is powerful enough to handle it) and it provides the player with a vast variety of graphical options to choose from.
The only downside is that the game looks so good, that the lack of tesselation on walls becomes slightly distracting (if you're not busy solving the puzzles, that is).
If you're looking for an action game, this isn't it.
If instead you are looking for an intellectually challenging and stimulating game, this is a must-buy.

This is a team-based massively multiplayer first person shooter. While there are several games out there in this genre, Planetside is unique due to the scale of the battles. Players fight across massive continents consisting of dozens of bases. A battle at a single one of those bases will usually involve dozens, sometimes hundreds of people on both sides.
There are 6 classes, each of which has a unique role on the battlefield. For example Medics can heal and revive teammates, while Light Assaults can use their jetpacks to ambush enemies from above. And even within a class there is room for customization, for example my Medic is equipped in such a way that he is optimized for small arms combat on the front lines in addition to healing. But you could just as easily equip a Medic as a specialized healer, carrying a bandoleer of many "revive grenades" to bring back multiple fallen allies fast in a major battle. There are also numerous ground and air-based vehicles to choose from, and like classes these can be customized as well.
There are three factions and each has their own faction-specific equipment and vehicles in addition to generic stuff that is available to everyone.
The game is free, and I know everyone's first reaction to hearing that is to ask, "Is it really free, or is it free-to-play-pay-to-win?" And thankfully, the answer is yes, it really is free.
That's not to say the devs don't want you to spend money on the game, they do, but the stuff you'd be spending money on would be things like cowboy hats, pink camoflauge, or other things which have no impact on combat. All the actual combat equipment in this game can be gotten with the in-game currency known as "certs", and cert gain is accelerated for new characters. It's very possible to be successful at this game without spending a penny. As for myself, I'm currently Battle Rank 95, meaning I have been a successful player, I also have not spent any money on it, although I do intend to buy some stuff in the future (not because I care about cowboy hats or pink camoflauge, but I do want to keep the servers running on this fun game).
Teamwork is very important in this game. It's great to join a squad of strangers, have your squad leaders come up with a plan, and have that plan actually work and turn the tide of a major battle. There is also support for "outfits" which are basically a group of your friends that you would squad up with regularly.
I must warn you that compared to other first person shooters, the time-to-kill in this game is very short. So you WILL be dying a lot! Thankfully the respawn times are short!
It's a fun game, if you're a fan of other multiplayer first person shooters you'll probably love Planetside 2!

From a graphics standpoint the game looks quite beautiful but I found a lot of the in-game community complaining about optimization. Personally I was able to run the game in  1080p on the “epic” setting. I am not sure what my FPS was exactly because the game seems to not let any overlays on the screen but I would estimate it at being 50-70. My only complaint was that the sun rays that come through the trees and around buildings are too bright and form a wall of light.
One of the biggest aspect of an online game is the community it fosters. This game, unlike several other games such as Battlefield and ARMA 3, actually requires not only teamwork but real leadership to come out on top. This makes the game very interesting to play and will really make certain people shine when they lead their squad to victory.
Building to the community aspect of the game is one of my personal favourite additions, local and team chat. With the added radio sounds it creates an even more immersive environment for the player. Something the ARMA series has repeatedly left out and modders have had to add in. When you’re in the fray and the bullets are flying,  it sucks you that much further in as a teammate screams for a medic.
Overall I think Squad has started out as a great game full of potential for the future. I will continue to keep a close eye on development and also hope it doesn’t suffer the same fate as Insurgency did. I can’t wait to see vehicles released and how that changes both the balance of the teams and the way people play the game.
Final ratings:
Mechanics: 8/10
Graphics: 7.5/10
Sounds: 10/10
Community: 8/10 (subject to change in the future)
Total: 8.3/10

It would seem that today’s gaming market would be full and there would be no space for a new FPS shooter game at all. Assumption is surprisingly faulty, the market have been out of product at least a decade that is focusing on realistic yet smoothly rolling tactics, strategy and teamwork over pedantically modelled simulator mentality or overly simplified score hunting block busters. That void is filled today when SQUAD did hit to the Steamstore as Early Access product.
The game is realistically unforgiving, but at the same time you can concentrate to the actual doing of things as the game is built in mentality of "easily accessible, but hard to master", so no need to spend first hours reading manuals of how interact with game world or hunting down a game mods to get access to online server to get your daily dose of online fragging.
As game is unforgiving it will mean that basic Battlefield games tactic of sprinting to point A taking some damage while shooting enemies popping around the corners along the way there and to just sit top of the medic box afterward that someone dropped randomly on the ground, will not work in this game. The harsh damage model combined with the fact that there is just not any kind of visual spotting system hovering above enemies makes the headless running around a one way ticket to under the soil. The game needs one to hook up with the team and think before actions, it is a thinking man’s battlefield.
The size of the Squad is stunning, maps are just huge compared most of anything. This is increased by the fact that the spawn system makes you at times to walk from the main base back to the action, if your team’s strategy of building the respawns were faulty, although when the vehicles are implemented later on the development of the Early Access your time is more used in battle zone than traveling around. Once again after long time of zwarms of restricted world military FPS games the flanking of the enemies are just as valid tactic as breaching the defences with the force and actually the flanking is working even better. Success in Squad comes from finding the weak spots of the enemy defence and not just throwing all forces to the grinder, similar philosophy is found from many traditional martial arts.
"The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy." - Sun Tzu

While none of the gameplay mechanics are as revolutionary as, say, portals, Talos Principle creates a lot of excellent puzzles using boxes on buttons, aggressive obstacles, and a lot of spatial reasoning with a dash of Braid-esque time manipulation, all in a very pretty environment.
More than a few puzzles stumped me to the point of going off to do other things and then coming back, and I spent more than a little time trying to unlock doors with tetrominoes and getting frustrated with "SO CLOSE!" sentiments, but the world of the game is rewarding and the various world-building details certainly add a lot of intrigue and mystery while pushing you to try and find one more clue, one more hint into what happened to get you where you are.
Obviosuly, game-play time is going to vary a lot depending on how inclined you are to power through puzzles, though the game provided easily 20 hours of play-time for me, and I still lhaven't collected all the stars or rewards from puzzles.
If you're in the market for a thought provoking puzzler, this is a 10/10.

There are 2 types of questions: straight-forward and deep-thinking.
Do I like this game?
No
Do I love this game?
Yes
Those were simple questions that I could answer in a flash. But what about a difficult one:
What does being a human mean?
Stop right there! Don't even try to answer this one.
Forget what you know about your own life and take a leap of faith. Try to follow this game's course and find out what it really means to be a human...by experiencing a replica of the world God created for us.
Of course, there is no Adam and Eve here. It's just you, the Devil and the God. Will you let yourself tempted by the Devil, or get immortality by following God's rules? I will be honest. I let myself tempted and I found it rewarding. The Devil's phylosophy...no...the entire game's phylosophy conviced me that defying God would  bring me satisfaction. It did, but it also raised a whole new set of questions.
Back to the question we left a few moments ago.
What does being a human mean?
I'd like to spoil it for you, but i won't. I think you should find out for yourself. If you pay enough attention, The Talos Principle will slowly reveal the answer. But as I said before, finding the answer might raise other questions.
So here I leave you some of these thought-provoking questions that this game has raised:
Was Eve right to eat the Forbidden Fruit? What if God actually wanted her to do so? What if eating the Apple was actually what God had intended for the human kind from the very beginning?

If you told me at the start of the year that a puzzle game with philosophical undertones from the developers of Serious Sam would be one of the year’s best titles, I probably wouldn’t have believed you. However this is very much the case as The Talos Principle is a fascinating and mentally invigorating experience with clever puzzles and a highly intriguing philosophy laden science fiction backdrop. The game slowly generates an atmosphere of mind-bending contemplation unlike anything I have experienced before in games thanks to a potent mixture of clever writing and music that starts to get under your skin. I think only 2001 A Space Odyssey has given me the same feeling before.
The puzzles themselves are the star of the show however with a good difficulty curve and consistently excellent design. Some puzzles which have you dodging floating mines can be annoying, but the vast majority require clever thinking rather than quick reflexes or good timing. The puzzles are short but require you to use existing mechanics in new and surprising ways. The game lets you figure almost everything for yourself, from the story to the mechanics, but the world and puzzles are laid out in such a way that this is generally not a problem. There are loads of secrets/optional challenges that help add further substance to the game after you finish working through the main set of puzzles. I did not spend a lot of time going after these and finished the game in about 15 hours, I would say it is well worth the forty dollar asking price.
If you have even a passing interest in puzzle games and don’t mind confronting some heavy philosophical/nihilist ideas (among some more hopeful ones), I can’t recommend The Talos Principle highly enough.

The Talos Principle is an amazing first person puzzler experience held together by a story building on elements of philosophy. However, if you're looking at this game, you probably know that already. Yes, one could summarize a recommendation for this game as: "Liked Portal 2? Get this.". In all honesty, it is damn good.
Instead of reiterating the same things everybody says about this game, I'd like to present maybe a more differentiated opinion, discussing what I did not like - make no mistake, the game is fantastic and I'd recommend it without hesitation, but even such games have flaws. If you're just wondering whether you should buy the game: Yes; yes, you should.
In this case, you're being presented a puzzler with distinguished rooms, between which you can switch and which unlock you sigils that you need to progress. Essentially these sigils are tetrominos that form sets which in turn once completed can be used to unlock new parts or to open doors.
My problem here is that these tetromino puzzles sometimes permit a logical approach implying certain symmetry relations or similar, so you can solve them using a determined strategy - but most do not. Especially tetromino sets consisting out of 14 parts feel rather tedious and time consuming, as they detoriate to a matter of trial and error, and ultimately trigger frustration.
More precisely,
Had they eased on that components I feel the game would have had a somewhat better pacing.
Nextly, some puzzles later on just become tedious. Especially those with multiple mines in them can be frustrating as a single misstep will result in a reset. Moreover,
.
It's a bit weird as some extra puzzles introduce some new mechanics unseen in the main puzzles. Again, it appeared to me the game would have profited from taking these mechanics and moving the tedious extensions in the extra puzzles instead.
Furthermore, a lot of text - both from QR codes and in-game messages - is 'enciphered' by just showing their ASCII representation in hexadecimal numbering, for example "I like 54 49 54 53!". I don't see the purpose thereof: Either you are technically adept enough to know what ASCII is, in which case this is something you translate maybe one of the messages and then ignore that or it is just confusing.
Lastly, I found the collectible stars being too easily missable.
As of such, if you've missed a star, but have already solved all puzzles in the given world, you're bound to revisiting things you've already seen.
My ultimate impression all things considered is that they wanted to squeeze in as many puzzles as possible. Per se, that would be a good thing but tieing them all in with the story and with extras leads to the aforementioned issues I have with the game. Furthermore, the story feels at some points badly paced because small fragments that progress the narrative are separated by long puzzle sequences.
While playing the game, I felt this giving it some pacing issues. What I mean is that the story would have could have also been presented with much smaller sets of sigils.
Had they
extracted the other puzzles in some extra unrelated to the story, I suppose the story's occasional drought periods would not have been there, while the game would have provided the same content, just in a different arrangement.

My initial reservations about The Talos Principle were rapidly swept away. [hah! a Portal wannabe!]. Superlative puzzle design that is decently challenging with plenty of "red herring" to keep you on your toes. The music is atmospheric and really adds to the sense of personal transportation as you engage with philosophical debate, reasoning and conjecture at various points throughout. There are many hidden levels to navigate, and you could take a somewhat non-linear approach to exploration of the worlds and puzzles that must be solved in order to find "sigils", a tetromino used in mini puzzles that allow player progression. Its rewarding to take the time to absorb the story and smaller side puzzles that are scattered about. The ongoing discussion with the unknown and difficult entity via the computer terminal may actually leave you puzzling for a minute about the consistancy of your own logic and reasoning - an easy trap to fall into with certain scripted systems :-) [some people even are still stymied by Eliza...] This is one of the best games I have played in recent years. You get to question reality, your own moral standpoint, and solve some briefly challenging, (but sometimes brilliantly simple) puzzles while you're at it.
One of the best f2p games.

A bittersweet experience. Great gameplay, cool new setting, and plenty of content for your buck.
However, replacing the great, gripping storylines and scripts from the first two with pretentious GTAIV-era Rockstar writing was really hard to sit through. It makes me wish that Remedy was still at the helm. As a long time fan, it was cringing to hear some of the bizarre social/political commentary that Max and others were making. Most of it didn't even make sense for the messages they were trying to get across. The first two titles were closely knit together with returning characters and ideas, and while it's impossible to expect those things from three, I simply wish I cared more. Throughout the game (especially the 2nd half) I didn't understand why things were going down the way they were, why Max was doing it, and frankly, I just didn't care. Max himself is a mixed bag. I like the whole broken, beat down, aged mess he is, but there is something truly missing here in his character. The whole thing just seems to forget what Max Payne was all about. Somehow the effort to make the world more 'realistic' just had the opposite effect of 'realism' to me. I couldn't take it serious.
Like I said before, the new setting is very welcome, though I wouldn't have minded New York a third time, or any familiar American location to maintain the 'noir' feeling. However, the new locale and variety in environments was very awesome. Gone is the noir feeling yes, which I can accept losing, but with the cool new locale we sadly are given excessive cutscenes and bizarre visual effects that can't be turned off. The combat to me is the best it has ever been, and the limit to how many guns you carry makes the combat a little more interesting and intense, though it feels a bit clunky at times. It instead makes you feel like John McClane and not a walking armory.
Long story short, if you're a fan of Payne, new or old, who played the first two games, I'd try it, or study it a bit to see if it's up your alley. The action is great like I said, even though that last-stand mechanic has plain not-worked for me many times. For me though, action alone is not good enough. The story kept me going in the past games and I just didn't care what happened here. The terrible script, though at least very well acted doesn't help. The whole thing is just an experience that when it ends you can't help but think about the simple fixes and changes that would have made it a much better ride.

Portal 2 is a sequel to Portal where you play as the same main character, that was waken up from a long sleep by a friendly companion robot who you see throughout the game, the game is a first-person puzzle-platformer and is a very good game, while keeping many of the mechanics from the first game, it still seems to be new and fresh without getting repetetive or seeming like an exact copy of the first game. Although this game was challenging in some parts it wasnt too difficult and I wasnt constantly looking up solutions to the puzzles it threw at me.
PROS:
-Storyline is interesting and keeps you on the edge of your seat
-Puzzles are very well thought out and some have more than one way of solving them
-Difficulty is just perfect as I only had to look up 1 or 2 answers to puzzles I couldn't figure out
-Many secrets hidden throughout the game
-Co-op is equally as fun as the main campaign
-Great ideas/mechanics
CONS:
-Little to no replay value as the puzzles stay the same
-No remaster so graphics arent up to date (good for the time though)
-Holds your hand too much in some puzzles and not enough in others
In my opinion Portal 2 was a fantastic game and although it is old it still deserves to be praised. It is definitely worth the $20 you pay for it. It took me around 10 hours to beat which is a lot longer than the first game and it was enjoyable throughout the entire game.

Dont know what to say about this game so here is a recipe for chicken curry
Roughly chop the onion, transfer to a small food processor, and add 3 tablespoons of water - process to a slack paste. You could use a stick blender for this or coarsely grate the onion into a bowl – there’s no need to add any water if you are grating the onion. Tip into a small bowl and leave on one side.
Put the chopped garlic and ginger into the same food processor and add 4 tbsp water – process until smooth and spoon into another small bowl. Alternatively, crush the garlic to a paste with a knife or garlic press and finely grate the ginger.
Heat the oil in a wok or sturdy pan set over a medium heat. Combine the cumin and fennel seeds with the cinnamon and chilli flakes and add to the pan in one go. Swirl everything around for about 30 secs until the spices release a fragrant aroma.
Add the onion paste – it will splutter in the beginning. Fry until the water evaporates and the onions turn a lovely dark golden - this should take about 7-8 mins. Add the garlic and ginger paste and cook for another 2 mins – stirring all the time.
Stir in the garam masala, turmeric, and sugar and continue cooking for 20 secs before tipping in the tomatoes. Continue cooking on a medium heat for about 10 mins without a lid until the tomatoes reduce and darken.
Cut the chicken thighs into 3cm chunks and add to the pan once the tomatoes have thickened to a paste. Cook for 5 mins to coat the chicken in the masala and seal in the juices, and then pour over the hot chicken stock. Simmer for 8-10 mins without a lid until the chicken is tender and the masala lightly thickened – you might need to add an extra ladleful of stock or water if the curry needs it. Sprinkle with chopped coriander and serve with Indian flatbreads or fluffy basmati rice and a pot of yogurt on the side.

Croteam, after their hallmark series Serious Sam managed to create the first puzzler game on the level of Portal 2, which was unexpected, to say the least. After having played through the game, it is definitely my game of the year 2014 for various reasons, which I'll break below into several sections:
At the start of the game, you awaken as a android which is tasked with solving puzzles, for which Elohim - your maker, promises you eternal life. The story is told mostly through logs found in terminals scattered around the world, but also serve for communication with Milton, a library assistant and an intelligence with which you discuss some intriguing philosophical dilemmas. While Elohim encourages the player to explore it's creations, he explicitly prohibits venturing into the tower, which soars into the sky. As the story progresses, Milton encourages the player to act independently, and motivates him to enter the tower and find out the truth for himself.
The game starts slowly by introducing gameplay elements (some of which are unlocked by solving specific puzzles) and the difficulty of the puzzles ramps up pretty fast, but they are never unfair - even if some of them may be excruciatingly hard. If there is a situation where the player may get stuck, it's because some specific mechanics and uses of elements aren't expected or explained beforehand. Example: some puzzles utilize your own body for intentionally blocking lasers, which the player himself might not think for some time. One thing that may get on some player's nerves is the reset ability, which you will use at some point to unstuck yourself from an unsolvable jam. It resets the entire room along with all the progress you might have made, which can be somewhat annoying in longer puzzles which take some time to progress through. Once you do solve a particularly tricky puzzle, you are glad you persisted and managed to solve it on your own. On most puzzles there is a shrine you can use to get a hint if you get stuck (although some hints are too vague and don't help as you might expect), but getting that hint requires solving some hidden puzzles which are not a part of the main story, but are worth exploring any ways as they have the most beautiful locations in the entire game. If you find yourself a bit short on hints, you may want to play Sigils of Elohim, a free companion mini-game in which you may get an additional 3 hints.
There are four worlds in the game, which go as follows:
- ancient Greek/Roman themed world
- puzzles spread out in the desert, borrowed aesthetics from Serious Sam 3
- typical medieval style with ruined castles in a forest
- the "main" world in which the tower and the three other hub worlds are located
You start your adventure in the Mediterranean world and gradually unlock the Egypt and medieval worlds with puzzles, which are spread out into different rooms in every world. You can play the puzzles pretty much in any order, which is welcome if you are stuck in a particular puzzle, so the player can skip that particular one for the time being and return later on with a fresh approach, unlike in fully linear games like Portal.
The game has some very nice visuals, particularly if you look at the texture quality (Example: look closely at the greek-style fresca scattered through the ruins of the first world, or just looking at the floor mosaic in the third world hub cathedral). There are some hidden locations with truly great visuals, so I definitely encourage anyone to explore the game fully, which will not go unrewarded. The game runs pretty well on older hardware, but don't expect wonders - the game likes stronger hardware, but it knows how to use it. If you played Serious Sam 3, you pretty much know what to expect, it's a visually slightly upgraded game, which is fine for my taste.
This game has one of the best soundtracks this year, which you can listen for free in full here
It's one of the few games where I didn't have to turn the music off after some time as it blends in fantastically with the game. If you buy the sountrack DLC now, you might be a little bit dissapointed to find out that there's Elohim's voice in pretty much every track, making it a bit weird if you listen to the game's soundtrack in the public or at work. The game's developers promised to offer a versions without voiceovers, but we'll see.
I haven't had this much fun with a game in years, and Croteam did a stellar job with this game. If you like puzzle games, especially Portal 2, pick this game up immediately, you definitely won't regret it. For now the game the game doesn't have content beside the main campaign and the prototype maps DLC, but they shipped the game with the editor and full Steam workshop integration, and already the community started putting out stuff days after release, so we might get an abundant amount of content as time goes on.
If you've played through the base game I highly recommend you pick up the "Road to Gehenna" DLC as it adds a good amount of hard puzzles which advance on both the mechanics and difficulty of the base game.

tl;dr this game made me think about stuff, buy it.
the easy comparison to this game is portal, and as i played, i did think of portal, it is a very obvious influence for the gameplay of The Talos Principal, but what makes this game stand out is it's conveyance of story, and it's themes.
portal gives you fun hoops to jump through, which you do, without question, until the game, through it's surprising story, shows you that there was a man behind the curtain the whole time. it's interesting, and surprising the first time you play through portal because it gives you a story which directly correlates with the game. it answers a question you didn't even ask: why were you playing the game? why were you doing all of these strange things?
to us, that's the game, it's fun, we don't question it. so it is interesting when the game makes us question it.
The Talos Principle takes this question and follows it to the absolute extent possible. it doesn't just make you question the game, it makes you question yourself, why do you exist? are you happy existing? have you ever thought about it? why are you picking up the cube? why is that fun? why do you seek the prize? is it part of your nature? what is nature? what is the mind? etc etc etc etc
etc.
it is a brilliant game which shows you the sadness and beauty of death without killing anybody, without violence.
but that's just the general theme of the game, the story itself is ALSO very engaging and interesting, and the gameplay...
the gameplay is pretty great. i wouldn't say the puzzles in talos principle make it amazing, but they are fun, and the difficulty ramps up very gently and satisfyingly, being sure to introduce new mechanics, only, when you have mastered previous mechanics. you never feel rushed in this game, you never feel badgered and harrassed, you can take as much time to solve a puzzle as you need which is really refreshing from the usual puzzle game which has you running around, juggling mechanics to exhaustion.
i can't recommend this game enough. honestly i would put it above portal, as extreme as that sounds, based on the fact that it made me think, a lot, which is a thing a lot of games don't seem to care about.
price point is high, but my playtime is accurate to the length of the game, and i didn't bother with the extra ending, so you could easily get 20 hours if you wanted to.

Well it took me long enough to finally play this game. And I gotta admit that though short, it was pretty damn fun....mostly.
Graphics: For its time, it looks great. Still holds up I think; though I had to play it on low-ish graphics due to my gaming laptop showing its age. But even on low, it looked pretty good (other than low textures, of course. If you're having trouble playing this game, save lowering the textures for the last option. Lower everything else first and see how it works for you.)
Gameplay: Max Payne 3 is pretty much just like all the other Max Paynes, only with a bit more flourish and alot more on rail shooting going on. This is not a downside, however, as such segments are far inbetween each other and they're actually pretty fun and action packed.
And that's really the name of the game here. It's a very action packed game. Lots of shooting, killing, slo mo, and so on. If you liked the other Max Paynes, you'll certainly enjoy this one. One thing they did do is add certain moments where you really see just how incredibly awesome Max is during gun fights.
However, it's not all rainbows... Enemies immediately hit you rather hard, but that's par for the course with Max Payne. But as the "Chapters" roll by, the more and more tanky the enemies get. Near the last chapter, I sat there and emptied a clip of an smg into a guy, and he didn't die. You're basically forced to use high powered revolvers/assault rifles and ALWAYS aim for the head. And even then, headshots go from being one-hit kill to two or three or sometimes even more, depending upon what weapon you're using. And then there are quite a few enemies with helmets and masks that soak up even more damage. I found myself raging hard when I perforated an enemy, he goes down, and as I'm taking out another group, that same guy gets right back up and kills me or makes me waste a painkiller. Truly, truly aggravating. This was on Medium, by the way. I'd hate to see how rage-worthy Hard is.
Controls: You really realize quite immediately that Max is not a spring chicken. His running speed is very slow. This is not the game itself having "slow" running speeds. MAX HIMSELF is slow. There are a few times when you're with an npc partner and they just run right past you while you're lumbering forward. You're even given a few jibes here and there by them at times. This isn't a bad thing, however. The game of course acknowledges Max's slow speed, and you're given the ability to roll or use his famous ShootDodge to dodge incoming bullets.
One thing that is definitely different from MP 1 and MP 2 is that there's a cover mechanic. People nowadays like to bash this mechanic at times, but it's definitely prevailent here in Max Payne 3, and you'll be happy it is. However, it can be a bit wonky at times. Sometimes I like to roll from cover to cover. So I'd Roll, and then press the Cover key (which is Q). It's...very hit and miss. Sometimes it works, other times he just stands there like a derp. This also happens alot after "Last Man Standing" mode, where if you have painkillers and you're fatally shot, you go into slo mo and are able to shoot the guy that shot you to revive. This happens ALOT while you're in cover, and right after you succeed, he just...gets right back up, standing all nice and tall for enemies to shoot him right back down again. It's...annoying, to say the least.
Story: Now this is where this game shines. Shooting things until they're dead is all fun and good, but it's the story that makes you want to continue. I think I only had maybe...4 gameplay sessions throughout the last 2 days not just because the game is short, but because I wanted to keep the story going.
Max Payne...is a catastrophe. That's all there is to it. He's a catastrophe that knows he's a catastrophe, and yet there's this tiny, little candle amidst the dark horrors within him that shows brightly when he's fighting for something he believes in. Constantly does he berrate himself over and over for who he is and what he's doing and failing impossible odds. He does this alot in this game, and one particular npc tells him "It's not your fault." During cutscenes certain words are focused upon and written on screen. Those words were focused on...and it was certainly a powerful moment.
He may hate himself, but his soul is strong and his resolve is stronger. He's not some deadbeat that doesn't care. He does...and that's what makes the torturing he gives himself mentally even more painful.
As for the story itself, it's full of interesting twists and turns. Some you'll see a mile away, others will surprise you completely. But really, the story is all about Max redeeming himself. Not in others' eyes, but in his own eyes. Does he? Maybe, maybe not.
Online Multiplayer: I didn't play it. I tried, and no one joined me nor could I join anyone else. Didn't seem like a connection problem. But really I'm not interested enough to try again. I wanted to play Max payne 3 for the story, not for the multiplayer. Which...in itself, aggravates me. Max Payne 3 was created during a time where EVERYTHING NEEDED MULTIPLAYER. Call of Duty and its ilk poisoned pretty much every developer's minds with their popularity. "Hey, if CoD has multiplayer, we should too!" No! Nooooo!
I feel that if they didn't add this crappy multiplayer to Max Payne 3, then the story would've been even better...and longer. There is a hint that not everything is completely "finished" if you find a particular "Clue" within one of the later missions. What's worse, is that you can create a character and one of the character archetypes is the name of this particular group that never really saw the light of day in the campaign. That...saddens me. What saddens me even more, is that there is no single player DLC that could've fixed this. Nope...ALL multiplayer. Maps, skins, overpowered weapons, you name it, they threw it in CoD style. *sigh*
And thus I think that ends my review. Overall, I'd give Max Payne 3 a....
8/10
The storyline was brilliant. Maybe a little convoluted with all the different groups and game changers, but Max's story within the story is what brings it home. Gameplay was (mostly) tight and fun. Difficulty in the form of enemy damage output was fine....but their tankiness really ruined the enjoyment in the latter levels.
As stated before - if you liked Max Payne 1 and 2...you'll like Max Payne 3 (Then again, they added cover mechanics, so if you're not a fan of that, then....go download some zany MP 2 mods and have at it.)

And then there are quite a few enemies with helmets and masks that soak up even more damage. I found myself raging hard when I perforated an enemy, he goes down, and as I'm taking out another group, that same guy gets right back up and kills me or makes me waste a painkiller. Truly, truly aggravating. This was on Medium, by the way. I'd hate to see how rage-worthy Hard is.
Controls: You really realize quite immediately that Max is not a spring chicken. His running speed is very slow. This is not the game itself having "slow" running speeds. MAX HIMSELF is slow. There are a few times when you're with an npc partner and they just run right past you while you're lumbering forward. You're even given a few jibes here and there by them at times. This isn't a bad thing, however. The game of course acknowledges Max's slow speed, and you're given the ability to roll or use his famous ShootDodge to dodge incoming bullets.
One thing that is definitely different from MP 1 and MP 2 is that there's a cover mechanic. People nowadays like to bash this mechanic at times, but it's definitely prevailent here in Max Payne 3, and you'll be happy it is. However, it can be a bit wonky at times. Sometimes I like to roll from cover to cover. So I'd Roll, and then press the Cover key (which is Q). It's...very hit and miss. Sometimes it works, other times he just stands there like a derp. This also happens alot after "Last Man Standing" mode, where if you have painkillers and you're fatally shot, you go into slo mo and are able to shoot the guy that shot you to revive. This happens ALOT while you're in cover, and right after you succeed, he just...gets right back up, standing all nice and tall for enemies to shoot him right back down again. It's...annoying, to say the least.
Story: Now this is where this game shines. Shooting things until they're dead is all fun and good, but it's the story that makes you want to continue. I think I only had maybe...4 gameplay sessions throughout the last 2 days not just because the game is short, but because I wanted to keep the story going.
Max Payne...is a catastrophe. That's all there is to it. He's a catastrophe that knows he's a catastrophe, and yet there's this tiny, little candle amidst the dark horrors within him that shows brightly when he's fighting for something he believes in. Constantly does he berrate himself over and over for who he is and what he's doing and failing impossible odds. He does this alot in this game, and one particular npc tells him "It's not your fault." During cutscenes certain words are focused upon and written on screen. Those words were focused on...and it was certainly a powerful moment.
He may hate himself, but his soul is strong and his resolve is stronger. He's not some deadbeat that doesn't care. He does...and that's what makes the torturing he gives himself mentally even more painful.
As for the story itself, it's full of interesting twists and turns. Some you'll see a mile away, others will surprise you completely. But really, the story is all about Max redeeming himself. Not in others' eyes, but in his own eyes. Does he? Maybe, maybe not.
Online Multiplayer: I didn't play it. I tried, and no one joined me nor could I join anyone else. Didn't seem like a connection problem. But really I'm not interested enough to try again. I wanted to play Max payne 3 for the story, not for the multiplayer. Which...in itself, aggravates me. Max Payne 3 was created during a time where EVERYTHING NEEDED MULTIPLAYER. Call of Duty and its ilk poisoned pretty much every developer's minds with their popularity. "Hey, if CoD has multiplayer, we should too!" No! Nooooo!
I feel that if they didn't add this crappy multiplayer to Max Payne 3, then the story would've been even better...and longer. There is a hint that not everything is completely "finished" if you find a particular "Clue" within one of the later missions. What's worse, is that you can create a character and one of the character archetypes is the name of this particular group that never really saw the light of day in the campaign. That...saddens me. What saddens me even more, is that there is no single player DLC that could've fixed this. Nope...ALL multiplayer. Maps, skins, overpowered weapons, you name it, they threw it in CoD style. *sigh*
And thus I think that ends my review. Overall, I'd give Max Payne 3 a....
8/10
The storyline was brilliant. Maybe a little convoluted with all the different groups and game changers, but Max's story within the story is what brings it home. Gameplay was (mostly) tight and fun. Difficulty in the form of enemy damage output was fine....but their tankiness really ruined the enjoyment in the latter levels.
As stated before - if you liked Max Payne 1 and 2...you'll like Max Payne 3 (Then again, they added cover mechanics, so if you're not a fan of that, then....go download some zany MP 2 mods and have at it.)

I'll start off by saying MP3 is a good game.  But it's a good game with some huge, glaring issues.  I felt the game was too long - at around the half-way mark, I just wanted to get it over with.  I can't remember the last game I finshed with this attitude.  The second chapter seemed to go on forever and the entire chapter took place in uninteresting run-down favellas.  At times, it seemed too frustrating.  Sometimes you just want to walk through a room and shoot some dudes in their face and you could never really do this, even with Bullet Time.  You had to constantly be in cover.  In regards to the Bullet Time feature, it was pretty useless.  The game has a "last Stand" mechanic that allows you to survive deadly damage provided you have Paynekillers in your inventory and if you are able to shoot the guy that shot you.  There were too many times where I died because the guy that shot me was at too great of an angle or was out of sight, making it impossible to find and hit him.
The story was good and interesting.  The graphics were great.  Overall, I enjoyed the game and would recommend it, but it does have several things that keep it from the "great game" category.

Planetside 2 - Do you like huge maps, a vast assortment of viehicles, from flying and ground vehicles, airdropping into 32 man+ battles? Then this might just be the game for you.
Pros:
Big Maps
Variety of Weapons
Multiple Strategies
Team Play not required (but reccommended)
Variety of Vehicles
Variety of map terrain/maps
Territorial based
Earn Certs even when offline
F2P
NOT Pay to Win
Upgradeable Vehicles/weapons
Customizeable armor/skins
Beautiful Graphics (assuming you have a high end rig to render thousands upon thousands of particles in a Firefight)
Cons:
Certs to purchase weapons take a bit of time to unlock
Attachments cost a good amount of Certs
Some weapons are only Purchaseable with Certs
Travel in maps can take a good amount of time, depending on how you play
That's just some of the games pros/cons, but overall, if you want a game that incorporates Battlefield Physics (to a certain extent), with large battles involving everything from tanks to aircraft, people airdropping in, and fire from all directions - then this can be good for you. Especially if you have friends who play the game as well. It is reccomended to play with a team of people, to be able to take over territories, but you can just as easily play solo and take over the quiet territories on your own and have a good time. The amount of hacking (as far as I have seen) doesn't seem to be there too much in the game. I haven't seen one myself, but others may have other stories to that account.
The graphics are amazing, especially if you have the ability to run it at max capacity, with all particles on. Collision and hitboxes are decent, and it incorporates bullet speed and drop, so don't forget to lead or adjust your aim. Overall a very good F2P game that has entertained many, including me, for hours.
It has a bit of a curve from how a traditional shooter would play, based off of how the bullet physics react. vehicles drive, and how the general mechanics work in the end. Overall, a game I think most FPS gamers would enjoy - and a GYMAH. And hey, it's free!

I think 'the best puzzler since Portal' is a lazy turn of phrase. One: It immediately compares your game to Portal, which has an amazing gameplay framework and some of the best writing I've seen in a video game. Two: It implies that Portal is unbeatable in the genre, which makes me think 'Oh, the best game since Portal? Why don't I just play Portal then, since we've all agreed that Valve has set a benchmark we all can never beat? Gather copies of Antichamber and Quantum Conundrum, throw them on the bonfire! We've reached the pinnacle of the genre, there's no point now!'
Anyway, The Talos Principle is the best puzzler I've ever played since Portal. This is because the game itself has a great framework for puzzles and manages to remain consistently good for two-thirds of its playtime (25-30 hours). Not only that, it's got decent storytelling qualities. Not as good as Portal's, but still, I can't fault a game that actually has you engage in existential debates with an artificial intelligence. (You won't be asked to brush up on your Immanuel Kant, but if you are familiar with his work you'll get more out of the game!)
The puzzles are fantastic - they are small but they get difficult. But not too difficult. Just enough to provide that 'ah-ha' moment when the solution comes together. There's only six props to solve puzzles with and you have to earn them first. But when you do, they're like getting new toys - barely learning how to use them at first, but the further and further you get, the more efficient you'll get, and in turn the game gets harder, and you use the secret tricks you've learned with these toys to beat the harder puzzles, leading to another set of delicious 'ah-ha' moments and smug satisfaction. Eat it, computer game. The student has now become the master of putting things on boxes! Oh crap, how do I beat this puzzle?
Exploring the world is a treat to be done between puzzles. You can take in the lush scenery of rotting architecture and poking computer terminals to read the scraps of data left behind in the simulation. Sometimes when you poke one of the terminals a filthy computer smartass with a liberal arts degree pops up and questions you about whether you're really human. I told it "I am human, because I think, so go to hell!" and it told me "Yeah, but PHILOSOPHY KARATE CHOP, HAHA! Not so smart now, are you?" and I have to end up conceding because the meager amount of Kierkegaard I read from a comic book was about as useful as a rock in the middle of an artillery strike. I make this sound like a dry pseudo-intellectual slapfight, but it's all just theatrics for the storytelling itself, and you can finish the game whether you win the 'debates' or not. Throw yourself as hard as you can into it, it's fun!
Speaking of finishing video games: There are so many puzzles that this game is The Puzzle Warehouse. The puzzles themselves are wonderfully constructed, but there are so many of them that even the 'ah-ha' moments started to wear off and I literally groaned at the thought of there being more puzzles. It's like reading a good but wordy novel - a lot of fun but finishing the damn thing requires a bit of dedication. Like an Umberto Eco novel, for example.
Anyway BEST DAMN FIRST PERSON PUZZLER SINCE PORTAL BUY IT. THERE'S A KITTEN ON THE STORE PAGE, YOU LIKE THOSE RIGHT?

The gameplay is OK, but unremarkable. A standard third person shooter in just about every way. But it works and it is fun. I was blown away by the variety and detail of the environments, this game has visual atmosphere overload throughout. Such a beautifully crafted game with great, crisp texturing. The music is also top notch and keeps you on edge.
Technically I had absolutely no issue with the game itself. It ran beautifully at 60 fps with a maxed out DX11 renderer.
One big, fat blemish on the game is Social Club, that piece of garbage is utterly useless. How can this not work properly two years after the game was released? Even though it doesn't prevent me from playing I have to manually sign in every time I launch the game. I also have to link my Steam account every time, even though it is supposed to be a one time affair. It baffles me that a massively rich company like Rockstar Games offer their customers this atrocious, useless DRM garbage. Steam should be enough, with Social Club being entirely optional.

This is easily the best puzzle game ever made. I recommend this whole heartedly to all puzzle fans, it has a lot of unique puzzles with a very gentle difficulty curve but a decent amount of tough puzzles in the 2nd half of the game to give even the best lateral thinkers something to really get their teeth into. It's accompanied by absolutely fantastic visuals, if you can max out this game is looks beautiful in places, it also comes with a really great soundtrack that doesn't distract from puzzle solving and adds great ambiance. The game features an intruiging story which is drip fed through a series of emails and archived electronic messages and ultimately opens up an interactive discussion on life, death, purpose, free will, what it means to be human and many other similar topics which add together to form a cohesive over arching and masterfully crafted plot. There's multiple endings depending on what degree you venture into the depths of the game and there's a huge number of secret collectibles which open up secret and unique puzzle areas which ultimately lead to unique endings, but there's also many other irrelevant easter eggs and references to other games which reward exploration and an inquisitive nature.
My 100% playthrough with relatively little getting stuck clocks in at 26 hours, this is 120 puzzles 30 hidden stars and many other easter eggs, value for money cannot be greater here.
If you are a puzzle fan and you enjoyed the portal games but ultimately found them lacking in depth and length especially relative to the price then you should absolutely buy this game. This is easily the sleeper hit of 2014 and easily my GOTY. If you're unsure pick up the free demo on steam and give it a whirl.

Splash Damage is making efforts to address DPC stacking due to single process of UE3 executing on just one core of the CPU.   Still, it has symptoms that develop over a game time of 20minutes and the only sure fire to maintain quality of experience is the inconvenient way of stopping the game, quitting to desktop and returning to the game.
The game implements a balance system that favors the winning team. ELO System in ranked forces you in an unbalanced match outside of your bracket.  Developers attribute to the low player population, however, their matchmaking algorithm has obvious flaws, in that out of balance exceptions are frequent and observable random match making is taking place.
The game has no sense in balancing players based on the latency; and due to the games' unrestricted regional connectivity, it will not take into account how a player performs.   It also applies unfair penalties for technical problems caused by either server/client or WIn10.
Packet losses/server chokes makes the game choppy.
So SD has implemented EAC and still, the netcode is the same and DPC stacking is still an issue.  There are also micro-freezes, unkonwn crashes, out-of-bounds-error, and recurring bugs found, not to mention, incrementing incidents of cheaters in game despite EasyAntiCheat introduction.
Similar to another league where I participated in, it will be to the demise of this title if the current trends continue to proliferate beyond July 2017.
It is now August 2017 and DPC stacking is still an issue.   I'm practically out of ideas in diagnosing what is the root cause of this problem.    I have been advised that it is even beyond the Operating System's capacity to address a misbehaving application so it means that it is definitively not a driver issue nor an operating system fault but rather an application implementation problem that Splash Damage may or may not know about, but simply they are not being open about it.
Game updates are now frequent and game content are now regular.
Ranked Matches (season 2, 3 and 4) are a constant source of problems from balance (due to smurf accounts), cheaters, mismatches (desguised as lack of player population) and technical issues.
We now have credible leads as to how UE3 is causing DPC/ISR stacking but are awaiting developer response regarding our queries.   Apparently, interrupt driven analogue devices attached to the PC are polled by the game engine somewhere in the code and potentially disabling the code making those interrupt polls could fix the issue.
