Max Payne, the eponymous gravel voiced "anti-hero" has returned after a hiatus of nearly a decade. Developed by Rockstar Studios, the latest game features a change of location, a new story and a number of fresh elements.
When Max first burst onto the 3D shooter scene he delivered new features and a fresh, adult story. The original Max Payne easily stood out as the most innovative 3D shooter of its age and spawned a superb sequel as well as a gaggle of imitators. In particular "Bullet Time" - the ability to slow down enemies and make precise shots - was a huge innovation and has been copied often.
Fast forward to the present day and much has changed. There are now many top notch shooters, most of which have features that help them to stand out in the current hyper competitive climate. In this tough new world does Max still have the skills to pay the bills?
When you fire the game up for the first time the lavish production values and strong narrative will bowl you over.
That said Max Payne 3 delivers a tale of woe that isn’t quite as compelling as the original game. Max has fled New York to pursue a new life as a hired bodyguard in Brazil. As soon as he has landed the fecal matter hits the spinning air conveyance facilitator and one of the people he is hired to protect is kidnapped. From here Max quickly discovers his employers are not popular people and he is constantly chasing hordes of bad guys as he tries to get to the bottom of the vendetta.
The story has many twists and turns and it moves along nicely, but it doesn’t have the emotional impact of the first game which saw Max trying to avenge the murder of his wife and baby. You still find yourself caring about the sad old veteran though, even as he binge drinks his way through most of the artfully animated segues.
Bullet Time has returned and we still like it, but there are other features that clamor for your attention. The game delivers a new obstacle based cover system, as well as a "last man standing" shoot-out mode that sees you survive a near fatal hit if you can fire back successfully. This mode is really cool as the game employs clever blur effects to make it feel like you really are about to expire if you don’t blast the guy who just shot you.
Max Payne 3 also features a number of fun multiplayer modes and these do add something, even if for this particular shooter the single player game is still king.
The game keeps you guessing with helicopter sniper stages, swamp boat chases and flaming buildings to escape as well as some really cool set piece battles with enemies and boss characters. The action is also punctuated by superb visuals. Never has the nebulous maze of refuse and ramshackle housing of Brazil’s favela neighborhood looked so good.
Max has a good, but not great selection of weapons to play with this time around. Compared with the earlier releases the current offering lacks variety boomstick wise. You do get to use an excellent sniper rifle from time to time, but you can never keep it. Instead it is sometimes snatched from your inventory in a way that doesn’t make sense. Indeed this applies to all of the weapons in that, after some passages of play, you lose your guns with no real explanation. This hurts the narrative’s sense of credibility, as Max wouldn’t have just tossed such valuable firearms away. He loooves his guns!
Also while the gameplay is very good, for me the essence of any Max Payne game should be Bullet Time. In the current offering the cover system ends up being the most regularly called upon gameplay dynamic and this feels odd.
During some stages Bullet Time is for the most part unnecessary. It isn't driving the gameplay forward as it did in the earlier incarnations of the series. It has gone from being the turbo, giving the game its extra impetus, to being a mere hood ornament. You will kill enemies more efficiently and with less risk to yourself by simply propping behind cover and popping up to take shots when foes show themselves.
Bullet Time, and in particular "shoot dodging" works, but it can be quite risky too. At its best shoot dodging is all about leaping into the air, spinning around and blasting a bunch of hapless enemies as they flounder about in slow motion. Bodies fall and you survive because of your incredible acrobatic skill. In Max Payne 3 your agility is annoyingly hamstrung. You can't draw a bead on foes fast enough. Worse than this, you often land with a thud that sees you recovering too slowly, leaving you horribly vulnerable. So while it looks really cool, you will use shoot dodging sparingly, as popping away at bad guys from cover is more effective ... it just doesn’t look as exciting. Even with the aiming speed cranked up to maximum the game still lacks the dizzying speed and precision we'd expect.
Also, and I know I am nitpicking here, many of the segues feature colorful motion blur visual effects that are totally unnecessary. The game looks stunning enough without this additional graphical garnishing. For me the developers were at times self indulgently showing off their luminescent toys merely for the sake of it.
Fans of the ketchup will be far from disappointed as the game splashes it around with enjoyable abandon. You also get treated to an animated slow motion kill sequence when you have polished off the last foe from a group of bad guys and some of the finishing moves in melee combat are slicker than baby poo. If this wasn’t enough the lighting effects and sun flares are also delightful to behold.
So, while there has been much discussion in this review of the things I didn’t quite love about this game, Max Payne 3 is still well worth your time and spare shekels. Indeed, it is only because I love the game so much that I feel the need to be picky with the critique. Max Payne 3 is that close to being perfect that we’d love it to have those few remaining foibles sorted.
Fans of the previous two outings will enjoy this and those of you who have never played a Max Payne game will love the acerbic wit, style, and narrative depth of the game. The game delivers old school ballistic bliss with aplomb. Gun toting gangsters and militia are everywhere and the action just keeps propelling you forward.

They took everything special about the Max Payne series and turned it into a standard, cover based shooter. I guess that makes sense because this game isn't devolved my Remedy, this time Rockstar did everything.
There's no more noir, no dream sequences, no graphic novel cinematics, no focus on Matrix-style shoot dodging, or fun for that matter.
Only in the first few missions is it optimal to Jon Woo dive at people, and it's admittedly very fun and over the top violent but that all changes 3-4 hours in. After this, the only enemies you'll be facing are fully armored PMC/UFE soldiers who are are nothing more than bullet sponges. Playing like this around them will get you killed and you're forced to use all your slow-mo sitting in cover and taking head shots. It's stupidly stale...
The only really good thing about the game are the cutscenes and acting. Max Payne himself may be a bitter, depressed husk of a human being who never has any growth, but dammit James McCaffery's voice and performance are rock solid, this guy is a great voice actor.
Everyone else still does a good job as well, if anything Rockstar is always on point when casting people, it's just a shame the actual "game" part of the game became so bland.

The Talos Principle is, at its core, a very simple puzzle game.
You have six different tools at your disposal, and using these, you must traverse three different worlds, all filled to the brim with puzzles, but, oftentimes you only have one or two available in a given challenge.
I decided from the first puzzle that I would not use any guides or walkthroughs for this game, and I haven't been this frustrated or had this much fun with a puzzle game since I played Portal 2.
The comparison to Portal 2 is pretty apt, its a first-person (can be switched to third, though) game, that rely only on your puzzle-solving skills, there are no weapons or combat of any kind.
Where you can't really compare the two games are in the story department, although I have read other reviews that doesn't share my feelings in that regard.
I found the story to be pretty trite, pocket-variety philosophy and a lot of text that didn't really seem to take the story anywhere, although I should mention the voice diaries you find in the world are pretty good in setting a mood.
The lack of any real story didn't bother me at all, though, the game and puzzles are simply so challenging and entertaining that you don't really need a story to push you through the world.
With plenty of hidden puzzles, and multiple possible endings, there are a lot of value in the game, and I can't recommend it enough.

tl;dr - Buy it. Buy it and try it, without reading anything about it. Talos Principle is well worth your money. It would be if it was 60 bucks even. It's a crime to buy it at it's current price.
Now for the proper review - Talos Principle is a puzzling game, in more than one way. It has incredibly well designed puzzles for the ones looking for a surface level puzzle game, but it also puzzles your mind - your beliefs, your thoughts, your
. If you want to go deep down the philosophical rollercoaster that Talos Principle offers, get ready for many loop-de-loops, spirals going down and many other things that will make you barf your mind out.
Gameplay wise, Talos is
solid. It offers incredible gameplay, with very well thought and increasingly challenging puzzles. If you're aiming for 100%, get ready for some
out of the box thinking. 100%ing it
any help is NOT for the faint of heart and will require a LOT of thinking. With that said, if you're not THAT hardcore (like me), there are guides that will partially aid you in your quest. I recommend, as an easier challenge, looking up the star
and trying to figure out how to get them at first. There is also a pack with puzzles that didn't make it into the final game - over 100 of them. I absolutely recommend buying that pack along with it, if you think the already big sized game isn't enough for your fix.
Story wise, Talos is ♥♥♥♥ing impeccable. Each and every bit of story is impeccably done, and you're doing yourself a disservice if you don't explore at least the story contained in the main monitors. Reading is part of the game, if you want to understand the nuances of the story, a concise entanglement of many philosophical questions, theories and literatures that will make you think about how
but
(or not) you are.
One BIG problem with it though, and that goes for all brazilians reading this review: This game has the WORST localization I've EVER seen. EVERYTHING is wrong. Then again, I blame the translation studio - Please, Croteam, don't EVER hire Studio Nixa or Gorgone Productions EVER, for ANYTHING.
On another hand, the voices of Elohim and Alexandra, Gil Cardoso and Zuleica Alem, did a fantastic job. HUGE props to them!
Music and sounds wise, this game is also spectacular. The tracks go from calming ambience to sort of sad and depressing   tunes - I absolutely recommend buying the OST along with the main game. It's ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.
Replayability will eventually be high, as this game also has Workshop support.
All in all, this game will stand the test of time - it's puzzling nature and excellent writing will make it still be a cult classic at the very least 10, 15 years from now.
The only (and small) con with this game is that, in some areas, it was really easy to break. I could exit some puzzle areas with some unintended pieces and managed to get some stars via some unintended clipping.
But then again,
Talos Principle, 9,5/10!

Summary: The best adventure game since Myst... and maybe even better than that
All I can say is, bravo!  Forget about the limited context of computer games, this games does what ART is supposed to do: evoke a response in its audience.  The Talos Principle forces you think about some pretty heavy stuff, but it does so without sacrificing a shred of entertainment value.  It's fun, challenging and addictive from a gameplay perspective, and all the while you're being exposed to ideas that you're probably quite unlikely to otherwise encounter in the video game world -- a synthesis which I for one consider to be the holy grail of *any* kind of science fiction.
The only knock I have on the game is that as someone who has actually studied both artificial intelligence and cognitive science, I found the philosphy in the game to be a little antiqated at times.  For example, the eponymous "Talos Principle" is introduced as a revolutionary and complex idea, but in reality you'd be hard-pressed to find a single contemporary cognitive scientist that would consider it to be the least bit controversial.  They'd refer to the idea by its converse, "Cartesian dualism", which as one colleague put it, "is as close to a dead theory as anything you'll find in science".  In other words, the "Talos Principle" is essentially already universally accepted by science, and has been for decades.
That highlights the key difference between science and philosophy: the latter doesn't concern itself with trifles like "experimentation" and isn't swayed by anything as crass as "data" or "evidence".  Some of the ideas that it still insists we ponder have already been examined and conclusively accepted or discarded by science, and subjects it has long considered inscrutible, such as the nature of consciousness (which plays a central role in this game), are now well on their way to being objectively understood.
But that's being nitpicky.  For the most part the philosophy in the game is delivered with a minimum of bombast or pretense, and the fact that it's there at all is a triumph.  Plus, the puzzles (which constitute 95% of the game) are challenging without being frustrating, the story is engaging, and the game engine is solid as a rock.  I hate to use hyperbole, but it applies in this case: this game is a tour de force of the adventure genre.
Buy it, and support this kind of game!

First-person puzzle game from the makers of Serious Sam? Well pardon me for being suspicious, because when I finally got over myself and purchased The Talos Principle, I experienced a two day puzzling binge the likes of which I'd not seen since Portal 2. Yep, this game is the real deal.
Not only is the puzzle design really solid and varied enough; The storyline isn't afraid to delve into the deep end either. The Talos Principle attempts to tackle some pretty heavy philosophical questions such as the nature of consciousness, and while the treatment isn't perfect, it's certainly one of the better ones seen in video games yet.
My only gripe lies with the Serious Engine, which I feel is not the best fit for this kind of game since it's built primarily for speed and performance, not beauty. It's a shame, because everything else, starting right from the music, is very graceful and serene in its pacing. The puzzles are never about testing the mechanical skills of the player, just the wits.
A late sleeper hit of 2014, The Talos Principle game definitely wormed its way into my top ten list this year.

Truly a brilliant game at 8 hours in.  Challenging puzzles, interesting philosophy, very compelling narrative thus far.  There are multiple levels of challenge, so there are harder puzzles and hidden collectibles for those who are particularly skilled.  It has to be one of the best I've ever played, without a doubt.  Calling it "Portal meets Plato" might be a bit blunt, but for the people who need to be explained things in those terms, that phrase would be appropriate.  I think it lacks a single mechanic as cool as the gravity gun but has more than enough complexity to make up for it from a strictly puzzle point of view.  There have been some challenging puzzles that have taken me some time, but I've only not solved one or two so far.
And it's a funny game with a lot of personality, and even a couple "holy ♥♥♥♥" moments.  It's not only intellectual, but it engages players in multiple ways.  It is much better paced than either Portal game is by far, and is better as a game I think.  I've found a lot of the messages in this game to be very funny, and actually sometimes giving a feeling of melancholy.
Basically, if you treat the game like a puzzle game, then you will have fun, but you'd be limiting your game experience greatly.  There is as much depth in this world as you are willing to put the effort into finding.  Beautiful graphics, beautiful set pieces and level design, not a single bug thus far, performs great on my 780ti, and is one of the more intelligent games I've ever played.  It's one of the more intelligent pieces of entertainment I've ever consumed, of any form outside of a philosophy book itself (and it's a great introduction to a lot of that without burying you in reading).
Congrats to the team for making such a beautiful game.  I understand Serious Sam is tongue-in-cheek and fun, but I hope that more games like this one are in the works from you guys.  This is truly an accomplishment.  I've not been filled with wonder by a game like I have been with this one in probably a decade.  Can't wait to see how it ends.

Truly a brilliant game at 8 hours in.  Challenging puzzles, interesting philosophy, very compelling narrative thus far.  There are multiple levels of challenge, so there are harder puzzles and hidden collectibles for those who are particularly skilled.  It has to be one of the best I've ever played, without a doubt.  Calling it "Portal meets Plato" might be a bit blunt, but for the people who need to be explained things in those terms, that phrase would be appropriate.  I think it lacks a single mechanic as cool as the gravity gun but has more than enough complexity to make up for it from a strictly puzzle point of view.  There have been some challenging puzzles that have taken me some time, but I've only not solved one or two so far.
And it's a funny game with a lot of personality, and even a couple "holy ♥♥♥♥" moments.  It's not only intellectual, but it engages players in multiple ways.  It is much better paced than either Portal game is by far, and is better as a game I think.  I've found a lot of the messages in this game to be very funny, and actually sometimes giving a feeling of melancholy.
Basically, if you treat the game like a puzzle game, then you will have fun, but you'd be limiting your game experience greatly.  There is as much depth in this world as you are willing to put the effort into finding.  Beautiful graphics, beautiful set pieces and level design, not a single bug thus far, performs great on my 780ti, and is one of the more intelligent games I've ever played.  It's one of the more intelligent pieces of entertainment I've ever consumed, of any form outside of a philosophy book itself (and it's a great introduction to a lot of that without burying you in reading).
Congrats to the team for making such a beautiful game.  I understand Serious Sam is tongue-in-cheek and fun, but I hope that more games like this one are in the works from you guys.  This is truly an accomplishment.  I've not been filled with wonder by a game like I have been with this one in probably a decade.  Can't wait to see how it ends.

I'll start off for anyone that doesn't know by saying that this game is a spiritual successor to Project Reality, the popular BF2 mod.  I have played Project Reality for about 8 years now and still play it today, so most of my opinions in this review will reflect a comparison with PR, for better or for worse.
This game is not PR with better graphics, but it gets pretty darn close. There are many changes from BF2 PR that do change the experience somewhat, but there is no other modern game on the market that delivers a teamwork experience quite like this.  There are still some tweaks and changes to be made with regards to this but already you can jump into a game and see 9 man squads working together to accomplish a goal.  You can find this nowhere else.
Because this is an early access game, the damage values still need tweaking, the suppression system needs tweaking, amongst many other tweaks that I think need to be made, and likely will as this is still an alpha.  But what exists now is extraordinary, and you can see that the dev team has the right mindset to deliver us a game that PR vets have been waiting 10 years for, and a game that the general public will find just as rewarding as we do.
The gameplay being sought here is not like Battlefield, Call of Duty, Counter Strike, or Insurgency.  It is completely unique in today's crowded FPS offerings. That's what makes this game worth getting. Look past the present lack of content and the occassional server crash, and see the game for what it could be in just a years time.  This is an experience you will want to have tried.
Pros:
-Great teamwork and squad based gameplay where communication is key
-Fantastic models and sounds
-Did I mention the sounds
-Clear forward direction by the devs that promises to not disappoint
Cons:
-Present lack of content
-Occasionally frustrating crashing (as to be expected)
-Some balancing issues etc.

Due to the fact that The Talos Principle is a science fiction based first person puzzler, it’s hard not to make comparisons to Portal. However, while Portal is a more lighthearted game, the Talos Principle is more somber and thought-provoking. Drawing inspiration from writers like Isaac Asimov, Philip K. D*i*c*k (Apparently Steam doesn't like his last name), and John Milton, as well as a number of philosophers, it takes a much different approach to the puzzle genre.
With heavy philosophical undertones, you will find yourself thinking beyond the puzzles as the very world around you is questioned. This, in combination with a visually stunning environment, creates one of the most wonderful and unique experiences that I've had in a game.
Playing as an android, you must solve puzzles while at the same time being posed a series of increasingly introspective questions about your existence. I am going to refrain from saying anything more about the story so as not to spoil anything. This is a highlight of this game and is best experienced by going in to it knowing as little as you possibly can.
The puzzles are very unique, with various elements being added throughout to provide for an experience that never once felt repetitive to me. In these puzzles you will collect sigils using boxes, jammers, crystal prisms to connect lights, avoid mines, and float high up in to the air with fans. The most notable tool at your disposal is undoubtedly the ability to record yourself, allowing you to create what is basically a clone of yourself, which will act out your previous actions while you work with it in real time to solve the puzzle at hand.
The puzzles are very scattered in difficulty. Most were able to be solved in very little time, with a select few that I found myself having to really think about. If you want some more difficult puzzles, or you’re like me and want to squeeze every second out of this game that you possibly can, then I highly recommend doing the extra puzzles which are marked by the stars. These are not required to finish the game, but I found them to be some of the most enjoyable ones to complete as they can be more challenging and mind-bending, forcing you to really think outside of the box (or designated puzzle areas).
The world is huge, often times even a bit overwhelming. There are quite a few secrets hidden around, so you will be rewarded for exploring. There are also messages and words scattered throughout which provide backstory as well as give you insight to other characters. These can be found on computer terminals, audio logs, and QR code graffiti, and really do add something special to the story. I really enjoyed finding these, and felt that it added a nice touch.
Not only are the graphics superb but the music is lovely and perfectly suited for the various environments as well as puzzle solving.
There is also a huge amount of customization available in the options menu, which is always to be appreciated. This allows you to change the size of the game hub (or remove it entirely), remove cross-hairs, change from first-person view to third-person, etc.
This is a lengthy game, and at my time of completion of the storyline I have clocked about 37 hours of playtime. For this length and the high quality of this game, I feel that the current asking price is more than fair.
10/10 would erase from my memory and play again.

- Quitting the game one more time through the Task Manager.
- Launching the game again and being lucky enough that this time RSC didn´t put any stone in your path.

Due to the fact that The Talos Principle is a science fiction based first person puzzler, it’s hard not to make comparisons to Portal. However, while Portal is a more lighthearted game, the Talos Principle is more somber and thought-provoking. Drawing inspiration from writers like Isaac Asimov, Philip K. D*i*c*k (Apparently Steam doesn't like his last name), and John Milton, as well as a number of philosophers, it takes a much different approach to the puzzle genre.
With heavy philosophical undertones, you will find yourself thinking beyond the puzzles as the very world around you is questioned. This, in combination with a visually stunning environment, creates one of the most wonderful and unique experiences that I've had in a game.
Playing as an android, you must solve puzzles while at the same time being posed a series of increasingly introspective questions about your existence. I am going to refrain from saying anything more about the story so as not to spoil anything. This is a highlight of this game and is best experienced by going in to it knowing as little as you possibly can.
The puzzles are very unique, with various elements being added throughout to provide for an experience that never once felt repetitive to me. In these puzzles you will collect sigils using boxes, jammers, crystal prisms to connect lights, avoid mines, and float high up in to the air with fans. The most notable tool at your disposal is undoubtedly the ability to record yourself, allowing you to create what is basically a clone of yourself, which will act out your previous actions while you work with it in real time to solve the puzzle at hand.
The puzzles are very scattered in difficulty. Most were able to be solved in very little time, with a select few that I found myself having to really think about. If you want some more difficult puzzles, or you’re like me and want to squeeze every second out of this game that you possibly can, then I highly recommend doing the extra puzzles which are marked by the stars. These are not required to finish the game, but I found them to be some of the most enjoyable ones to complete as they can be more challenging and mind-bending, forcing you to really think outside of the box (or designated puzzle areas).
The world is huge, often times even a bit overwhelming. There are quite a few secrets hidden around, so you will be rewarded for exploring. There are also messages and words scattered throughout which provide backstory as well as give you insight to other characters. These can be found on computer terminals, audio logs, and QR code graffiti, and really do add something special to the story. I really enjoyed finding these, and felt that it added a nice touch.
Not only are the graphics superb but the music is lovely and perfectly suited for the various environments as well as puzzle solving.
There is also a huge amount of customization available in the options menu, which is always to be appreciated. This allows you to change the size of the game hub (or remove it entirely), remove cross-hairs, change from first-person view to third-person, etc.
This is a lengthy game, and at my time of completion of the storyline I have clocked about 37 hours of playtime. For this length and the high quality of this game, I feel that the current asking price is more than fair.
10/10 would erase from my memory and play again.

I'll start off for anyone that doesn't know by saying that this game is a spiritual successor to Project Reality, the popular BF2 mod.  I have played Project Reality for about 8 years now and still play it today, so most of my opinions in this review will reflect a comparison with PR, for better or for worse.
This game is not PR with better graphics, but it gets pretty darn close. There are many changes from BF2 PR that do change the experience somewhat, but there is no other modern game on the market that delivers a teamwork experience quite like this.  There are still some tweaks and changes to be made with regards to this but already you can jump into a game and see 9 man squads working together to accomplish a goal.  You can find this nowhere else.
Because this is an early access game, the damage values still need tweaking, the suppression system needs tweaking, amongst many other tweaks that I think need to be made, and likely will as this is still an alpha.  But what exists now is extraordinary, and you can see that the dev team has the right mindset to deliver us a game that PR vets have been waiting 10 years for, and a game that the general public will find just as rewarding as we do.
The gameplay being sought here is not like Battlefield, Call of Duty, Counter Strike, or Insurgency.  It is completely unique in today's crowded FPS offerings. That's what makes this game worth getting. Look past the present lack of content and the occassional server crash, and see the game for what it could be in just a years time.  This is an experience you will want to have tried.
Pros:
-Great teamwork and squad based gameplay where communication is key
-Fantastic models and sounds
-Did I mention the sounds
-Clear forward direction by the devs that promises to not disappoint
Cons:
-Present lack of content
-Occasionally frustrating crashing (as to be expected)
-Some balancing issues etc.
If you want to be a part of a squad-based shooter that is actually worthy of the title "Squad-based", then this is your game.

This is a 3D puzzle game using an FPS engine, so of course it'll inevitably be compared to P.O.R.T.A.L. in every review. Let's do that.
Portal is nonstop comic relief while Talos Principle is much more serious in tone, with a few bits of unexpected humor hidden away. I'd say one is like reading Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy while the other is like a Philip K♥♥♥♥♥♥novel. They may both star robots and AIs, but Talos focuses much more on questions of philosophy and religion.
For the puzzles themselves, obviously there's no flashy physics gimmicks like the Portal gun or bouncing paint. Mostly you'll work with basic elements like lasers and lines of sight, and that's just fine. There's a nice challenge curve, and it's very non-linear anyway so you can choose your order. The Tetromino door puzzles between areas get a little tedious though.
I love puzzle games, so they both feel like equally amazing titles in very different styles. Few games accomplish being as fun & amusing as Portal, but even fewer games accomplish being as intelligent & thought-provoking as Talos Principle.

Now you see my hours on this and you think, feck he hasn't played it at all, but I've had it before it was on steam (pre-alpha access). Anyways, the sounds in this game are amazing, you really feel like it's a battlefield out there. People have MICROPHONES and actually COMMUNICATE. It's nice. When you're getting shot at and your squad is yelling as you frantically try to figure out what degree it's coming from, those are the moments you play this for.
It's got a long way to go, but it's come so far from its initial first release of pre-alpha, they've updated it alot with optimization and features. The interface, menus look alot better and it's running way better. I trust these developers will make a fantastic game in the end.
In the end, with any early access game. Buy at your own risk sort of gig, but considering alot of these folks have worked on the Project Reality game (originally a mod for BF2), and kept it consistently updated for over 10 YEARS, that gives me alot of faith. I'd recommend this.

Below you'll find a video and written impression on the game.
The Talos Principle is a philosophical first person puzzler. You'll be exploring gorgeous environments as you solve puzzle to puzzle, so you can collect pieces to complete other puzzles! While you tickle your brain, the game slowly unfolds a loose narrative that explores themes of the self, and the existential. Philosophy majors, this game is practically made for you!
Though it all could sound slightly pretentious,  the creatively designed puzzles that seems to hit just the right mark in difficulty and satisfaction, that I think even the most modest of puzzle players (like myself) can find a lot of enjoyment from The Talos Principle. If you're not into heavy philosophical themes, the good news is the gameplay is more than enough as the focal point.
The Talos principle also features some of the best graphics I've seen this year in games. Not only are the texture, model, and lighting quality expertly crafted, but the design, the idea of mixing multiple timeline motifs, is equally worth praising. Those who enjoy a great sound track from their games won't be disappointed here either.
To be honest, I have a hard time coming up with a negative for this game. I am really enjoying it so far, and I find most every aspect of it very satisfying. I think the only thing that might be keeping some potential players away is the price point. $40 is defiantly a higher end price point for what a lot consider and indie game. I don't agree with the notion that indie games need to be set at a lower price point, but I am also aware it does exists. What I will say is that the game has a presentation quality that in my opinion, is on the same level as many AAA games, while retaining that creative freedom that indie games have come to be known for.
Pros:
- Creative and satisfying puzzles
- Gorgeous art and design
- Great OST
- Intrigueing narrative
Cons:
- Might be pricey for some

I've spent the last couple years looking for a game to replace the impressive but outdated Project Reality mod, the run-n-gun Battlefield FPS and the overly complicated Arma MilSim… and then I found
.
Squad is still in its infancy but the infantry combat, team & squad based communication and ability to apply tactics combine to create my ideal FPS game -- fight together or die alone.  Add in the large scale maps, base (FOB) building, upcoming vehicles, and some of the (known) planned features.  All of the sudden I’m looking to be one happy camper for the next decade.
As with any EA game,  there are some bugs and performance issues, but I expect stable 50 vs 50 player server in short order as well as everything balanced to meet player expectations.  Bugs will be an ongoing issue as new features are added but the developers have been quick to address them when found.  That's the nature of and EA process.  I'd also recommend that you have a newer CPU and GPU until the game matures a bit more.
The thing I like the most is how much the developers have listened and reacted to player feedback during the closed alpha.  Granted the developers have spent much more time thinking about Squad’s future and many major ideas have already been thought of, things still change from concept to application, and they respond accordingly.  I also really like the fact that, since most of their core team came from a modding background, they have been building the game with modding in mind.
So, if you have a bit of patience for early access games or just wished Battlefield, PR and Arma had "one baby to rule them all", then I’d highly recommend Squad.

Voolf-en-shteyen: TNO is a straight-forward action game with simple mechanics. For better-or-worse, Nazis continue to captivate our imaginations 60 years after the end of the war. The combination of immeasurable callousness and Hugo Boss super-villain outfits is burned into our consciousness. But Nazis are also hard to take seriously, much like the Kim family. They were so wrapped up in the fiction they created that they became parodies of themselves. Because of this, I don't feel this game trivializes their atrocities in any way. Nazis are goofy and delusional and that is how they are portrayed in the game.
The graphics are fantastic. The developers somehow took the imagery to the edge of taste without going over the line. The entire game is tongue-in-cheek. There are some moments of cruelty, but cybornetic German Shepherds and mecha make the game feel more comical than terrifying. There are a few moments that are eerie, but it seems the developers wanted to make a pure action game like Half-Life 2 rather than try for anything philosophical or truly frightening.
Wolfenstein is a blast. It goes by in a blur but it is obvious it was made with a lot of passion and that is a welcome treat in the age of corporate shovelware.

So, having finished every puzzle, found every star, and seen all
endings, I must say that if I were to never play this again, I would still find my experience with The Talos Principle to be worth every cent and minute put into it.
What's funny is that I don't even know why I bought this game in the first place. I hate puzzlers. I absolutely loathe them, even, yet I found myself drawn in, and simply could not resist. So, excellent job on making a game that managed to draw me in to a genre I avoid the best I can.
The graphics and music are perfect. Enough to make things great, but not enough to drown you at any point. The music especially stood out to me, it seemed that no matter what location I found myself in, the music fit the ambience and climate of the current world. The graphics were quite gorgeous, but the game handled just as well on my gaming desktop as it did on my three and a half year old laptop. Overall, I found this to be a rich experience, and gotta say, you did not dissapoint in the slightest.
The story, however loose it was, was also great. It gave a nice grand appearance of some sort of mystery, and how much the entire game was steeped in philosophy... It definitely added to the experience. I especially loved
The audio logs, I think, were the best narrative as far as all of the asides go. It was quite enjoyable playing them all back to back before ending the game. Also, piecing together the events that led to the simulation... very well done.
The puzzles... God, I came to hate seeing anything using the
item. I'd have to say that some of the hardest puzzles involved it. The developers of SQUAD set out with many goals in mind. Not only did they want to bring to life a new iteration of a game we all played and loved (Project Reality), they wanted to do it their way, which meant trying to achieve a relatively transparent dev. process, and do away with the trust issues we all have from early access games. Squad is in an Alpha stage of development that would pass for a complete game by the standards other EA games have set in the last few years. On top of these things theyre also on the way to achieving the rush that only people who truly played Project Reality could get, when you value youre game life enough to actually have your heart skip a beat, and you get to see how you really react under the stress of fire. Something i find very tough to explain, but you will know once you play SQUAD.
The GOOD:
-High quality audio, textures, models, and effects. seriously you can just sit and watch a  firefight and still get a rush
-Accurate models and factions with proper equipment. A must for vets and military nerds alike!
-In-game VOIP allows a level of communication not seen in other FPS's. you can talk to people near you with positional audio, or you can talk to another Squad Leader across the map.
-Speaking of maps. even without pushing the engine to its limits the maps are HUGE compared to alot of FPS's. im not talking ARMA scale, but 4kmx4km will give you plenty of flanking room.
-Very few gamey elements. A big part of the idea of SQUAD is that you should be able to get easily immersed. Your enemies dont pop up as red dots anywhere, the only way you can know where the enemy is is by communicating with other team-mates, or walk towards the gunfire.
-Buildable FOBS! this is one of the things brought over from PR, and with the new engine it is just awesome! You can make your own objectives within a game. Stuck in a stalemate, or just dont like the flag you have to attack? Build a giant fortress at the top of the hill and make the enemy come to you!
-Medic System. If you get wounded, you dont just wait 3 seconds and spawn on your squad leader. in SQUAD you rely on a medic to heal you even if youve been dropped, he first has to bandage your wounds, then heal you, then you can get back in the fight. the system is still being worked on all the time but it is already a nice mechanic, and the long spawn or walk times to get back to your squad are a good incentive to keep the squad together and keep your medic safe!
The BAD:
-Game pretty much requires a microphone to get the most out of it, you can get pretty cheap mics, but some people cant be screaming at insurgents all night while their baby/family sleeps. an unfortunate problem.
-Performance issues. Incase youve forgot at this point, this game is still in ALPHA, theres gonna be problems. the devs work constantly to resolve these problems. dont freak out because you cant play, go to the forums and report it and it will be fixed sooner :).
-Bugs. again from the above point, ALPHA. there are still some bugs to flesh out, none of the major bugs are game breaking so it shouldnt be a point against buying the game, just report them when you find them!
Conclusion:
If you're looking for more out of your FPS experience, if you get frustrated by the stupidity you see in other games, if you just need to blow something up, join us in SQUAD. It's like if ARMA and Insurgency got freaky, and then their baby got raised by Project Reality. What more could you want?

The Talos Principle is a first-person, Portal-inspired puzzle game with a philosophical narrative as a backdrop that makes for a truly intriguing and remarkable experience. The game delivers a wealth of challenging puzzles compiled with a thought-provoking story. It's a fantastic combination that makes this title a prime GOTY contender.
You begin by not knowing who you are, what you are or why you exist before you are propelled into a mysterious world in where you seek answers for your existence. Your progression in the land is unfolded by completing puzzles and collecting Silgils. Only you and a strange voice seemingly from the sky reside in this strange place but can whoever or whatever is there be trusted? You'll have to progress to find out..
The game houses a vast selection of smart and beautifully crafted puzzles which were designed to an amazing standard by the developers; Croteam - the development house behind the Serious Sam games. Some are fairly routine in the early stages as expected but the more Sigils you collect; the harder the puzzles become especially in the latter stages of the game. You will find yourself deeply confused, frustrated and dumbfounded at times but it's all worthwhile for the satisfaction on completion of a tricky task and is a testament to the developers for their creativity. The supportive writing and story complimenting the game is also of a very impressive standard and you really have to admire the effort that has gone into producing a game that's more than just a puzzle title.
Overall; I hadn't heard of The Talos Priniple this time last week and now I am the proud owner of a truly fantastic title that is worth every penny. The narrative is deep and compelling and the puzzles on offer are of the highest standard. The developers have done a truly fantastic job in their design and execution and should be commended in the highest order for what has been a dreadful year in gaming. The Steam Workshop potential is also another selling point to what is a beautifully produced title.

Squad or as others may know it by "The spirtual succesor to the Project Reality mod for battlefield 2."
Is a great standalone installment to the project reality formula made by many of the same devs that worked on the mod,
Squad is a great return to the genre of Tactical shooters,  it promotes and relies heavily on teamwork and communication and working with your team in Squads hence the name.
Now what separates this game to other tactical/milsim shooters you might ask?   Well first of all Squad is a very easily accesible game,  unlike other shooters like ARMA for example,  where if you want to get around 60-100 players in a good scenario mission and then also be coordinated and communicate with something like ACRE or Task force radio mods  you almost always have to be in a milsim community and schedule events for such things to get that experience.
But with Squad all you have to do is just join up on any offical or community ran public server with good admin moderation, to get that experience since the gamemodes and mechanics in Squad are all very well made to kinda force that kind of gameplay and interaction with other from the get go, (Built in Local voip and radio channels through built in mumble to the game) ( Very harsh penalties to getting shot and dying) (Almost all objectives require more people too accomplish/capture) if you start running around and trying to lonewolf you will not have a very good time and most likely die very much and not accomplish anything good for the team.
Now Squad isnt exactly a milsim shooter,  but it tries to bridge the gap between a pretty realistic military shooter and still a fairly simple game in terms of understanding and controls and it wont sacrifice any good gameplay just too add in something that would be more realistic,  it still wants to be a fun game to play in the core,  It wants to be both realstic and fun at the same time!
The current main gamemodes in Squad are Insurgency and AAS, which if you have played PR previously you are probably pretty familiar with them,  In AAS you have to capture flags in a specific order, and which locations are also dynamically set after each start of the round,  and the amount of flags that are in play may also be just one are several,  and in AAS theres also always one flag that you have to defend or attack. which creates some really unqiue and interesting gameplay.
In Insurgency the goal for blufor is to find enemy weapon caches that are unmarked on the map until you gain enough intelligence by killing/interrogating enemies/civilians  the latter which was part of PR but not currently introduced in Squad, The first Cache intel however is given to you after a few minutes at the start of the round, but the rest of them you have to gain intel for or just find them yourself by searching the map and looking for enemy activity,  after a certain amount of caches have been destroyed blufor wins,  and opfor needs to defend them all and deplete the blufors reinforcement tickets,  however  Insurgents dont have any tickets.
Theres also some new and smaller modes like Conquest and one more at least that I cant remember right now, but they are not as polished or popular currently.
The maps are all pretty big, detailed and all well made, the locations of them will also vary a lot,  currently we have some maps set in eastern europe and afghanistan but in the future we will also see urban maps like the one thats currently being remade from PR Fallujah West one very popular urban map set in Iraq,  and the current size of them are between 1 square km to 4 km Which PR had about the same sizes,  but I think they have been thinking about making maps even up to 16 square kms in size once the next thing im most excited for with this game gets introduced.
Yes VEHICLES!  Vehicles of all sorts will make their introduction in the future, everything from  ground transport humvees/technicals to apcs,tanks and helicopters. And as youd expect you will need to have several crewmen in them to operate them, you will not just be able to solo a tank or APC,  This is not battlefield!
One of the coolest and most unique features in Squad has to be the FOB building system (FOB is one of the 3 types of spawn points in Squad) while it was in PR it was just very basic then,  now in Squad you can make huge  bases for your FOB's  or make them as tiny as you want, as the basebuilding is very easy to do,  currently the requirements to place down a FOB radio is only to have a couple of teammates by your side and to not be too close too another FOB,  but in the future you will have to establish supply routers with  Logistic Trucks and Helicopters that have to come and deliver supplies before you can build up your FOB,  and you will also need additional supplies to upgrade it even more and  too keep it up and running.
Besides FOB's you can spawn on Squad Leader dropped Rally points, which also require some of your squad mates near to be able to be dropped,  it also only has a certain amount of respawns, and if enemies get too near to a rally point they will disappear.
The 3RD type of spawnpoint is your Mainbase which will probably get seen more used in the future once things like Helicopters are introduced,  where you will be able to jump in and get your transport back to the battlefield that way.
Now lets talk about roles and kits,  The kit selection system works in the way that once you are a part of a squad and the bigger that squad gets, more kits and roles (classes)  get avaible for  you and your squad to pick from, altough most kits also have certain  limits to them,  like for example you can only have 2 medics in a full 8 man Squad,  same with AR's Same with LAT's  but if we were only example  just 4 people in a squad,  we would only be able to have 1 medic etc. This is just another way to promote playing in a squad and with your squad, and aslo for realism and balance reasons certain kits are limited.
Now I could go and on and keep talking about the features and mechanics of this game,  but nobody wants too read tha many pages right? ;)  So im gonna stop it here, I think I touched on the most important parts of the game.
But all in all Squad is a very great tactical shooter with a focus on teamwork and communication that will just get better with time, and that I can also see lasting a very long time thanks to the everlasting and growing PR community, and now with us being on steam it's probably only gonna get better :)

The Talos Principle is a first-person, Portal-inspired puzzle game with a philosophical narrative as a backdrop that makes for a truly intriguing and remarkable experience. The game delivers a wealth of challenging puzzles compiled with a thought-provoking story. It's a fantastic combination that makes this title a prime GOTY contender.
You begin by not knowing who you are, what you are or why you exist before you are propelled into a mysterious world in where you seek answers for your existence. Your progression in the land is unfolded by completing puzzles and collecting Silgils. Only you and a strange voice seemingly from the sky reside in this strange place but can whoever or whatever is there be trusted? You'll have to progress to find out..
The game houses a vast selection of smart and beautifully crafted puzzles which were designed to an amazing standard by the developers; Croteam - the development house behind the Serious Sam games. Some are fairly routine in the early stages as expected but the more Sigils you collect; the harder the puzzles become especially in the latter stages of the game. You will find yourself deeply confused, frustrated and dumbfounded at times but it's all worthwhile for the satisfaction on completion of a tricky task and is a testament to the developers for their creativity. The supportive writing and story complimenting the game is also of a very impressive standard and you really have to admire the effort that has gone into producing a game that's more than just a puzzle title.
Overall; I hadn't heard of The Talos Priniple this time last week and now I am the proud owner of a truly fantastic title that is worth every penny. The narrative is deep and compelling and the puzzles on offer are of the highest standard. The developers have done a truly fantastic job in their design and execution and should be commended in the highest order for what has been a dreadful year in gaming. The Steam Workshop potential is also another selling point to what is a beautifully produced title.

Planetside 2's problems stem from several sources inwards in the way of the development team and the playerbase, as well as integral problems in the way the game's made.
The game's optimization problems which've existed since beta have still yet to be resolved. It takes a decent amount of time to get from A to B in the way of loading screens. It doesn't seem to enjoy being meshed in with Steam, either, as Shift-Tabbing results in further slowdowns in loading.
The stutter that's been there forever, from my measly rig a decent time ago to the relatively decent rig now, has not been fixed. You are likely to encounter stuttering when going into a populated area, whether from deployment straight into it or from moving from one area to another. This adds further a sort of "loading screen" where you will likely have to sit in spawn for a few seconds to a minute just so the game stops stuttering. Before you say "well that's just the game loading in everything, of course it takes time," you must understand this stuttering is after spending some bit of time waiting on a loading screen beforehand. This stuttering can last for a good bit of time and catch you unawares, leaving you in a sort of lag that is absolutely deadly in a firefight.
The game doesn't even try to load in any blips on the minimap if there are loads of players in an area. I'm willing to say it works both ways, in that you may not see enemy blips at farther distances on the minimap or on the main map as well as friendly blips.
The game's based on grind which has become so horribly common in any massive multiplayer game of any sort, whether a typical MMORPG or MMOFPS, as is here. It takes a painfully long time for to get any experience enough to gather CERTs, which are the means by which you upgrade your gear. They're more than happy enough to tell you, however, that you can spend real-life money on virtual money to buy virtual gear for a dying game. Some weapons are, without a doubt, more effective than others in different respective areas, and these weapons can be purchased by way of this real-to-virtual currency, allowing you an immediate upper hand in, say, anti-vehicular battle or anti-air battle. CERTs are used to upgrade things like armor and utilities like smokescreens to tell lock-on weapons to screw off and cannot be purchased, but then you have to grind to get those relentlessly. Shouldn't be bad if the game's fun, right?
The game's horrid alone, owing to the "massive" nature of the game ("Massive" being used loosely as, as I will touch on further, the game is nowhere near what it was in playerbase). Sure, you can chip in a vehicle here or there, or even do some decent work carving through ground troops, but the game won't be as fun unless you're in a squad of decently organized individuals. Even then, it won't last long unless you join an outfit or at least form an acquaintanceship with a few players so as to sustain the gameplay through teamwork alone. I'm unsure whether to rank this positive or negative for two conflicting opinions: One, every game is fun with friends, thus nullfying the simplistic solution of "get friends and the game becomes better"; Two, the game is a teambased game that requires a relatively organized team to get the most fun out of it, as would be necessary in a different sort of game as, say, Project Reality (which is completely different in gameplay but requires faintly similar in the way of teamplay). Therefore, I won't hog on that. The gameplay itself is just "Massive Multiplayer Online First Person Shooter" otherwise, just like the box says.
The playerbase has dwindled to extremely low numbers compared to the amazing amount it originally had, more obviously due to the normal occurence of the Beta-Bugout: when someone "releases" a game as an open beta, letting people play their fill in a broken, messy, sorry state of a "game" and everyone grows extremely tired before the game officially releases.
The playerbase is now filled with, for the most part, Battle Rank 100's (which was the highest you could get before a recent update which increased the cap to 120, which is now quickly being sought after). Due to the fact you have to grind to get the best stuff in the game, you are definitely going up against uneven odds. They've played the game longer, have better gear and better knowledge because of it, and will definitely have a one-up over you. The fact that people with Battle Ranks anywhere from 50~100 make up the game means new players will definitely be getting, forgive the brashness,♥♥♥♥♥♥on by everyone else, which only further adds to the deterrence to any form of new player.
I doubt there's much that will be done to salvage the game. The only thing left for Smedley to do is to do what he's always done: milk this cash cow.

A Quick Review - A Shooter With A Soul and a Story.
Well, I must say I really enjoyed the game. I played the original and the various iterations of the shooter genre since, and none of them had the heart this game does. All the characters are very well drawn and presented as powerfully and a realistically as any I have ever played. If you are a person who prefers to focus on the game solely as an exercise in trigger pulling this may not matter to you, but I was amazed at the quality of the writing and the character development. It is the best writing I’ve experienced in any game, and the main character in particular has a compelling inner dialog and a broad personl scope of the sort you’d normally find in a movie.
The game also does a wonderful job of defining the ideas and methods of the Nazis and it does it in a way that does not interfere with game play – you hear snippets of conversations for instance, and they are chilling. You truly get a sense of the stakes and the sacrifice that is needed to stop them. Again, rather than slap together another tired shooter the people behind this game made it all very personal and human, and went to great effort to produce a cast that meant something. Great heroes, great villains. There is a mountain of carnage and gunplay along the way, horror and stomach churning moments, set pieces with massive scale and excellent cinematics, and a world that is well composed and frightening. All of the voice acting is stellar.
I strongly recommend turning on all the subtitles and allowing the personal and emotional parts of the game to play out if you want to understand what this game was supposed to be – not just a shooter, but a story about people fighting to save the world. Wolfenstein is really a tribute to those in uniform and what they choose to give up to defeat evil. And you do get to kill a lot of Nazis. It is not perfect, but it definitely is one of the few games I liked so much I wrote a review.
In the end it is not a simply “shooter”. It is a game about waging war. If you let the dialog and story work you will find a lot to like. The effort was successfully made to convey an understanding of why you’re fighting and make you care about the outcome and the main character. I recommend it.

Squad is a satisfying, genre defining, and focused shooter. Squad is the spiritual successor to the BF2 mod 'Project Reality', and it does it great justice.
Squad pulls inspiration from many shooters in the genre, from fidelity to design. Some people say it's like Insurgency with bigger maps, vehicles, and more people. It is, and it isn't.
The gameplay is suspensful, firefights happen often unexpectedly.  While trying to lead your squad to a safe place in order to put down a FOB so that your team has a spawnpoint closer to an objective; you may stumble into another enemy squad attempting the same in the forest, or an APC may see your squad cross a road.
The game really feels more like a modernized Project Reality, rather than a bigger Insurgency. It brings in familiar gamemodes, which have been time tested and a joy to play. AAS - Advance and Secure - has your team capturing flags in sequence, while the enemy does the same. Insurgency - The gamemode - has you either searching for, or defending weapons caches. The BluFor team doesn't know where the OpFor team's caches are, but can get a general area marker on their map after killing enough insurgents, or enough time passes. The Insurgents don't need to worry about tickets, they have an infinite amount, but they must stop the other team from destroying the caches and wear down their respawn tickets without being overrun.
The environments are beautiful and intelligently designed, featuring large, dense urban warefare as well as sprawling eastern European farmland. The animation and sound design are both notably stunning, and really do create a real sense of immersion, the lovely special effects work brings it all together.
Offworld Industries has created a game that breathes new life in to a niche genre; with an attention to quality that could drive it to the mainstream, and a modding community to keep it there.
The app runs smoothly and is highly customizable.

After my Steam stats clocked around 52 hours straight for Talos Principle, I finally can write my own mini-review.
First and the foremost - this game is
. Year 2014 wasn't really rich for good puzzle games and Talos Principle was definitely a lovely addition to the end of spoken year and, I believe, definitely the best puzzle game of it.
Now, the comparisons with Portal 1-2 is pretty much inevitable a t this point. And while most of the reviewers and people tend to draw direct parallels up to the point saying "it is a good Portal clone" - I have to strongly disagree.
Good? Oh yes, indeed.
Clone? Not so much.
And it is not just about the usual argument "well, duh, first person puzzle is not an exclusive genre introduced by Portal" but more about the fact that Talos Principle feels rather unique and genuine. Essentially, the game uses the same tools and instruments to represent slightly familiar gameplay, but it resolves around original core concept so it feels fresh. And that comes from a guy who quite a sucker for puzzle games.
The story aspect of the game is somewhat original in its position as well. Videogames tend to explore mostly technical aspect of Artificial Intelligence and consciousness (System Shock, Deus Ex, etc), but deeply philosophical? Not very often. Game's lore masterfully blends existing work on the subject with a fiction that does not deviate so much from its base material.
Visual and technical sides of the game is a quite nice showcase of something I can call Serious Sam 3.5 engine. It is pretty. It is lovely. It is fast and customizable. The engine is very scalable, supports a lot of API natively and someone even managed to run and play the game on old IGPU with 32Mb VRAM,
All that being said, most of the criticism Talos Principle receives for its price. And while I do agree with some of the arguments on the topic - I do not regret my purchase in the slightest. More than that, since it is all goes to SS4 budget as well... yeah, win-win to me.
Long story short: do you love Portal 1-2? Did you have fun with Antichamber? Do you like good puzzle games in general? Get this one ,end of story.

The Talos Principle does a number of things remarkably well. First and foremost: the puzzle design is as near perfect as I've ever encountered. The only other games that I would consider at a similar level are Fez and Portal. Without ever explicitly explaining any mechanics to you, the game presents the levels in a way that makes you intuitively understand the way things work. The open level design leaves you with dozens of puzzles to choose from at any given time, which means that if you get stumped on something you can just walk away and work on other ones until it comes to you. No one particular level is ever required to progress, and multiple levels will provide you with the same credit towards progression, so you can skip one for a very long time before you'll actually need to complete it. The challenging puzzles are just hard enough to push you and make you think, without pushing you to frustration. I haven't gotten to a point in the game where I was so frustrated with a seemingly impossible puzzle that I just went and looked it up online. And the "hidden" puzzles, the puzzles within the puzzles, solving those may just be the best feeling ever. Figuring out how to break the rules and solve a puzzle outside the sandboxes you're meant to play in is incredibly rewarding. Some of the easier puzzles border on totally obvious, and can feel a bit repetitive, but that's really my only complaint about the level design.
Second, the game mechanics, while not particularly groundbreaking (pulling mainly from Braid and Portal, from what I've seen so far), are impressively polished. For example, the way that the laser reflectors work is incredibly easy to use, allowing you to simply select the targets you want the reflector to hit and then place it. It will then attempt to connect to all the targets you requested, preventing the annoyances of fussing about with angles and trying to get microadjustments perfect that other puzzle games often suffer from with spatial puzzles. The gameplay as a whole feels very fluid and polished. The game almost always translates my input into a result that matches my intent.
Third, the performance. This games scales from stunningly beautiful at max settings to totally fine at the lowest, but the best part is that it runs buttery smooth on low settings even on very old hardware. My old laptop can play this game at 60fps without even kicking on the fans on low settings, and can even be pushed to halfway between low and medium before I even start to see framerate drops. It's got more precise customization options for performance than any game I've seen in recent memory. If you've got a computer that was ever considered decent in the last 5 or so years, you can probably play this game just fine.

This is easily one of the most polished puzzle games I've ever played. Just about everything in the game is wonderful but it's the amount of polish on the puzzle mechanics that really impresses me. Play the demo and see what I mean: objects show you exactly where they'll be when you put them down, things snap to places that you need to place them precicely, and whenever there's a place that you're actually supposed to jump the game will show you that you're able to and just let you press spacebar to do it without requiring your precision. Most of all I like how when you are placing the laser connectors, which need line of sight to everything they connect with, the game will shift where you are able to put them down to try to make sure that your planned lines of sight work when you place it, and will tell you when they don't. Almost never in the game did I feel like the game was preventing me from solving a puzzle I knew how to solve; if you've figured out what you need to do then solving the puzzle will go very smoothly.
The puzzles are very well made and very well paced. The game has a very loosely ordered selection of puzzles such that you can easily skip any that you get stuck on and come back later when you're more skilled at the game. The puzzles which you need to beat to progress to new areas are straightforward practice for the game mechanics. You don't unlock new mechanics unless you can solve the more involved puzzles with the old ones. The fully difficult puzzles aren't needed for anything except the ending, so the game makes sure that by the time you're actually forced to solve a puzzle to progress that you'll have had plenty of opportunities to work your way up to them. Alternatively you can just solve them all the order they're presented for a nice challenge throughout the game. Also present are the stars, which are their own puzzles which you thankfully never need to touch to get the most rewarding conclusion to the game. But they're always present, just out of reach, requiring you to do things that are very clearly cheating (How do I even get a blue laser? There isn't one anywhere in this puzzle!). If you're into following clues to secret passages and discovering "exploits" in the game, they're a lot of fun. Still, every puzzle, even (especially) the stars, is extremely rewarding to complete and makes you feel good about yourself for figuring them out. There's also easter eggs of some sort or another hidden in basically every level, almost all of which I missed until the late game.
Aside from the joy of solving the puzzles themselves, the game also rewards you by slowly drip-feeding you story as you enter new levels and complete their challenges. The whole thing manages to sit comfortably on the edge where it feels enigmatic and philosophical without becoming awkward or overly pretentious. You find yourself searching around looking for more (thankfully either noisy or contrasting-colored) things to read. I recommend this game more than anything else I've played in recent memory. Assuming of course you're into this sort of game. Play the demo! It does a really good job of showing off the game and I would have never considered buying this at all had the demo not made such a good impression on me. There's a whole lot of content in it and it's definitely worth the steep price asked.

Max Payne 3 presents a true successor to the Max Payne franchise. Although made by a different team, the tone and the overall feel of the game are very much consistent with the Max Payne universe. Sure, the game mechanics have changed in order to suit the contemporary shooter playstyle, but the overall impression is that Max Payne 3 is a brilliant nod to the thousand times tested but rarely perfected formula of a third person bullet time shooter.
Mechanics wise Max Payne 3 is a very good game. The shooting feels natural, the guns recoil just right, and the movement of both Max and the Enemies is brilliant. Rockstar's ability to use Euphoria engine presents a real treat for the gamers since it allows the game to shine in the physics department. Shattered glass, natural movement and insanely detailed animation of both Max and the enemies really adds to the believability of the entire thing.
Graphic wise the game looks really good even by today's standards, while the sound quality just goes a long way in adding to the overall impression.
Overall, Max Payne 3 is a great game, one that will offer you hours of fun, and what else can you ask from a title.

is a game that incorporates an effective balance of adventure and puzzle mechanics to create an engaging experience.
Puzzle design is well implemented and each element of the level is used effectively. The game introduces new mechanics through discovery in fairly straightforward levels, removing the need for explicit tutorials. Other levels are generally non-trivial and require some careful thinking and possibly some experimentation. Obstacles and items in levels are often useful in more than one purpose, requiring different strategies to solve rather than resorting to gimmicks.
One particular mechanic that's not as common in other puzzle games was the recording mechanic, allowing your character to record a short series of actions to do useful things such as activating additional switches and helping your character reach higher places. The mechanic also takes advantage of the terrain when combined with the ability to carry a platform above your character during recording to gain extra height.
The game also exploits the fact that several puzzles are interlinked in a hub area. For players who want to collect all the stars for access to more difficult levels, interacting between puzzles in an area or going outside the level boundary is necessary, as the obstacles in each puzzle can be interacted with within other puzzles in some cases. It's not necessary to complete the game, but it shows that the game takes advantage of being in a more open space. It also shows that the difficulty has been set effectively, as the main game has a decent challenge but is not overwhelming, while the end game requires thinking (literally) outside the box.
Backstories and texts enhance the game world. While only a few are strictly required to be read near the end, these help the player to learn more about the characters in the game and what the truth may be. More importantly, these readings make the game world and decisions meaningful, rather than having arbitrary puzzles for no reason.
Through the combination of level and world design, the game produces a unique and engaging experience that goes beyond standard expectations of a puzzle game and easily stands out among some other popular games this year.

Squad is a large-scale FPS with support for up to 100 players in various gamemodes. The development team, Offworld Industries, is largely made up of former developers for Project Reality: BF2, one of the oldest and most popular mods for Battlefield 2.
The focus of Squad is on semi-realistic teamplay that revolved around squads. There are a few different gamemodes, such as Conquest, Assault And Secure, and Insurgency. All of these gamemodes have varying objectives and ways to win.
My personal favorite mode is Insurgency, which pits a faction of insurgents against US forces. The insurgent team is tasked with protecting a series of weapons caches, the position of which is unknown to US forces at the beginning. By gathering intel, the US forces can get the rough location of a cache and with enough intel they can determe the exact location of a cache. After destroying a certain number of caches, the US forces win. However, they have limited tickets so casualties are not something they can afford as opposed to the insurgents who have an unlimited number of tickets, but only a few caches.
The majority of the Squad community is mature and helpful. There are many community servers with good people that inhabit them. When playing with a proper squad you will have one of the best times ever.
The sounds and the graphics are pretty solid, although the game is currently rather demanding on the spec side. This will change as the game is optimized.
I definitely recommend Squad, even  in early access. This is going to be one of my few go-to games for a long time coming. There are bugs and glitches that may pop up every now and then, but the developers are working diligently to make this one of the best tactical games available.
I look forward to seeing and playing with you all. I'll be playing on the server that my community (CIA Gaming) hosts.

This is easily one of the most polished puzzle games I've ever played. Just about everything in the game is wonderful but it's the amount of polish on the puzzle mechanics that really impresses me. Play the demo and see what I mean: objects show you exactly where they'll be when you put them down, things snap to places that you need to place them precicely, and whenever there's a place that you're actually supposed to jump the game will show you that you're able to and just let you press spacebar to do it without requiring your precision. Most of all I like how when you are placing the laser connectors, which need line of sight to everything they connect with, the game will shift where you are able to put them down to try to make sure that your planned lines of sight work when you place it, and will tell you when they don't. Almost never in the game did I feel like the game was preventing me from solving a puzzle I knew how to solve; if you've figured out what you need to do then solving the puzzle will go very smoothly.
The puzzles are very well made and very well paced. The game has a very loosely ordered selection of puzzles such that you can easily skip any that you get stuck on and come back later when you're more skilled at the game. The puzzles which you need to beat to progress to new areas are straightforward practice for the game mechanics. You don't unlock new mechanics unless you can solve the more involved puzzles with the old ones. The fully difficult puzzles aren't needed for anything except the ending, so the game makes sure that by the time you're actually forced to solve a puzzle to progress that you'll have had plenty of opportunities to work your way up to them. Alternatively you can just solve them all the order they're presented for a nice challenge throughout the game. Also present are the stars, which are their own puzzles which you thankfully never need to touch to get the most rewarding conclusion to the game. But they're always present, just out of reach, requiring you to do things that are very clearly cheating (How do I even get a blue laser? There isn't one anywhere in this puzzle!). If you're into following clues to secret passages and discovering "exploits" in the game, they're a lot of fun. Still, every puzzle, even (especially) the stars, is extremely rewarding to complete and makes you feel good about yourself for figuring them out. There's also easter eggs of some sort or another hidden in basically every level, almost all of which I missed until the late game.
Aside from the joy of solving the puzzles themselves, the game also rewards you by slowly drip-feeding you story as you enter new levels and complete their challenges. The whole thing manages to sit comfortably on the edge where it feels enigmatic and philosophical without becoming awkward or overly pretentious. You find yourself searching around looking for more (thankfully either noisy or contrasting-colored) things to read. I recommend this game more than anything else I've played in recent memory. Assuming of course you're into this sort of game. Play the demo! It does a really good job of showing off the game and I would have never considered buying this at all had the demo not made such a good impression on me. There's a whole lot of content in it and it's definitely worth the steep price asked.
