is a game that incorporates an effective balance of adventure and puzzle mechanics to create an engaging experience.
Puzzle design is well implemented and each element of the level is used effectively. The game introduces new mechanics through discovery in fairly straightforward levels, removing the need for explicit tutorials. Other levels are generally non-trivial and require some careful thinking and possibly some experimentation. Obstacles and items in levels are often useful in more than one purpose, requiring different strategies to solve rather than resorting to gimmicks.
One particular mechanic that's not as common in other puzzle games was the recording mechanic, allowing your character to record a short series of actions to do useful things such as activating additional switches and helping your character reach higher places. The mechanic also takes advantage of the terrain when combined with the ability to carry a platform above your character during recording to gain extra height.
The game also exploits the fact that several puzzles are interlinked in a hub area. For players who want to collect all the stars for access to more difficult levels, interacting between puzzles in an area or going outside the level boundary is necessary, as the obstacles in each puzzle can be interacted with within other puzzles in some cases. It's not necessary to complete the game, but it shows that the game takes advantage of being in a more open space. It also shows that the difficulty has been set effectively, as the main game has a decent challenge but is not overwhelming, while the end game requires thinking (literally) outside the box.
Backstories and texts enhance the game world. While only a few are strictly required to be read near the end, these help the player to learn more about the characters in the game and what the truth may be. More importantly, these readings make the game world and decisions meaningful, rather than having arbitrary puzzles for no reason.
Through the combination of level and world design, the game produces a unique and engaging experience that goes beyond standard expectations of a puzzle game and easily stands out among some other popular games this year.

Squad is a large-scale FPS with support for up to 100 players in various gamemodes. The development team, Offworld Industries, is largely made up of former developers for Project Reality: BF2, one of the oldest and most popular mods for Battlefield 2.
The focus of Squad is on semi-realistic teamplay that revolved around squads. There are a few different gamemodes, such as Conquest, Assault And Secure, and Insurgency. All of these gamemodes have varying objectives and ways to win.
My personal favorite mode is Insurgency, which pits a faction of insurgents against US forces. The insurgent team is tasked with protecting a series of weapons caches, the position of which is unknown to US forces at the beginning. By gathering intel, the US forces can get the rough location of a cache and with enough intel they can determe the exact location of a cache. After destroying a certain number of caches, the US forces win. However, they have limited tickets so casualties are not something they can afford as opposed to the insurgents who have an unlimited number of tickets, but only a few caches.
The majority of the Squad community is mature and helpful. There are many community servers with good people that inhabit them. When playing with a proper squad you will have one of the best times ever.
The sounds and the graphics are pretty solid, although the game is currently rather demanding on the spec side. This will change as the game is optimized.
I definitely recommend Squad, even  in early access. This is going to be one of my few go-to games for a long time coming. There are bugs and glitches that may pop up every now and then, but the developers are working diligently to make this one of the best tactical games available.
I look forward to seeing and playing with you all. I'll be playing on the server that my community (CIA Gaming) hosts.

Age of Empires 2 is in my opinion the best game ever made. It's a timeless classic that is still just as enjoyable today as the day it came out. In my opinion it is the best RTS game of all time and for that to still be true 10 years later, it is certianly worth full price.
However, this is the HD version so it is slightly different. Graphics are practically the same - which is ok for such a timeless game. However it doesn't quite live up to it's HD title. However, I came back for the game - not for anything new.
This HD version HDifys the gameplay rather than the graphics. It adds a new map size and increases the highest pop cap to 500 - allowing for much better games if your PC can handle it. The new map size hurts the PC more than the pop cap though and I've played 500 pop games on a laptop on the old standard map size. I don't recommend doing that with more than one player though. Nonetheless, huge armies are very fun to play with and add that little thing that we probably would've modded in. However - if this is what sold you then make sure you have a decent PC for it because it gets unbearably laggy on certian systems.
Another update is the new AI which they patched in at some point. As a man who prefers to do single player, this new AI added a proper challenge to the old game when I played all the time during my childhood. I used to be able to take on  6 other AIs on the hardest difficulty all on the same team. Now I struggle against them on equal footing. However, you do have the option of playing against the original AI if you want. Even a mix if you really want. The only problem I've found with it is that it will focus on water whenever there's a significant amount of water on the map. This can be good at times but when they attempt a galley rush on highland and you walk right around them it's limitations can be quite apparent.
One big flaw is it's multiplayer. They've removed the LAN function for some reason. Despite this I still play this at LAN parties but we play through the online mode. A little bit annoying. Another thing is the lag. There's a noticable lag between when you click somthing and when it notices. This did cause problems but they are working on patching these problems out. The lag still exists but I'm no longer having the problem of me putting many houses in a line and it registering the house I accidently placed rather than the ones I wanted. However, I have played an entire game which was full of unbearable lag. However, it has multiplayer (the original's doesn't work anymore) and it actually lets you try the new civillisations from the expansion packs in it.
Overall, this is still the Age of Empires 2 that I loved all my life. It didn't need updating but they gave it a go and basically refreshed the experience a bit by letting me play on larger maps and with larger populations. Still the same game and therefor worth full price in my opinion. I'd personally say that the fact that the game is still being updated and you've got expansion packs if you want more, it's somthing you should get. Even if you've never played it you should try this game as it is the best game of all time in my opinion.

Max Payne 3 should have been the ultimate deconstruction of the modern Third-Person Shooter.
Instead, it was the epitome.
The first two Max Payne games were noirish -- gritty and bold. They had a protagonist who wasn't a military genius or commando supersoldier. He was a cop who popped pain pills and was just looking for some way to avenge his dead loved ones. This, along with an innovative bullettime mechanic and a dark noir setting should've transitioned beautifully into the modern day.
Instead, the third Max Payne game completely eschews all but one of these values. It updates the Bullet Time gameplay and makes the guns fun to handle, that much is true. But alongside this, it strips all the Noir Styling and Personal Background that the story has. They try to desperately tie the game's plot into the past games, but to no avail; it has no connection of relevance, here. Max Payne is in Brazil. Why? Because he's getting paid to. That's really all there is to it. And alongside the new setting change comes an unwelcome change in style -- from dark and noirish, reminiscent of The Matrix, to a gritty shootout more reminiscent of Black Hawk Down.
What it comes down to is the fact that Max Payne 3, while a competent third-person shooter, brings nothing new to the table, and outright betrays its' roots. If you want to have some fun over the weekend, pick it up, and you won't necessarily regret it. If you bought this as a Max Payne fan, understand this:
Max Payne 1 ended with Max Payne ending his spree of bloody revenge and being led away by the police.
Max Payne 2 ended with Max Payne cradling his lover's limp body as the corrupt police force closes in.
Max Payne 3 ends with a grenade launcher car chase.

This is a puzzle game to rival Portal.  It's much harder than Portal and features about 100 levels that will take an average adult about 18-20 hours to complete.  It's not as enjoyable as Portal or as highly polished but what it lacks in quality it makes up for in dastardly quantity of hard puzzles.
My only major gripe is the story/plot.  It impedes gamplay and adds no value to the game.  I started to completely ignore the plot (which is presented to you with God like voiceovers and PC terminal text messages) after the first 5 minutes.  In fact I took off my headphones for almost the entire game.  It requires user interaction for plot devices and they are fed in mind numbing text messages that you are somewhat forced to read.  It would have been better if the text messages were all voiceovers and all the current voice overs were text messages.  They got it completely backwards.
Sound is completely unecessary for the entire game and the voiceovers are very annnoying.  I enjoyed the game much more in silence which is a tragedy to the potential for a game like this.  If the puzzles weren't so mind blowingly good this would have been a bad game due to everything else that I found annoying.
Portal did a phenomenal job on the plot compared to Talos Principle.  You'll get the most enjoyment figuring out puzzles in silence and completely ignoring the plot.  It could have been worth more if it had a good plot.  Obviously story creation is not something that Croteam is good at.  We all figured that Serious Sam was supposed to be funny because of the horrible plot.  Talos Principle proves that wasn't the case, Croteam just sucks at it.  At $30 it's definitely worth scratching your head for up to 20 hours.  Talos Principle attempted to rival Portal as the king of the first-person puzzle game but falls just shy of the mark.  That doesn't mean it wasn't worth every penny and is an A+ quality title for anyone to add to their steam library.

I have mixed feelings about the game. There are some distinctly "Rockstar" things about the game, such as implausible / irrational / insane characters that don't make any sense, and a lopsidedness to the game design in terms of difficulty ramp, etc. That said, it is strong in many other "Rockstar" ways, such as the incredibly well realized world and a fallen hero that you're excited to redeem as the player.
My biggest negative about this game is that often failure feels largely out of your control. You often don't know where enemies are coming from, when they're gonna pop-out, how accurately their bullet-spray is gonna be. I appreciate that the game kills Max realistically when he gets hit in the head with a bullet, but when the combat is often unpredictable, you can quickly end up in a loop of death, reload, death, reload, ad nauseum. In these cases, when you finally succeed, you don't really feel like you did anything better, you just... got lucky.
My favorite thing about the game is the pacing. There's some boring cutscenes where you watch Max get drunk for like the 50th time, but other than that, the game keeps you going from combat section to combat section, often doing backstory exposition through combat, etc. It's rare for me to play such a linear, focused action game like this where I will say something like, "Just to the end of this part," and then the narrative throws me so well into the next that I just end up never putting it down. Seven combat encounters later, It's 3am and I'm wondering where the time went. That's saying something for sure.
At the end of the day, I can't really recommend Max Payne 3. While I did enjoy it, it's a somewhat frustrating rollercoaster corridor shooter that's a little more conservative with its best feature (bullet-time dive-shooting) than it needs to be to make up for its obnoxious encounter designs. I don't regret playing it, but I do feel like the next item on my backlog that I tackle would've been more worthy. If you love rollercoaster narrative with characters that are slightly less shallow than your generic call-of-duty garbage, maybe Max Payne 3 is a diamond in the rough for you.

Seriously, play this game. It is one of the greatest experiences I have ever had in gaming. The story is quite good although feeling somewhat angsty at time, albeit that is not a bad thing in a game made by Rockstar. Overall the story and presentation was mind blowing and the connection felt with max was unbelieveable. I truly think Rockstar outdid themselves on nailing the handling and shooting of MP3 making it feel as weighty and dare I say realistic as possible. Much of the plot (without spoilers) revolves Max providing security for a family of rich ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and his path of revenge. As expected of a Max Payne title, there are somes seriously messed up moments in this game which I won't spoil but more than a few times did my stomach grumble at the violence/horridty displayed. As for the visuals, they are outstanding to comment in the least. Lighting is spot on, character models for even the typical cannon-fodder enemy are incredibly detailed and don't even get me started on the weapon modeling. I could write a whole paragraph at how entertaining and intriguing it is to simply watch the show of firearms, well firing as shells fall ♥♥♥♥ing from chambers opening and recokcing repeatedly it's simply beautiful to watch a game truly nail gun operation visually. As a Max Payne title, you will be spending quite a bit of time shooting and it's quite a delight to know that the shooting is akin to the other aspects of the game, outstanding. Enemies use the euphoria procedural animatiion system which realistically models and renders physical impact (e.g enemy getting shot in the arm, his shoulder will flench) and the detail Rockstar put into the wounds and "gore" is a little unsettling at how convincing it can be. There are several weapons to acquire which include the plethora you'd expect, assault rifles, submachine guns, handguns, and even a high caliber sniper rifle at one point in the game. I won't go into more detail about the gameplay and visuals as I mentioned, I could go on for days about how good it really feels and looks. Additionally, the characters and cast are SUPURB although some characters are slightly annoying, you really feel as if they are people at times and even disdain others due to their deplorable actions. That's basically all I can spout about the game without revealing too many plot details (which you will be in for some suprises!) Overall, Max Payne 3 is probably my favorite Rockstar with a close seconds being Red Dead Redemption and Max Payne 2. Typically the GTA series outshines Max Payne as Rockstar's signature series, but in almost every aspect (disregarding the world size) in Max Payne 3 is more enjoyable in my opinion. If you have a spare 20 dollars, you most likely won't be dissappointed in this game at all, as I pre ordered it when it came out.

I don't play First Person Shooters that often these days, that said Wolfenstein: The New Order is certainly the best I've played in a year or two.
Graphically it's no slouch, showing off id's engine to good effect - a good sign for Doom 4. As well, from a sound perspective they put a lot of thought into the game: the music is appropriate, the voice acting is occasionally wooden but suited to the characters, and the atmospheric sounds - public announcements, the occasional conversation in the background (try lemon coffee!)  and even the audio journals, it serves to place you firmly in a dystopian alternate 1960.
From a gameplay point of view, I found it to be a welcome mix of nostalgia and modern shooter styles. Although there is very limited health regen, most of your recovery comes from picking up armour and health packs scattered around the fround or off fallen enemies. In firefights, the action is smooth but constant, keeping you on your toes. Various weapons are effective against different kinds of enemies, and ammo for guns can be limited, ensuring that you never get too married to any one weapon. The ability to dual wield most weapons is also great fun, although it burns through so much ammo you only do it in the direst of situations.
Storywise, things are interesting enough to keep you going, with plenty of little surprises along the way. Although it can be very camp (pun intended) at times. If you tend to shy away from blood and guts, please note that Wolfenstein has both in plentitude...
Overall, a game well worth giving a go - a pleaser for fans of the original Wolfenstein 3D as well as for those trying out the series for the first time.

SPOILER ALERT
Wolfenstein: The New Order is set in a universe where the Nazis won WWII. They have taken over practically the entire world, and most people do not even resist anymore. As BJ Blazkowicz, you get to travel to a bunch of places, including reimagined Nazi versions of London and Berlin, and even a Nazi moonbase, in your struggle to reunite the resistance and bring the Nazis down.
There are loads of collectibles to find along the way, some of which improve your character and all of which add replay value. Also, there are two separate timelines based on a choice you make early in the game - so far I have only played through one, and look forward to seeing how the events of the game change when I make the other choice. Your use of various weapons and techniques throughout the game determines what perks your character unlocks in a realistic and sensible way - for example, throwing your knife a lot gives you a perk which lets you carry an additional knife for throwing.
The game isn't perfect, though. I felt that the stealth department was especially lacking. You can kill any lightly armored Nazi by throwing a knife at them, regardless of whether it hits their knee or their head. Also, enemies seem to  have no reaction to the death of other enemies unless they witness said death as it takes place.
With all that said, W:TNO is exactly what a shooter should be: a great story seen (mostly) through the eyes of the player while mowing down a delightful mix of enemies including bosses and minibosses with a delightful array of retro-futuristic weaponry. Buy it. Play it. Play it again. You won't regret it.

Never has a game that I have played on Steam to date ever urged so much me to write a review until about ten minutes ago when I finished the game.
I bought The Talos Princible on a whim because I was in desperate need of something new to play. Although I very much enjoyed Portal, puzzle games really aren't up there with my favorite genres but after reading a couple of the reviews I was swayed to buy the game.
And good gravy I'm glad I did.
From the first puzzle I was hooked in to the deep, complex plot and literally played in every free moment I had. Who am I? What is this world? Why am I being forced to do all these puzzles? Who is the voice in the sky? Not only are you asking yourself these questions but as the plot continues you find yourself being prodded to question your own opinions on humanity, consciousness and all of the universe's philosophy inbetween. Now tell me another game that does that.
In terms of gameplay, the puzzles are a nice balance of challenge and fun and you feel a sense of achievement when you complete them. Unique and interesting game mechanics really keep you invested in powering through the puzzles and the learning curve as puzzles get progressively harder is fair to say the least, although certainly in some of the later puzzles I found myself being stuck for quite a long time and getting rather frustrated with myself. With a crazy amount of puzzles (including the huge amount of bonus/secret puzzles) and easter eggs (hot diggity I love easter eggs) the The Talos Princible offers at least 20 hours of gameplay and that's if you just want to finish the game. If you want to collect all the stars, all the audio files, ALL THE DAMN EASTER EGGS, and explore the world fully, you could easily get 40 hours+ out of this game.
Visually, the game is stunning. Lord only knows how many screenshots I took to replace my desktop background. Every location from the Egyptian desert to the blue skyed mountains, this is a fine looking game even by todays standards. Something else to mention also is the soundtrack and voice acting which both really help immerse you in the game world.
To summarise:
+ Gripping plot
+ Challenging but fun puzzles
+ Interesting and unique game mechanics
+ 40+ hours of gameplay
+ Beautifully modelled world
+ Emmersive soundtrack
- Puzzles can sometimes feel a bit tedious, especially towards the end of the game
TL;DR - If you liked Portal, you will love The Talos Princible.
Overall rating: 9.5/10

The Talos Principle is a very good first-person puzzle game in the mold of Portal. You play the role of an anthropomorphic robot who hears the voice of God (Elohim) telling it to solve puzzles to gather sigils (small tetris pieces). The puzzles themselves revolve around several mechanics, the negotiation of mazes with force fields and the use of various devices. Around this gameplay you learn about this world through messages on terminals spread around the world - echos of a post-apocalyptic scenario, although for the most part you are on your own with the puzzles.
For the most part I would agree with other reviewers that this is an interesting title, well worth your time. However, there are a few problems. Firstly, the difficulty curve is all over the place. There are three colours of sigil: green are mostly trivial (these unlock areas), yellow are fairly easy (unlock abilities), red are variable between easy and frustrating. For the most part the puzzles are on the easy side, there were only 4 or 5 puzzles in the entire game that I needed to revisit. On the other hand, the gameplay is very fair - no insta-kills or required pixel perfect jumps (you lock on for jumps, so you should never miss). Some of the puzzles are very neat, and you'll feel good about yourself when you've managed to solve them.
Secondly, given how easy the green and yellow sigils are to solve, you will have unlocked almost all of the mechanics of the game after only a few hours. To my mind there isn't as much variation as I would like from a puzzle game. The mechanics are all related to objects you pick up in the world: jammers stop forcefields and other mechanisms, connectors power doors etc., hexahedrons are blocks you can jump on, fans allow you to move things around a level, recorders allow you to record your action and replay it with a clone, and platforms can be used to carry things around. Combinations of these allow for some level of complexity, but quite soon you are repeating the same sort of thing again and again. Of all the items you have to work with, the platform is the least developed, in the normal levels at least it is only used in combination with the recorder so that your clone can carry you around - it feels a bit of an afterthought. The tower puzzles at the end of the game add some nice variation, but are also quite simple. So on the whole I would have liked a bit more variation to keep me interested.
Finally, the physics of the world aren't very realistic. For example if you put a block on a fan, it will float - if you want it to float higher you can float another block underneath the first one. This is not how physics works, and whilst this isn't game-breaking it does feel like you are playing in a world with made-up rules which you have to learn and not a real physical environment (I know it isn't, but the look and feel of the game gives that impression). There are quite a few examples of this. Piles of rocks are lying around in the world, but you can't place anything on top of them, they're just pretty background texture. You can simply run through most interactive objects. You can't aim lasers through railings. You can't climb through openings which are clearly big enough, or climb on most things. You can't push objects through gaps in walls. These are all things which games such as Half-Life 2 were doing over a decade ago - and it feels like the developers are constraining the creativity of the player in how they solve the puzzles.
This review may sound very critical, but for the most part I enjoyed this game very much. It is very good looking, some of the puzzles are very challenging, there is a nice tone throughout, and there are plenty of secrets to discover. It's a good game, but I would argue that there are many ways in which it could be improved, hopefully there will be some dlc which can expand on the variety of mechanics currently in the game. In summary:
Good:
- beautiful game
- great score
- good to have a completely non-violent puzzle game
- feels good to solve the more challenging puzzles
Bad:
- many puzzles are very simple
- uneven difficulty ramp
- small number of puzzle mechanics
- doesn't use realistic physics

The best description of this game I've heard is "Portal meets Myst." If you liked either, you'll love this game.
It's very good and has proper challenging puzzles. The gameplay has depth and secrets. It looks beautiful even on low settings. Plus it's extremely well-optimized for running natively on Linux.
The design team definitely walks the line well between "too challenging" and "just challenging enough to keep you interested." There weren't any puzzles I was stuck on for too terribly long -- usually a good night's rest would help me when I came up against a wall.
Like I said, the puzzles are in the same vein as Portal. The puzzles have more elements than Portal does, and the solutions come in about the same amount of time. The challenge in later levels is applying what you know about one element to another, and getting them to work together. It's really well-thought-out.
This game is deep. There's a lot to be discovered, and the solution to a mystery is gradually revealed to you as you play. There are tons of secrets and at least 3 endings.
My only complaint is the visuals can be a little overwhelming at times (!!!), and I sometimes found myself hurrying though an area because I just couldn't take it all in.

While Wallpaper Engine is very solid when it comes to options, there is no choice to purchase a multi-PC license. Attempting to run it on multiple computers at the same time causes issues with Steam and it's licensing. Having an option to purcahse a second license on one account is one feature that should be added. Overall it is well worth the money and I would recommend it to anyone who want's a more intersting windows experience.

This is probably one of the best games I have ever played… you know, after fixing it so my computer doesn’t melt whilst playing it. (That isn’t a stab at the game at all!)
I’m gonna do a simple Pros and Cons list for this game because I’d end up writing an essay about it. TL;DR located at the bottom.
PROS:
-  Genius ideas. It takes on an FPS style obviously but it keeps your interest for the entire duration of the game. The enemies are so creative and original that I was honestly curious as to what the game would throw at me next.
-  Graphics. Are. Godly. There’s detail where detail wouldn’t even be necessary, helping to complete the atmosphere the game wants to create.
-  Music. This is more of a personal thing but I personally loved the music. At certain parts too, it just knows how to get your adrenaline pumping.
-  The STORY. I loved the story so much. I grew a love for characters and I grew an unrelenting hatred for characters too. If you want to have your heart cycle between loving the characters and experiencing extreme bloodlust, this game is for you.
-  Weapons are pretty awesome too. I loved using the missile launchers, in the few instances that I could.
-  The game knows how to balance between explosions, chaos, fire and death and the calm “just go around and explore” levels. It makes you appreciate both of them if you’re someone that gets annoyed when there’s too much of one or the other.
CONS:
-  If your computer isn’t the absolute best, this game will decimate it. Initially when launching the game (I can’t remember if it detects your computers specs and sets graphics accordingly beforehand) it was very de-synced. The video was slow and the audio seemed to had to repeat itself because the video was so slow. But after fixing the graphics so my computer can tolerate it, it ran pretty well.
-  I don’t know if it was just me being bad at video games in general, but it’s pretty easy to get lost. The path isn’t given to you with a giant neon green arrow screaming “GO HERE.” The good thing about this though is that it sort of encourages you to explore more. Though when you explore everything you might get a bit frustrated. All the more satisfying when you make progress, though.
-  Some of the robots can be a bit of a pain to figure out how to kill.
Honestly though I can’t come up with many Cons. The Pros definitely dominated in my opinion.
TL;DR:
Would definitely recommend this game for anyone looking for something that will give you a satisfying feeling when you launch rockets and grenades and Nazis and see them explode all over the floor. The game bombards your senses with the most detailed atmosphere I’ve ever seen in a video game, and takes a pretty frightening and nightmarish idea and makes a badass game out of it. A bit expensive though. I bought it when it was on sale for $20, mainly since I don’t want to spend too much on games. A truly spectacular game. Took me out of reality for the time I played it.

Skyrim graphics had a love child with Portal puzzle design to produce The Talos Principle.
Basically the game includes a series of puzzles set in a variety of very pretty mythic backdrops including Greek, Egyptian and medieval castles. As you progress through the game, more objects become available (Eg. Lazers, Fans and self recording machines), allowing for a greater variation and difficulty for later puzzles. The aim of each puzzle is to gain access to a tetromino block, that later, through arranging them into a set shape, will unlock a lift to allow you to advance into the next area. The game also keeps one intrigued through the addition of an all seeing god whom claims to have created you, and a computer system which asks you philisophical questions and psychoanalysis' you. All of this building up to the great question, will you defy god and reach the heavens by climbing the tower? Or will you obediently follow his rule in the hopes of attaining eternal life?
And for those puzzle fans out there that thoroughly enjoy a challenge, the game offers a harder difficuly by attempting to gain access to stars spread throughout the levels. Along with a certain level of replayability in trying to 100% the acheivements, with some only accessible if completed again.
This game had me questioning what it is to be human and scratching my head as i stared blankly at several pieces of a puzzle in hopes that an answer will just appear in front of me.
As close to a perfect game as one can get,  a nice 9/10 for The Talos Principle

In the hands of any other developer, this game would be the messiah of FPS games.  As it stands it is a game with enormous potential, but it has deep-rooted flaws that have been neglected for years.
My thumbs down has large caveats.  You can get on this game and have a great time here or there, in fact I recommend it because there are experiences in this game you just can't get from any other shooter.  If you decide to play it long-term however, the issues will grow on you fast.  The largest issue is a general gameplay one.  Terrible base design turns most fights into shooting at spawn doors.  The way spawning in general works is flawed.  Taking a base requires several mobile spawns that have to be created and maintained by players, without these spawns, attackers don't stand a chance.  Therefore it is the defense's objective to take out these spawns, but as a result a fun and engaging battle will be ultimately lost.
Attacking in this game is extremely punishing.  Everyone loves to head to a base and defend it, you get a fun firefight that usually results in a win unless the attackers drop so many people on the base you can't even step a foot outside the spawn shield.  Attacking takes a ton of effort and the game doesn't help you out any.  If you want to run to the next battle, you'll die and have nowhere to spawn except back at your base a mile away.  If you want to try and deploy a mobile spawn to the next base, unless you have a whole squad of back up, your mobile spawn will be destroyed before you even reach the base, or maybe last a few minutes if you make it there.  After all, it is the defense's objective to destroy it.  So it gets destroyed, you're back at square one at your base.  By this point the other side is trying to attack your base, but you do the same to them, and on it goes.
The bottom line is the funnest engagements in this game are so rare and fleeting that most of your time spent in this game feels like frustration.  You might find a good firefight, it might last for 5 minutes, then a friendly squad may redeploy from a nearby base and zerg the attackers spawn and destroy it.  You no longer have targets to shoot, and you're left with the only option of trying to mount your own attack, but you know it will only end in wasted time, resources, and punch a hole in your stats.
The funnest time you will have in this game is running with a zerg platoon as they run around crushing everyone during a world event.  You won't be experiencing the game at its best, but you'll get to do some fun coordinated teamwork actions while making decent experience, though most of your time will be spent idling next to objectives as the enemy is hopeless driven before the zerg.
The best thing for this game would be a competitor.  Major gameplay changes need to be made, but development has been slow since the business was bought out.  The future is uncertain, and I can't quite recommend spending any money on the game.

Absolutly love this game. Have played for over a decade and can never get enough. Its just one of those games that grow on ya and always have a place in your heart.
Not worth the money alone.

Story wise it's pretty great for a 3rd person FPS and ties in pretty well to real world 'agendas' for politics, dodgy corporations and has some pretty solid reasons why you are murdering the locals on each chapter. The constant voiceovers are well done and don't detract from the action. It does drag on a little too much and is probably a few chapters that could have been shortened somewhat or a couple of side story pieces cut.
Graphics, excellent throughout - plus runs really well even on hardware a few years old and the mouse is really well presented so no crappy acceleration throwing your aim off. It's a very pretty game and a lot of the ingame cutscenes are  better than the forced video ones.
Music and sound is spot on, every weapon sounds gutteral and the relevant screams and splat noises are in abundance. The soundtrack is pretty good later on but gets a little tedious at the start as it's just different mixes of the same piece of music - the 'max payne theme tune'.
Combat is the same as it's always been but with soldier of fortune style gore with entry and exit wounds all present and people bleeding through places they shouldn't have holes created by one of your many guns.
The only real annoyance is that you are often killed by enemies who insta headshot you unless you know to round that corner in slow-mo mode which is where the crutch of the game lies. It often makes it a must to use rather than a tool. Many areas are just plain tedious learning which enemies are where and need to be shot in which order unless you use copious amounts of bullet time.
Overall It's worth playing through, especially if you get it on a sale for single player at least though if you don't like the repeated retrying of gunbattles or the over use of bullet time - chuck the difficulty down and enjoy the action and gory story a lot more.

Being a Max Payne fan of the original game and playing it to death back in 2001 when it first hit the PC this was a must buy.
So lets look at what we get with our rather large 30Gb install.
The answer is a disappointing one, most of the size is due to large cutscenes that like to go on and on and on.
CONS:-
Very linear game play which often takes the control of the game away from you, for example you creep up to a door with your favourite weapons ready to launch some Max Payne goodness on their♥♥♥♥♥♥and it takes over to a cutscene which you have no control over and have to watch.  It then releases control after dropping you in the brown stuff with a whole different       choice of weapons.  Now this sounds very petty to mention but this happens alot through out the game.
This suggest the director of the game wanted a limited feel of the game and in turn it takes alot of control away from the end user / player.  VERY ANNOYING!
Also the game lacks any inovation is areas, this makes the gameplay feel repetitive quickly and the boredom factor soon creeps in.
Another annoyance to make are the extremely long first load time which you are forced to watch the long cutscene when first launching the game.
Settings the keyboard is another area where the game lets you down.  After binding your keys unless you have every action assigned to a key it will not save the settings and want to default the keys.  There a lack of information is this area to inform you that you have not assigned a key or need to complete the list before it will save any alteration to the defaults.
Pros:-
Graphically the game looks very good and gives you lots of GFX eye candy.
The game is also aimed at the adult gamer with lots of profanity and adult content which gives the game a darker gothic feel than alot of other games in this genre.
Story line of the game has lots of twists which keep you guessing where the plot will take you and who are the bad guys.
For me the cons outweighed the pros and after a full play through of the single player campaign it felt more like a chore to get through with the repetitiveness and lack of control over cutscenes.

Before I begin, please note that I suck at FPS games and fast paced games in general.
Dirty Bomb is a fast-paced objective-based multiplayer class shooter set in London after the detonation of an RDD or dirty bomb, which, if you hadn't noticed, is the game's namesake. The Government (The CDA) and a group of terrorists (The Jackal) fight for what's left of London, using mercenaries because they needed a reason for the same characters to fight for both sides. You play as one of these 19 mercs and try to either complete the objectives (Jackal) or defend until time runs out (CDA). The maps are multi staged, having 2-3 stages each, and are quite well made. There is one primary objective per stage, and a few secondary ones that open up new attack routes or obstruct the enemy team. All in all, the maps I feel are pretty good, although the escort sections are more or less just both teams eitherspamming airstrikes or repairing constantly. (Yes I know I missed Execution but it's basically CS:GO bomb defusal)
Characters:
There are 19 characters, each with an amusing little backstory and personality, divided into 5 classes:
Assault:
Crowd control characters with heavy weapons and usually spammable small AoE abilities. They kill people, and that's it.
Medic:
Weaker characters with a healing ability and the ability to instantly revive downed teammates (I shouldn't need to explain what they do). You start off with one: Aura.
Engineer:
Have the "Objective Specialist" perk, so they plant/defuse C4, repair EVs and build generators twice as fast as other mercs. They also have some sort of deployable ability (Turret/Mine/Sticky Bomb). These guys play the objective.
Fire Support:
These characters have decent weapons, the ability to resupply teammates with ammo, and very powerful AoE abilities with a long cooldown. You start off with one: Skyhammer
Recon:
These characters do some supporting in the form of spotting or disabling deployables, but they are mainly focused on precise killing. Armed with sniper rifles or heavy melee and a stealth suit, they target important enemies, such as medics,  engineers or the poor sod trying to complete the objective before he suddenly gained a third nostril via your rifle.
The characters are quite varied, interesting and have mildly amusing personalities, as well as being mostly well balanced, apart from a couple, such as Thunder (Press Q to force the target enemies to stand there gawping like idiots for 5 seconds), but overall, I like them.
Pay-2-Win:
No. it isn't, thankfully. Any loadout card (the bizzare loadout system's way of changing weapons for a character) can be bought directly from the store for ingame currency. secondly, the rare Silver/Gold/Cobalt cards are only cosmetic upgrades from Bronze. While Bronze cards are better than defauly, lead and iron cards, the difference is very minor, and bronze cards are easy to get anyway through crafting. The characters themselves don't take too long to unlock either, I did the maths and worked out that you could get one new character per week with very little effort if you handled it right.
Things I don't like:
The matchmaker. Firstly, in a very high skill variation game, it does not take skill into account AT ALL, and so you often get steamroll matches. Secondly, it requires manual effort to shuffle the teams, which is a problem I'll get into now:
The community. Quite a few high level players are elitists, refusing to shuffle a clearly unbalanced match, saying that you are a "whining noob", or that "It's a challenge". The new players all seem to not understand the concept of teamplay, and rarely give ammo/healthpacks or play the objective. While there are some nice people on the steam forums, like Pizza Delivery, most ingame players are either clueless or elitists.
Conclusion:
Do I recommend? It depends. If you can deal with the matchmaker having the IQ of a block of concrete, then yes. If you cannot, wait and see if the matchmaker gets changed. If you are on the fence, try it for a while. Maybe you'll like it, maybe you won't, but it's free, and the only thing it will cost you is a little time.

Skyrim graphics had a love child with Portal puzzle design to produce The Talos Principle.
Basically the game includes a series of puzzles set in a variety of very pretty mythic backdrops including Greek, Egyptian and medieval castles. As you progress through the game, more objects become available (Eg. Lazers, Fans and self recording machines), allowing for a greater variation and difficulty for later puzzles. The aim of each puzzle is to gain access to a tetromino block, that later, through arranging them into a set shape, will unlock a lift to allow you to advance into the next area. The game also keeps one intrigued through the addition of an all seeing god whom claims to have created you, and a computer system which asks you philisophical questions and psychoanalysis' you. All of this building up to the great question, will you defy god and reach the heavens by climbing the tower? Or will you obediently follow his rule in the hopes of attaining eternal life?
And for those puzzle fans out there that thoroughly enjoy a challenge, the game offers a harder difficuly by attempting to gain access to stars spread throughout the levels. Along with a certain level of replayability in trying to 100% the acheivements, with some only accessible if completed again.
This game had me questioning what it is to be human and scratching my head as i stared blankly at several pieces of a puzzle in hopes that an answer will just appear in front of me.
As close to a perfect game as one can get,  a nice 9/10 for The Talos Principle

Okay since some vets of PR are complaining and Some people are a bit confused i will explain this better.
This game in its current state is a facepaced FPS similar to the game "insurgency" but with a larger engagment range. There will be close quarters to longer range little dots of people range. But At this stage that range is not very far to the final product.
The current game has you fighting Infantry vs Infantry, Fobs are easy to contruct, squad rally points(spawn points for squads) are easily put down, and last a long time. Flags are close together and fobs are destroyed by just being near them. This gamplay allows for fast paced gameplay where lonewolfing is easily achieved and can be effective, but is frowned upon. That being said, working as a squad is MUCH more effective in general and allows you to be much more ticket effective vs larger amounts of enemies.
That is the current gameplay, but the game will be going away from that in the next month and two with things like.
Vehicles, These assets can punish lone wolfing as to get from flag A to B is no longer just a single sprint away, you may need to drive from one to another to get anywhere in a timely manner, so if a squad takes a humvee and you are left alone at base with no transport, good luck trying to effective. This addition makes lonewolfs join squads even just for transport, but it also shows how being a squad can be more effective.
Fobs are currently♥♥♥♥♥♥easy to build, These will later require logistics brought up to contruct, slowing the construction of these key functions of the game, and making them much more valueable then they are now, which will force squads to be more wary of the defence and contruction of these, These will also then be less likely to be able to have a lone wolf be able to destroy these structures as such you will need a larger squad sized force to be able to deal with these.
Squad rally points last forever in time, and dissapear after 9 spawns or enemy overrun it (you have to be pretty close) These rallies only add about 10 seconds to your spawn vs a FOB as such they can allow for almost instant fob creation and sustained battle capablities to a squad. In PR rallies will disspear after about a minute. They are designed for regrouping, not sustained battle. Their current design is not the final design, they will change heavily over time.
The maps themselves are mostly smaller sized maps, they have released larger maps but use only a fraction of the map. They are pushing the whole server into a close quarter situation, As such it is a twitch shooter right now, But later when it changes into you having to worry about that APC sitting on that hill all the way over there you will be taking  your running across open ground a bit more carefully. This will make you have to scout the hills and area before you do actions, a lonewolf wont have the benifit of so many eyes.
So over all This game is currently designed as a closer quarter about the sized of the current BF4 maps(which really is pretty small) you will run into enemies pretty quick and have a good twitch shooter experience.
In a few months this will all change(except for when the server is designed to play close quarter maps only) to a more squad based tactical shooter where tactics are seen over gunplay skill.
And side note $40 is a steep cost, it is designed to allow the kick starters a bit more room as they paid $30, if $40 is seen as to expensive for you, just don't buy it for now, but if you got cash, go nuts. i would say for $40 you are kinda buying two games, the current twitch shooter, which will evolve into a larger battlefield game, so $20 for each isn't to bad =].
So i recommend this for people who don't mind laying down the $40 you will have a good time, but don't look for super serious team work just yet, it will come, but right now it will be more of a insurgency game, then an ARMA or PR game.

game is kinda buggy atm, crashes and disconnects during loading maps is a bit common, these are sure to be fixed but til they are be warned, AMD people are complaining of larger problems, but a fix seems very soon to be released. FPS in general is a bit on the lower side with FPS drops on things like smoke grenades, So be warned if you have a♥♥♥♥♥♥rig. But when in game, if you have the machine that can run it, it runs smooth enough during gameplay, just loading times are when you have to cross ya fingers.

Don't get me wrong the game is good like the sector capturing, map mechanics, factions, maps, freedom, roleplay and different variety of weapons and vehicles is amazing but the actual gameplay is quite poor. I am talking about the gun, killing and movement mechanics.
Movement: Strafing is non-existent which makes it feel very slugish, only pressing "W" to move and nothing else. Your character moves extremely slow which makes it very easy for people to kill you. Not being able to get out of battle when you're getting shot at just gets repetitive and annoying. The Vehicle's are just plain terrible to drive. Cars weigh about 50000kg then they just drop to 5kg. Trying to turn right or left in a ground vehicle takes you about 4 seconds and by that you've already crashed. Trying to turn around in the air is like expecting the enemy to wait for you to turn around because by the time you've gotten half way they could of killed you 3 times. So it's so hard to turn but when you crash you fling up in the air and start bouncing all around the place.
Gunplay: There's many weapons to choose but unfortunatley there are only a small majority of weapons that are actually good and useful. Weapons feel and sound very weak in as it takes 7-8 shots to the body with a decent auto weapon (140-160 damage) Doing 2v1's is practically useless head-on so don't expect getting kills if you're outnumbered. I know some of you will say "WELL I'VE DONE IT BEFORE". Yeah, read the sentence again. I have done 2v1's and even 3v1's and won before, but I ambushed or sneaked up on them. I am talking about head-on combat. They all see you and they start shooting at you at the same time as you. Combine that with the movement and you have no chance. The range of the assualt rifles is just horrible. I was shooting a guy with the default heavy weapon 20m away from me, I shot him about 5-10 times and I destroyed half his shield + heavy shield. You know what's crazy. I was playing as the vanu's. THE GUYS WHO HAVE THE MOST ADVANCED TECHNLOLOGY IN THE GAME! But you know, 20m. 20m? 20m?! Are you out of your mind! Thats way too far!
In conclusion the games main premises of capturing and defending territory for a faction is amazing. The game is definitely not bad, there was epic moments with huge battles going on. People dying, tanks, aircraft explosions. There was just so much going on. Sadly you will see the gameplay as stale or just plain bad if you remove all the big battles and maps and make planet side 2 a 5v5 small mapped comp game. Imagine that. You will see how bad the gunplay and movement is.
In short games premises is good but gameplay is bad. 6.8/10

The guys behind Project Reality have made a masterpiece!
That being said, I will try to be objective in my review of this game.
I originally bought the game a while back, in part to show my support to the development of the game, and in part because I was to excited to see what the game offered. Fearing I was going to be let somewhat down, I started the game up for its first run.
I was not let down. My initial thought was, and still is, that it's a sort of mix between Insurgency and the Arma series. I think in a lot of ways, the game will address itself to both groups of players.
It has the simple controls and management of Insurgency, but at the same time offers combined arma warfare in a scale similar to Arma, not to mention that the maps are quite large, and the different fireteam roles actually matter in this game.
The ability to set up outposts as spawnpoints, and the need for a tactical plan, is something that appeals to me in this game. While some might feel the urge to go Rambo in the game, you could say that there is no room within fireteam for such actions. Fireteam tactics and coop play are a priority when playing this game.
The game has quite good graphics, and will appeal to those looking for something more serious than COD of BF, but without losing the simple control scheme. The game also offers in-game VoIP, letting you utilize three different radio channels, one for direct chat, one for fireteam chat, and one for company chat.
All in all this is a game I look forward to playing a lot more, and also seeing what the future has in store for. I highly recommend this game if you like playing Insurgency, but maybe want a little more realism, or if you're an Arma player looking for a similar experience, but without the Arma problems. (If you're an Arma player, you'll know what I mean).

A nice touch.  Most of the characters seemed fleshed out enough that they were interesting, though some could have used a bit more involvement.  The music was awesome. The one used in the last section of the game stuck out the most. I didn't really encounter any glitches besides shell casings being stuck in the air for a bit, though there was a major glitch in the water level. A raised body of water transitioned into a lower section of water. So you literally were walking into a wall of water. Other than that, no problems. If I had to nitpick, it was kind of a letdown that you had to Rambo most sections of the game. So you can't  really 100% stealth in it. One area I silently killed everyone, but as soon as I transitioned to the next area, everyone was alerted to my presence. Not a huge deal, but problably something to keep in mind if you plan to go stealth. The game took about 30 hours to finish, but I went REALLY slowly trying to find the collectibles. So far, I would definitely recommend it. It's too early to decide if I like it more than Portal 2 but they're two very different games.

Might be the best game of 2014. What distinguishes "The Talos Principle" from others is an incredibly detailed background for a philosophical question - what is the difference between an AI and a human being? While you progress through those levels reading all the rare pieces of information you form your own understanding of a problem. This game is a very rare occasion when being able to predict the ending (after completing ~2/3 of a game) is not a sign of developer's incompetence but the very opposite - the conclusion that you came up to yourself. The one you thought about even before you realised it and, what a relief, the developers have also used it.
It is quite difficult to express what you like about this game without any spoilers - let's just say that it is the fist game after which I read several psychophysical articles just to know what people thought before and how things changed in this area. The puzzles, the story - everything is extremely engaging.
As for negative points I can only mention three:
1). Awful support of Nvidia 3DVision - unable to read any text as the eyes can't just focus on it (it might be fixed in future versions)
2). Sometimes puzzles are a little bit redundant. They can be made more difficult and thus more challenging. Especially with the fan blade. It's as if developers sometimes forget that this blade can also be placed on pressure plates.
3). "Tetris" puzzles become annoying in the second part of a game just because of the amount. I have completed every single one in "Sigils of Elohim" and than I had to complete even more of those here. First 30 times were fun. Other 100500 times - just irritating.
Solid 9.9/10

I am going to be Frank here. I have grown out of mindless games that only is about leveling up and hitting buttons (or keys) as much as possible. I get bored after five minutes with most games like that.
A lot of Beat 'Em Up games (which this basically is) are like that. For mostly nostalgic reasons I can now and again play classics like Golden Axe, Final Fight or TMNT: Turtles In Time. But other than that... No. Beat 'Em Up is nothing that interest me anymore.
This game though is very enjoyable. There is lots of humor in it. The game never takes itself too seriously which I enjoy. While some humor is very childish I bet most people will laugh at least a few times during the game or smile frequently.
It isn't all about hitting buttons either. Whilst not being that difficult there are places where you actually have to use your brain to get through. I like that.
The replay vaule is quite big mostly because of two reasons:
1) You can play with up to four people which make the game more fun (but a bit more chaotic). I would say the game is easier alone though in some ways. Which leads me to 2).
2) The system to upgrade your character. There is four elements you can upgrade during the game.. Depending on which you upgrade the game can get easier or harder. It's also fun to choose different strategies. You get experience directly for all hits you do on enemies in the game. So if you friend get fifty hits on an enemy and you one. You still get one experience. It isn't always much.. But it keeps the game in a good flow and is very fair. The more you level up the longer time it takes. Getting all upgrades will definitely demand more than just playing the game through once without going back. Playing alone, you will upgrade faster.
From what I noticed the diffculty playing with friends or alone is hardly notable. But there is minor differences like more enemies in different spots. The diffculity goes up and down in the game. Some places you just run through and others will take a few tries. The game is quite long for a Beat 'Em Up but not compared to other genres of games today. You won't finish it in one hour the first time you try it though.. *cough* Final Fight 3 *cough*.
All in all. It is a fun game if you want a break from the longer more serious games you got. Comes recommended all the way from Sweden!

Whether you love them or hate them, there's no denying that the FPS genre is quite possibly the biggest of all genres in modern gaming. We've seen hundreds, if not thousands of shooters developed over the past two decades. Most gamers would say that Doom was the game that really put shooters into the spotlight, and they'd be right, but Doom wouldn't have even existed if it weren't for a certain FPS made back in May 5th, 1992. That game was Wolfenstein 3D. Sure, the genre stretches all the way back into the 70s, but Wolf3D was the game that put FPSs on the map. It invented the basic mechanics that all future shooters would build upon. Despite having this most impressive distinction, the series never really took off like Doom did. There were few entries released over the years, but they didn't really stand out amongst the enormous sea of other shooters. For a while, I was certain that Wolfenstein would die out. It was a shame, but I couldn't see how it could stand up to the sheer amount of competition it was facing.
With the release of Wolfenstein: The New Order, I am glad to say that I was proven wrong. The New Order is quite possibly the biggest surprise hit of the year. I came into it expecting another mindless shoot-em-up, so I was caught completely off guard by how brilliant this game was. It's kind of an odd case, really, since it does many things that you don't really see too often in most modern shooters. This only serves to make it stand out more amongst its peers.
Mechanics-wise, I think the best way to describe TNO is that it's an old-school shooter augmented by more modern shooting mechanics. This is a brilliant design choice because it allows for several different playstyles, and all of them are equally fun. You can go for the classic playstyle, running and gunning through hordes of Nazi mooks like a badass out of hell with an impressive array of weapons, go tactical and systematically eliminate your targets from the safety of cover, or take the stealthy route, stalking and asssassinating your foes before they even know you're there. All three of these playstyles are completely viable, and they're further supported by the perk tree. Perks are unlocked not through monetary means, but by completing certain feats in the game, like getting a certain amount of kills while sliding, getting stealth kills with throwing knives and overcharging your health all the way up to 200. It works great, because it forces you to mix up your playstyle over the course of the game in order to unlock them.
There are different enemy types throughout the game, each requiring different tactics to defeat, like the average Nazi troopers, rocket launcher-bearing Fire Troopers, flying drones and minigun-wielding Supersoldaten. The majority of your enemies will be regular soldiers, though. Fortunately, they're kept challenging by their consistently solid AI. They make intelligent use of cover, lay down fields of fire to keep you suppressed, throw grenades to flush you out and constantly stay on the move to try to outflank your position. I would've liked to see a little more variety in the enemy types, but still, mowing down hordes of hapless Nazis is still as fun as it's ever been. There are four difficulty levels to choose from, and they all modify the challenge level significantly. It's not done perfectly, though; for the most part, the difficulty curve is reasonable, but there are certain parts of the game where it's suddenly cranked up by a surprisingly large margin, to the point where these sections can be, if I may be so frank, a pain in the rear to get through unless you play very carefully. It would've been nice if it was more balanced, but even so, while the game may seem a bit unfair sometimes at the higher difficulties, it's never impossible.
Graphically, the game is quite gorgeous. The textures, character models, lighting effects and environments look awesome. However, it's not perfect. Some textures are noticeably lower res than others, and the game's engine has a rather irritating quirk: it streams models and textures in when you turn to look at them, which results in a lot of texture pop-in and models appearing out of thin air. It can get pretty jarring at times. However, these complaints are minor, compared to the rest of the game's merits.
One of the things that really surprised me was that the game doesn't have multiplayer, but to be honest, it doesn't need multiplayer. I'd say it's actually better for it, because it allowed the development team to focus on delivering a polished, satisfying experience.
Ultimately, Wolfenstein: The New Order's gameplay is fantastic. In a way, I think it's poetic, how the game is designed. Wolfenstein 3D invented FPSs as we know them. Now that the conventions of first-person shooting have been fully established, Wolfenstein: The New Order takes the best aspects of modern FPSs and combines them with the frantic, aggressive gunplay of old-school shooters, creating a polished, complete experience that pays tribute to the genre's roots while also holding up with the best of today's shooters.
Now this may come as a surprise to you, but as fantastic as Wolfenstein's gameplay is, it's not what impressed me the most. No, what truly blew me away was the storytelling. When I first heard about The New Order, I figured that the gameplay would be decent, at least, but the story would be ultimately forgettable, and now that I've actually played the game, I can say with full confidence that I was completely and utterly wrong. Wolfenstein delivers a highly character-driven narrative experience that is remarkable in its execution. The writing is magnificent, the pacing is solid and the characters are all memorable. Special mention must be made for B.J. Blazcowicz, the player character. B.J.'s been the protagonist throughout the entire series, and through all that time he was the definition of a flat character. His whole shtick was literally just being a badass, nazi-killing, one-liner spouting one-man-army. The New Order changed that, giving his character a much needed injection of depth. Blazcowicz is still the unstoppable Nazi killer we all know him as, but something about him has changed. He's no longer the cocky badass he used to be. He's a brooding, haunted shell of a man who's seen and brought enough death to last several lifetimes. The experiences that at one point drove and hardened him are starting to eat away at him, and now, all he wants is to see the war end. B.J. proves to be a very dynamic character as the game goes on; his monologues can be heard over the course of the game, revealing tidbits of his psyche and history. He's not just a violent meathead; B.J. is eloquent in his musings, and he's quite capable of connecting to people. For the most part, he puts on a hard exterior, but he's more sensitive than he lets on, even showing hints of vulnerability to certain characters, especially Anja. He's a flawed man, one who often acts on his emotions, even when it ends up being more harmful than not, and he wonders if there's even a place for him in a world without the Nazis.
The amount of emotional depth in The New Order stunned me. The story's quieter moments thrive on subtlety and chemistry between the characters. Of course, being a shooter, it certainly isn't lacking in action either, which it delivers with gusto. I will admit, the tone of the story isn't always consistent, but I don't think that detracts from the experience. The absurdity of certain elements in the setting and characters, mixed with the emotional strife the heroes go through actually made the story more memorable for me. The story's emotional strength is further supported by the absolutely stunning soundtrack composed by Michael John Gordon. Give it a listen when you can.
In conclusion, Wolfenstein: The New Order is a wonderfully crafted experience. If you have even a passing interest in shooters, buy. This. Game.

The guys behind Project Reality have made a masterpiece!
That being said, I will try to be objective in my review of this game.
I originally bought the game a while back, in part to show my support to the development of the game, and in part because I was to excited to see what the game offered. Fearing I was going to be let somewhat down, I started the game up for its first run.
I was not let down. My initial thought was, and still is, that it's a sort of mix between Insurgency and the Arma series. I think in a lot of ways, the game will address itself to both groups of players.
It has the simple controls and management of Insurgency, but at the same time offers combined arma warfare in a scale similar to Arma, not to mention that the maps are quite large, and the different fireteam roles actually matter in this game.
The ability to set up outposts as spawnpoints, and the need for a tactical plan, is something that appeals to me in this game. While some might feel the urge to go Rambo in the game, you could say that there is no room within fireteam for such actions. Fireteam tactics and coop play are a priority when playing this game.
The game has quite good graphics, and will appeal to those looking for something more serious than COD of BF, but without losing the simple control scheme. The game also offers in-game VoIP, letting you utilize three different radio channels, one for direct chat, one for fireteam chat, and one for company chat.
All in all this is a game I look forward to playing a lot more, and also seeing what the future has in store for. I highly recommend this game if you like playing Insurgency, but maybe want a little more realism, or if you're an Arma player looking for a similar experience, but without the Arma problems. (If you're an Arma player, you'll know what I mean).

Wow... This game is great. The cutscenes are amazing and don't distract from the gameplay. I also appreciate that the developers give  the option to skip any one of them, which comes in handy when you replay the game. Believe me, you will be replaying it. Initially I found myself skeptical of the Nazi tachnology and construction, but as the game progressed, I started being enveloped in the world. It feels almost claustrophobic since there is nothing but concrete and steel, as well as the hulking threat of the Nazis always looming. The game has emotion and heart, and I truly believed this is a labor of love from the developers. The ending was not as satisfying as I had hoped, and I wasn't all that keen on the plot's reasoning as to how the Nazis attained all of thier amazing technology (a jewish cult? really?). Other than that, the gameplay is great. The sound effects are comparable to Battlefield. Weapons really sound beefy and have some punch. The game is loaded with little details scattered throughout the world which add to the narrative. I personally loved seeing all of these little stories and newspaper clippings, and think that they further draw you into the game's world. You are given information from the Nazi and resitance perspective. The characters are unique and very interesting, each with a detailed personality that you find yourself wanting to know more about.
I could write a book as to why you should by this game, but I'll just stop there. If you purchase this game, you won't regret it.

DON'T BE DISCOURAGED!
I'm not going to cover what is good and bad about the game, since I'm sure it's already been done thousands of times and you can see another review for that information.
I'M going to make something very clear and give you a warning.
When you first start playing this game, you'll feel completely out-classed. You will die a lot, you will be confused often, and sometimes you just won't know what to do. However, at the same time, it will be an awesome experience. This game's trailers speak the truth. There are lots of players of all classes waging war against the enemy. Aircraft of all kinds will be constantly flying overhead, chasing each other in dog fights and strafing the battlefield. There will be tanks and Armored Personnel Carriers dotted throughout the escalating battles.
And while it's a cool spectacle, you will be understandably overwhelmed.
"Where is the objective? What do I do when I get there? Where is my team? Where is the enemy? Why does the announcer keep saying random stuff??? AAAHHH!"
So I - being a fellow noob - am here to give you some advice.
You have to focus on one thing at a time.
Yes, it's ok to take the scenery and the battle into spectacle appreciation, but don't let it crowd your focus. Listen very carefully to everything the announcer is saying. Take a minute or two to collect yourself. Ask yourself a couple things before charging into battle:
"What is the objective?"
"What is the lay of the land?"
"Is my Team's offensive large enough?"
"What kind of support do they need / how can I help?"
Next, you should try every aspect of combat. Do you want to specialize in ground combat, air combat, or heavy armor?
And just because you aren't doing as good as you had hoped, don't get discouraged. EVERYTHING in Planetside 2 takes time to get good at.
I for example, decided that I'm very good at a supportive role on the ground and in the air.
On the ground, I'm an engineer, making sure all the tanks and other vehicles are in tip-top shape, and that every soldier has ammunition spilling out of their pockets. Or even placing turrets to provide suppressing fire.
In the air, I transport troops and other much-needed reinforcements to the field of battle, and that has been one of the deciding factors in battles more than once for me.
The point is, you need to find some way that you can contribute and make a difference in the battle.
But if you let your focus get away from you, you'll develop this mindset of "charging and randomly firing will work"
And that is a bad habit. You'll always die like that. You aren't just another player.
If by the time you stop playing for the day, you can confidently say:
"I made a difference"
Then you're doing it right.
Now get out there! The continents won't conquer themselves! You need to help!

After playing the free "The Talos Principle Public Test" and "Sigils of Elohim", I just had to get this game and I think it is worth the price I paid for it (about €33 as I pre-ordered and already had The Swapper). I loved both Portal games and this game is about the same difficulty, which means that it is challenging without being impossible to figure out (I was totally stumped with Kairo and needed a guide to get through it, although I still enjoyed it).
I have solved about half of the puzzles and some of the hard ones can be really difficult, but you can get some help in the game and of course there are already YouTube videos that can help you get unstuck.
There is no timer, so you can take your time to figure it out and if you first can't get it, you can go and solve some other puzzles and come back later to try again (after learning some useful new tricks). That's one of the really good things about this game, all the normal puzzles in a building are available for you to solve in any order you like, although you do need to solve specific puzzles to unlock the next building.
Let's not forget about the scenery, which is fantastic.  The developers have gone through a lot of trouble to make the environments and just exploring them is interesting. There are so many things that are not really needed for the gameplay, but are there purely for you to look at and enjoy.
There's also a back story to what is going on and it is interesting to uncover it piece by piece, although it does seem a bit predictable, at least so far, but who knows, maybe I'm in for a surprise when I finally get to the end.
So, is there anything negative about this game? Sure, the first thing being that I couldn't get it to work in full screen mode. However, the windowed mode works just fine, so I'm not too grumpy about that, especially as it could be a hardware problem (same thing happened with the Public Test).
Another thing I don't like much is that there are some puzzles, which require speedy actions. I have trouble with games that require me to react or move fast. Fortunately, there haven't been too many puzzles like that yet, so the frustration isn't getting too bad. Mostly you get all the time you need.
I have also noticed some lagging even in the windowed mode, but that could again be a hardware problem. There are a lot of settings to address those, provided you understand what to do with the settings. If you want to make sure before buying, install the Public Test and see how that works.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes challenging puzzle games and the ability to set your own pace - either rush from one puzzle to the next or take your time to enjoy the scenery and all the little bits of the back story scattered around.

There are plenty of games which are celebrated for their gameplay but lack anything in way of story or character. Max Payne 3 is a different type of proposition. The gameplay is simple yet satisfying, but it’s entirely in the service of a strongly-authored narrative. Players aren’t at the liberty to roam, to explore, or to shake things up. Some might find this too controlling, but in return for your freedom, you’re rewarded with a mature genre piece which is also a finely-realised character study. Action games continue to inch the dial towards 11, sometimes at the expense of their narrative integrity. Max Payne 3, however, has the conviction to reign in the action, imbue it with purpose - the spectacle still sparkles but it also makes sense.

Where to start? Sure, there are plenty of Multiplayer 1st Person shooters. Plenty of them are built in Unreal engine.
But this one has a legacy, and that legacy is Project Reality.
That's not to say that this will end up -being- Project Reality, so if you're looking for a direct, updated 1:1 match, this hasn't gotten there yet. But it is framed and inspired by PR at its core by Communications and Teamwork being the focus and most significant components of the gameplay.
In the (relatively) short amount of time since the Kickstarter concluded, this game has seen a lot of iteration and dedication put into getting things just right, in proving out the framework and all the elements that have gone into the game in order to make it possible for it to survive and be expanded upon and more importantly, for it to remain fun and engaging for the player.
There is still a lot of work left to be done: there will be bugs, hurdles, stumbles and changes. I look forward to seeing all of you on the battlefield and being a part of your Squad.
