Most of the reasons I love this game are well stated by every other review. Here's some buy/no buy advice based on what this game is and will be.
Reasons to Buy:
1. Teamwork. The thrill of accomplishing a common goal with a cohesive unit is greater than any other game I have ever experienced. (That's a lot of games)
2. Fellowship. It's fun to socialize with people like you and make life-long gaming friends. I certainly have.
3. Realism/Gameplay. Most people field these two as opposing forces that mark the difference between Arma and Battlefield; fun or boring; simulator or shooter. Gameplay > Realism? Realism > Gameplay? Squad has both. Realism = Gameplay. 'Nuf said.
4. Longevity. Squad's predecessor, Project Reality, has achieved a following since 2006 and has become a constantly enhancing game with updates still being pushed out. Squad is breathed by the same Gods and will be much the same.
5. Creators. The Devs will personally discuss with anyone on what they can do to improve the game just as they will watch your back during the heat of combat. This ain't EA. These guys care. They're giving it to you for $40 and someday it will be worth so much more. They deserve your money.
6. Renaissance. The concept that is this game is unique. Imagine Battlefield's combined warfare, Arma's teamwork, Red Orchestra's casualness, and Insurgency's flow. Add huge maps and much else and you get Squad. Why has no one made this game yet??
Reasons not to buy:
1. Early Access. Squad is not comparable or up to par with Project Reality. If you want a working game, patience you must have.
2. Immaturity/mic. Squad is designed for a mature player who can communicate by mic. You will not feel what this game has to offer if you possess neither of those.
3. Combat Pace. No 360' no scopin' fools. If you're partial to those games, you'll be disappointed here. Combat pace anywhere between Red Orchestra and Arma, depending on the map.
4. Walking Simulator. This will change when vehicles are added, but Squad will probably feel like a walking simulator to everyone at some point. Admirable graphics are an instant fix of this for me. IMO, most games don't give you the time to appreciate the finer textures and lights like this one will. Environment will immerse you.
5. Hardware. Currently in this un-optimized pre-alpha state, the performance is quite low when on populated servers. I probably would not be having fun if it weren't for GTX 780 + 4770k. Others may be frustrated if they purchase it so soon.

Everyone compares it to Portal, but honestly, I don't really see the connection. So because a game has puzzles, it's like Portal? I think not. The puzzles in this game are more diverse, imo more difficult, and have different mechanics. Okay, so there are boxes and pressure plates, but that's not the only usage for boxes. Also the whole religious/philosphy aspect of the game is VERY interesting and well done. I'm a Christian, and I find the situational comparisons to life as a religious person very stimulating. If you are turned off by religion in games, DON'T worry, you do not have to see it that way, get your own meaning out of the story then, it's not so forceful that you have to be religious to enjoy it.
Honestly, overall this is probably the best "game" (if you can even call this work of art a game) I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. I'm not sure how many hours I have logged right now, but it's got a good lot of content, especially for those that like to enjoy the scenery and soundtrack, and not speed-run it. Sometimes, I'd find myself just looking for good angles for screenshots because the enviroments are so beautiful.
I'd find it very hard to find someone I wouldn't reccomend this to. It is the hype, it meets the hype, and it's even better then the hype would lead to believe.

[IMPORTANT INFORMATION]
Pie recipe [VERY IMPORTANT]
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons UNSALTED butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Medium paced tactical shooter that encourages and rewards teamplay. In the future we'll have logistics, aircraft, ground vehicles (tanks, apcs, transport) and static emplacements which will slow the pace of the game down quite a bit. What the game offers now is a robust infantry based shooter, that has great Squad based gameplay. The games really come together when you have a squad leader who communicates and focuses on the objectives / winning and a Squad that is willing to listen and follow orders. I would highly suggest if you pick this game up to listen to and stick with your Squad Leader, especially if hes communicating and giving orders. If you end up in a silent squad that is all playing by themselves and not communicating I would suggest joining a different squad or give leading a go. It makes the game much more fun and your Squad will be infinitley more effective.
So far in the game we have some nice systems including the ability to build up bases anywhere on the map with a great building system, the squad leader places objects down and his squad can build them up with E-Tools. Large maps that will probably only get larger when vehicles are included, and various game modes including Advance and Secure (sector control gamemode) and Insurgency (find the insurgent weapon cache sites and destroy them). Also included in the game so fare are 4 different factions all with realistic loadouts and loadout restrictions within your squad based on how many people you have in your squad and how many of the kits are already taken.
If you play and enjoy Insurgency, Arma, Project Reality, and maybe even Battlefield I'm sure you can find fun and enoyment in this game. For $40 this game is very worth the buy, you'll be engrossed in the game at times and hours will just fly by as you have fun participating in large scale battles and securing objectives with your squad.
Final note: If your a player who doesn't like playing as a team, this game may or may not be for you. I believe "lone wolf" shouldn't be shunned away but if you refuse to play as a team and listen to your squad leader I only ask that you

This game is a masterpiece. Deep, interesting, moving storyline married with polished, beatifully realised gameplay. The graphics are beautiful, albeit heavy on the lense-flare at times. The music is apt and the sound effects are expertly done. Voice acting (at least for English speakers) is top quality - particularly the moving Alexandra sound capsules you will hear throughout the story. The final cut scene was suitably poignant and yet, given what you've been through and what the end represents, epic.
For folks that like to think hours-to-complete is somehow relevant, it took me 23 hours to "finish". I'd discovered three (which I think is all) of the secret rooms, plus one absolutely wierd "extra" secret area within a secret area and I went to extra lengths to find what turned out to be an easter egg that revolves around, of all things, Aperture Science. I don't know what the Croteam guys have in relation to Valve, other than perhaps being fans, but it was pretty awesome nonetheless. However, I'd only unlocked five stars by the end and I suspect there's many more to find. Probably around 25 or so. I also read all the "local resources" that you find at computer terminals. Who knows, but you could probably speed run the game in half the time I spent absorbing it all.
But don't speed run this. This game is fantastic and deserves a bit of your time to immerse yourself in. Not just the puzzles, but the story, the atmosphere and the many, many secrets scattered around this wonderfully realised world.
Couldn't recommend it enough.

If Arma 3 always was too inaccessible for you, but Bf4, Cod way too casual. You do enjoy games like RO2 or Insurgency or you are interested getting into more "serious/mature" gaming. This is the game you are looking for.
Squad offers some gameplay that you won't get anywhere else. Intense fire fights and teamplay with a great soundscape and decent graphics. There is a strong focus on "authentic" military gameplay, but without sacrificing playability. Meaning you can't take a lot of hits and have to work as a team to be successful, but you don't need a college degree to join the game or use any assets/kits in game. The game is all about combined arms warfare ("infantry-in-squads" focus with all kinds of ground and aerial vehicles planned or soon to be finished/implemented).
Admittedly this game has a certain learning curve (especially leading a squad) but its basics are still pretty easy to learn and enjoy. There are always people willing to introduce you to the game (just use the VoIP to ask for some advice). If you have any further questions, you can always head over to the official forums
.
In terms of graphics you could compare it to Arma 3, but as its running on UE4 it just runs way better for most of the people out there (there are some engine related problems with AMD CPUs at the moment).
You definitely don’t need the latest high-end hardware to run this game properly.
The gun/explosion sounds are very atmospheric and kept authentic.
I can recommend this game without any doubt that it’s going to be an even greater experience when its finished than it already is!
Don't bother buying the game if:
•	you are not into teamplay (don't lone wolf, always join a squad)
•	you have no microphone or do not know how to use it (there is a great in game VoIP, don't be shy)
•	you can't sit tight, defending a flag for several minutes (happens every single round)
•	you always have to rush in (you will die)
•	you think your aiming and shooting skills will give you the upper hand in every situation (correlates to lone wolf)
•	you can't follow simply orders (sounds harsh, but it’s not that bad)
•	you like trolling or destroying the experience for others by wasting team assets, ghosting etc.

College days, year 2000... I played this game for hours and hours when I should have been studying.  There were at least four of us who played constantly with each other and made our own scenarios...  Simply put, I think Age2 set the standard for what a real time strategy game should be.  Plenty of civs across eras to choose from, each with their own strengths and weaknesses.  The HD remaster changes little, but makes for a more smooth gameplay than I remember. Menus are the same as well. Additionally, after such a long progression in time, an expansion was made for this HD edition that adds more civs, AI, and content to an already great game. Word is that yet another expansion is to be released in the future as well. One negative I will add, however, as it is a negative I had with the original Age2 as well, is that stone mines still hold less amounts than the gold mines and are just as scarce as they have always been, even more so on some of the newer style maps... It would be nice if they addressed it so at the very least they appeared and contained as much as the gold mines. Highly recomended with much replay value.

This game is simply amazing with its engaging and brain-tingling puzzles. It will make your head spin a couple of times, but the "A-ha!" moments are the best, better than in Portal. In fact, I would argue that it is better than Portal in many ways. First of all, the multi-tier story is more mysterious and intriguing, the levels are HUGE, the secrets actually play a role in discovering even more levels, and the variety of instruments you unlock as you advance through puzzles is much better than just the companion cube and portal gun variety,
In brief, you have three main stages (A - Greco-Roman Antiquity, B - Egyptian Antiquity, C - Middle Ages), each with its own 7 levels of puzzles. They are all connected in a limbo-like environment with a huge tower at the center that an ominous voice from the sky claiming to be God tells you not to climb.
As you solve puzzles in each of the three stages (can be done at random, but they are interdependent), you collect tetris pieces to open new puzzle areas and unlock new solving equipment (connectors, jammers, cubes, fans, platforms) which grant you access to more complex puzzles.
Once you solve all stages the voice will invite you to join him in eternal life by walking through a door of light in the lobby of stage C, but I recommend you wait and instead collect those secret, hard to reach stars, which will grant you access to secret levels in each stage, where you collect special tetris pieces to unlock levels in the Tower.
So basically there are two exits out of the game world: either through the door of light in stage C after completing all main puzzles, or through the top of the tower after unlocking all secrets. Each option has its promise: eternal life from the Creator, or enlightmentment by trial at the top of the tower. I suspect the former option is bogus, so I will strive to reach the top of the tower.  :)

I have been playing for over 3 years now, created YouTube content for 2 of them and I am still in love with this game. Planetside 2 brings unprecedented size of fights to the FPS front, in a format that challenges battlefields joint combat arms set up. You might see hundreds of tanks come over a hill whilst infantry spill through a valley as bombers and fighters weave through flak in the air. Which all happens on a huge continent sized map with no transitional borders. This just isn't possible in any other games to date. But it is not just that Planetside 2 is a one of a kind game that makes it good. The tank gameplay, FPS mechanics and flying are all enjoyable in their own right. And the variation in each loadout can give birth to a wide style of play that can keep you playing for a long time.Oh and did I mention it was free? The weapons are all side grades and almost everything you can buy with money you can also grind as a new player, so forget calling pay to win. It is a little rough around the edges, with patches occasionally breaking the game, but that seems thematic with most MMO games. But a big plus of being an MMO is the outfits and faction chatter that can also immerse you not just in the battlefield but the community, which other shooters don't have. So if you want to play a game that actually feels like a battlefield, then I would 100% recommend Planetside 2 to you.

Two years ago I would have definitley recomended this game. Fun gameplay, fun to design your own robots, yada yada. The only issue back then was optimization: things would get exceptionally laggy if there was alot going on in one area. Nowadays, the game is fantastically optimized, but you can not progress. For playing a match, you are rewarded with crates of parts (four or less), and depending on how you performed during the match, your crate is better or worse. So here is a fun for instanse: you are on a team that is suffereing, and it goes on for a good while. You are the top performer, getting kills out the♥♥♥♥♥ but your team still loses. Lets say the match lasted 10-15 minutes, ok?  Guess what! You get the second to worst crate of parts you can! Even though you did really well, and you wasted 15 minutes.
Rewards go something like -
Winning Team
1st - Protonium Crate (best crate)
2nd - Diamond Crate (second best)
3rd - Gold Crate (third best)
4th-8th - Silver Crate (fourth best)
Losing Team (not totally sure if I am correct, but I am close)
1st-4th - Bronze Crate (fifth best)
5th-8th - Rusty Crate (worst)
Now this may seem fair, except you being the best on your team when you lose could have more points than some of the enemy team, yet you get♥♥♥♥♥♥for reward.
Basically, this game is only fun to win, and it absolutely sucks to lose. If you win, of course its great. If you lose, it sucks doubly; for one, you don't get rewards, so you can't upgrade your bot to perform better, and second, because you can't upgrade, you are stuck with a lesser bot doomed to perform poorly.

Honestly this game should have blown up by now. I'll give you a few reasons as to why:
Pros
- NOT PTW.
- Balanced combat. No one person is better then another, it's all on your playstyle and how you use them.
- Loadouts. Or more accurately, loadout cards. Every one can be earned though random drops (much like a cs:go case) but requires nothing special to unlock it.
- Face paced combat reminiscent of Brink (To me at least) with parkour like movement when it comes to jumping.
- Classes or characters with each to their own special abilities and weapons. All of which can be earned and used though the weekly hero preview
- Little to no hackers
- Cannot stress enough that everything that makes up gameplay advantages CAN be earned.
Cons
- A little wonky to queue with friends for public matches.
- Unfortunately not always the best servers. High ping in some or just bad netcode, either one.
- A bit of a grind to unlock heroes. Not impossible but still a fair amount of time.
- Limited maps, still in "beta" even though it's been out for quite some time. I'd love to see more map selection.
- Not overly small playerbase but not exactly large. In lower level lobbies you can find the uncommon empty lobby or near empty.
Personally I find if this game did add more content like maps or whatnot this game would of the best FTP shooters out there without a doubt.
Overall I would strongly recommend this game to anyone who likes fast paced and class based combat.

The audio is out of sync during cutscenes, and texture popping is horrendous. Some objects in the game don't even render until you're right next to them - including enemies.
I spent hours researching fixes to these performance issues. Many people are having the same complaints, but every fix I tried did nothing to help. I've concluded that I am unable to play this game on my computer and I have wasted my money.
Do not waste your money unless you have an extremely high performance desktop that FAR surpasses the posted "minimum requirements"

I have been playing FPS games since Doom first came out, and I have to say that in comparison to every other shooter that I have played, the gameplay in Max Payne 3 is truly disgusting.  Rarely will you ever come across repetitive tedious hard labour as hideous as this.
The occassional bug that lets you fall thru the floor or get trapped in a wall comes as a refreshing break in the horrid mix of broken gameplay and cut-scenes which take away any weapon upgrades you have fought hard to achieve, either by switching you back to the single hand gun or simply removing all other weapons from your inventory, leaving you wondering why you worked so hard to get other weapons and ammo supplies, or even why they were dangled there to temp you in the first place.
The most horrid aspect of fighting in MP3 would have to be this "last man standing" feature which takes away all control in a gun fight and forces you to target on a single enemy who has dealt you a mighty blow, and somehow you are supposed to enjoy suddenly ripping your attention away from the fierce battle that had your full attention, and shoot just one enemy in slow motion, if you can, before dying.  Personally I would prefer if the game let me just do my own thing in a battle, and if I am hit with a killing shot then so be it.  Let me use my meds and battle sense to do it my way.  Last-man-standing is probably the most hateful feature I have ever encountered in a game.  Have I missed a feature that lets me turn that off?
The greatest wonder I am left with is WHY I have spent so much time trying to complete this game and why I have not simply deleted all traces of it from my pooter.

Honestly this game should have blown up by now. I'll give you a few reasons as to why:
Pros
- NOT PTW.
- Balanced combat. No one person is better then another, it's all on your playstyle and how you use them.
- Loadouts. Or more accurately, loadout cards. Every one can be earned though random drops (much like a cs:go case) but requires nothing special to unlock it.
- Face paced combat reminiscent of Brink (To me at least) with parkour like movement when it comes to jumping.
- Classes or characters with each to their own special abilities and weapons. All of which can be earned and used though the weekly hero preview
- Little to no hackers
- Cannot stress enough that everything that makes up gameplay advantages CAN be earned.
Cons
- A little wonky to queue with friends for public matches.
- Unfortunately not always the best servers. High ping in some or just bad netcode, either one.
- A bit of a grind to unlock heroes. Not impossible but still a fair amount of time.
- Limited maps, still in "beta" even though it's been out for quite some time. I'd love to see more map selection.
- Not overly small playerbase but not exactly large. In lower level lobbies you can find the uncommon empty lobby or near empty.
Personally I find if this game did add more content like maps or whatnot this game would of the best FTP shooters out there without a doubt.
Overall I would strongly recommend this game to anyone who likes fast paced and class based combat.

While the Talos Principle may not be up to Valve's level of complete quality when it comes to Portal 1/2, The Talos Principle is a very good first-person puzzler with an interestingly-enough story to keep you driving towards the end.  The quick concept is that you are working through 3 worlds with a total of about 100 puzzles to solve while learning the rules of the strange world that you have found yourself in.
The puzzle elements are sufficiently different from Portal or other similar games to be fresh enough, and for those that were more spatially challenged by Portal's puzzles will find that those in Talos are much more two-dimensional. Elements like the use of the light connectors to create virtual circuits and using a recording of your actions create some more interesting challenges. One factor that I will warn about is where Valve is well noted for developing Portal with the concepts of "platform learning", carefully bulding puzzles that guide you carefully in the use of all the tools, Talos is a lot less hand-holding, at least after the first few puzzles.  Not that they don't try to guide, but it stumbles in some areas as where Valve has it perfected. But all this likely means is that you should not get too stumped on any one puzzle, and instead  work on others; as the narrative voice mentions, you might learn more in other puzzles that can be brought back into earlier ones. As such, only about 4-5 puzzles I found to be difficult until I figured out the right trick.  But one thing is true for Talos as it is for Portal - there was a deep satisfaction in discovering the solutions to puzzles on my own, and that's why I'd definitely recommend the game.
Add in the promise of future legit campaigns, and Workshop ability, and Talos looks like it has a good long tail, making it well worth the price.

Written at 12/10/2015, five days before early access to public.
Before I start, I just wanted to tell you that the predecessor of Squad is a mod based on Battlefield 2 called Project Reality, it features ground combined arms combat, aerial warfare which includes helicopter and jets, and small portion of naval warfare. The overall ideology of this mod is to create a team-based tactical shooter game that looking towards to some degree of realism. I'm not gonna talk too much about PR here, this is just a peek on where Squad is heading to.
So let us go back to Squad. So far Squad only features infantry combat, ground light vehicles will be available within most likely a month, so my review will only focus on the infantry combat for now.
This game is all about tactical cooperation and sticking together as a SQUAD while obeying orders from your squad leader. It goes so far that not only it encourages you to stay with the squad, you will get penalites from being a lone wolf.
For example, not join a squad will limit your select-able kit to basic rifleman,  dynamic role limitation system(or whatever it's actually called) allows you to choose from more kits progressively if certain number of players is in your squad and your team, and if you decided to go for getting the kits you want from other squad and quit then good for you, because the game will take away your kit at the moment you left and re-assign you with a "recruit" kit with the ammo you left before you quit the squad. Without a squad you can easily get pinned down and killed from enemy gun fire while no one can help you out.
This game binds players together so tie that even you don't know each other you can still play as a squad and win the game easily, and that's the whole point of realistic tactical shooter game isn't it?
Though it's only in Early Access with just infantry combat for a large scale FPS, and it does have many many incomplete and unpolished aspects (such as animation glitch, spawn glitch, FOB camping, etc.), irritating bugs exist here and there (medical reviving is buggy as fxxk which includes not properly located, teleporting fallen one to nowhere when getting them up, etc.) But it does find a well balance between realism and gameplay as its predecessor PR, you can't hide a shinning gem like Squad from anything.

I've been a Max Payne fan since the day the first game in the series was released back in 2001. I approached Max Payne 3 with caution and without high expectations, because I already assumed that Rockstar won't capture the specific atmosphere that made the previous installments shine. The game did not disappoint. The new setting (no more snowy nights in shady places) is figurative to the transition of Max Payne - a character we are given deep insight into, as Max comments bitterly on nearly everything that happens around him. The gameplay itself is tight, shooting mechanics and destructible environments make every firefight quite an experience, looking like it was an action movie sequence. The story gets a bit predictable midway through, but strong writing pushes it forward. Beside single-player (15-20 hours, depending how fast one plays, I was taking things slow) campaign, the game offers a lot of content to keep players occupied; there are time trials, collectibles and a very solid and intense multiplayer, which feature an intriguing choice of special abilities as well as different kinds of weapons. Overall, Max Payne 3 is a very solid game. Recommended.

This game is absolutely incredible and I recommend it to anyone who enjoys puzzles, exploration, deep/complex stories, and more. Let's look at what makes this game so enjoyable:
Graphics: This is the first thing you're going to notice when you start the game...so how are they? Quite honestly, they're pretty darn good. They most certainly get the job done and immerse you into the mysterious world you're exploring. Additionally, weather/lighting effects really jazz up the environment while you're solving puzzles.
Gameplay: You're going to be solving puzzles. Lots of them. If you're a fan of this particular genre, you'll love it. There are a ton of elements that come into play slowly and gradually. Lasers, boxes, keys, jammers, fans, time manipulation...the list goes on and on. You won't be dealing with all of these elements right off the bat, however. The game does a wonderful job pacing itself and introducing you to each element thoroughly before moving on. It doesn't hold your hand though...you need to figure things out on your own ;) Exploration is important as well, if you wish to uncover the story or find all of the side content available (there's a ton of it).
Content: The amount of content in this game is enormous. you essentially have 4 buildings packed with puzzles. At first, you'll only have access to the first. As you complete puzzles, you obtain these things called 'sigils' (basically tetris pieces). You use these to unlock new areas. Once you collect a set of 'sigils', you put the pieces in a lock, and solve this little rectangular puzzle by arranging the pieces so they fit together. These 'sigil locks' unlock everything from new buildings to more puzzle elements, and are your key to getting around. You can also collect stars, which are typically harder to obtain than sigils, to unlock some extra, harder puzzles. There are other secrets to be found too; keep your eyes open!
Story: The story is very interesting and told in a unique way. It's very philosophical in nature, and will leave you thinking as much as the puzzles themselves do. The game tells this story through a few different ways; first, ELOHIM, basically god, a talking voice in the sky. Next, computer terminals. You talk to an AI and try to uncover documents and emails that reveal more to the world. Finally, there are voice recordings scattered around as well. It's really fun to piece together this story, and I never felt it was tedious or boring.
Overall, I can't really think of one complaint for this game. It's brilliant, and honestly surprising it came from the creators of Serious Sam. I love how mysterious the story is, and how philosophical it is. I love how tight and smooth the gameplay is; something absolutely imperitive, especially in puzzle games. I love how much content there is in this game, and how many secrets you can find while exploring the beautiful world(s). I love it all, and hopefully you do too!

Normally I'd wait for at least one full playthrough before choosing to recommend a game, or not as the case may be. But The Talos Principle receives an early, wholehearted recommendation with a game that I can't wait to see to it's completion.
Portal is the obvious immediate comparison both in its puzzle solving but also the intrigue in what's behind the puzzles and the world that's been created. Why are you here? What are you? Why are you solving puzzles in Greek and Egyption ruins?
It's intriguing and I feel like you'd be doing the game a disservice if you ignore the text(s) you can read and just steamroller through the puzzles.
Speaking of which, the puzzles seem to find that sweet spot between too easy and too hard, where some you'll solve quickly and others will be left with you scratching your head. Irrespective, finding the solution will make you feel clever and this is the sign of a puzzle game with a good sweet spot.
Unless things take a very unexpected turn for the worse from this point on, I would definitely recommned this for anyone that's a fan of puzzle games, loved Portal and like a bit of intrigue and wonder to their games. Those that like moving around in a beautiful envirionment are well catered for too; it's a gorgeous game.
Highly recommended.

TL;DR: Have you ever worked on something where no matter what you did, it would reset, and you spent days doing the exact same step over and over praying that it'd make progress but it never seemed to?  PS2 is like that except there's no hope of moving forward.
I've been trying to play PlanetSide 2 for a long time, but now I've finally got my chance, since my computer is now decent.  I cannot fault the action or character progression.  Both are amazing.
Character progressions is the standard unlock/upgrade with mods system, with boosts only being enough that you'd win a one on one fight, and slow enough that it provides interest in continuing to play.
One on one fights sound like a lot?  I can see that, in pretty much any other FPS.  In this game, if you're getting into 1 on 1 fights, you're playing so wrong.  The game gives you a maximum snipe range of 1,000 meters (but I've only been able to get reasonable kills at 500 meters with the assault rifles).  The long range combat is incredible.
That's not to say one on one fights are unsupported.  There's a class designed for it, Light Assault, which has a jetpack to allow you to sneak ontop of your targets.
This game has mixed arms combat.  As in, the tanks, aircraft, and infantry all have to fight the same battle on the same map, and you can destroy tanks as infantry, or aircraft as a tank, and ect.  This creates an epic feeling when you shoot a rocketeer with a rifle and kill them before they can take out a friendly tank.
So, why don't I recommend this game?  Staff abuse?  Rude community?  Just angry that I'm no good at it?
No.  I don't recommend this game... Because there is no win or lose state.
Seeing as there is only 4 maps in the game, that are all going at once, they don't want players to take over a map and lock their enemy out of that map, as that might make their enemy have a less fun experience.  I can agree and see that.  it'd probably be very common for a faction to get wiped off all maps and thereby prevent their spawning.
If the game had several maps, it'd be near impossible for a faction to get wiped off of all of them, and even then, they could swap to another map.
They don't want to do this.  Instead, the way the game works is only 2 of the 4 continents in the game can be controlled at once.  If another gets taken, it'll unlock one of the previous maps.
So the entire game is just a constant struggle where no one will ever be ahead or behind.
I wouldn't be too upset about this except every thread online I can find about it has people DEFENDING this choice as if it's a good idea!!
It's not a good idea.  It's putting a bandaid over a missing arm.
That said, the gameplay is fun.  If you're 12 years old and like brainlessly shooting people for no reason, it's a good alternative to school shootings.

One of the better Free to Play titles I've seen, not really pay to win as any loadouts above bronze (the third rank) the only improvements are purely for the looks.
You unlock other mercs by earning credits by doing missions that refresh every 3 hours (for example: Earn X amount of support xp)  which earn you 500, 750, or 1000 credits per mission, you also get a base fee based on your playtime.
The crafting system is alright if you don't want cobalt cards, because the cost goes up (both in fragments and credits) ridiculously after silver. You get fragments by recycling other loadout cards based on their rank.
In my opinion the gameplay is extremely fun, different mercs mostly have different playstyles, and you can tweak their playstyles a bit more with different loadout cards.
The maps are well-designed and fun, however there aren't a lot of them. Splash Damage has said they are working on new content after they recently fixed loads of bugs and did a visual overhaul of all the maps, so I remain hopeful.
tl;dr The game is great, especially considering it is free to play. A bit low on content, but it's fun enough that you can get hundreds of hours out of the content that's there.

If Insurgency, Battlefield and Arma had a Child
The better way to describe Squad is a casual military first person shooter with realism elements. Perhaps it's not a diehard simulation like Arma 3, but like Arma 3, the challenge you'll get from Squad, despite it being about as casual as the Battlefield series of games, will keep you coming back for more.
Rich, authentic and downright chilling sound design and detailed environments which explore a range of variety in both scale, terrain type and infrastructure which can and will impact maneuverability of vehicles and foot soldiers.
Projectile arching is very much a thing to realize and compensate for with either firearms, rockets and of course grenades with grenades having an optional underhanded throw for shorter distances for those over-the-fence or out-the-window tosses.
Overpressure from explosions withing confind spaces like building interiors and backblast from rocket launchers exist as well. So even if you're fairly far away from a grenade when it goes off in the same building you're in, you'll still feel it or possibly even die from it. And think twice before firing an RPG inside of a building. Your eyeballs and lungs will explode and you'll also probably end up harming or killing other friendlies inside your building.
Moving is pretty good. The weapon sway/bob is a bit like Battlefield which gets annoying if you fail to work with it. But movement is pretty solid. This makes firing while absolutely stationary being the ideal position to fire from.
And keep in mind for this next body of text, there're differences between walking, jogging and sprinting. Jogging being the default speed which isn't stamina intensive.
Like sprinting, jumping requires stamina too and consumes stamina based on how many times you jump over a short period of time. This also limits how much you can jump as you need stamina for both sprinting and jumping. Although there is a key for switching between jogging and walking, there's almost no difference from what I can tell. I think walking increases the amount of stamina regenerated while still moving, but by an extremely small amount. Jogging from left to right is much slower than jogging back and forth but I guess it helps with clearing around corners with your sights up.
Moving up and down ladders in Squad is the most intuitive ladder mechanic I've ever seen in any game. Just walk into a ladder to go up and walk backwards to go down. Or vice-versa if you're turned around.
Moving around while prone is pretty cool. You always have  your weapon pointed outward and ready to fire like you would actually be able to do by crawling on your opposite forearm as your forward method of movement.
The communication is terrifically crisp and audible with a realistic radio audio filter slapped on for authenticity and immersion. Individual squad leaders can communicate with each other while the lower ranking soldiers are only able to communicate with their designated squad leader and vice-versa.
If you want the scale, infantry combat, communication and minor simulated elements of Arma, the sound quality, ease of movement and weapon aspects such as backblast of Insurgency and the casual accessibility and gameplay of Battleifeld then this is your game.
And it doesn't look half bad to boot! Unreal Engine 4 is quite pretty.

I think this game is good if you love FPS games and a well written story.
This doesn't mean the game is without flaws, but in my opinion it's well worth the investment.
Let me list a couple of pros and cons (fairly subjective) so you can see for yourself if you would like this game or not.
Pros:
- Great graphics and atmosphere
- Storyline is very well written, with nice use of flash-backs (as game chapters)
- Bullet-time is still as fun as ever!
- The game as a whole feels solid, it's not overly long, but certainly long enough on your first play-through
Cons:
- Aiming could have been a little better (example: when running, you can't look up or down)
- Grinds (achievements) can be a drag
- Once the story is complete, there's nothing new (the story is linear)
- Some problems with crashing between cut-scenes and some scenes you can't skip (which is a nuisance in some modes)
Personally, I'm not a big fan of multiplayer in this game, it doesn't "feel" right with the controls/aiming that this game uses, but you might have a different opinion on this.
Bottom-line: I'd recommend getting this game, maybe wait for a sale so you can get all the DLC to get all your achievements.

If you don't trust Early Access titles, then this game may change your mind. I can honestly say that I have NEVER in my time playing Early Access games, seen a developer team that works so closely with the community, and even comes on the servers and plays with every one and asks questions and makes sure that the communities voice has been heard. But to get down to an actual review of the game, here goes.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay for it being an alpha early access game is PHENOMENAL, the firefights that you get into are intense, and really get your blood flowing. The game is so well designed that from the standpoint of gameplay, you actually gain a sense of fear before assaulting a compound, or hearing footsteps outside a wall unsure if it is a friendly or not, and being unwilling to check your map for fear of potentially getting shot. The in-game comms are very well done, Local positional voice, Squad voice, and Squad leader voice (For SLs talking amongst other squads). The medical system is an ever changing system, but it is also a system that works, and it works damn well. The weapon handling is fantastic, it really emphasizes not blasting full auto, unless of course you are in a CQB situation then it works perfectly fine. Fob building is great as well, clear images of what is going to be there once it has been built by squadmates, and what direction it faces. Overall, coming from Project Reality myself, the gameplay for Squad gets a solid 10/10 from me.
AUDIO
Honestly, I have never heard a military shooter with such crisp audio. From the footsteps of friendly and enemy soldiers, to the supersonic crack of a bullet flying passed your head. Nothing in my opinion beats Squads audio team and I really commend them for doing all the research they can to get the sounds as close to what they are in real life. The weapon sounds are crisp, clear, and sound powerful. Not like other games where they sound like peashooters. The death screams are a nice touch, and help with identifying allies that have gone down and need a medic and confirming kills. The music score in the main menu is also phenomenal, it really brings to life the thought of being sent to a warzone and not knowing if your squad is going to make it, although the music isn't featured in the actual gameplay, it's a welcome and very well done touch to the main menu.
GRAPHICS
The graphics are a huge step-up from Project Reality. I've played games like Arma 3/2 and before that, I've also played the entire battlefield series (but stuck with BF2), and countless other games that are very intense when it comes to graphics. Squads graphics in some aspects are some of the best I have seen. From the backblast of an RPG or LAW, to the actual explosion of hand grenades, 40mm grenades, or the warheads from the LAW/RPG they are fantastic to watch and truly a sight to see, and gives a sense of danger when you see this huge cloud of smoke land just feet away from you as you are taking cover behind a wall waiting for your moment to break cover and return fire. The player models are always being updated, with the new Russian, Militia, and the Insurgent factions getting a welcome makeover since I started playing in September. The Americans are due for a makeover as well, but this will come in due time.
CONTROLS
Unlike the Arma series, Squad doesn't feel even close to as clunky as arma, but offers the same range of movement(Save for free look which is a possibility in the future). It offers a rich and rewarding movement system that causes you to think before you make an action as the momentum of your soldier is what propels you towards the direction you are facing, unlike games like Battlefield 2/3/4 where it feels like you're constantly sliding around with a constant momentum in either direction where you can turn on a dime and get a headshot. Squad isn't a milsim, but it also isn't a twitch shooter, and it really finds it's balance by bringing the two together and taking the good parts from both, while getting rid of the bad parts as well as incorporating a lot of the phenomenal things that Project Reality has done.
TEAMPLAY
I'm going to say it simple, and blunt. If you DON'T communicate with your squad/team, you WILL fail. I play in a highly organized clan where we are all comfortable with each other, and understand each other. We know what is expected of us from our Squad Leaders, and the #1 thing that you can, and have to do to be successful, is LISTEN to your squad leader and COMMUNICATE what is going on around you. Giving valuable information such as enemy movement in a certain direction (0 to 345, 0 being 360), letting your squad leader know when you have stumbled upon an enemy FOB, or even letting the medics know you've been tagged and need medical attention. I cannot stress enough how valuable communication and teamwork is in this game, working as an effective squad where that squad is helping the team will make or break your experience.
All in all, I recommend squad 110% the game took my breath away from the moment I stepped on the sandy hills of Logar pressing through hostile fire coming from the central village, or stepped into the deep desert valley of Kohat. Now with the addition of Fool's Road, I can add the intensity it was when we had three squads all communicating together storming up the side of a steep hill, to overtake an enemy FOB and release the capture point from their possession. If you pass up the opportunity to buy and play this game, I guarantee that you will regret it, Squad has been the best money I have spent on a game in a long time and I couldn't be happier. To give you some perspective on what I mean by teamwork, here is a link to a video I recorded tonight (2015-12-14) that should shed some light on what it's like to really play as a team.
The game takes time to learn. There are bugs yes, but the game is still in early development and the developers are very active in the community and do their best to fix every bug they can find before the next build update. With regards to the learning curve, it's not as steep as Armas learning curve, and it's designed so that the average FPS player can hop in and start playing basically. But, there are still concepts that are not present in other FPS games, like listening to your squad leader and doing what he says, building FOBs, taking defensive positions etc. The game isn't about rushing in and trying to get the most kills, it's about playing as a team, moving as a team, and making sure everyone is ready in your squad before moving in to attack.
There aren't any bugs in the game that are gamebreaking, AMD users have a bit of trouble playing, but that's not completely on the devs side, that has to do with Unreal Engine 4 not really liking AMD processors and graphics cards. I myself have a Core i5-3570k and a GTX 970 and I usually get between 40 and 50 fps right now while recording video. To end the final edit on this review, the game is great, it's still in alpha and being developed by only 30 people, now for 30 people to do something like this, it's amazing. When you get a company like EA/DiCE who have hundreds of developers at their disposal, and they still turn out a bad game (E.g. Battlefront, Battlefield 4, Battlefield Hardline etc) or Treyarch/activision (Call of duty games = same thing every year no real ingenuity) then what exactly are those devs doing to make sure they put out a good game? Anyways, YMMV with this game, but it's up to the individual to decide whether or not this is the game for them.
I chose to replace the original video with one that shows what you will see more of in Squad. This is what you will experience 95% of the time while playing. Or at least what I have experienced 95% of the time while playing.
A must have, no questions asked.

(Disclaimer: This game used to not be on Steam and ran off its own launcher; thus, I have more hours on the game than what it states here.)
As the spiritual successor to Project Reality, this game surpasses the mod it was largely inspired by. The gameplay is extremely intense, and you often find yourself ambushed or getting pinned down while trying to capture one of the objectives. The suppression mechanic in this game is not overbearing like the one in Red Orchestra 2, and it adds a nice feel of urgency and stress to gunfights. If you've played Project Reality, a lot of the mechanics like healing, grenade launchers, and spawning will be very familiar.
For those that have not played Project Reality, you spawn through rally points or forward operations bases that squad leaders are able to put on the map. In addition, squad leaders can build various types of fortifications that require players to build them. Other features like grenade launchers, rocket launchers, grenades, and smoke grenades are self explanatory.
As for the gameplay itself, it requires coordination and teamwork to win the game. Unlike most shooters in the market, you cannot lone wolf and spawn willy-nilly unless you want to run your team's tickets down. Instead, you have to work together with your squad leaders and other squad members to be effective. Gun damage has weight, and one to three shots can end you within a moments notice.
Sqaud members can communicate with each other over squad radio, and sqaud leaders can communicate to each other over a sqaud leader to squad leader radio channel. All players can communicate to each other over a local voice chat as well. In addition, there is a squad, team, and global text chat players can use, but a mic is the best option when playing this game.
At the writing of this review, there are four teams: the U.S. Army, the Russian Army, a Russian militia force known as Militia, and the Insurgents, who are the game's equivalent of the Taliban. Each team has a unique array of weapons, and each weapon spawns in a different variant, whether it be its camo or variant (i.e. an AKMS when you select AKM). As of right now, there are no vehicles, but humvees, tanks, and planes are planned, as well as more factions and weapons (U.S. Marines and the M16 gun family).
The people currently playing the game (donators) have all been polite, willing to work as a team, and fun to play with. There have been only a few instances where people have been rude or unresponsive, but every game has its bad apples. To top it off, the devs are very active with the game, and I have often been in servers with them.
All in all, if you ever wanted a game that is hybrid of Project Reality, Insurgency, and ARMA, this is the game to go with. Squad is a great game, working together and killing enemies has a certain satisfcation to it, and this game will only get better as time goes by. It is one of those rare Early Access games that will fulfill the potential it has.

Believe the hype. Believe the 10/10 net reviews. They are the truth.
I hadn't heard of The Talos Principle and frankly can't remember where I heard of it. I think the PC Gamer RSS feed. No matter. I'll be the first to admit that puzzle games aren't in any way my genre of preference - I'm much more likely to be found playing games such as Unreal Tournament, Mechwarrior Online or a hard-core flight sim. Puzzle games, until now, really haven't captured my imagination or interest.
The thing that drew me to the Talos Principle was the notion that it combined a puzzle game, and a beautifully rendered one at that, with notions of the meaning of intelligence, the question of how "life" can be defined, what "artificial intelligence" would look like. I have a keen interest in philosophy, something that the reviews stated was very much at the center of the Talos Principle. So, I decided to take the plunge and I'm *extremely* glad that I did so.
The game is beautifully presented. The Serious engine (as in the FPS game Serious Sam) presents a very nicely rendered world. Each of the puzzles is set in themed ancient Roman, ancient Greek or medieval settings. Having recently spent a week in Rome the ancient Roman themed portions were very familiar and very well representative of ancient Roman remains.
The puzzles themselves ramp up very well in terms of difficulty, with early ones being very simple to solve. Later puzzles and in particular special puzzles that grant access to bonus areas can be absolutely fiendish. That being said, unlike most puzzle games I've never given up in disgusted frustration - the puzzles and tools that you unlock to assist you are intuitive enough to make you want to solve the puzzle to progress or to unlock more of the thematic content.
Speaking of which, this game is superbly grounded in philosophy, well presented themes from science fiction and indeed theology. Far from being a simple solve-this-puzzle-then-on-to-the-next, this game makes the player really think about such questions as who they are (in game), what they are and whether you are in fact merely a metaphorical rat in a maze. It should be noted that the game absolutely does not require any knowledge of philosophy or sci-fi tropes, but if you are familiar with the concepts developed by the likes of Soren Kierkegaard, Lev Shestov, Carl Sagan or A.C. Clark the game is absolutely that much more immersive and enjoyable.
I'm really, really impressed by the Talos Principle on many different levels. This is one of the most intelligently designed and presented games I've ever had the pleasure of playing. Everything from the graphics, quality of the voice acting, in-game presentation, music, even the controlls have obviously been developed with a lot of thought.
Bored of yet another generic, mindless, so-called "AAA blockbuster" game that was identical to the last 5? Give this game a try, you'll be amazed and impressed by how fun it is to play and perhaps more importantly how it makes you really think.
Absolutely 10/10. Unhesitatingly recommended.

After watching the trailers and after taking a look at the screenshots

NO cutscenes, NO all knowing narrator !

As other users pointed out, it is a very philosophical story which wants you to think by yourself rather than presenting you with a solution.
But even if you are not interested in this kind of stuff, don't worry. You can still solve puzzles without knowing anything about the world you live in.
Presentation:
Graphics are okay but I don't think that anyone plays this kind of game because of how good it looks. ;)
The only thing I don't really like are some invisible barriers around certain walls which prevent you from climbing them, even if they look like you could jump on them.  Which can be quite frustrating if you have an idea on how to get somewhere but it just doesn't work. ToT
Summary:
All in all a solid 8/10 from me, which is quite alot.^^

If you don't trust Early Access titles, then this game may change your mind. I can honestly say that I have NEVER in my time playing Early Access games, seen a developer team that works so closely with the community, and even comes on the servers and plays with every one and asks questions and makes sure that the communities voice has been heard. But to get down to an actual review of the game, here goes.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay for it being an alpha early access game is PHENOMENAL, the firefights that you get into are intense, and really get your blood flowing. The game is so well designed that from the standpoint of gameplay, you actually gain a sense of fear before assaulting a compound, or hearing footsteps outside a wall unsure if it is a friendly or not, and being unwilling to check your map for fear of potentially getting shot. The in-game comms are very well done, Local positional voice, Squad voice, and Squad leader voice (For SLs talking amongst other squads). The medical system is an ever changing system, but it is also a system that works, and it works damn well. The weapon handling is fantastic, it really emphasizes not blasting full auto, unless of course you are in a CQB situation then it works perfectly fine. Fob building is great as well, clear images of what is going to be there once it has been built by squadmates, and what direction it faces. Overall, coming from Project Reality myself, the gameplay for Squad gets a solid 10/10 from me.
AUDIO
Honestly, I have never heard a military shooter with such crisp audio. From the footsteps of friendly and enemy soldiers, to the supersonic crack of a bullet flying passed your head. Nothing in my opinion beats Squads audio team and I really commend them for doing all the research they can to get the sounds as close to what they are in real life. The weapon sounds are crisp, clear, and sound powerful. Not like other games where they sound like peashooters. The death screams are a nice touch, and help with identifying allies that have gone down and need a medic and confirming kills. The music score in the main menu is also phenomenal, it really brings to life the thought of being sent to a warzone and not knowing if your squad is going to make it, although the music isn't featured in the actual gameplay, it's a welcome and very well done touch to the main menu.
GRAPHICS
The graphics are a huge step-up from Project Reality. I've played games like Arma 3/2 and before that, I've also played the entire battlefield series (but stuck with BF2), and countless other games that are very intense when it comes to graphics. Squads graphics in some aspects are some of the best I have seen. From the backblast of an RPG or LAW, to the actual explosion of hand grenades, 40mm grenades, or the warheads from the LAW/RPG they are fantastic to watch and truly a sight to see, and gives a sense of danger when you see this huge cloud of smoke land just feet away from you as you are taking cover behind a wall waiting for your moment to break cover and return fire. The player models are always being updated, with the new Russian, Militia, and the Insurgent factions getting a welcome makeover since I started playing in September. The Americans are due for a makeover as well, but this will come in due time.
CONTROLS
Unlike the Arma series, Squad doesn't feel even close to as clunky as arma, but offers the same range of movement(Save for free look which is a possibility in the future). It offers a rich and rewarding movement system that causes you to think before you make an action as the momentum of your soldier is what propels you towards the direction you are facing, unlike games like Battlefield 2/3/4 where it feels like you're constantly sliding around with a constant momentum in either direction where you can turn on a dime and get a headshot. Squad isn't a milsim, but it also isn't a twitch shooter, and it really finds it's balance by bringing the two together and taking the good parts from both, while getting rid of the bad parts as well as incorporating a lot of the phenomenal things that Project Reality has done.
TEAMPLAY
I'm going to say it simple, and blunt. If you DON'T communicate with your squad/team, you WILL fail. I play in a highly organized clan where we are all comfortable with each other, and understand each other. We know what is expected of us from our Squad Leaders, and the #1 thing that you can, and have to do to be successful, is LISTEN to your squad leader and COMMUNICATE what is going on around you. Giving valuable information such as enemy movement in a certain direction (0 to 345, 0 being 360), letting your squad leader know when you have stumbled upon an enemy FOB, or even letting the medics know you've been tagged and need medical attention. I cannot stress enough how valuable communication and teamwork is in this game, working as an effective squad where that squad is helping the team will make or break your experience.
All in all, I recommend squad 110% the game took my breath away from the moment I stepped on the sandy hills of Logar pressing through hostile fire coming from the central village, or stepped into the deep desert valley of Kohat. Now with the addition of Fool's Road, I can add the intensity it was when we had three squads all communicating together storming up the side of a steep hill, to overtake an enemy FOB and release the capture point from their possession. If you pass up the opportunity to buy and play this game, I guarantee that you will regret it, Squad has been the best money I have spent on a game in a long time and I couldn't be happier. To give you some perspective on what I mean by teamwork, here is a link to a video I recorded tonight (2015-12-14) that should shed some light on what it's like to really play as a team.
The game takes time to learn. There are bugs yes, but the game is still in early development and the developers are very active in the community and do their best to fix every bug they can find before the next build update. With regards to the learning curve, it's not as steep as Armas learning curve, and it's designed so that the average FPS player can hop in and start playing basically. But, there are still concepts that are not present in other FPS games, like listening to your squad leader and doing what he says, building FOBs, taking defensive positions etc. The game isn't about rushing in and trying to get the most kills, it's about playing as a team, moving as a team, and making sure everyone is ready in your squad before moving in to attack.
There aren't any bugs in the game that are gamebreaking, AMD users have a bit of trouble playing, but that's not completely on the devs side, that has to do with Unreal Engine 4 not really liking AMD processors and graphics cards. I myself have a Core i5-3570k and a GTX 970 and I usually get between 40 and 50 fps right now while recording video. To end the final edit on this review, the game is great, it's still in alpha and being developed by only 30 people, now for 30 people to do something like this, it's amazing. When you get a company like EA/DiCE who have hundreds of developers at their disposal, and they still turn out a bad game (E.g. Battlefront, Battlefield 4, Battlefield Hardline etc) or Treyarch/activision (Call of duty games = same thing every year no real ingenuity) then what exactly are those devs doing to make sure they put out a good game? Anyways, YMMV with this game, but it's up to the individual to decide whether or not this is the game for them.

(Disclaimer: This game used to not be on Steam and ran off its own launcher; thus, I have more hours on the game than what it states here.)
As the spiritual successor to Project Reality, this game surpasses the mod it was largely inspired by. The gameplay is extremely intense, and you often find yourself ambushed or getting pinned down while trying to capture one of the objectives. The suppression mechanic in this game is not overbearing like the one in Red Orchestra 2, and it adds a nice feel of urgency and stress to gunfights. If you've played Project Reality, a lot of the mechanics like healing, grenade launchers, and spawning will be very familiar.
For those that have not played Project Reality, you spawn through rally points or forward operations bases that squad leaders are able to put on the map. In addition, squad leaders can build various types of fortifications that require players to build them. Other features like grenade launchers, rocket launchers, grenades, and smoke grenades are self explanatory.
As for the gameplay itself, it requires coordination and teamwork to win the game. Unlike most shooters in the market, you cannot lone wolf and spawn willy-nilly unless you want to run your team's tickets down. Instead, you have to work together with your squad leaders and other squad members to be effective. Gun damage has weight, and one to three shots can end you within a moments notice.
Sqaud members can communicate with each other over squad radio, and sqaud leaders can communicate to each other over a sqaud leader to squad leader radio channel. All players can communicate to each other over a local voice chat as well. In addition, there is a squad, team, and global text chat players can use, but a mic is the best option when playing this game.
At the writing of this review, there are four teams: the U.S. Army, the Russian Army, a Russian militia force known as Militia, and the Insurgents, who are the game's equivalent of the Taliban. Each team has a unique array of weapons, and each weapon spawns in a different variant, whether it be its camo or variant (i.e. an AKMS when you select AKM). As of right now, there are no vehicles, but humvees, tanks, and planes are planned, as well as more factions and weapons (U.S. Marines and the M16 gun family).
The people currently playing the game (donators) have all been polite, willing to work as a team, and fun to play with. There have been only a few instances where people have been rude or unresponsive, but every game has its bad apples. To top it off, the devs are very active with the game, and I have often been in servers with them.
All in all, if you ever wanted a game that is hybrid of Project Reality, Insurgency, and ARMA, this is the game to go with. Squad is a great game, working together and killing enemies has a certain satisfcation to it, and this game will only get better as time goes by. It is one of those rare Early Access games that will fulfill the potential it has.
Definetly worth two dollars even though in my opinion it should cost way more.

Just finished the game and to be honest .... I am impressed. I personally known Croteam as makers of Serious Sam ... run,gun,fun and seeing them joining forces with Tom Jubert (FTL, The Swapper) and Jonas Kyratzes (The Sea Will Claim Everything) to create a PUZZLE GAME was a surprise.
Now I wont be talking about the story since its something that should be experienced though can say that the idea is something like Stanley Parable. Now lets talk about the puzzles.
Your point in the game is to collect sigils(tetronimos) that you later gonna use in puzzles(Sigil of Elohime). There are 3 kinds of sigils serving different purpose: green are needed to unlock areas, orange - unlock tools, red - for the tower(its one of the endings,nugh said).Each area contains 7 islands filled with puzzles that you should solve.You start the game with jammer and with collecting orange sigils you unlock more tools. So on and so forth to the end. Puzzle's difficulty starts low and increases with each area.
If you like reading you can take a look at computer terminals on each island  to reveal more parts of the story in the game. Also in the world you can find time capsules with recorded message also serving part in the story.
And for all hardcore collectors there are stars that are hard to obtain and often requires to link together parts from different puzzles on the island.
Graphics : They are gorgeous and often breathtaking. You may stop doing puzzles for a moment to take a break and look at the environment around you. There are glitches in the texture but they are intentional because they have to remind you that you are in virtual world.
Sound : To be honest ... I was barely noticing it and the reason for that is it was fitting the moments.
There is one thing I didnt like in the game though : the fact that you cant save during puzzles so often you may need to redo something a lot of times until you figure it out.
Overall if you want a tough puzzle game with a great story you need to get this when you can. Else.. move along.

This game is extremely good as a puzzle game. It might be the best puzzle game I've played. I enjoyed playing games like Portal I, Portal II, and Quantum Conundrum, but the Talos Principle is even better in terms of puzzle design. It also mixes in some philosophy surrounding the situation you find yourself in, but that's not the reason to play this game.
The puzzle designs in this game are so expertly done because, despite the large number of puzzles, there are almost no puzzles that are difficult due to shear complexity or obscurity. Despite this fact, the puzzles actually do increase in difficulty to the point of being seriously challenging. It would be trivial to make puzzles increasingly difficult by just making the puzzles more complex or requiring more obscure actions. Instead, The Talos Principle manages to increase in difficulty by constantly requiring the player to think of using previous tools in a new manner.
The most difficult puzzles are far more difficult than what can be found in the other games I mentioned. I was never truly baffled or boggled by any puzzle in Portal I, Portal II, or Quantum Conundrum, but some of the puzzles in The Talos Principle really left me at loss for what to even think about. But the brilliance of the puzzle designs really showed when, once I did figure out the solution, I was never mad. I didn't feel cheated by the solution being something ridiculous, obscure, or overly complex. Instead, it was like witnessing a simple magic trick, wondering how in the world the trick was done, and then having the cleverness of it revealed. If you've ever experienced that, it's not something you get mad at, but something you want to congratulate someone on for being so clever.
The puzzle designs alone make the game worth buying, but some people might also like the philosophical nature of this game. It's pretty clear from the start of the game that you're an AI running inside a computer program along with an AI god figure. A little bit later you can run into an AI serpent figure that tries to make you go against and doubt the AI god. The exact nature of this whole situation is slowly revealed throughout the game, but saying more might spoil that. However, the main reason for all the philosophy is to make you think about what it means to be human and how much the AI character you're playing would think of itself as human. It's not particularly in-depth, and the AI serpent who's driving this philosophical exploration gets annoying very quickly. For nearly every dialogue option you choose in response to the AI serpent, it just resorts to straw man and ad hominem fallacies to argue against what you say. This aspect of the game could have been done much better.
Overall, though, the game is amazing as a puzzle game and I strongly recommend it for that reason alone.

Max Payne, he was a drunken son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ who got dealt a terrible ♥♥♥♥ing hand. The destructive emotion of entropy had not one drop of sympathy for Max Payne. Since the first one to this most recent third game of the series. Max, I would like to think of as a good friend by now (considering what we've gone through), was a man filled with so many conflicting qualities that whether it was in the heat of a slow-motion shootout against paramilitary drug cartels, or, the dreadful conversations with stoned secondary plot characters. That is until the story takes a few twists and turns that end up creating more questions than answers. This left many questions unanswered, and a sense of disappointment at the end. The graphics are most definitely stunning (check out my images, I have many pictures from the game I played through). This game is extremely good as a puzzle game. It might be the best puzzle game I've played. I enjoyed playing games like Portal I, Portal II, and Quantum Conundrum, but the Talos Principle is even better in terms of puzzle design. It also mixes in some philosophy surrounding the situation you find yourself in, but that's not the reason to play this game.
The puzzle designs in this game are so expertly done because, despite the large number of puzzles, there are almost no puzzles that are difficult due to shear complexity or obscurity. Despite this fact, the puzzles actually do increase in difficulty to the point of being seriously challenging. It would be trivial to make puzzles increasingly difficult by just making the puzzles more complex or requiring more obscure actions. Instead, The Talos Principle manages to increase in difficulty by constantly requiring the player to think of using previous tools in a new manner.
The most difficult puzzles are far more difficult than what can be found in the other games I mentioned. I was never truly baffled or boggled by any puzzle in Portal I, Portal II, or Quantum Conundrum, but some of the puzzles in The Talos Principle really left me at loss for what to even think about. But the brilliance of the puzzle designs really showed when, once I did figure out the solution, I was never mad. I didn't feel cheated by the solution being something ridiculous, obscure, or overly complex. Instead, it was like witnessing a simple magic trick, wondering how in the world the trick was done, and then having the cleverness of it revealed. If you've ever experienced that, it's not something you get mad at, but something you want to congratulate someone on for being so clever.
The puzzle designs alone make the game worth buying, but some people might also like the philosophical nature of this game. It's pretty clear from the start of the game that you're an AI running inside a computer program along with an AI god figure. A little bit later you can run into an AI serpent figure that tries to make you go against and doubt the AI god. The exact nature of this whole situation is slowly revealed throughout the game, but saying more might spoil that. However, the main reason for all the philosophy is to make you think about what it means to be human and how much the AI character you're playing would think of itself as human. It's not particularly in-depth, and the AI serpent who's driving this philosophical exploration gets annoying very quickly. For nearly every dialogue option you choose in response to the AI serpent, it just resorts to straw man and ad hominem fallacies to argue against what you say. This aspect of the game could have been done much better.
Overall, though, the game is amazing as a puzzle game and I strongly recommend it for that reason alone.

Very nifty and unique puzzle game, best of its kind I've played since Portal. Definitely worth checking out if you want a smart game that'll actually challenge you to think (outside the box too). It's actually rare to find a game experience like this nowadays that isn't all about linear action or a single "goal" but more progressing at your own pace and provoking thoughts about the world you're in. Well optimized with great graphics too.
Difficulty is lenient unlike in many other puzzle games and you're not forced to complete every single puzzle which is a huge plus. Instead, should you face an "unbeatable" puzzle (as you no doubt will, there's plenty of them :P) you can just opt to go to another area for an easier puzzle instead. And the world to explore is huge and you have no shortage of various puzzles to engage in, so the possibility of getting "stuck" is much lower than in other games of its kind.
All this coming from a developer that previously made much simpler Serious Sam shooters, so give them some props, this game deserves your attention. The leap from Sam's storytelling and gameplay to this is just huge.

Portal 2 is an excellent first person puzzle game. It has the interesting mechanic of using actual portals to solve puzzles designed around it, which are fun and interesting to think out of. The game has a surprisingly good amount of length to it (especially compared to the first game) and, despite using the same mechanics throughout, didn't feel stale. All the while, you're treated to a nice story that's easy to get invested in while also pretty dang funny at the same time.
Portal's main story can carry it on its own, but one thing I LOVE about Portal 2 is its level editor. Sure, you can spend the time to make your own levels and that's cool, but the real prize here is that there are a TON of great test chambers made by people. If you want unlimited Portal puzzles, this is a pretty darn good deal.
Portal 2 also has a multiplayer mode where you have to solve portal puzzles...but also while having to use four portals and maneuvering two people. It can be rather tough and fun not only to figure out puzzles, but just getting a friend to cooperate. The multiplayer story isn't going to drag you in, but the stages are well-designed and, of course, the level editor bonus extends to this as well.
With a great base for singleplayer and multiplayer alongside a ton of additional levels for both from fans, it's very hard to not recommend this.

Huge Battles, and enormous amounts of players makes this game up there with in my opinion one of the best, real time strategy first person shooters. Not only must you defend Tech Plant from Infantry, but you must regain top floor defenses from hacking infiltrators, ward off troops from going to Alpha point, get out their air support with AA, and counter their tanks, all in ONE battle. Trully a good time for anyone out there wanting to sit down in a game where strategy is key and teamwork is the foundation of this playstyle. Every team is unique in their own special way, and the people of the community vast in numbers. Don't like your current battle? Go to another one. Don't like your world? Go to another one. It's simple and fun. I totally reccomend it to gamers out there looking for much more then just a simple first person shooter deathmatch!
P2P Atmosphere Note: This game gets alot of mixed feelings on the due spot that it's considered a Micro-Transaction type of community, which I will hope to re-describe. Like any Free to Play game, it can't just be there and exist, even with such huge amounts of these servers hosting hundreds of players at one time, and not go bankrupt. They require money to run this game, just as any game out there, and you can pay if you so choose to support and get things in return, such as Member Benefits, but that is far from a battlefield wiping upperhand.
-Like I say to anyone who complains that paying for the game shows you support P2P trash then let me say this.
If you genuinely like a game, is it hard to really input money to enjoy yourself and time with the game more? No. We pay for games, which is a given factor. So why is it in a Free to Play the concept of purchasing anything so bizzare? It's not. It's just the twisted belief that we feel that a Free to Play game needs to ONLY stay Free to Play and any form of inserting said real life currency for said passive monthly benefit is wrong. It's not. They need money to survive and keep this amazing game thriving. And of in that, I am very fine with putting some money over to enjoy myself, and I hope you to can find to enjoy this game.
