I usually don't write reviews on games but I have to say something about this game.
I read a bit about it before I bought it but I never imagined a game could play mind tricks on me.
It's one of those games that have a higher purpose of sort, a game that is made by a developer who thinks of games as an art form.
Can a puzzle game be an art form? they sure try to make it so here.
First of all the game world itself is beautifully rendered and it's pretty big, each area is big and there seems to be a lot of areas in the game - after playing only two hours and opening only 2 areas I realize there are a lot more areas to open...
But, about the size of the areas, it's keep on puzzeling me, why are they so big?
We already know that an FPS puzzle game can work (Portal 1 and 2) and their world wasn't that big, but in this game the areas are way bigger then they should be and it drives me nuts! I feel like I'm missing things in places where I "shouldn't" reach.
Second of all, all the philosophical text and incomplete messages are weird and interesting. The whole vibe of the game - with Elohim (God in Jewish) is the narrator guiding you around with a very clear biblical intent that may or may not be helpful to the player.
So, to wrap it up:
A stunning world with a strange vibe to it with interesting puzzles.
It's not as fun as the Portal games - which were faster and more comic - but it's way more interesting and make you think more than you thought you should think while playing games. In my honest opinion - this of it's own is a great achievment for a video game.
Highely recommended for all of you thinkers who don't care spending hours wondering around in an unexplained world searching for stuff you didn't know you should have looked for in the first place. And in the meanwhile reading some philosophical text about existance issues...

A first/third-person puzzle game with beautifully themed environments and captivating original soundtrack.
You solve world puzzles to collect Sigils (Tetris pieces, essentially), and you use those collected Sigils in Sigil puzzle locks (which unlock doors or new puzzle mechanics.) To solve a lock you must arrange the Sigils in a preset rectangular pattern. Along with Sigils there are collectable stars which are used to unlock more difficult content. The stars themselves are often fairly difficult to collect, but are very satisfying.
The game plays at your own pace, as puzzles are solved with theory and execution as opposed to timing and platforming. Due to the design of puzzles being self-contained experiences, you can play casually, only completing a few puzzles during a session without worrying about losing progress and having to redo a bunch of them. You can't manually save in the middle of a puzzle, but progress is saved as events get triggered, and your last puzzle/world location is kept track of, so it's easy to continue where you left off.
The game does not hold your hand as you play... you aren't told how to use puzzle mechanics, but rather you learn how to use them through natural play and experimentation. The learning curve is very gradual but you will find yourself dealing with fairly complex puzzles later on in the game as you become accustomed to the mechanics. The game isn't a linear progression of puzzles so if you get stuck on a puzzle you can skip it and come back to it later (and often solving it after having an epiphany.) The only barriers are Sigil Locks, which do require you to collect at least certain  "easy" Sigils before advancing too far.
The story of the game is conveyed through various means... through ELOHIM (the voice in the sky), audiologs (from a female scientist), journal entries (archived data in computer terminals), and messages written on the walls (by various characters.) A big, unique part of the story is done through interactive events in the terminals, where you will interact with an AI character through dialogue trees. The AI will make you think, articulate your thoughts, and ultimately question yourself. If you wish to partake in the story and get the most of it, you'll find yourself having a lot to read, but it's all completely optional and can be skipped if you really just want to solve puzzles. The writing and voice acting are all super high-quality with perfect execution.
The level design is based on real-life environments and themes primarily from Roman, Egyptian, and Medieval architectures, with a few "fantasy" environments thrown in. Weather and time of day add a lot of variety to the worlds and keep them fresh and feeling unique from one another. Environmental textures and models are very detailed and are made from real life photographs and 3D scans, as I understand it. Puzzle mechanics clearly stand out from the detailed environments by being pristine and more technologically advanced in nature, as to not get in the way of solving the actual puzzles. Puzzle areas are designed to feel open and allow you to see to other areas so you get a good sense of what all you have to work with and the area you have to utilize. Areas such as walls, fences and stairs feel natural while still retaining very distinct purposes, often aiding you in coming up with the solution without you necessarily realizing it.
There's a ton more I could say about this game, but all in all you're looking at around 20 hours or more of content spanning around 120 puzzles (not including Sigil lock puzzles or additional secrets.) A second play-through is likely if you're wanting to explore alternative dialogue trees, get all the achievements, find all the secrets/messages, or attempt speed-running. There is also a level editor included as well as Steam Workshop support for user-generated content. The PC version of this game has more settings than you have ever seen before, so it can run smoothly on rather low-end hardware, and you can adjust to your liking.

Full disclosure: I was a volunteer beta-tester for this game for ~3 months prior to release, and I have ~180 hours of play in ~4 playthroughs. I highly recommend this game and supporting the developer, Croteam!

Max Payne 3
Story: This game is about Max Payne, (captain obvious strikes again) here's a variety of words he describes himself as throughout the game "drunk, gringo, fat, killer, american has-been". Well, I cant say he's wrong. Nevermind. Max is broken from the events of the previous games when his family was killed. He lives in New Jersey in an apartment and is one day approached by a man that goes by the name of Passos. Raul Passos. They take out the mob/gangsters in New Jersy and passos offers Max a job. Private Security for a family in Brazil. The game starts in Sao Paulo, when a family member gets kidnapped, I dont want to be spoiling the game for you so that's all you have to know for now.
Gameplay: The gameplay plays out smooth as you walk around on the streets of Sao Paulo while jumping in slow-motion and taking out 9 guys in 3 seconds, that's called bullet time and you are EXTREMELY overpowered while in it, srsly though, you can take out NINE FREAKING GUYS IN THREE FREAKING SECONDS!!! And then take some medicational drugs to feel better. You can choose from 3 options regarding aiming, free aim, soft-lock aim and hard-lock aim. I personally prefer the free aim but it's up to you to decide which one you'll use. Summary: It is awesome.
Graphics: The graphics are topnotch, it runs very smoothly on slower systems like my own, it CAN be compared to GTA V's graphics. Might as well take attention to detail in this column too. This game is not a open world game like Red Dead Redemption, or GTA. And you know what that means, maybe not but who cares, MORE ATTENTION TO DETAIL, YAY!!!
Summary here too: It is awesome
Immersion: This game fails to immerse you by making it possible to jump one meter forward at the same time as killing everyone in the room, that kind of breaks immersion to me. But in other cases, like that they actually speak portugese sometimes instead of just ALL english like there is in some games. So it is not bad, but not entirely good either.
Length and extra features: The campaign can be around 10 - 20 hours long, it depends on the player and the difficulty you choose. AND above that there is golden guns in the game! So you can go and chase the golden gun parts for your favourite gun, YAY!
FINAL VERDICT        IS        AN EXCELLENT 8 out of 10
But keep in mind, the final verdict is my opinion only, I've given you information that should be able to help you decide if you want to buy the game. And if you want to know more about the storyline then give me a PM and I'll tell you a bit more. Some people dont want the game spoiled.

My recommendation is "maybe" tending towards "possibly not". I was pretty excited about a game made by many of the same team as Riddick, one of my most favourite recent games and one I've played many times over. But somehow... this game doesn't quite gel. It's not sure what it wants to be. It's overly long, and it just tires towards the end.
There's dual wielding most guns. That sounds fun, right? But there's no point. It isn't any much more effective than a normal gun and working the environment. Most enemies, and bosses in particular, are just annoying bullet sponges. There's an extended car scene in which you travel maybe fifty metres before some other annoying thing blocks your way and you have to deal with it. There's sort of stealth, but it's mostly just effective to pew pew pew your way through. Later, you get a driving tutorial where you press "up" to drive the car, and... that mechanic is never really used again.
The resistance gets these absurdly overpowered sphere things (which conveniently destroy things creating a perfect path of things for you to navigate), yet they only see fit to use them twice. Something about Jewish magic or something? I don't know, I'd stopped paying attention to the plot at this point.
The game has BJ mumbling random things throughout. I think they were supposed to be deep and meaningful? Then suddenly he'll be making some joke or other. I'm just not sure whether they wanted to be serious, lighthearted, ironic, horrific. The story is likewise all over the place. Especially when they decide there's a nazi base on the moon. Uhh... okay. NOLF did this really well, but NOLF's tone was camp James Bond, and it worked. The whole settling in this game is underutilised. You walk around in space for about three or four minutes before you're back inside a base with gravity. What was the point of this, again? I forgot. Something about shooting nazis. Because, nazis.
In the end, I just didn't really find this game all that fun. Functional, maybe, but its combination of average gunplay, wildly inconsistent story, endless brown/grey corridors and tiring shooting, maybe I've moved on past this kind of shooter. For me, I can't really recommend this. Still, if shooting nazis is all the justification you need to play this game, go for it. You'll probably enjoy it.

This game is a sequel to the high acclaimed Max Payne 2, unfortunately it does not live up to the franchise's reputation.
First, the story is completely disconnected from the Max Payne universe, this game should be titled something like "Max Payne's Retiring Adventures" or something like this. The main character from previous games is depressed and accepts a job in Brazil, where he works as a body guard for a rich family. Of course everything goes wrong, it gets even funny how he tries to fix not only his problem, which should be only regarding his work, but the whole country's problem, without even understanding what is going on.
Second, the gameplay and controls. The cover controls are so sluggish that I preferred not to use it. The game allows you to have 2 simple weapons like pistols and UZI, and 1 main weapon, but every time a cutscene takes place (which is about every 1-2 minutes, almost every door you have to open leads to a cutscene) it scrambles your inventory, changing the weapon you have equipped or even dropping your main weapon, and usually the cutscenes leave you in the middle of a firefight, surrounded. Great huh? This was even more annoying when I had an AK47 and after opening a door I was left with a useless UZI to take out a room full of special forces solders.
Third, DRM. This was plain stupidity. There were several times I wanted to play this game but I could not, because I was unable to log in to Rockstar Social Club, which left me hanging on the title screen, having to CTRL+ALT+Del out of the game. I believe this is due to server traffic from GTA 5 players, although this was so frequent that it was a show stopper for me and I did not uninstall the game because I am (or was) a Max Payne fan and wanted to see how the story ended.
In summary, it is not worth the 10 hours, I should have replayed Max Payne 2 which is a lot better than this. By the way, forgot to mention that the graphics are good. That's all.

This is a masterpiece. I even got a little baffled by some reviews out there - namely, my dear RockPaperShotgun - which, despite saying all sorts of great things about this game, missed the fact that few (or maybe none) FPS has achieve what this one has, since Half-Life 2.
It's focused on single-player, and that's what I am talking about: a full, single-player experience with a strong storyline and vicious combat sequences. Yes, HL2 did it a little better - you had more variety in encounters, like tripods and giant antlions, but New Order does its best to give you a variety within the proposed setting, with robot dogs, choppers and supersoldiers. The guns may be also not very expansive in design, but firing a machinegun here reminded me immediately of shooting a shotgun in Doom: a rewarding experience in seeing your enemies shaking and ultimately undone over your firepower.
If the gameplay doesn`t rise as high as HL2, the story does. Yes, it`s silly, contrived, but it`s also a great story, told by the eyes of true character, with emotions and personality. It's a action flick - you won't find dense moments like Bioshock - but it's all there: the damsel in distress, the moral choices, everything.
Another thing it does right is the diversity of its environments, something that I find lacking on most games nowadays. Except for a jungle setting, you got it all: a castle, a dungeon, a city, a house, bunkers, a war setting and even the moon.
You maybe not love this as much as I have, but trust me: if you like single-player FPS, you want to play this.

Portal 2 is an excellent first person puzzle game. It has the interesting mechanic of using actual portals to solve puzzles designed around it, which are fun and interesting to think out of. The game has a surprisingly good amount of length to it (especially compared to the first game) and, despite using the same mechanics throughout, didn't feel stale. All the while, you're treated to a nice story that's easy to get invested in while also pretty dang funny at the same time.
Portal's main story can carry it on its own, but one thing I LOVE about Portal 2 is its level editor. Sure, you can spend the time to make your own levels and that's cool, but the real prize here is that there are a TON of great test chambers made by people. If you want unlimited Portal puzzles, this is a pretty darn good deal.
Portal 2 also has a multiplayer mode where you have to solve portal puzzles...but also while having to use four portals and maneuvering two people. It can be rather tough and fun not only to figure out puzzles, but just getting a friend to cooperate. The multiplayer story isn't going to drag you in, but the stages are well-designed and, of course, the level editor bonus extends to this as well.
With a great base for singleplayer and multiplayer alongside a ton of additional levels for both from fans, it's very hard to not recommend this.

Oh boy, where do I begin? I've been playing this game since it was released as a demo for maximum pc back in 1998. My father showed me it at a computer store that he used to work at in the small community that we used to live in. I was only 4 years old at that time, and I remember the only civilizations you could be were the Brits and Celts. I first laid eyes on the scout calvary, would ignore the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everything else, because he looked cool in my eyes at 4 years of age. Since then, Ive been playing this game on and off, I'm 21 now, and I still find myself latched on to it. I now have a daughter of my own, although she won't know what it was like to see the game evolve over the course of 16 years, she will still know how it came to be, assuming she would even find it as cool as I have growing up. I think for me at least it was the growing anticipation of seeing something new with every civ, while still keeping the basics of the game simple and the same in it's own ways. I used to play this during lunch break in middle school from 2006-2009 with all of my friends, for the most part, I came out on top, even had our own little community of players, formed our own club, and we made a board game out of it. It was pretty cool that not all of us were premature nerds that played this, at least half of our little community were jocks that just loved it as much as we did, and there was no discrimination involved in any of it.  We amassed to a total of 20 or more people in this community, and for a small amount of us, our community is still strong with new members and old. This game is called Age of Empires II, and it will stand the test of time for the ages. I'm happy and delighted that people are still playing this game 16 years later, and we're still finding newcomers for this game at as faster rate than before. I've come to realize that just since early 2014 I have ended up spending hundreds of hours playing this game, teaching people both young and old what to do in this game. I'm so thrilled to see that this game is coming out with new expansions still to this day, even after 16 years. I think that if I were to find the gold edition realeased back in 2004 without the package being opened or torn, I would keep it as a collector's item, this game has so much potential and I'm happy to see that it's not being thrown away in to the trash. I honestly believe that when I die of old age, assuming that I don't die any other way, I will more than likely have a copy in my coffin for when my body gets discovered generations later, people will know what kind of influence this game had on my life as much as anyone else's life. I honestly didn't even play the Conqueror's expansion pack until 2007, even though I knew about it unpon release date, my mother refused me video games, so I never got to play it on time like most of my friends did, but I knew that I would at some point in time. Due to my parents seperation back in 2001 shortly after my mother's mother died, I ended up living with my mother, as she got the majority of custody except on holidays when I would be with my father. Whenever I was with him, he would let me play games, even though it was against my mother's wishes. I really loved playing as the Celts, Britons, Franks, Goths, and Vikings, at the time, they were my favorite. Now and again however, you will find me riding along Genghis Khan's horde as the Mongols, however, you can also find me still enjoying the company of the Goths and Britions. I love all of the civilizations very much, I know that they all have their strengths and weaknesses, some are greater than others. My best advice to you is to rush your enemies into the dirt while still keeping up with your economy via micro manage. I would rate this game a solid 10/10 and would also highly recommend it to anyone who still finds the old RTS game to be complexed and fun. I can't wait for the new expansion to come out November 5th 2015 African Kingdoms will have without a doubt in my mind as many new features as it pre successors. I hope you all have a try at this game, it's for sure my favorite game of all time.

I was looking for a shooter that required little thought, plenty of action, a good setting and decent story. Which is exactly what Wolfenstein: The New Order is.
The levels are very linear, but you do have some choice in how difficult you want them to be. You can try to stealthly kill the 'commanders' before they notice you and call in reinforcements or you can go in guns blazing and enjoy the blood as new order Nazis brains splatter against the wall. I always tried for stealth, taking particular satisfaction in a well thrown knife landing in the back of a patrolling guard.
The weapons are fairly typicaly (pistol, machine gun, shotgun) but also have an alternate fire mode. The shotgun for example allows you to fire ball bearings which rebound off walls. You also have some more futuristic energy weapons but for the most part you can continue to use what you feel comfortable with. I was still using my machine gun through the later levels. There are only a few parts where you feel really pressured into using a particular weapon.
The story kept me engaged but it did not require me to pay attention too much. You could get as involved as you wanted, but if you skipped any dialogue then you would not go far wrong by following the instructions in your journal.
On Hard difficulty I completed it in around 13 hours.
A solid fps that does not innovate but is very enjoyable. It delivers on what it promises; Blood, action and guns.
Overall a 80 / 100

Probably every FPS player knows the Max Payne series. The first game is known for being perfect in every way - it had great graphics at the time, smooth action gameplay, great dark story and nice comic-style storytelling. The second game was worse. The protagonist wasn't cool or funny anymore and the story had unnecessary "romance" (which actually had nothing to do with romance). It still had good action and nice graphics though.
And after many years comes Max Payne 3. And boy, is it a disappointment! It has so many problems that I don't even know where to start.
Let's start with the story. You are once again Max Payne, even though he looks even less like himself than Max Payne 2 did. But now it's been a few years, so it is tolerable. You move to South America because some dude makes you go and so you work as a bodyguard for some rich guy whose family seems to have problems with unknown terror threat. After his wife is kidnapped, you go bust some balls again and reveal who's behind it. Here you see the first major issue. Why the hell does the game take place in filthy South America? Max belongs to New York. Sure, there is one chapter that takes place in NY, but that's it. Wrong decision.
Graphics of the game is above average. It looks okay, but not good enough for the game to have such over-the-top requirements. During cutscenes (which actually replace the cool old comic pages, but still somehow resemble a comic) you may often see that the objects in the background have some weird squares over them (probably some unfinished blur).
I can't judge game sounds, because I'm no expert. The soundtrack is forgettable, with the exception of two tracks that stand out.
Gameplay has changed a lot. You now hardly have any bullet-time, but instead a cover system was implemented. And you will be using it all the time, otherwise you get killed in a few seconds. Not only is the game much harder and annoying now, but it also resembles CoD. No kidding - most action scenes are so over-the-top and improbable that you won't believe your eyes. The only good gameplay addition was some kind of "second chance". Instead of getting killed, you get a chance to shoot the enemy who mortally wounded you and then get back to life. Unless you run out of painkillers. In that case, you die.
This is the first Max Payne game to feature multiplayer. And guess what. It sucks too. 99% of "players" are pathetic aimbotters and morons. One shot anywhere and you're dead. It's a joke.
On the other hand, arcade modes are quite fun. There are "Score attack" and "New York Minute".
The game also has numerous technical problems. The most remarkable is random crashing to desktop during cutscenes. There are no apparent reasons for it to happen. You may often get stuck on loading screen too, because either your Rockstar account refuses to connect or you can't click any button to get to the menu.
You're probably wondering if there's anything good about the game. And to be fair, yes, there is. The gameplay, even though very awkward, can sometimes be called fun. The best thing about the game is Max Payne himself. He's a wreck and a drunk. He sounds depressed or down all the time, which is actually nice to see, because that's what almost everybody would be like after all that happened to Max since the first game.
Overall the game is average at best. It feels nothing like Max Payne, it is unpolished,  has awkward gameplay, weak story, many technical problems and lacks proper optimization. I recommend this game only if it gets VERY cheap.

Oh boy, where do I begin? I've been playing this game since it was released as a demo for maximum pc back in 1998. My father showed me it at a computer store that he used to work at in the small community that we used to live in. I was only 4 years old at that time, and I remember the only civilizations you could be were the Brits and Celts. I first laid eyes on the scout calvary, would ignore the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everything else, because he looked cool in my eyes at 4 years of age. Since then, Ive been playing this game on and off, I'm 21 now, and I still find myself latched on to it. I now have a daughter of my own, although she won't know what it was like to see the game evolve over the course of 16 years, she will still know how it came to be, assuming she would even find it as cool as I have growing up. I think for me at least it was the growing anticipation of seeing something new with every civ, while still keeping the basics of the game simple and the same in it's own ways. I used to play this during lunch break in middle school from 2006-2009 with all of my friends, for the most part, I came out on top, even had our own little community of players, formed our own club, and we made a board game out of it. It was pretty cool that not all of us were premature nerds that played this, at least half of our little community were jocks that just loved it as much as we did, and there was no discrimination involved in any of it.  We amassed to a total of 20 or more people in this community, and for a small amount of us, our community is still strong with new members and old. This game is called Age of Empires II, and it will stand the test of time for the ages. I'm happy and delighted that people are still playing this game 16 years later, and we're still finding newcomers for this game at as faster rate than before. I've come to realize that just since early 2014 I have ended up spending hundreds of hours playing this game, teaching people both young and old what to do in this game. I'm so thrilled to see that this game is coming out with new expansions still to this day, even after 16 years. I think that if I were to find the gold edition realeased back in 2004 without the package being opened or torn, I would keep it as a collector's item, this game has so much potential and I'm happy to see that it's not being thrown away in to the trash. I honestly believe that when I die of old age, assuming that I don't die any other way, I will more than likely have a copy in my coffin for when my body gets discovered generations later, people will know what kind of influence this game had on my life as much as anyone else's life. I honestly didn't even play the Conqueror's expansion pack until 2007, even though I knew about it unpon release date, my mother refused me video games, so I never got to play it on time like most of my friends did, but I knew that I would at some point in time. Due to my parents seperation back in 2001 shortly after my mother's mother died, I ended up living with my mother, as she got the majority of custody except on holidays when I would be with my father. Whenever I was with him, he would let me play games, even though it was against my mother's wishes. I really loved playing as the Celts, Britons, Franks, Goths, and Vikings, at the time, they were my favorite. Now and again however, you will find me riding along Genghis Khan's horde as the Mongols, however, you can also find me still enjoying the company of the Goths and Britions. I love all of the civilizations very much, I know that they all have their strengths and weaknesses, some are greater than others. My best advice to you is to rush your enemies into the dirt while still keeping up with your economy via micro manage. I would rate this game a solid 10/10 and would also highly recommend it to anyone who still finds the old RTS game to be complexed and fun. I can't wait for the new expansion to come out November 5th 2015 African Kingdoms will have without a doubt in my mind as many new features as it pre successors. I hope you all have a try at this game, it's for sure my favorite game of all time.

This is one of the best RTS's of all time, and until version 4.x it was a fantastic remake for modern systems. Unfortunately, 4.x messed around too much and now it's pretty broken. Most mods that worked with previous versions won't work any more and there are no available workarounds other than manually editing game files. So mod support is pretty much useless other than cosmetic mods. Any mods that make changes to mechanics (like resources, population, units, etc.) require convoluted procedures.
Also, the game will no longer let you create custom MP matches by yourself. Before, you could always go into Multiplayer and host a game against AI, and set it up however you wanted, but now you get an error "You cannot start a game with only one player." and it won't let you start the game. Single player won't let you customize the number of opponents or anything like that.
The game is pretty much broken. The original HD version was fantastic, but the developers kept fiddling and making things worse and worse, and I can no longer recommend this.

The game is relatively good given its Age of Empires 2. Forgotten Empires adds some cool stuff and a lot of cool new campaigns. The community on the other hand is a mixed barrel; I will personally say I did not have a good time given the inherent elitism this game has brewed over the course of many years in its game communities and the lack of variety in maps that people play;
(and do note that this is not a problem of a lack of maps in the selection list, this is the community im speaking about)
especially on this release of this version of the game; I've gotten sick of teamgames on Black Forest pretty fast.
People either refer to the same old maps and those who don't are normally very good players in terms of skill level, which can be intimidating for anyone who is rusty and returning to the game or completely new. The ELO system also tends to encourage this elitism and can (and I don't blame them because lower ranked players in a game can severely drop elo scores) end up in people getting the boot and not finding good games.
1 vs 1's have also largely died out. The only people who really play lots of them tend to be more experienced players high in their performance, so you will not find a variety of skill levels typically.
Scenario maps exist and you will find a few people hosting the odd game of castle blood and some of the old favourites, but the mapping community is nothing really new when it comes to day to day play. But then again this game has been out for over 15-16 years so go figure.
Overall the game content is good, but while online play exists and there is a modest amount of games about, they are mostly unvaried and to be frank filled with toxic attitudes.
Buy it for the new campaigns and civilization content; if you're looking to rehash your glory days from the zone or find a nice community to play with don't bother.

Where to start here.. Well, not even the devs could sort out this mess so lets jump right into it.
Pros
Fast paced
Unique characters
Interesting (Sometimes overpowered) Healing/Medic elements
Certain mercs give out ammo
Movement Mechanics are very smooth
Cons
All loadouts are fixed so you have no customization options
Game has very little variation in gun options (Many mercs share the same weapons)
Devs have had to put out multiple updates to make the same limited content acceptable
No merc limits on teams (Can have up to 8 of the same merc on one team, I,E Medics circle jerking each other)
Very little maps in the game
Takes devs months (Or longer) To put out new content
Shotguns are overpowered (Can 1 tap all light mercs/ 2-4 tap any other merc)
Many matches are poorly balanced (Casual Matchmaking on the way currently but it more than likely won't do anything)
Devs very often have to pour time into things that should've already been fixed or that they just can't find a way to fix
Long story short after about 2,000+ hours and having my love for this game slowly fade away due to the devs sheer ineptitude with handling content updates, as well as adding new content (Which is basically nonexistant over a 6+ month period at the time of this review) I've given up on Dirtybomb. It appears that at this current point in time the devs no longer care about veteran players and only want to attract newer players (Which is understandable given the very little growth DB has shown over the last 18 months) And with certain upcoming additions to the game, The main one being Casual Matchmaking, Any veteran player will only ever have the luxury of playing against any of the few other veterans that have managed to stick around leaving diversity amongst them almost non-existant.
Dirtybomb could've been, and still can be a good game. In the hands of another team of developers.

Only a few hours played on steam because I had hundreds of hours played on my initial ProSieben Games account, which was erased when that third-party company's contract with the developers ended.
Players had a window to move their accounts over to Daybreak, but if you happened to be burnt out and not playing the game at that time, and therefore not keeping up with news from the developers, the investment of time and money you put into the game has been taken away from you.
If you're an EU player returning from a long break, don't bother. Your characters and unlocks have most likely ceased to exist and Daybreak's support couldn't care less about that fact, nor do they care enough to reimburse you for real money that you invested and effectively lost, even with a virtual currency that effectively costs them nothing. If they had possessed the thoughtfulness to at least do that, I would probably still be playing the game. I've also heard a number of horror stories about people who were automatically banned by the system simply for achieving a high kill/death ratio, and with support like this, they're pretty much out of luck too.
Since I refuse to spend money on the game after this shoddy business practice and refuse to spend hundreds of hours grinding unlocks to get close to where I was while being farmed content for experienced players who haven't lost all of their gear, I'm not going to play Planetside 2 again, nor am I going to play anything else Daybreak ever produces.
I definitely wouldn't risk spending money on something operated by such a shady company and wouldn't risk playing it if you don't like having things that you have invested a significant amount of time into taken away from you through sheer negligence. If you can ignore that and play it for free and still have fun, enjoy what is, despite everything, still a good game.

I gave this a shot.
I saw the screenshots and it immediately reminded me of Brink, a good game that really didn't age well. Actually it died before most people even knew it existed. And just to be clear i really like the game, it definetly has potential. I do realize the game is in "Beta" and will most likely turn into a decent game in the end, but until that day comes i can't really recommend this to anyone looking for a solid multiplayer fps game.
I don't think this company needs an introduction, and i know from experience there's a whole lot of people who feel the same about them.
So the game is Free to play, and i believe you can get your hands on any playable characters, loadout cards and items without any real pay-gates, but at an ridiculously slow rate. I mean the concept isn't revolutionary, heck it's probably the most mainstream thing for free-to-play games to do these days, and in some cases it's acceptable, in other not so much. So unlocking a new mercenary costs 50'000 credits. A decent round will give you anywhere between 30-150 credits, and if you use a credit booster, the double. So let's say if you WIN 100 games, you'll average anywhere between 3000 and 15'000 which is one third of what a merc costs. So if you do really well for roughly 350 rounds worth of playing, you can buy any character you want! Yay!
But there are also additionl bonus objective that gives you credits for completing them (Updated after a few hours) but from personal experience most of them just pushes you toward playing the "execution" gamemode, which is literally Counter Strike. You attack bombsites and plant the bomb, or defend the points from the "terrorists". So no, i think i'm fine. Because if i had any plans on playing a bomb and defuse kind of game, i would be playing Counter Strike instead.
Oh by the way, there are 18 mercs atm. Two are free, and three random mercs (each week i think?) will be available for anyone to play. But for you to actually be able to play any character you want at any given time would obviously require you to unlock all of them. And without waving your wallet at Nexon i don't see many players making it. Unless any of them are on sale each merc costs a whooping 9,99€! Hows that for a "free to play" huh? So unlocking 5 mercs is gonna cost you as much as the game would cost if it wasn't "free".
Talking about Counter Strike. This game has cases too! Don't worry, you don't need to buy keys. But this introduces yet another unrealistic aspect of the game.
Every merc has several "Loadout cards" which gives you characters minor/major perks, different weapon loadouts and different skins. These Loadout cards has SIX different rarities, so getting your hands on the exact type you want from a pool of Loadout cards, ranging anywhere between 4 and 20 different combinations of different weapons and different perks (Depending on rarity), the odds of you getting what you really really want is ASTRONOMICAL!
HOWEVER, you CAN scrap unwanted loadout cards and make it into currency. Not credits mind you, just scrap. For the very purpose of making a new card that perhaps doesn't suck as much. However, apart from you now choosing the rarity of the card, it's still seems random which one you get. Crafting a golden one (The rarest one being cobalt) however costs 25'000 CREDITS. Half what a character costs!
Proximity mines clipping into objects so that you won't see them! A barrage of air and artillery strikes on less than a minutes cooldown! And oh-boy, heals that only take a second to heal any merc to maximum health. Just to name a few!
ALL the healing in the game is ridiculously potent. Anyone standing next to a healing station won't be going down unless you're able to either kill them in one shot or if you are 4 guys spraying like you're in a freaking Jason Statham movie. OR you can just kill the healing beacon (Which doesn't seem to happen too often, i think i've seen two or three teammates ever shooting at an exposed health or ammo station). But the worst thing about it is that placing it strategically behind a corner that the enemies can't reach behind will not only make it impossible to hit without explosive devices, but it will just start healing up anyone standing in it, practically the very same second they take damage.
Not only is this OP to the point that i want to barf, but it is by far the best way to get experience points. I'm a decent run and gunner in most FPS games and i do fairly well K/D wise, but getting 40 kills a game will give me somewhere between 6000-12000 exp per game playing objectives and doing what i should be doing, anyone playing an efficient healer with healing station will easily get 10000-25000 doing nothing but camping good spots and healing people. Not only is it the most efficient way to defend on any given objective map, it is actually so freakishly powerful that a good Aura healer not firing a single shot in a round, just camping healing stations and ressurecting people will carry the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of even the worst players along with giving you more experience points than you would earn playing the freaking game with an aimbot! And the best part is that there is no limit on how many players can pick the same class, so imagine what TWO not-so-braindead healers can do!

I'm quite disappointed so far by my experience playing it on the PC.  Surprisingly little effort seems to have been made to actually support the keyboard, considering this version is being sold for the PC and not the Xbox.
Let me explain the issue with the keyboard controls.
Pro: The game options offer you the option to map in keyboard controls.
Cons: The mapping option tells you what ability you're binding the hotkey to and not the controller key.  This is a con because then as you go on throughout the game, it keeps popping up tips to hit this controller key (hit B! hit X! hit Y!) and you have absolutely no clue what keyboard hotkey that corresponds to.
To make it worse, the game seems to only partially support your keyboard controls and remapping.
1) In some parts of the game (such as the part where you transition between game episodes), when it says hit Y or X, it literally does mean hit Y or X on the keyboard.  But in other parts, such as in battle, X or Y refer to the controller buttons which you have no idea what the keyboard controls correspond to.  So each time you have to sit there trying to figure out if it's referring to the keyboard hotkeys or the controller buttons.
2) In the stats screen, the game completely forgets your remapped hotkeys and reverts to the original keyboard mapping.  This is rather disorienting--on top of the previous problem described--as you then have to keep attempting many different keys to see what the problem was this time and make it work.
Needed fixes:
- Just let the player toggle controller support on or off in the menu.  If it's off, then give all tips (press X! press Y!) etc. for the keyboard hotkeys bound, instead of controller buttons.
- Fix the remapped hotkeys not being recognized in some parts of the game

In Max Payne 3, your primary objective is to move from point A to point B and kill everything in between.  Do not attempt to go to point C, because that door is closed and inaccessible until a cutscene opens it.  Do not attempt to sneak past someone without killing them, because killing them is required for the cutscene, as well.  So yes, you will be killing a lot of people.  Approximately the entire population of Brazil will die to your guns, all to trigger that next cutscene where Max Payne laments his terrible life and how he's sad.  Chin up, Max!  A new door opened with more people to kill!  Oh, but don't shoot them in the chest, because they are wearing T-Shirts, and Brazilian T-Shirts can negate 3 bullets from an assault rifle.
The game isn't without its merits.  The trademark bullet-time allows you to play aggressively, without hiding behind cover like pretty much every other shooter made in the last decade.  The character models and animation are phenomenal, although the entire game takes place moving from one rusty corrider to another, so the same can't be said about the environs.
Overall, it's a hideously boring game with extremely tired game mechanics.  It's a glorified tablet game - press button on bad dudes, watch them die, get a cutscene, repeat.  There are no exploration or choices.  Your decision making is strictly limited to "Do you want to pick up this gun with 30 bullets or keep the one you have with 14?"

I've just not been able to get in to PS2 at all however.  The primary reason for this would likely be because it plays nothing like the first game - it retains the same kind of scope, but for the most part the core mechanics are completely different.
I realise now I was hoping for a graphically-updated clone of PS1, and while I accept that wouldn't exactly constitute 'progress', I'm not convinced that the design decisions made here push the game on in any great leaps and bounds.  As an example, it's worth comparing the inventory or loadout system of the two games.  In PS1, players built their own loadouts from the ground up with overall carrying capacity dictated by the type of armour worn.  The weapons and equipment available were restricted by the branches of the various combat disciplines that had been unlocked - using points gained by levelling one's character.  This approach allowed for HUGE variation between loadouts for individual characters and meant that genuine mulit-tasking was possible.  By contrast, PS2 has a much more rigid and defined class system which will be more familiar to players of 'traditional' shooters and is arguably less daunting to get to grips with - if ultimately more generic and unsatisfying.
Less tangible - but equally off-putting, for me at least - is the feel of the battles.  PS1 often had very clearly defined battle lines and it was possible to sense and react to the ebb and flow of battle.  I don't get this in PS2 at all.  Large outdoor fights give the impression of many self-contained deathmatches all going on at once and seem utterly disorganised.  Is this a result of the pacing of the game?  Possibly.  I believe the TTK may be generally lower than it was in the original and this coupled with the faster character movement undeniably makes the game a very diffeerent proposition to the first.
I'm quite sure than in its own right, the fare on offer is enjoyable to many - just don't expect anything like the slow(ish) pace of the first game and the almost 'trench warfare' scenarios that could develop.
Overall, I really wanted to like this game but the sad truth for me is that it's lost too much of what made the original so special.

Ok. So I feel I need to do this review since I recently got back into this game. I started playing back around late 2013, and I heavily enjoyed the game. Unfortunately, my original account got wiped during the daybreak transfer, so I kinda gave up on the game. So now it's time for a fresh start review.
I’ll start with talking about the game's scale. Love this game or hate it, no one can deny that this game is impressive from a technical standpoint. The ability to fight with and against several hundred to several thousand players at once, combined with maps measuring over 100 square kilometers, all while handling real time ballistic calculations is an impressive technical achievement to say the least.
Now, as far as gameplay is concerned, things get a little interesting. Fights are often fought by huge numbers of players contesting small regions of the map. Because of this, small individual mistakes have a minimal result on the outcome of a fight, but the right plan executed at the right moment can turn an entire battle. It is certainly a nice set up, as it allows for great tactical creativity, with minimal risk.
Each faction is also set up differently, with each relying on similar, but distinct tactical doctrines. I won't go into detail here, but put simply, each faction has a different approach to weapon and vehicle design that ensures variety, while avoiding a rock paper scissors situation.
Unfortunately, this game has had some long standing problems, and with a shrinking player base, I doubt they are ever going to get fixed. First on the list is an economy that can be considered almost punishing to players without premium, and persistent issues surrounding vehicles. There also exist several facilities that are effectively impenetrable, and reside at key strategic positions, making strategic gameplay a frustrating affair at times. Also, impalants. I have hated the implant system since it was first introduced, and my opinion of it has only grown worse with time.
Summary:
Pros:
+Amazing combat scale for an FPS that still today remains unmatched.
+Easy to get into ground combat.
+Time to kill is such that fighting is always intense, while mitigating lag issues.
+Distinct weapon set ups for each faction.
+Amazing when played with others.
+Squad and platoon system are simple and effective in their design.
+Excellent chat system.
+So many cosmetic options, it's like this game has a soldier dress up mini game built into it.
Cons:
-Numerous facilities exist in key locations that are almost impenetrable (the crown on indar, the bastion and heydoka armoury on amerish as examples).
-To keep continents populated, continent locking is in heavy use now, which means you often can't fight on your favorite continent.
-Economy is incredibly grind heavy, even for things that have serious impacts on combat, which overall proves punishing to newer players.
-Premium accounts feel like they have a bigger impact then they should. I’m fine with 50% gain rate jumps, but up to tripling, or even quadrupling just seems like kicking people in the teeth for not spending.
-Aircraft handling system is in desperate need of work, despite the game's age. Handling is often difficult to work with, and given that most modern titles use a “chase the mouse” style, it really shows. It not ineffective, but it is really hard to get used to.
-Many unlocks don't transfer between classes, which means either you main one or two classes, or end up feeling underpowered at all times. Unless you have premium.
-I had a lot of misgivings about implants when they first got introduced, and I think the problems with them have only grown since.
-Cosmetics are not cheap, and only available with real money.
Final thoughts:
I have my misgivings about this game. It takes time to get the feel for the gun play, and stop being insta killed by level 1000 players as a level 16. The economy is incredibly punishing, and premium can often feel like a must have. Despite that, the scale, the fluidity of combat, and the amount of random shenanigans that can occur are really nice to see. It's a game where you have to take the good with the bad, and decide what's right for you.
Do I miss the old days of planetside 2 before implants? Oh you bet your♥♥♥♥♥I do. Is the current game set up worse then it was a few years ago? most likely. Is it unplayable? NO. Its still fun, even if its worse for ware.
Final score:
7/10 if playing free.
8.5/10 if premium.

This game is actually better than I'd been led to believe. I came into the game expecting it to be a competent, if fairly brainless shooter. It's more than 'competent' though. In fact - I think it might be one of the best games of the year. Given that the game is an over-the-top, Nazi killing simulator, I was expecting the story to be more of an afterthought. Surprisingly though, the game's alternate history story is compelling and the game does a good job with world building by peppering the levels with optional conversations and newspaper clippings that help make the world seem more alive. I was expecting the story to go for camp humor, but the game takes itself very seriously at times and the quality of the writing is such that it doesn't come off like some 12 year old's idea of what's is dark and gritty.
I also admire the game's design philosophy, as it does a good job of combining the better elements of new-school and old-school FPS design. For example, the game's health system is a hybrid between health pickups and regenerating health. The way it works is that you can only regenerate health in blocks of 20. If you were to start with 100 health and then lose 95, you'd only be able to regenerate up to 20. I like this system a lot, since it alleviates some of the 'die and retry' repetition from older shooters, but still encourages you to keep moving instead of just hiding behind a wall while you wait for your health to recharge.
The levels are well-designed, with lots of large open rooms, secrets and multiple paths. The controls are nice and responsive, and there's a decent selection of weapons with balanced strengths and weaknesses. You can slide into cover, or shoot while sliding. You can also dual-wield almost every single weapon in the game for an increase in rate of fire while sacrificing accuracy. There are situations where you can take out enemies using stealth, or just go in guns blazing. There's also a perk system that levels up organically based on things you do in the game rather than experience (like x number of head shots with the pistol, or stealth kills using throwing knifes).
The game is just... a lot of fun. There isn't any one thing that makes this game stand out when compared to other shooters, but it does many things very well and manages to feel very fresh while not doing anything particularly new. Machine Games did good here. I really hope that we'll see a sequel from them at some point!

This is for fans of the cooperative-FPS genre, or anyone curious.  It's free as in free-to-play.
Try it? YES. Here's why.
This is fast-paced, cooperative first-person-shooter. It's smooth, good visuals, fair audio variations. The different player classes come in the form of different "mercs", with very different personae attached, armed with an addition of "loadout" cards which determine their weapon and special abilites, if any. The personae are purely cosmetic, but adds some quite nice personality to the game; not unlike say Overwatch, though I personally prefer the aesthetics or these personae.
After sixty hours of play I'd say I've gotten a good impression of the game. While I recommend trying it, I do have criticisms:
DB gets repetitive as there are only six maps at present. Everything has a price tag and the indication that whatever you can get is purchasable is everpresent. There isnt't much you can't get in the game on playing it without paying anything, but that is a heavy grind, so don't go into this hoping youll get the phat loot in short order, because you won't. It's for those with patience and a willingness to play this for a long time.
I have been able to scrape together enough credits to buy two mercs. People with less skill will have a tougher time earning, which might make the game a disappointment to them as it will seem a dead-end to grind the characters they think look interesting. At that point a price tag of 10 euros per merc (though some cheaper) might seem insulting.
Now, ameliorating observations:
While the relatively few maps become monotonous, that opens a new dimension which is to explore them properly, because they are detailed and LARGE. There are several ways to get from A to B, some not very visible obvious, especially in the heat of battle. This adds quite some long-term replay value. Additionally, others I've shown the game agree that the map layouts seem quite pleasant and "natural" in their look and flow, making the many battles you will find more agreeable instead of the everpresent and over-monotonous labyrinths of walls and corridors found in virtually all other games.
Those who hate one particular game mode or map will like the game, since it explicitly allows you to solo out the ones you prefer.
Wallet warriors cannot buy themselves to easy kills or victoriries since the extra abilities on the loadouts only add a marginal edge to the individual mercs. They cannot buy themselves to skill; purchase a merc that sounds super-duper-powered, but unable to use it effectively because the player chose to buy herself to power instead of building the skill through hard work will do little.
Now, there are and will always be players that are very experienced and very skilled. Fact of life. You will run into Level 106 snipers that have taken your head off by the time you notice where she stands. This is always annoying as duck when you are new, and it is part of the lerning process. The only players that are realitically capable of using the bigger loadout card abilities are these, but is that unfair? No, because they'll still be capable of killing you just as easy as without it.
Stability-wise, the game has proven stable. I have had one single crash over two weeks and it was non-fatal for my system.
Performance is decent, a fairly recent-model gaming lappy will have this running between 100-something and 25-ish fps, with 40-50fps most of the time. I do experience some times where the fps drops somewhat, but it hasn't impoacted my gameplay much.
Servers are plenty across the continents and offer good capacity and low ping rates.I think I've been dropped from a server a single time.
Others complain that the matchmaking (MM) is ducked up. I think it can be made better, yes, but not much. Many complain that team balancing can be off, sometimes heavily. I think this is true, but I have a hard time seeing how it can be improved, because it certainly cannot be properly balanced based on player level/XP only! Also, matches can be completely destroyed if one very good player leaves the game early, so that the team loses the match togetehr with its best player. Or such. Or a very good player joining the opposite team mid-match. You will have a hard time compensating for this if you want to keep matches well-populated. The alternative is long wait times, which ALSO makes players complain.
Lastly, whilere there are 6 different grades of loadout cards spanning LEAD to COBALT, only the first three offer progressively better extra abilities; the latter three is pure "bling"; and the game clearly indicates this to be the case, so credit where credit is due to the developers for informing the players of what they're getting. Players with gold or cobalt cards just want to look good, they aren't supermen because of the colour of their loadout.
I plan to stick with this for a good while since it offers me a decent explerience without tying me up for very long for one round to finish. Easy in and out. No expense if you don't want one, just less bling.

I remember playing this game when I was even younger with my next door neighbours on their old Toshiba laptop.....oh those were the days of not knowing hwo good PC Gamign would get. Anyways the game is great, a prime example I love to use when describing the "strategy" section to my friends. The game succeeds in almost all places, including but not limited to: animations, variety, content and overall fun. Now that this game is on Steam, don't hesitate! if you have any interest in the strategy genre you will love this game.
Gameplay
You will spend most of your game hours organising your village/kingdom/town/empire (the word varies from culture to culture damnit!) This usually involves sending your settlers to build things or sending your troops off to war. What I really love about the gameplay is when you get into battle, you can control troops to utilise rush tactics as well as flanking. You will put many hours in the game just testing out strategies on AI just to see what happens. The game is that fun and honestly I don't think they could have done a better job considering the time period for when this game was originally released.
Performance
This is one of the few things I dislike about this game, performance. Now because it is an extremely old game, I must obviously recognise that they didn't use 60 FPS back then and that the technology then wasn't capable of pushing the types of textures and frames per second I route for. However, when you call your game a "HD Edition" yoru customers will assume it is a scaled up version, thsi includes texture quality being improved (significantly) and frame rate being modenised to a solid 60. AOE 2 does not do that, instead of actually taking the time to change the game at all, they converted it onto a file and shipped it off to steam to make a further profit. This is not the route they should have taken, I don't care if your game was originally released in the 90's because if you re-release that product as a "remaster" or a "HD Edition" then you MUST and NEED TO update the game to include better FPS and better Texture Quality, those should be requirments.
Conclusion
if you were a big fan of this game when it released, you will still like it now.....mainly because nothing has been changed to improve the game. With that being said, I still really enjoy the game despite its technical issues as it allows good, juicy nostalgia to flow through me once again. Hurray!
-JoshuaUpham

Easily my favorite beat 'em up of all time. Don't have too much time on the Steam version, but I've got about a billion hours into the console version.
Castle Crashers is a game that can easily be beaten in one sitting in an afternoon if you've got time and buddies to play with. YOu start out with four characters, and quickly unlock a fifth. Each of these characters unlock a character when you finish the game with them, and then each of those characters that you unlocked also unlock characters when you beat the game with them. You can unlock other characters through other means (mostly just beating arena modes that are scattered around the map), and those characters unlock characters as well. It's designed for insane replay value and it succeeds in a big way.
There are very simple RPG elements in the sense that you can level up and place your stats into strength, defense, magic, and agility. Strength makes melee stronger, magic makes magic stronger (and unlocks different types of magical attacks/extends your magical range), defense is defense, and agility is your movement speed and bow shot speed and damage. You can find a ton of different weapons that alter your stats in some way, so there's actually a lot of options.
Fun gameplay, a comical storyline brought to life by a simultaneously great and hilarious art style, a million unlockables, bosses to fight, princesses to rescue, and a new game+ mode where the challenge is ramped up.
Now the PC version does have some issues, namely input lag when playing with people who are far away or have slow connections. That said, this does NOT happen for everybody and you're probably good to go if you and your friends are in the same area. The occasional dropout does happen on the PC version but it's not a deal breaker. And of course, local multiplayer is always an option, even on the PC port.
Also, do yourself a favor and don't even try to play this one with a keyboard and mouse. This is a controller game through and through.
But yeah, not only my favorite in the genre, but one of my favorite games ever, period.

First off, let me say that I would normally never spend more than $35 on a solely single player game. Wolfenstein (with backup from FC3) changed that for me. My main reason for why I liked this game so much is because of sheer graphical fidelity. In short, the graphics are top notch. You can tell that Machine Games has poured their soul into this game.
When the game kicks off in 1946, there is clearly a sort of punk-ish look to all the Allies' tech. This contrasts with the sleek and highly advanced Nazi killing machines. Then, boom, when you're thrust into the 1960s, things literally get cracking (Nazi's necks). The action is almost non stop except for a handful of well placed cinematics that really help pull the story together. Regardless, the game isn't without its drawbacks. The amount of blood and gore in this games is staggering . After a while I had to take breaks and play lighter hearted games such as
and

One thing I do have to mention is the 1960s awesome futuristic aesthetics. The sleek designs fit very well with the white and orange or white and orange color schemes. The Many posters scattered around the game offer a break in somewhat endless walls of super concrete. The guns are on a whole other. My favorite was the LazerKraftWerk. An engineering masterpiece that didn't require me to scrounge ammo like some pauper. My other favorite was the fully upgraded marksman rifle. I mean come on, it shoots lasers and is also a sniper rifle. who doesn't want that.

All in all, Wolfenstein: The New Order is a must play if you enjoy killing a lot of Nazis in a multitude of beautifully created settings.

Not yet in terms of how the way things currently are in the game.
One of the basic aspects of the game is how much it does not educate the newer players well enough to help to survive the game in general. When a player is being a medic or an support, there are no visible prompts to tell the newer players how to revive teammates or drop ammo. The icons are still there to be seen on the screen but it does not help that the simple mechanics are not being clear to the thumb sucking morons that you WILL be paired with in this game. All Medics have to do is press their "E" key to revive teammates yet it's the hardest thing the world to be clear. The tutorial is not mandatory which keeps the problem unsolved.
It took the devs close to 2 years to finally get some serious updates for the game. Much like any other shooter you follow. Be prepared for long waits for serious content in terms of maps and legitimate balance updates. Javelin was the newest Merc took a month to updated so that her Shoulder mounted launcher would provide a visual cue when she is prepared to fire at you and your teammates.
What separates this games from a pay to win model is how there are these things called "loadout" cards. In other words predetermined perks and weapon loadouts that will visible alter the colors and skins of your mercenary. This is a welcomed aspect since that means that the weapons available to you will be at the result of RNG. Much of how anything that is related to RNG, IT WILL SCREW YOU over. There is a roulette system on what you will be recieve on for the various mercs. So sometimes that there will be a time of a specific set of weapons and or perks that you will want but the RNGods will not be there for you.
On "Ranked" the situation there is even worse on the terms of rewards for the amount of time that it wants from you to earn limited edition Ranked Cards. It's not bad enough that you are meant to suffer about 10-20 hours of terrible matchmaking to barely scrape enough points to purchase a limited edition crate. To only be given the CHANCE to get the loadout card for the Mercenary that you want.
So speaking of Mercenaries, after when the noobs purchase Vassili as their first mercenary. The game is divided up into various classes. Snipers, Air Support, Assault, Medics and Engineers. Snipers range from the most experienced players to the quickscope wannabes will use to aim down range with their spotting equipment. The Air Support are the teammates that will drop ammunition for the team with packs or stations, keep in mind that Air Supports are the best in keep pressure on the enemy team. Medics are the classes that revive downed teammates that no one wants to be while your team will get stomped on. Engineers are the ones that repair the objectives and plant/disarm C4 the fastest. (Besides a single line of text in the loading for matches. There will be instances where non-engineer teammates will arm, disarm C4 or repair objectives without the knowledge that Engineers can do it with much more efficiency.)
The game is reliant on a fast paced system for the combat and the emphasis of precision aiming. Which is a major selling point one how this game operates. It demands a lot team work as the composition of the team is what will win the day. Just be prepared when you're stuck with two snipers that dont defend the objective, medics that dont heal and air supports that never drop ammo. Typical frustrations related to Class Based shooters.
You earn in game credits from completing matches. These credits can be used to purchase other mercs, load cards or used to craft cards. Much like any Free to Play, be prepared for the grind if you dont plan to spend a penny on this game. When you level up, you are given a crate that will give you various rewards ranging from credit boosters, crafting kits and more basic loadcard cases.
The new match making system has been applied in recent weeks and has little fruit to bare since the match making works and sometimes it doesnt. It could be an issue of the lower overall player count since there is not much of a wide enough range to keep players on their level. So sometimes a team will be given a godly teammate as your fellow randies and you will have to sprint head first to be massacred to take the first objective.
There is a lack of an identity to the OST that this game has. Sure there is the main menu music but it gives off a hopeless vibe yet when the Mercs burst at the seams in personality. When a match is close to ending, there is the usual "Oh No! Hurry up!" music but is overall bland and is meant to be the what the game has to offer. Games like Ballistic Overkill, Blacklight Retribution, LawBreakers and even Brink have better music to make the game memorable.
Give on how much the game has it problems. I cannot help to love it on how the gameplay is still solid and with it's numerous flaws to just work with the player. It just deserves at least a try. I am saying that the game is not a excellent state because of the reasons listed above. But when it continues to work on improving itself, I will gladly eat my words when that day comes. It's just that today, is not that day.

Just finished this game.  Glad I bought it on sale.
SUMMARY: Awesome premise.  Excellent style and aesthetic.  Decent gameplay.  Horrible script.  Bad level design.  Laughable action sequences that destroy suspension of disbelief (and annoy).
The bad dialogue and lazy storyline ruined what could have been a great game.  The worst were the interstitial gopher missions clearly designed to stretch out the gameplay.  Sadly, they had the opposite effect of, what I guess, were their other purpose; namely, help me get to know the characters.  I did everything in my power to avoid slowing down the pace of the game by finding toys or welding torches carelessly thrown down sewers by my so-called friends.
Unfortunately, the real levels aren't much better.  I was railed through so many interesting and atmospheric locations that I wish I could have explored and interacted with more fully.  As it was, it just felt like I was checking boxes on the plot outline.  Walked underwater a bit: Check.  Shot a few globes to make stairs: Check.  Push a button: Check.  Fiddle around with some junk: Check.  Watch a cutscene: Check.  I guess I'm done with the secret underwater stockpile.  Mazel tov.  Next.
The game started out with promise but hit so many sour notes that I had checked out half way through.  I found myself rushing through just to get to the end, skipping the increasingly eye-roll-inducing cutscenes, and telling the main character to shut his word hole and just get on with it.  Seriously Blaskowicz, enough with the maudlin monologue.  We get it.

First off, let me say that I would normally never spend more than $35 on a solely single player game. Wolfenstein (with backup from FC3) changed that for me. My main reason for why I liked this game so much is because of sheer graphical fidelity. In short, the graphics are top notch. You can tell that Machine Games has poured their soul into this game.
When the game kicks off in 1946, there is clearly a sort of punk-ish look to all the Allies' tech. This contrasts with the sleek and highly advanced Nazi killing machines. Then, boom, when you're thrust into the 1960s, things literally get cracking (Nazi's necks). The action is almost non stop except for a handful of well placed cinematics that really help pull the story together. Regardless, the game isn't without its drawbacks. The amount of blood and gore in this games is staggering . After a while I had to take breaks and play lighter hearted games such as
and

One thing I do have to mention is the 1960s awesome futuristic aesthetics. The sleek designs fit very well with the white and orange or white and orange color schemes. The Many posters scattered around the game offer a break in somewhat endless walls of super concrete. The guns are on a whole other. My favorite was the LazerKraftWerk. An engineering masterpiece that didn't require me to scrounge ammo like some pauper. My other favorite was the fully upgraded marksman rifle. I mean come on, it shoots lasers and is also a sniper rifle. who doesn't want that.

All in all, Wolfenstein: The New Order is a must play if you enjoy killing a lot of Nazis in a multitude of beautifully created settings.

Portal 2 is a first-person puzzle game developed by Valve Software and released in 2011.
let's start this review by saying that I like this game A LOT.
I like it so much, in fact, that is in my top 5 favourite games of all times.
In Portal, you solve puzzles with the help of a very special and iconic tool: the portal gun! wich allows you to shoot portals (captain obvious) and teleporting (captain obvious #2) anything that passes through them instantly, this is not only a very creative way to create puzzle games, but also allows to solve puzzles in potentially countless different ways.
The learning curve is just right, teaching the player how each mechanic works without any text or verbal output.
The player is always capable of guessing how a mechanic works with experimentation, starting with a very simple and short puzzle, and adding more and more complexity as you progress.
Not only Portal is set in a very cool location and, thanks to the sound design, has a very nice atmosphere, but it's also one of the very few games that I qualify as "comedic".
Every single line of dialogue by GLaDOS or Wheatley is simply a gem, and these characters are one of the main reasons why so many people love this game, each of these character's voice performances is terrific, along with the great writing and character design, you have two of the most admired characters in the gaming industry.
Here are a few of my favourite quotes from GLaDOS:
-"Here comes the test results: you are a horrible person. That's what is says, a horrible person. We weren't even testing for that."
-"I hope you brought something stronger than a portal gun this time. Otherwise, I'm afraid you're about to become the immediate *past* president of the being alive club, ah ah."
it's clear how much detail the developers have put into creating the world of Portal, as the textures always have very high resolution and the ambience has its distinct style. Also, as repetitive as the Aperture Science's laboratory may be, the developers made the setting look different over time, changing location drastically to keep the player in a fresh environment.
The game, as expected on Source Engine, ran smoothly through all the 76 hours of playtime I had, and never suffered from a framerate drop.
What else can I say? The music is great, it fits perfectly with the sci-fi atmosphere of the game, the sound effects have a really high quality, and if all that wasn't enough, BOOM! 6 extra hours to spend with a friend in co-op puzzles! But wait...that still isn't enough...what about a test chamber editor connected to the steam workshop, so you can play an infinite amount of puzzles for the rest of your life or create your own to share with the world? Seriously though, is there any game as filled with stuff as this one?
This game doesn't have many downsides, the only problem I had is that I didn't quite like some rare sections of the story set in gigantic, asymmetric spaces, finding it confusing most of the time to get through. The only other problem that you may have with this game is your taste, of course. A must-buy if you like puzzle games.
After rating all the aspects of the game, I've come to the conclusion that there is no reason for me to not giving this game a 10/10. No game is perfect, but this one comes really close to such achievement.
