Max Payne 3 isn't a good game, it does a disservice to fans of the Max Payne series, and it disrespects every gamer with its requirement to log into the Rockstar Social Club every time you want to play a single-player game.
On the plus side, the graphics are nice. But on the minus side...
The game lacks the well-honed excitement found in Max Payne 2. The combat in Max Payne 3 is repetitive and predictable. The enemies are much tougher now. They have no problem continuing to fight after you've shot them in the chest three times with an AK47, and they continuously and magically spawn all around you, which requires that you spend almost all of your time in cover. That might be fine if it's what you're looking for, but it's not the great run-and-gun gameplay of the earlier games. The controls aren't well-honed either. Max Payne often doesn't move the way you want him to, so expect to have more annoying deaths than you should.
The game also lacks the exploration component of the original games. Max Payne 3 constantly drives you forward in a completely linear fashion, and as you pass through doors and gates they automatically and inexplicably lock behind you. If you stop to look around, the game will repeatedly berate you for "wasting time". This is especially annoying in conjunction with the game's collection mechanic, where you have to find hidden items strewn throughout the levels. If you try to explore there's a good chance you'll pass through the doorway leading ahead (since you don't know in advance which paths lead ahead and which lead to secret items), whereupon it'll lock and you'll have no way to go back and try another path.
The game frequently takes control away from your character and doesn't hesitate to make him act like a complete idiot. Example: You're supposed to rescue a girl captured by a gang. Over the course of the past five hours, you've killed 99% of the gang's crew and seriously♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the gang leader. He would like nothing more than to hurt you. When you get to the room containing the hostage, the gang leader, and five of his cronies, you notice that the girl's sister and brother-in-law are also there, held captive, with guns to their heads. So naturally you should bust in with bullet time and shoot all the baddies before they know what hit 'em. But the game takes control away from you in one of many annoying cutscenes and has Max Payne run into the room, put his gun down, and say "Don't shoot her!" What the hell?!
that won't help anything! So of course they shoot the girl, and her brother-in-law, and grab the sister. Then Max Payne starts whining about how he failed once again to protect a girl... Yeah, because in this game they make you out to be an idiot.
Max Payne doesn't just suffer from bouts of idiocy, he's unlikeable. He spends a lot of time drinking, drugging himself, passing out drunk, staggering around drunk, vomiting... you get the picture. Sure, they want to portray Max Payne as a down-and-out character. And he is. He's certainly not the Max from the previous games. It might be okay if he was part of a good story, but the story is poor and apparently full of holes.
Finally and perhaps most seriously, the game requires you to create a Social Club account and permanently link it with your Steam account in order to even get to the game's main menu, and you have to log in every time you want to play. If I'd known that, I would not have bought the game, and I will not buy any future Rockstar games that work this way. I don't want to support this kind of behavior, where companies try to control when and whether you're allowed to play the games you've purchased, even in single player, and I recommend you don't either.
Because of the aforementioned problems, I didn't bother finishing the game, and stopping a game in the middle is something I almost never do.
In short, if you want a repetitive, poorly tuned, linear cover shooter that disrespects you as a gamer, buy Max Payne 3. Otherwise, buy something better.

Played through single player numerous times and co-op several times with different friends. A solid, enjoyable experience of relatively easy and sometimes moderate puzzles.
The single player is very cinematic at times, linear and story driven, all the while adding new elements into the game's puzzles, accompanied by voices of GladOS and Wheatly, the latter being a silly little comic relief ball who decided to help free you from Aperture's decaying facility. The characters and environments all have a certain charm to them, all the way down to the little turrets that try to kill you but scream helplessly when they are flying left and right after being knocked over by some flying companion cube. Sounds silly right? Portal mostly is.
The controls are smooth, the visuals easy to read, the soundtrack variable and appropriate; sometimes haunting, othertimes calm, pensive or even tense in some situations. The story is alright, I'm not going to say stellar, because for me personally, the pacing is a little off in places and characters are annoying and old
.
The issues with pacing come in so far as the middle section of the game where you find yourself exploring the lower layers of Aperture's facility which predate GladOS etc; the setting is different and unique, but the game just feels SO SLOW at this point. I remember my time on my first playthrough thinking "I wish I could get back to the modern stuff". I don't know about anyone else, but the contrast between old and modern aesthetics really contributed to a sense of boredom within me, even though you are getting backstory to Aperture in an amusing way all the while.
The issues with the characters merely depend on how much you like the characters and their personalities, because GladOS is, well, GladOS; taunting, condescending, dispassionate and amusing. Meanwhile Wheatly is supposed to be funny, clumsy, bumbling, stupid (fact, not opinion), and interfering. While I enjoy the feeling of GladOS watching me go about my merry way in puzzles because there is usually some quip that is a little left-field and as such surprising and amusing. Whereas Wheatly is silly by design and there is only so much "Oops I made a mistake, lets break things to make it better" humour before it gets really old, REALLY FAST.
These latter criticisms of Portal 2 have a common theme; an element of boredom. Even with the interesting environments and things happening within the story, ultimately it boils down to the same actions over and over again, to a very linear, single-solution puzzle solving experience where at times it feels a little more like 'Do what you're supposed to in order to progress' than straight up puzzle solving. The locations can feed into this as well as aesthetics get boring (hence why they probably felt the need to change it mid-game. Equally, the characters are very limited in their interaction with you, and it really depends on your sense of humour as to whether you will either love or hate Wheatly. But with a style of humour quite so divisive, you will either find yourself bored or enthused for much of the game.
The game does come into it's own though in 2 ways; the process of changing the status quo (i.e. running amok in aperture outside of established puzzle rooms) as this gives you backstory and fleshes out the world in a variety of ways, and in the co-op wherein the potential for puzzles are magnified because of a second pair of portals flying around. There are some really creative and different challenges in co-op which are unlike anything you will have come across in single-player and is defintely worth exploring with a friend - as long as you can cope with many a foolish death from both of you.
There is now even support for community made puzzles in the workshop and these can provide some of the most challenging puzzles you will probably ever try to solve with portals - orders of magnitude better and more difficult than in the game itself. Sadly this only feeds into the contrast and a feeling that the game is just too easy and is less puzzle solving and more "Put the portal where you are told like a good little human".
Overall however, most definitely worth it's asking price based on the inclusion of co-op and workshop support. Might want to give the first portal a go first though, to get you up to speed with what is going on in the world before you begin. Plus, it's a nice nostalgia trip into old-game land, introduces you to portals and GladOS, and is a short, compact experience.

This is pretty much what you'd expect from today's generation of FPS games. The campain took me roughly 30 hours on hard, but could probably have been completed in 20 if I hadn't idled around. Every level is your typical led-by-the-hand, linear tripe with interactive set pieces and quick-time events. The graphics were pretty but nothing to write home about. Stealth exists but has no depth and feels broken (Soldier A doesn't even suspect something is wrong when he sees Soldier B is a bloody mess on the floor). Enemy AI is adequate, but at times laughable. Absolutely zero replayability unless you're a completionist or interested in the other outcome for the single potentially meaningful choice you make. Overall I'd say the game is as advertised, yet still underwhelming. Defeating the last boss left me far more satisfied to be done with the game than with my accomplishment - frankly. Felt like candy... tasty enough to keep eating it, but leaves you with an empty feeling at the end. All that said, I did largely enjoy the characters, interactions, and the story was entertaining enough. Also, nothing but respect for the ending.
I would only recommend this to Wolfenstein fans, FPS enthusiasts, and people who just need something new to play. Personally, I would be upset if I hadn't purchased this for 50% off. I CANNOT recommend this at full price. For $25 or less I feel you get your money's worth.

Wallpaper Engine is a neat piece of software that replaces your wallpaper with a tweakable animated render.
So far the functionality is pretty tip top. It supports optional audio playback features. It can start with windows when it turns on. It has tweakable settings related to things like anti aliasing. And different wallpapers are customizable. Ranging from the ability to change the color to the speed at which the animation plays.
So far it's in Early Access but I've mostly been pretty satisfied so far with it. I'm interested to see where it goes in development. Since it is a very neat idea that I've only really seen on Linux operating systems and not so much on Windows.
Whether a little bit of eye candy is worth your 5$ is up to you though. But for me having an animated wallpaper that displays soundbars for your music tickles an itch that my usually static wallpapers can't scratch.

Problem I have with the game is on one occasion the game failed to load and I had to do an "End Task" in windows. The story is pretty boring and there are slightly too many cutscenes.
All over I would give the game a 8/10.

I had such high hopes for this game, but alas, I've been disappointed again by Bethesda Softworks and, surprisingly, ID (ID titles are usually awesome). This game is nothing like "Return To Castle Wolfenstein". The simplicity of the previous title is completely gone. You literally have to control everything your character does; NOTHING is on automatic. For example, I shouldn't have to manually pick a lock, lining up all the pieces, etc. etc. I shouldn't have to manually pick up ammo and other goodies. I shouldn't have to perform acrobatic feats just to move into a room. I shouldn't have to manually reach for a NPC's hand when he's trying to help me up from a firefight. You get the idea. These things should be done for you or at least made into a skipable cutscene.
There is also a tremendous lack of anything that points you to where you're supposed to go. Occasionally you'll see a small diamond in the distance, but it only appears when you're almost right on top of your obejctive. It's very easy to miss it and find yourself lost in the back and forth of a castle dungeon, plane wreckage, or whatever. Many of the missions are timed, and not knowing which direction to head and failing that mission just because you're turned around isn't fair. There is a map, but there is a "fog" over unexplored regions, so it's pretty much useless. That and there's no indication of above and below on the map. I see no reason that the developers couldn't have made pages to the map showing each level individually instead of cramming the entire maze of hallways for a giant complex on one sheet of paper.  Having a simple arrow or radar on the HUD would've helped immensely.
I also noticed a fair share of slow-downs and graphical glitches; usually from the textures forming on something only after I've looked at it. Come on, guys, what is this, 1996? I have a top of the line system and graphics card, so this shouldn't be happening. This same bug haunts another ID title, "RAGE", which came out in 2011. You'd think they'd figure it out by now.
I also could've done without Blaskowicz's voiceovers during the missions. Other than being an obvious ripoff from Max Payne, it only serves to annoy the player. Half of what he says doesn't make any sense anyway. There's an underwater swimming level about halfway through the game, and all through it, he's blabbering on and on, about his childhood memories and blah blah blah.... Dude, you're here to kill Nazis, not to get in touch with your inner child. Shut up.
I realize that this is going to be an unpopular review, but no, I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone unless it's being bargained price at under $10.00.

Age of Empires II was always one of my favorite games when I was a kid (playing it on an old Windows 98 machine!), and seeing it remastered and put on Steam makes me happy on so many levels, especially because of how well it was done.
So I'm writing this review to answer the key questions of two primary audiences.  First, if you're like me and you're a fan of the original one that came out way back in 1999, let me put your main questions to rest: yes, the game has aged extremely well and is still just as much fun now as it was then.  And no, this is not a remake of the original - it is a remastering of the original.  It's the same game, same engine, same game mechanics.  The rerelease of AoE2 has done nothing but improve it.  Some of the menus have been streamlined, and because it's now on Steam, multiplayer support is an absolute breeze compared to the hoops you had to jump through on the original.  The game is now displayed in full HD resolutions, and some of the animations and sprites have gotten a graphical update (most noticeably fire and the fact that water is now animated).  If you're playing against the computer, there have been a lot of AI tweaks that will make the game much more of a challenge than the predictable, clumsy AI from the original.  I also love the Forgotten expansion and the civilizations and campaigns it adds to the game; it really does seamlessly merge old content with new, so you're getting a new game experience but with all the things that made this game such a classic in the first place.
Now, to the newcomers who perhaps aren't familiar with the Age of Empires series: AoE2 is probably the quintessential medieval real-time strategy game.  The real beauty of Age of Empires (compared to a lot of the more modern RTS games) is its simple mechanics and streamlined gameplay.  It's one of those games where you can really focus on the gameplay without the meta getting in your way too much, and there's really limitless options on how to enjoy the game - between all the different game types (conquest, king of the hill, etc.) and all the civilizations available, it really is a challenging experience every time you play.  Sparing you all from reading a wall of text, here's the simple things that make this  game worth the purchase price:
-High replayability: the game contains multiple storyline campaigns and has a good "skirmish" mode.
-Outstanding multiplayer: the multiplayer aspect really is the star of this game, but it's still very enjoyable even if you don't do multiplayer games much.  But the way Steam handles the multiplayer aspect of the game is really very nice and very simple - this is especially a bonus if you compare it to the original.
-Simple mechanics but deep gameplay: the game is very like chess in that it's very easy to learn and simple to play, but the finesse of being truly competitive in AoE2 is very nuanced.
-Reasonably lightweight: this game runs pretty well even on fairly middle to low-end computers.  The graphics aren't anything super spectacular; the game is over 15 years old, and aside from updated resolutions and a few new animations, the graphics really haven't been updated since then - nor do they need to be! The artwork from this game is quite gorgeous, even rendered in 2D.
-Full of historical goodies: sure, that's not really much of a selling point, but still worth saying.
In all, this game has easily given me over 100 hours of fun (and if you count the original since 1999, probably closer to 500 or 600 hours), and despite the fact that it's a rerelease of an old game, it's a classic for a good reason :)

This is pretty much what you'd expect from today's generation of FPS games. The campain took me roughly 30 hours on hard, but could probably have been completed in 20 if I hadn't idled around. Every level is your typical led-by-the-hand, linear tripe with interactive set pieces and quick-time events. The graphics were pretty but nothing to write home about. Stealth exists but has no depth and feels broken (Soldier A doesn't even suspect something is wrong when he sees Soldier B is a bloody mess on the floor). Enemy AI is adequate, but at times laughable. Absolutely zero replayability unless you're a completionist or interested in the other outcome for the single potentially meaningful choice you make. Overall I'd say the game is as advertised, yet still underwhelming. Defeating the last boss left me far more satisfied to be done with the game than with my accomplishment - frankly. Felt like candy... tasty enough to keep eating it, but leaves you with an empty feeling at the end. All that said, I did largely enjoy the characters, interactions, and the story was entertaining enough. Also, nothing but respect for the ending.
I would only recommend this to Wolfenstein fans, FPS enthusiasts, and people who just need something new to play. Personally, I would be upset if I hadn't purchased this for 50% off. I CANNOT recommend this at full price. For $25 or less I feel you get your money's worth.

I like this game. I really do. From a technical standpoint I marvel at it, although I doubt many others do. The building mechanic is nice, and the creativity of the game is there. My issue is with certain mechanics of the game. For example, the matchmaking system is somewhat subpar with games such as league of legends. Maybe I'm just bitter from having my tanked up mech with snipers and a shotgun being repeatedly blasted to bits by the same brick with wheels fifteen times who has the superior weaponry and has fifteen homing turrets on the back. The loot system is absurd in my eyes, you have to spend an abhorent amount of in-game money to afford ONE minigun, TWO out of the six spider legs you need to complete your ant robot you've been working on for weeks, or that set of anti air guns to deal with the OP fliers that kill you ten seconds after the shields go down. I wasn't in the era where you had to unlock loot, but that sounds a lot more balanced than the current system. And the "Premium" Shtick. Yikes. You need to pay a fee to keep using the color red? Who comes up with this? I don't want to pay a monthly fee just to fill in the red parts of the apple shaped robot I built because I could! And the loot crates. Half of the stuff out of them wouldn't be considered the "Epic" that the purple coloring implies. I mean, how can a strut, something that connects things together and is rather common throughout the game, be considered epic? How is a headlight, something logic dictates would be a rather common and inexpensive item, or a spedometer or altimeter, things that I'm not sure really are useful in this game, be considered rare commodities? I mean, what world are lightbulbs expensive but massive mechs can be made for a relatively small amount of money?
I reiterate. I like this game. It has creativity that hearkens back to minecraft, and glorious amounts of gratuitous destruction. But the current systems they have in place for both loot and matchmaking are sub-par at best, and I hope these will be adressed in the future.

And that's exactly what it does on the other hand : I really felt playing an HD old FPS : the Call of Duty franchise, for example, made a tradition in modern FPS of holding only two weapons (usually a rifle & a gun), well in this game you have all the weapons accessible to you, you can switch weapons like you did in old FPS, you can also hold double weapons for each kind, which pretty awesome. The musics too have had some serious work, which is another thing I missed from previous FPS (I mean I could remember Doom's songs, Duke Nukem songs.... but I got nothing whenever I think about FPS like CoD or Crysis.... except maybe for Crysis 2's main theme. The biggest exception to this would the Halo saga which has fantastic pieces of music). There was a lot of attention and care to what they did, they didn't just made a generic FPS hoping to cash on nostalgia, which was my biggest fear.
The end of the game might be dragging a bit to my taste, but it didn't felt too long either. The difficulty spikes a bit towards the end, but generally it's nothing undoable, especially if you consider one of the last weapons you get, which has somewhat infinite ammo (you need to recharge it every now and then, but there are plenty of places to fill up), so you can exploit the hide & kill tactic with this weapon if you get cornered by too many ennemies with low health.
I think this is a game you can enjoy, especially if you miss the old FPS era where you could wield 9 different guns. For my collection : this game is a winner.

I am a fan of Max Payne and Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne. The second is in my top ten games of all time. When I heard Rockstar had taken over I was happy. When I heard it would be set in Brazil I was concerned. The end result - a great story that stays true to the character in a new setting.
I am reviewing the single player story only here. Haven't played much multiplayer so far. There are a few reviews that complain there are too many cut scenes  - don't listen to these ADHD kids. The single player experience is a story, something the majority of gamers just don't get any more. The Michael Bay School of Game Playing is alive and well (look at how many reviews haven't even given a game an hour of their time).
There are a lot of cut scenes between each Chapter but these are very well produced with a top notch story and great voice acting.  The tell the story of Max Payne - a man who has lost his family, lost his self respect and lost his way. It takes over from where MP2 left off and shows a Max that thinks he has hit rock bottom and yet still manages to dig a little deeper. Taking a job in Brazil seems like easy money, a much needed excuse to get out of New York and should give him ample time to drink and pop pain killers. All is not as it seems as thigns go from bad to worse in a way only Max Payne can achieve.
The game mechanics are solid even if you may have to tweak the mouse sensitivity to get it where you need. Plenty of different weapons are on offer, including duel wielding and of course no Max Payne would be complete without the series' greatest creation - bullet time. There are collectibles in golden guns and "clues" for the story but it is the story that shines. It's told from Max's point of view - jagged and distorted as seen from a man who is high or drunk most of the time. It's a stylised film noir that is a welcome deviation from MP2's very traditional NY City film noir. Rockstar do pay tribute to that with several flashback missions set in NY so everyone is happy.
Overall this game tells a story, a good story, that uses cinematic cut scenes as well as game play to tell that story. Enjoy it. If your eye starts twitching and you get distracted after not shooting something for ten seconds then save your money and load up Call of Duty.

The original Portal had the element of surprise. Its style of first-person physics-based puzzle gameplay was unique. GLaDOS, the murderous robotic villain, was new and vibrant and evil in the most charming way. Cake jokes and songs about surviving dismemberment were still hilarious. It was short, succinct and essential. Creating a sequel without playing all the same notes and making it feel like Portal: The Longer Version is a tough task. For Valve, it's apparently no problem.
From the first moments of waking up in the rusting Aperture Science facility to right before the credits roll, Portal 2 rarely falters. The world is bigger, the story thicker, and the character development more surprising. The mania of GLaDOS, the facility's operator, is molded into unexpected forms alongside a host of brutally funny personalities. The history of the Aperture Science facility is filled in, character origins discussed, and though its pacing suffers as it occasionally strikes a more serious tone, an abundance of cruel jokes and cheerfully sincere death threats prevent it from losing its sarcastic charm. When you're not staring at your screen with wrinkled, pained expression on your face trying to figure out a puzzle, expect to be laughing.

Right after finishing Portal for the first time the other day I felt compelled to play through Portal 2 immediately after. Portal ended on a cliff hanger. The ending of Portal may have been spoilt for me but Portal 2 was a completely fresh start for me. I was curious how they could improve on the original when the original worked so well, felt polished and satisfying to play through in a sitting or two. Now after it being out for several years my experience with Portal 2 was as follows.
The game starts us off in what seems like a post-apocalyptic setting. We are immediately introduced to our new companion Wheatley who guides us out to more familiar grounds. Shortly after we find our trusty Portal gun among the wreckage and the real fun begins. The game remains the same for the most part. It feels similar to the first person puzzle action was saw in Portal but with a lot more polish. To begin with I was impressed by how the tutorials were again clever in getting you familiar with the new mechanics but also at how quickly they trusted you to go nuts with experimenting with the gun. Truthfully the first part of the game was great but they outdid themselves in the second half of the game by allowing us to explore new environments, mess around with new mechanics such as gels which allow you to run faster, jump higher or create portals in different places. All in all the core mechanics from Portal are still here but there’s an added touch of polish that can definitely be seen.
I didn't do any of the co-op missions but I understand that there are new levels that you can try. Definitely worth a go if you’re interested and can add a lot more fun to the game with a player 2.
The story was very entertaining, the characters are full of personality and charm. Particularly our new companion Wheatley. We re-encounter some familiar settings in Portal 2 and dive into the lore of Portal much more this time around. In Portal 2 there is an emphasis on explaining why this technology exists at all and what happened to those who created it. The game from beginning to end was very entertaining and the voice acting was top notch. Like Portal each level prompted some voice over from GLaDOS and this time it’s no different. As with the original it’s a pleasure to listen to the characters banter and how they develop throughout the course of the game.
Technically speaking the game like Portal looks good, it’s not the flashiest of games but it feels like a further polished version of Portal with a lot more added to it in all areas. Portal 2 ran smoothly throughout the entire play through. It features Ultra-wide support and look great at 3440 x 1440 without mods.
Portal 2 is a step up in many ways to Portal. It holds up as a game that is constantly celebrated by its community and holds up to this day. Portal 2 doesn’t get much wrong, the only things that frustrated me were some of the puzzles and that was on me not being able to figure them out. Portal 2 lets you test and play around in these environments and allows you to take the approach you want to progress further. This is a game that improves upon its predecessor in many ways while retaining the original mechanics it creates an identity of its own that gamers shouldn't miss. I for one wish I'd played through both Portal and Portal 2 sooner.
I would not recommend to buy this unless microsoft fixed the fps issues.

When this game came out I didn't pay it much attention even though I was a huge fan of Max Payne 2. It just looked like another rushed and overpriced "Triple A" game with nice graphics to hook you in.
I recently bought it when it was on sale and realized I was very wrong. Max Payne 3 is a really good game, and although it certainly can't compete with the second in the series, it does a lot of things right and some others not so much.
The action in the game alone is enough to keep you going through the end. The game is really linear but in this case it's not a bad thing since it constantly pushes you forward from gunfight to gunfight with some great setpiece moments. This is coming from a guy who has a really hard time finishing games. I normaly go through 80% of a game, get bored, set it down for a few weeks and then go back to finish it just to see the ending. That was not the case with this game, it doesn't let you put it down. The bullet time is very nicely done and will never get old. There is a great variety of guns but it doesn't really matter since the enemies are bullet sponges. You don't want to get anything else but headshots in this game. And since it's an instakill, the gun with which you do it doesn't really matter. It's a bit odd that none of then have any actual recoil but it suits the playstyle of the game, especially in bullet time.
The parts in between the gunfights and action however are not that good, and it's where the game has its biggest flaws. Between every action scene you normally have to get close to a door or ledge and Max starts to walk instead of run. At this point you are treated with a cutscene of Max opening said door and going into the next area and bad guys soon follow. Then you get control of Max again. These cutscenes feel really pointless and most of the time switch between the weapon you are holding or drop them altogether without any reason whatsoever.
The rest of the cutscenes are not that good either. The visual efects they use are nice but they are too overused and too random. The way I see it, the neon glare you sometimes get is suposed to outline the fact that Max is wasted or has a massive hangover through most of the story, but they should be used at the right time, rather than every 5 seconds. Also for the first half of the game, all the cutscenes at the begining or end of a chapter seem to be Max drinking by himself in his apartment with no dialogue whatsoever. Just Max holding a glass, drinking, filling it again, and drinking again, repeated 4 or 5 times until he passes out. It feels really drawn out and unnecesary. Do it once, we'll get it.
All in all I feel the game has too many pointless cutscenes. Some drag you out of the action for no reason and some are just weird and overdone, but none of them hurt the game that much.
The last thing I would like to talk about is Max himself. Even though he is one of my favorite videogame characters of all time, in this game, and especially towards the end, I end up getting tired of him and his constant whining. I really think this is more the story's fault then his. Max usualy talks about things that didn't happend the way he wanted and how bad he feels, but since the story isn't that good I don't feel the same way and as a result Max's constant self pitty feels overused. I don't care about anyone who dies in the game, buy Max won't shut up about how he could have saved them even though he himself had no emotional attachement to them. It's not like in the first game where he grieves over his wife and daughter or the second one where he is second guessing Mona's intentions and his feelings for her. This time its just rich people who party all day and don't give a ♥♥♥♥ about anything. Yeah, we should all cry.
Oh and the multiplayer....didn't play it, not gonna.
Even with all the things I mentioned I really liked the game a lot and highly recommend it if you played the previous two.

Dirty Bomb has the
to be the best online FPS game in a a long time. It's fast paced, challenging, well themed and fun.
+ Maps (although there are not a huge number of them) are well designed.
+ Gunplay is focused on skill, landing headshots is a necessity no matter what weapon you are using. Spray and pray doesn't work, skill determines who walks out alive.
+ Highly objecitve based.
+ Several mercs (classes) allow multiple playstyles and different team builds.
+ Free to play and no pay to win elements. Spending your real money only helps with progressing faster, but doesn't give you any advantages over others.
- Earning credits (used for buying mercs, loadouts etc.) is rather slow, so it takes quite a bit of grinding to get what you want.
- Team balance is a bit too often bad. You will have a fair share of unbalanced matches, but this isn't anything new to online games to be honest.
Hence Dirty Bomb is a free game, I really see no reason why you wouldn't give it a go. After leaving TF2 (1000+ hours played) behind, Dirty Bomb has become the number one shooter game for me. This game will be a good experience for anyone who enjoy challenging and team based shooters. Hop onboard, and play dirty!

There's been a lot of hubub recently about Wolfenstein being the sleeper hit of the year, and after hearing it was made by most of the same team that worked on the Chronicles of Riddick and The Darkness (both fantastic games that are criminally overlooked), I was excited to try it.
Does it succeed? Mostly. The general premise (your character is in a coma for 14 years and wakes up to a world where the Nazis won WWII) works, largely because of solid storytelling and a fantastic art direction. Up to this point, BJ Blaskowicz's defining trait is being "that dude who kills Nazis," but Machinegames does a really good job of making him a belivable character thrust into an unbelivable situation.  Except for the romance stuff. Ech, that romance stuff. The various newspapers and decorations throughout the levels do a great job of establishing the world and overall tone.
The actual gameplay doesn't break any new ground, but it's really good for what it is.  The guns have a great feel and weight to them, the enemy types encourage a vareity of strategies, and the pace is fast and frantic.  There's also a stealth element, where the game often encourages you to silently kill generals in the area to prevent backup. This works most of the time, but not always - the AI has some weird quirks where sometimes it'll notice you from miles away and other times it has no idea that you're right next to it.  Also, the game loses some steam towards the end - they run out of new enemy types and the new environments just aren't exciting enough.
I think some of the "surprise GOTY" talk is a bit overblown, but having said that, Wolfenstein is a great FPS with a surprisingly good story that stands above a lot of games in its genre. Recommended, especially at $20.

Dirty Bomb has the
to be the best online FPS game in a a long time. It's fast paced, challenging, well themed and fun.
+ Maps (although there are not a huge number of them) are well designed.
+ Gunplay is focused on skill, landing headshots is a necessity no matter what weapon you are using. Spray and pray doesn't work, skill determines who walks out alive.
+ Highly objecitve based.
+ Several mercs (classes) allow multiple playstyles and different team builds.
+ Free to play and no pay to win elements. Spending your real money only helps with progressing faster, but doesn't give you any advantages over others.
- Earning credits (used for buying mercs, loadouts etc.) is rather slow, so it takes quite a bit of grinding to get what you want.
- Team balance is a bit too often bad. You will have a fair share of unbalanced matches, but this isn't anything new to online games to be honest.
Hence Dirty Bomb is a free game, I really see no reason why you wouldn't give it a go. After leaving TF2 (1000+ hours played) behind, Dirty Bomb has become the number one shooter game for me. This game will be a good experience for anyone who enjoy challenging and team based shooters. Hop onboard, and play dirty!

They really messed this up. I got this game when it had just come out (I always use the launcher so it shows I don't have many hours) and it was amazing - there wasn't really a pay to win. You had research points to unlock things so you could rush ahead to a certain item, or follow a specific path, you actually got cash after a battle and nothing was super over powered. But then... the big updates came.
Firstly they changed the tech tree (where you researched items) and then removed it completely, secondly they changed the cash system and then they changed it back and now they changed it, again, so you don't get cash after a battle, they removed items and added them back in and removed them, resulting in a loss of cash - e.g armour blocks and S-tier items - and the pay to win update was introduced: now you, technically, get 6x loot after a battle (with premium), can sell things for 3x more and get exclusive things - nearly everything can be done better with premium.
I'm going to explain the stupid process on how to get cash in this game:
1. Play a battle (terrible team balancing because they removed the efficient ranking system)
2. Get given a random loot crate (depends on how well you did in battle, probably terrible because of team balancing)
2. Unlock your crate (you get 2x rewards with premium)
3. Either keep or sell the items you get, that are mostly terrible (you sell things for 3x more with premium)
4. You gained about 100-300 cash (tier 5 stuff cost around 7500 cash, and the really good stuff costing about 150,000)
Or..:
1. Pay money and get everything that would take you maybe 24 - 48 hours, of non stop playing, to get (buying crates)
2. Beat people in battle easy (you get over powered items - e.g chain shredder, missile launcher etc because you get the best crates)
4. Get 6x rewards afterwards (with premium)
5. Get even better items and billions of robits
Why are the teams so unbalanced? and what was the ranking system? you are probably asking. Well the ranking system worked in tiers: tier 1 - 10 and the mega bot tier. The Robocraft devs. removed this feature so now you can put overpowered mega bots with around tier 7 stuff. There used to be a mega bot game mode, for tier 7/8s and up, where there would be 1 - 3 mega bots on one team and 6 - 10 (I think) tier 7 - 10s on the other team. These teams were balanced. Now, however, you can easilly be put into a game with 5 mega bots vs 5 tier 7 - 10s.
Don't play this game unless you've got £30 spare!

Portal 2 is the second and last official installment of the Portal Series, released in 2011 by Valve.
In my opinion, this game adds a lot to the original formula and improves a lot of aspects of the first game, this time you'll have to breakout of a destroyed Aperture Science using your skills and your beloved portal gun. You'll also have to master 3 gels, the repulsion gel, the propulsion gel and the conversion gel.
The Story, along with the characters are pretty well written and they feel alive. The humor is well done and the dialogues, specially in the later scenarios are totally hilarious. Even you haven't played the first game, you'll undestand the story.
The aesthetics are beautiful and you'll have a lot of this so called screenshot opportunities, even if you have a low end rig, you'll be amazed of the beauty that can spawn from the source engine.
And the last but not less important aspect of the game, the soundtrack, from the first time you awake from your long time sleep to the last song, Is not only fitting, but also, like grabbing science and adapting it into an mp3 format. You guys did a great work with it.
Overall, I recommend it to every time of gamer and non gamer, if you want to get into gaming, try this game. If you love fps, try the game, if you love puzzles, definitively try this game, and the first one , if you're a Valve fan, why are you reading this review in the first place? Get the damn game!

This is a story about a loser called Max Payne. He's always drunk and stuck in trouble. But this ex-cop is lucky enough to stay alive and kill well-prepared army of bandits, cops, terrorists etc. It's ridiculous. He's kind of superman who eats painkiller tabs faster than Dr. House can do. I don't see any point about this game that I can recommend. Here's list of things I don't like:
- Plot. It's s short and predictable. Even in chapter 1 you know who are bad guys. And it's obvious that Max will kill them. Story is short, it took less than 15 hours to pass the game on last difficult level.
- Gameplay. It's monotonous and boring. You only watch movie few minutes, run and shoot enemies, movie, enemies... boring.
- World. It's linear. You go though one door and can't came back because of it had become blocked. Levels are simple, you can move only in one direction.
- Competition. I played on last difficult level. It wasn't hard at all. Last boss took some time to pass. But that's all.
- Bugs. Weapons disappear from time to time, enemies can shoot you when you and they can't see each other.
- Graphics. Nothing special.
- Replayability. There's no replayability. You can play a multiplayer match or look levels for gold parts of guns, nothing more.
If you're Rambo or Chuck Norris or Terminator fan you'll probably like it as it's thriller and main action is shooting targets. Otherwise, I recommend you to save your money and time.

Wolfenstein, being the first "official" FPS, has always been a good game. The only soiled spot on the franchise's reputation was Activisions 2009 Wolfenstein which didn't suck at all, but just wasn't that great. Before that, there was the unquestionably epic RTCW - both in multiplayer and story - and it was a hard game to top.
I can safely say New Order tops RTCW and is the best game in the franchise. That doesn't mean it's without its faults, but Machine Games said they would deliver a fantastic single player experience, and they weren't wrong.
Sure, the story is a little bit cliche - if you can't just get overself and get into a story. So, whereas previous Wolfenstein games have always gone the occultist route - we all know dem Nazi's loved their occultism - New Order decided to go more of a Stargatey/Indiana Jonesy route where the Nazi's use ancient, high tech secrets as the source of their advancement. Frankly it's a breath of fresh air, even if it isn't so original, into a franchise that became a broken record with the exact same memes over and over again. More importantly, the story moves far away from World War II and tries something different: a world where the Nazi's won. It pulls this off well, but this is also something that hurts the game overall.
The story in this game unfortunately suffers under the weight of its own grandeur. Early on the story was established and it took an interesting road to develop into something that would be better suited for a mini-series, but ran its course like it was a Hollywood movie. The game comes in at about 13 hours, and that's including literally all collectibles and secret rooms, picking up all items, exploring 100% of the map, side quests, and dying about 10 times over the course of the entire game. As far as I'm concerned, MG had an opportunity to make a much longer game when they established the resistance - and it felt like that was going to happen, but it never did. To make matters worse, MG established this post-WW2 nazi ruled planet, yet did not fully explore it and killed any hope of a sequel - at least with some of the same characters - because of the ending.
Most importantly though, the story trolls everyone near the end, everyone who can follow story and understands writing anyway. Over the course of the game, a certain villain is built up - with personal interactions with Blazkowicz no less - and then suddenly, inexplicitly, off screen, the villain up and disappears. Is never seen again and the credits roll. There is no post credits scene, either. It's like the story writers all got kidnapped with the script for the end of the game and someone else had to step in and just♥♥♥♥♥♥out an ending in 1 hour. Someone who can't write very well, either. It's just so anti-climactic what happens, and that coupled with the disappointingly anti-cliche cliche ending (The type of ending that people started using to be somber and realistic and counter-cliche, except that now it's just as old hat as the standard action movie ending) should leave a bad taste in your mouth if you are at all a student of literature or have any ability to write on your own.
One thing I thought was really cool was the weapon design. You only get to see it in some of the guns, but in those guns it's very obvious that Machine Games took what existed in World War 2 and they naturally evolved it to be realistic and make sense in a fictional universe. The German assault rifle, for example, is based on the STG44. You can see in the 1960s version that they kept the standard HK style sight - the rear sight which all HK rifles, SMGs, and MGs use to this day - and kind of made it follow a realistic design progression of German weaponry.  The Luger also can be clearly seen in both the 1948 version of the pistol, and the 60s pistol - which looks pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥in a scifi way. MG60 is also another fine example of this. Better yet, all of the guns - pistol, laserkraft, MG, assault rifle, AR marksman, shotgun, knife, grenade, they all serve distinct purposes.
Pistols are absolutely perfect for stealth. Once you get the silencer, it takes 1 hit to the head to kill almost any enemy in the game except the more heavily armored super soldaten and rocket troops.  The assault rifle is good for all situations and frankly must be substituted for actually having a sniper rifle, because you're never going to get more than 30 bullets total for the AR marsksman. The laser AR marksman, a gun you'll only use twice, is very good at accurate and powerful fire, making it an alternative to the assault rifle. Knives are great for stealth and make for some fun situations, like a swirlie and a knife in the skull, and can also be thrown. The SMG only really exists in the first level so it isn't worth a mention, but it is good for close up encounters, just like the shotgun - which can also be used for ricochet madness in the submarine. Other than that, you have the laserkraftwerk, which serves as your main laser cannon, and your primary method for opening most crates, fences, and cutting chains in the game. Once you get used to it your arsenal seems kind of limited, but all the guns do their jobs well - if not with flair.
The only thing I can say negative about the actual gameplay is that even on normal, the game is dreadfully easy. There was one time in the entire game where I died and it was for no reason, on the Gibraltar bridge, until I figured out how to easily defeat all 294 Nazi's. Other than that and the first phase of the last boss, it's just silly how easy the game was. Will try again on superhard.
Also, Nazi Battlemech's. Everywhere. Oh and of course, mofoing space/Moon nazis. And, they of course threw in a nod to mechahitler, as all Nazi movies like this do.
I really, really wanted there to be a sequel, but I think the way MG left the story at the end precludes it happening without a brand new hero. I'm just saying, a major villain is still alive as far as you know and it's never explained - the end was just awful - but there is an entire planet of Nazi's to deal with.

The original Portal had the element of surprise. Its style of first-person physics-based puzzle gameplay was unique. GLaDOS, the murderous robotic villain, was new and vibrant and evil in the most charming way. Cake jokes and songs about surviving dismemberment were still hilarious. It was short, succinct and essential. Creating a sequel without playing all the same notes and making it feel like Portal: The Longer Version is a tough task. For Valve, it's apparently no problem.
From the first moments of waking up in the rusting Aperture Science facility to right before the credits roll, Portal 2 rarely falters. The world is bigger, the story thicker, and the character development more surprising. The mania of GLaDOS, the facility's operator, is molded into unexpected forms alongside a host of brutally funny personalities. The history of the Aperture Science facility is filled in, character origins discussed, and though its pacing suffers as it occasionally strikes a more serious tone, an abundance of cruel jokes and cheerfully sincere death threats prevent it from losing its sarcastic charm. When you're not staring at your screen with wrinkled, pained expression on your face trying to figure out a puzzle, expect to be laughing.

Right after finishing Portal for the first time the other day I felt compelled to play through Portal 2 immediately after. Portal ended on a cliff hanger. The ending of Portal may have been spoilt for me but Portal 2 was a completely fresh start for me. I was curious how they could improve on the original when the original worked so well, felt polished and satisfying to play through in a sitting or two. Now after it being out for several years my experience with Portal 2 was as follows.
The game starts us off in what seems like a post-apocalyptic setting. We are immediately introduced to our new companion Wheatley who guides us out to more familiar grounds. Shortly after we find our trusty Portal gun among the wreckage and the real fun begins. The game remains the same for the most part. It feels similar to the first person puzzle action was saw in Portal but with a lot more polish. To begin with I was impressed by how the tutorials were again clever in getting you familiar with the new mechanics but also at how quickly they trusted you to go nuts with experimenting with the gun. Truthfully the first part of the game was great but they outdid themselves in the second half of the game by allowing us to explore new environments, mess around with new mechanics such as gels which allow you to run faster, jump higher or create portals in different places. All in all the core mechanics from Portal are still here but there’s an added touch of polish that can definitely be seen.
I didn't do any of the co-op missions but I understand that there are new levels that you can try. Definitely worth a go if you’re interested and can add a lot more fun to the game with a player 2.
The story was very entertaining, the characters are full of personality and charm. Particularly our new companion Wheatley. We re-encounter some familiar settings in Portal 2 and dive into the lore of Portal much more this time around. In Portal 2 there is an emphasis on explaining why this technology exists at all and what happened to those who created it. The game from beginning to end was very entertaining and the voice acting was top notch. Like Portal each level prompted some voice over from GLaDOS and this time it’s no different. As with the original it’s a pleasure to listen to the characters banter and how they develop throughout the course of the game.
Technically speaking the game like Portal looks good, it’s not the flashiest of games but it feels like a further polished version of Portal with a lot more added to it in all areas. Portal 2 ran smoothly throughout the entire play through. It features Ultra-wide support and look great at 3440 x 1440 without mods.
Portal 2 is a step up in many ways to Portal. It holds up as a game that is constantly celebrated by its community and holds up to this day. Portal 2 doesn’t get much wrong, the only things that frustrated me were some of the puzzles and that was on me not being able to figure them out. Portal 2 lets you test and play around in these environments and allows you to take the approach you want to progress further. This is a game that improves upon its predecessor in many ways while retaining the original mechanics it creates an identity of its own that gamers shouldn't miss. I for one wish I'd played through both Portal and Portal 2 sooner.

This game is a lot better than I expected. As a big fan of the Remedy Max Payne games, a good chunk of the pre-release stuff was concerning me, but it all came together into a really good time. They've updated the gameplay in ways that still feel like Max Payne, and manages to be a shooter that's vastly more fun to play than the regular slow third person shooters, or twitch-based iron-sight extravaganzas.
I've been super cognizant of games that just pump endless waves of enemies, and wait for you to click on them to make them dead, lately, and it's soured a lot of otherwise good experiences (Bioshock Infinite, Space Marine, Dragon Age II). This doesn't feel like that (spare maybe one, or two instances across the whole game), and I really expected it to be. Whether it be the fun mechanics, or the encounter design as a whole, I really like how this game plays.
Also I feel like the story fits Max's character really well. While there's a definite charm to his melodrama from the previous games, Rockstar adds onto that in ways that make his character a lot more human, and helps balance things out a bit. The writing wasn't always as sharp as the Remedy games, but it surprised in other ways in equal amount.
I really like this game. You should probably play it, even if you're tired of shooters, or are turned off by the ludicrous 30GB install. It's a nice conclusion to two games that didn't really need elaborated further upon, and that's just pretty impressive to me.

The first couple of chapters in TNO I thought were more frustrating than fun, especially the scene where you first meet Deathshead and a couple of objectives where you have to sneak and avoid being detected. I hate mandatory stealth missions with a passion.
But once you complete that last annoying stealth objective you can pretty much play the rest of the game any way you want - using knives and silenced pistol to take out Nazis quietly, or mow down Nazis with both barrels blazing. The way the story unfolds in the game ought to hold your attention as you progress.
Overall, the beginning felt a bit dull, but the game gets better later on. And yes, there are direct references in-game to the original granddaddy of the FPS genre.
I like it a lot!

The perks are nice but not essential. In this game it works out great, because they are there if you're into persuing them but they don't get in the way of your enjoyment of the game. I went for MOAR BULLETS and avoided grenades, and my performance did not suffer in the least.
Overall gameplay was fantastic. The animations were really smooth, and the level design was well thought-out with some hidden bonuses/collectibles along the way. The controls in this game are really crisp. Like, crisper than an apple picked right off the tree after the autumn's harvest moon crisp. Just that right amount of light crunchiness without getting all twitchy (DAYZ I'M LOOKING AT YOU, you dry leaf crunching under the heft of my .45 caliber pistol rounds).
The overall plot concept was simple (and I don't feel this to be a spoiler as it's literally the first few seconds of the game): "The bad guy's name is Deathshead. Let's go kill Deathshead." As one would expect, he's not particularly interested in jumping in front of your bullets, and  trying accomplish that simple-sounding objective is where Wolfenstein gets it's pull from.
The atmosphere and aesthetics were brilliantly executed, as was everything about the characters. OMG dem characters doe! They had excellent writing, great acting, and an engaging development. The universe that Wolfenstein presents
the characters to further enhance the plot experience. In other words, there really isn't anything that's contrived in this game (such as, "IT'S JUST... uh...  BECAUSE OF XYZ, WHATEVER JUST ACCEPT IT" does not occur).
The weapons in Wolfenstein feel visceral, but are not anything particularly creative. Full auto rifle, pistol, shotgun, sniper, and so on and so forth. You also get a laser gun, but in a world set in "nazi engineering takes over the world," you'd be disappointed if you couldn't pew hard.
And pew hard you will. Wolfenstein presents its heroes, friends, and villians concisely and profoundly. I mean, I really hated Deathshead, and I was not going to stop holding down "Primary Fire" until I stuck my freshly shined GI boot into his mouth (via his butt).
Awesome weapon-feel, fantastic characters, well-executed universe, "strangling nazis." Not really much wrong with this game, Strongly recommended.
edit: The graphics are also stunning. The freaking in-game movies though, holy hell those are rendered with some next-level stuff.

Intro
----
Max Payne 3 is a solid action game, let down by issues with replayability and series continuity.
It's a cinematic third-person shooter, set in present day Sao Paolo (Brazil) and New York. You play an alcoholic, ex-NYPD detective-turned-bodyguard in a dark story about crime and corruption. As in most modern third-person shooters, the action is based around moving from cover to cover and popping out to take quick shots, but in this case you'll be aided with slow-motion and balletic dodging.
Playability
----
The gunplay is a great example of the genre. You'll find a ridiculously varied arsenal throughout the game, ranging from silenced pistols to grenade launchers, all of which are fun to use. You're rewarded for accuracy, are encouraged to switch weapons often, and can resort to other methods if you're running low on bullets (grenades, melee action if you're close enough, vehicle emplacements, and lots of objects which explode if sufficiently abused).
It feels like it's 'on rails', and you're mostly just doing what the game's producers want you to, but diving sideways in slow-motion to nail a perfect headshot feels great. You'll regularly find combat arenas that are complex enough to give you a variety of methods for tackling them.
The storytelling is less successful. With the exception of Max himself, the characters are all very shallow, and impossible either to care about or to genuinely despise. Voice acting is jobsworth (again with the exception of James McCaffrey's soulful Max Payne), facial animations are wooden. The story snakes around in such a way that I found myself frequently forgetting what the whole point of that section was; it doesn't feel like there's a unifying drive to it.
It's stylishly 'directed' though, feeling very much like a Tony Scott film. And HEALTH's soundtrack is utterly spectacular - the two elements in combination are highly immersive, feeling like you're powering through a monster hangover. This helps you get inside Max's head, as he tries to quit his vices and get his life back on some vague semblance of a track.
It's a good-looking game for the time, and there's a wide variety of options to scale the graphics back if you're playing on an older machine. Levels are bursting with detail, characters are rendered in gloriously high definition. Max himself has a vast number of costume and appearance changes over the course of the game, so every section feels fresh.
Replayability
----
This brings us to the subject of replay value. I haven't touched multiplayer, but there's quite a lot to do. For starters, it's a long game - 12 hours on my first playthrough - with several levels of difficulty.
Secondly, there are collectibles hidden throughout the game, which unlock various perks (upgraded weapons, cheats and new features). Other perks are unlocked by grinding out accomplishments (for example, number of vehicles destroyed). There's a regular, satisfying sense of progression on a level beyond the basic narrative.
There's also a score-based 'arcade' mode, in which you're awarded points based on how stylishly you tackle the level, and finally a very difficult time-based mode. These all take place during sections of the main story.
There's a big problem though. Most of the storytelling sequences are cutscenes, and these take up a huge chunk of the game (I'd estimate around 20%). During the cutscene, the next level loads, providing a seamless experience - but no matter how fast your computer is, **nearly all of the cutscenes are unskippable**. While that's fine on your first playthrough, it annihilates the replay value, and undermines the fun-factor. And as mentioned, the story you're forced to sit through isn't exactly The Godfather.
Series continuity
----
If you're a fan of the series, there are even bigger problems: despite the inclusion of Bullet-Time and voice of James McCaffrey, it does not feel like a Max Payne game.
Gone is the fluidity of the PC-focused older games - the new one borrows from console-based shooters like Gears of War, with an emphasis on squatting in cover, rather than balletic John Woo-ian carnage.
While the levels are dotted with hidden collectibles, there's very little interactivity. In the first two games, almost every object in the world could be manipulated in some way - you'd find yourself rooting through every cupboard for a stray magazine, a painkiller or a new weapon; scanning every roofline for a hidden area. In MP3, once you've found every collectible, on subsequent playthroughs you'll just be running through the levels and shooting people.
Gone are the mod tools, as is the "guns, lots of guns" approach - you can only carry a couple of weapons at once, and the system to toggle between them feels very awkward on the PC.
This is the first Payne game not to be written by Sam Lake, and it shows. Gone are the old characters. Gone are the OTT metaphors and verging-on-parody film noir musings. Gone is the eccentricity, fine detail, romance and sense of humour. The story is utterly disconnected from anything that's come before, and has nothing to do with Max as a person. It feels like Rockstar just wanted to create a game of Tony Scott's film Man On Fire.
And Max isn't written like Max. He swears, he's devoid of wit, he has a new and awkwardly fitting set of values. He even *looks* wrong in his facial expressions, lacking a sense of strength or focus. It's not the first time Max has changed appearance, but in every way except the (admittedly better than ever) voice, he doesn't feel like Max.
Then again, Max Payne 2 felt like a closed story, something which arguably didn't need another sequel. That's a shame, because it's such a beautiful thing to play, which more than a decade later the world feels like it needs more of. Max Payne 3 may be a huge break from the past, but remains a solid shooter, and unlike its predecessor it does feel ready for further sequels. Better ones, hopefully.
Conclusion
----
When you learn to disconnect it from the earlier games, you can't help but be swept up by the ride. It's well made, and a blast to play. But thanks to those unskippable cutscenes, you won't be coming back to it for a while.

Great story, horrible gameplay... that about sums up this game
But since I hate 1 sentence reviews here on steam, here's a summary of what I like/hate about Max Payne 3, and why I'll never play this game EVER again.
The good:
- great storytelling, it could have easily been made into a movie.
- fantastic voice acting (I can't vouch for the Portuguese conversations, since I don't speak the language).
- music fits the game well.
The bad:
- the game throws dozens of enemies at you way too often, I feel like they did it to artificially prolong the game length.
- two thirds of the game, all enemies will only be killed by headshots, since they all wear body armor (you can actually kill them by shooting at the legs and bodies, but it will take an insane amount of bullets, which you are almost always out of).
- too many bullet hell moments in the game, combined with enemies wearing body armor and the player having to conserve ammo often, it was just regular hell.
- the game TOTALLY relies on bullet time and bullet dodge, in other words slow motion.
- checkpoints are not frequent as they could/should have been (again, Rockstar artificially prolonging game length).
- enemies will spawn out of "monster closets" quite often, or even appear out of nowhere in a few situations.
- I hate the "pills are health" gimmick that Max Payne 3 uses, in the old games they had to do it, MP3 has no reason to use it, regenerating health exists, it's a thing now.
- bullets are way too scarce, I ran out of ammo in too many situations.
- the collectibles in this game are golden guns which give you a 50% increase in ammo capacity. You have to find and collect 3 golden gun parts in order to unlock a golden version of a gun. Well, here's the scummy part, you come up to a fork in the road, one path leads to a golden gun part, the other continues the story, if you choose the story path by accident (since you won't know which way is which on your first playthrough), you will not be able to collect the gun part in that playthrough, as the game only has an auto save system, so reloading a checkpoint does you no good since it auto saves the second you trigger a new area.
The verdict:
I had a horrible time playing this game. I did really enjoy the first third of the game as I wasn't forced to aim at each and every enemy's head in order to kill them, but for the major part of the game, I felt like I was playing an on-rails shooter.
So, the score... this game is a 6/10 in my opinion, but only because I really liked the story progression, everything else I just want to forget.

Easily my favorite multiplayer shooter, ever. There's nothing quite like Planetside 2's 50 player+ battles... and this is a REAL FPS, not a hotbar MMO.
I can't speak for the other servers, but the 3-faction system keeps battles on Emerald fairly balanced.
There is one issue: the MASSIVE noob hump. Most of the players are veterans these days, the mechanics take some time to learn, and the skill ceiling is quite high... For the first few hours, you'll be nothing but cannon fodder. But trust me, just just stick with a squad and stick with the game, you'll be addicted in no-time.
One more thing: the game is NOT pay 2 win. This is the only F2P game I've actually bought aesthetic items in, purley out of respect for the developers.

The perks are nice but not essential. In this game it works out great, because they are there if you're into persuing them but they don't get in the way of your enjoyment of the game. I went for MOAR BULLETS and avoided grenades, and my performance did not suffer in the least.
Overall gameplay was fantastic. The animations were really smooth, and the level design was well thought-out with some hidden bonuses/collectibles along the way. The controls in this game are really crisp. Like, crisper than an apple picked right off the tree after the autumn's harvest moon crisp. Just that right amount of light crunchiness without getting all twitchy (DAYZ I'M LOOKING AT YOU, you dry leaf crunching under the heft of my .45 caliber pistol rounds).
The overall plot concept was simple (and I don't feel this to be a spoiler as it's literally the first few seconds of the game): "The bad guy's name is Deathshead. Let's go kill Deathshead." As one would expect, he's not particularly interested in jumping in front of your bullets, and  trying accomplish that simple-sounding objective is where Wolfenstein gets it's pull from.
The atmosphere and aesthetics were brilliantly executed, as was everything about the characters. OMG dem characters doe! They had excellent writing, great acting, and an engaging development. The universe that Wolfenstein presents
the characters to further enhance the plot experience. In other words, there really isn't anything that's contrived in this game (such as, "IT'S JUST... uh...  BECAUSE OF XYZ, WHATEVER JUST ACCEPT IT" does not occur).
The weapons in Wolfenstein feel visceral, but are not anything particularly creative. Full auto rifle, pistol, shotgun, sniper, and so on and so forth. You also get a laser gun, but in a world set in "nazi engineering takes over the world," you'd be disappointed if you couldn't pew hard.
And pew hard you will. Wolfenstein presents its heroes, friends, and villians concisely and profoundly. I mean, I really hated Deathshead, and I was not going to stop holding down "Primary Fire" until I stuck my freshly shined GI boot into his mouth (via his butt).
Awesome weapon-feel, fantastic characters, well-executed universe, "strangling nazis." Not really much wrong with this game, Strongly recommended.
edit: The graphics are also stunning. The freaking in-game movies though, holy hell those are rendered with some next-level stuff.

I have over 550 hours invested in the game at the time of writing this review. Not all of it shows up since for my first ~350h I didn't have the game installed via Steam.
Planetside 2... what a game... You're looking at the Guinness World Record holder for the most players online in a single FPS battle. 1158 players participated utilizing all manner of land vehicles and aircraft, making it one of the most epic fights ever to grace the PC.
Alright, it's Free-to-play, so does that mean it's pay-to-win like a lot of F2P games out there? Nope, only cosmetics require you to spend real money as all weapons are available for in-game currency earned by gaining points. Balance is a little janky at times, but at no fault of the cash shop. Weapons are primarily sidegrades, and even the end-game achievement weapons are only variants on the stock equipment. Every vehicle from the humble Flash ATV to the gargantuan Galaxy troop transport are available from level 1, no questions asked. Even new players can score killstreaks on BR-100 players who have been playing since release (it's unlikely, but the possibility remains).
Onto gameplay, the sole objective is to capture territory from the empires opposing yours. This involves getting to a hostile base and moving people onto the capture points, then waiting until the timer counts down to zero. Sounds simple enough, but you will have to contend with defenders from the empire that owns the base, whether they be on foot, in tanks, or are raining hellfire down on you from their aircraft. Your job is therefore to eliminate the hostile forces, maintain your faction's offensive inertia (yes, it's a thing), and keep your friendly spawn points operational. You can switch between classes at will, provided there is an equipment terminal nearby, in order to cope with a variety of situations.

So would I recommend this game? Yes, without hesitation. Perhaps I'm addicted, but Planetside 2 is a great game that doesn't demand a cent from you. This game was pretty good, but I feel alone in my opinion so maybe me posting this will warn people of what they are getting into or point out for people that have played it though may have missed or have not realized some things about the game. .. So I thought I'd put my 2 cents in.
First lets start off with the things I liked about this game.
1. I defintly love the idea of the game. It's refreshing, interesting, and I think they pulled it off.
2. I like how the 'run and gun' gameplay style in this game almost pays homage to the popular believe that the orginal Wolfenstein practially super charged, if not created, the first person shooter. One aim. .. Killing Nazis.
3. I love that this game is sprinked with playable cut scenes as well as first person cut scenes, though, accented with regular cinematic style cut scenes.
4. I though it was great the weapons and the BEAUTIFUL level designs .. just makes you want to live in the game. ..
5. Most of all I really enjoyed the characters, they all felt unique and were played 'freaking awesomly'.
Out of the things that make the game good it is tragic, really, because they took all this time designing these beautiful levels, having great actors, and having an awesome cinematically balanced script- just to have broken cut scenes where one minute your fighting in a castle (you grab you beverage), next your in prison (you take a quick drink), and then you end up on the moon. .. if you even glance away for a moment you wouldn't understand why you are, where you are. In fact, i didn't glance away- and it was still unclear as to how/why I am where I am.. .. Ha.. You end up at the moon but theres no cutscene or even playble video showing how you've gotten there. .. You finish killing the enemys on earth, somebody radios in that the next stop is the moon (then a brief loading screen) and now your on the moon.
I'm not sugar coating that, either.
There are pleanty other situations like that throughout the game- though- that was just the obvious one. ..
It probabaly wouldn't of botherd me that much IF THE END OF THE FREAKING GAME DIDN'T HAVE THE EXACT SAME PROBLEM of you having to use your imagination to fill of these horrible gaps left in the game.
If i wanted to just 'use me imagination' instead of purpously vesting my time AND MONEY in an entertaining cinimatic story, which it puts out to be, I would taken my $60 freakin dollars and buy myself some paper and crayons for my hit Novel "Wofenstein: The Step by Step, Nothing Left Out, Picture Book Edition" .. .. And still would have some left over for lunch. .. And be more satisfied.
To sum it up and to conclude; I do like the game, especially because I love most things Bethesda puts out. Though they got so freaking obviously painsteakingly annoyingly vibrantly sloppy on this one.. .. Yeesh..
There you have it.

This game was nothing like the other installments of the Wolfenstein franchise that I have played (being Return and 3D). That is not a bad thing. This game has a stellar story with very few plot holes. The characters are compelling, as are the choices you have to make about them throughout the game. Be prepared for intense feels. The alternate history created by The New Order is believable and engrossing. Setting aside the fact that I'm a bit of a completionist, I made sure to find as many of the newspaper clippings as I could just to try and learn more about this world. While these clippings don't add anything to the gameplay, they are full of witty quips and references (Das Blauer U-Boat comes to mind).
As far as the gameplay, this game is quite unique in the approach it takes. You are given stealthy options throughout most of the game and can complete it in that way, which is very satisfying and surprisingly well-scripted for what I expected to be a shoot-em-up game. That said, if you want it to be a shoot-em-up game, pick up two assault rifles and wade through SuperNazis like they were hot butter and you're a lightsaber. I would also like to give a shout out to the LazerKraftWerk (sp?), or LKW. This is a weapon you receive fairly early in the game, and throughout the game you find upgrades for it. I found that the LKW was one of my favorite weapons, especially since it doubles as a cutting torch for getting through thin metal.
The perk system they implemented is inspired and fun to work with. Instead of getting XP and levelling up, there are a series of "achievements" in the game that are unique to each playthrough. Some of the ones I remember off of the top of my head include things like reaching 200/100 health, killing 5 or 10 enemies while sliding, and emptying the LKW's charge without missing a shot. Each of these challenges gives you a perk which benefits your gameplay in some way, be it through increased damage, bonus ammo capacity, or what have you. Some of the perks do require you to get others first, but they are grouped into separate trees so you can play how you want to play and get the perks that are best for you. Don't want to go stealthy? You never have to touch the pistol if you don't want to. Dual wielding seems to be your speed? Well, you'd better believe that you're getting extra ammo drops when you kill an enemy while dual wielding!
There were only a few things I didn't care for in this game. The first is the voice actor for the main character. While BJ has a rather deep personality, his voice is as deep as the shallow end of the pool. There's very little room for tone in it, and he always sounds tired. That said, I can see why he would sound tired, but it's still irritating. The second point is minor, just a revelation about where the Nazis got the inspiration for their technology. It felt like a cop-out, but it wasn't enough to make me not enjoy the game. The last thing I didn't care for was the Enigma system. It was cool that they threw in a reference to the Enigma machine and all, but the puzzles were annoying. Basically, throughout the game you found these Enigma code portions, and once you found all of a certain code, you could try and decode it in the main menu for an alternate gameplay mode. Really, it wasn't that cool, and the alternate modes didn't seem worth the hassle.
All in all, terrific game, and I would highly recommend it.
