I bought this when it was on sale - more out of an obligation rather than an interest in Castle Wolfenstein.  I remember "Return to Castle Wolfenstein" but paid little attention to it,  But I heard a lot about the competitive mod "Enemy Territory"
And then that mod team created
that was Epic enjoyment.
Installation
40GB in size download.  Wow, this was huge and, with a slow internet speed, took 5 days to download.  Standard Steam installation after that.
Graphics
Pretty good.
Detailed scenes,  Human faces were top quality and the hair was short but always well-crafted.  Animation was well-crafted ad very smooth.
But the big caveat is the texture pop-in.  Every time you rotated your field of view, the textures would pop-up and were horribly blurred. Every.... time.... you... turned.... Disconcerting with flashing doors and objects.
After some time, I adapted to the texture pop-in and got on with the game.
The art direction is excellent with a Fallout 50's feeling to the metallic creatures and machines.
Game-play
Of all of id software's games, this is the one with the best story, and a very compelling back-story.  Taking on the what-if possibilities of a world where the Nazis won was very exciting.  The guns were above average and there was an extra adrenalin boost when you dual-wielded weapons.  The set-pieces were interesting.  The bang-bang was usually challenging enough and at the correct level.

At only 10 or so hours in gameplay time, and with little replay value, $60 is a pretty high asking price for the new Wolfenstein, but it's a steal at $30 and would still probably be worth $45.  The gameplay is simple, but entertaining and avoids getting too repetitive like many other single-player shooters suffer from (like Serious Sam), and it's not excessively railroaded like the Modern Warfare games.
The game suffers from excessive load times, oddly jerky cutscenes (while actual gameplay is a rock-solid 60fps at maximum settings even on a lowly HD 7770), and some irritating controls (the slide move is almost never actually used beyond one or two set-pieces and makes it incredibly hard to sprint from cover to cover), but it's more than made up for with good acting, fun gameplay, and a surprisingly fun plot despite being, well... Wolfenstein.  Also, a word of advice: this game is MASSIVE, weighing in at a crazy 44GB, so be ready to spend an excessive amount of time downloading it.  All that voice acting, I guess.
Definintely worth $30, but you might want to wait for a better sale if it's being sold for much more than that.

I have to admit when I first heard that the Wolfenstein franchise was getting a reboot I had a number of mixed emotions. While the game was a bit before my time, I have to say that the thought of Bethesda remaking such an iconic series seemed unrealistic to me. Remembering how groundbreaking the first game was, I wondered how such a game could live up to it's legacy. Recreating this critically acclaimed franchise which had been virtually untouched for so long seemed like such a tantamount task for any developer to take on; but MachineGames pulled it off with it's hit: Wolfenstein The New Order.
Entering the Wolfenstein franchise as a new player I found myself to be quite entrigued by the immediate introduction into action in the game. having never played the previous games from the '90s I was unsure if I was going to enjoy the game or not upon first entry. Of course I'd seen the videos from E3 of all of the gameplay footage and such alike but I was unsure whether I would truly be imersed into the game or not. Well, I guess I found out later when four hours had passed and the sun was down. With this game I was expecting any old shoot 'em up action packed FPS, but I found myself pleasantly surprised at the end of the game. Set in a world where the nazis have conquered the planet after mystical occult powers lead them to their victor in WWII, the Nazi War machine now rules the globe. The main character B.J. Blackowitcz' main directive after somehow awakening from a decade and a half long state of paralysis is to find the resist and bring down the war machine. Now this might sound like your classic FPS however a combination of fantastic character immersion as well as a gripping plot development creates an experience which really gets you empathizing with the characters in the game. I couldn't stop playing this game and when I made it to the end found myself feeling very satisfied with the all around experience. I have to say that this game is a perfect embodiement of what I'm looking for in a modern day FPS. Looking forward to the next game!

There is no multiplayer in Wolfenstein TNO:
"If we could take every bit of energy and sweat the studio has and pour all that into the single-player campaign, it gives us the resources to make something very, very cool, compared to if we would also have to divert some of our resources to making multiplayer."
And I have to say, the dev was selling it short calling the campaign 'very, very cool'. It's absolutely amazing. This is the most fun I've had with a shooter since Bulletstorm.
I didn't expect the story to be interesting, but it is, mostly because the characters are well developed. You get a better feel for the resistance in the interludes, where you explore the underground base. These serve as a welcome break from the action, but also give more exposure to the characters.
This is no regular corridor shooter. Most levels have secret routes and sometimes there are multiple paths to take. The game offers a chance to approach a situation with stealth or guns blazing, but why not use both? For instance it's great fun to take out the commanders silently first (who can call for backup), then finish up with mayhem from your dual shotguns.
The arsenal isn't too big, but that's a good thing. Every weapon is fun to use (silenced pistol headshots hnnghh), with dual wielding and secondary fire modes adding variety to the combat. Some enemies are a bit too bullet-spongey when you use regular weapons, but that's a minor complaint. When you make full use of your arsenal, the encounters feel very satisfying.
If Wolfenstein: The New Order is what we get when developers ditch mp in favor of the campaign, I'm all for it. The focus shows, and I'm actually itching to go back in and replay the game. Machinegames have really delivered something special here.

This game has long been a childhood favorite. It was the first game I ever bought and owned for the PC. I played a lot of this game, mainly singleplayer back in 2006, but scratched the CD a couple years later. When I found it had been remastered on Steam I was quick to purchase myself a copy and have been playing both singleplayer and multiplayer since. For those of you who used to own a copy like myself, I highly advise purchasing this digital edition, as it offers both the same nostalgic gameplay and a great strategic outlet. The Forgotten DLC also gives you more to explore and adds even greater variety to an already extensive game. I highly recommend this title, as it has quickly (re)become a personal favorite.
For those of you who haven't played Age of Empires before, it was one of the older RTS games dating back to the late 90s / early 21st century. I'm surprised more people don't play it. You are given a wide selection of civilizations with specific perks each, and try to race each other towards an objective, be it a Wonder Race, Deathmatch, or King of the Hill. All of which are great fun! What really stands out with this game is that there are hundreds, if not thousands of ways to win. Granted, the mechanics may seem simple and outdated, but when trying to runn an entire empire with 200+ units against up to seven other players, every click counts as you try to out-maneuver, out-think, and out-micro your opponent. The graphics may take a while to get used to, but what you really should look forward to enjoying is the satisfaction of wrecking the strong defenses of an enemy with allies or alone, and conquering lands one by one. A great title, I also highly advise purchasing this for the newer community.

Max payne 3 is 3rd Person Shooting at it's finest.
Aiming and moving around is very tight and feels so natural, it's ridiculous. You can move in any direction while aiming in another, thanks to dynamic animation that supports pointing your gun behind you, over your shoulder or across your chest to the side, etc.
There have been a lot of great gameplay additions to Max Payne as well, such as the inclusion of a physics engine to the characters themselves. Now doing a shoot-doge has extra streategy involved as you can choose to throw yourself into an opponent, knocking him over, while you place a slow-motion bullet into his buddy 30 feet away. Another really cool feature is the last stand. If you have any painkillers, and you get gunned down, you'll have a chance to exact revenge on your killer before dying. If you suceed, Max dusts himself off and keeps going at the expense of a painkiller. This feature, however, doesn't make the game easy. There are times where it's frustratingly difficult, but those moments are few and far between. For the most part, Max Payne 3 provides an excellent challenge while managing to not make you want to rip your hair out.
Also, if you have a firend who plays, pick up the Deathmatch Made in Heaven pack to unlock the classic Dead Man Walking mode; Only this time, you get to bring your friend along with you. This mode is one of the better wave-based co-op modes that I've played in any game. There's a lot of awesome things going on here. My only gripe is that they only ever converted 2 of the multiplayer maps to work with this mode, despite there being a handful of new maps for other modes in the various content packs. Veteran Max Payne fans are used to having a sizeable number of maps for Dead Man Walking.
Lastly, the story. So many people, myself included, were worried about Rockstar taking Max out of New York, aging him, cutting his hair, etc. but they've taken care of the series, as they've been working with Remedy and Max Payne since the beginning of the series (be it as a publisher or handling console ports, etc.).
The story is great and does a good job at filling you in on the happenings in the last 2 games if you never had a chance to play them. You see what brought Max to Brasil and the story unfolds there at a good pace.

The A.I. in the missions are pretty good at moving around and thankfuly for me aren't "aim bots" and miss a high percentage of their shots.
The one major down side of Max Payne 3 is that the online multiplayer is basically dead and I didn't really get enough time to mess around in it.

I'd already posted a review some 2 years ago, but eventually deleted it because it was overly shallow.
After over 11 years playing AoE II, I can still say it's my favourite RTS ever. It's that kind of game you get really fond of, each year more, through your childhood and adolescence, Unfortunately, I must admit I'm absolutely unable to be fair in rating this game, because I have no idea what impression an Age of Empires neophyte would get in 2015 from a 16-years old game.
What I can say, is that it's quite pricey. After 2 years from the HD release, it's still sold for no less than 20 euros, and steam transaction history reminds me I bought it on April 11 (2013) for €18.99. As I doubt there is any RTS enthusiast who has never come across this game in the last decade and a half, and considering nobody but RTS aficionados would look up such a retro game, I suggest everyone reading to pass on until it's on sale.
Pertaining to the improvements allegedly made from the original game, I can't say they've done a great job. They merely noticed there was a massive on-line community after all those years and told themselves "oy vey we could make some good shekels with this geriatric". The 500 unit cap is great, but you don't exactly need to be a sagacious or creative developer to figure it out. 'HD'? Doesn't feel so. The textures were barely touched, although even if they'd been, I wouldn't have cared.
The Forgotten Expansion is objectively good. I have tested the Italians, the Slavs and the Magyars only, but except for the last one the other 2 really feel like unique factions. I generally don't play non-european civ's so I'm just going to say the Incas are a great pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ Playing against the Indians feels like assaulting pakistani mini-markets with trebuchets and knights. However, considering the expansion adds a bunch of new civ-related campaigns too, 9 euros aren't that bad.

The original Payne will always be close to my heart, and the second is right up there in the best sequels of all time list. I was highly suspicious about what Rockstar was doing to my precious Finnish game by making it a trilogy that ends with a bald fat John McClane in the tropical heat of Brazil,
?
Actually, no they haven't. It's definitely different than the two previous games and I think that's a decidedly good thing (hardcore noire fans calm down there's still segments of good old Jersey which isn't quite New York but it's the perfect place for Max). R* may have left Noir York behind but they're staying true to the originals in gameplay, with a few improvements added. Bullet time remains unchanged and you won't find regenerating health here, pop the pills and struggle on with the incredible new gunplay which is the single biggest plus point for the third game. Max's movements in all directions with any weapon are so fluid that it's hard to appreciate it at times, it just seems so natural that the player will rarely notice it.
For me the story wasn't an important point, but rather served as a great excuse to put the old warhorse out on the battlefield one last time. You get to shoot at the thugs of favelas, senseless paramilitaries and a few mafia goons, armed with a shiny new game engine it's a fun experience that surprised me positively. The story is there at least and it stands on it's own, but only just, if you ask me. No comments on the multiplayer as I haven't played it.

Dirty Bomb is free-to-play FPS game developed by Splash Damage (SD) and Nexon.
At the beginning of a match, the player is placed on one of two teams, either Jackal or CDA, and must complete various objectives in order to win the round whilst fighting both the opposing team and the clock. The player can choose up to three mercenaries, or 'mercs', to play as during the round and can switch between them freely between lives. Teamwork and communication are strongly encouraged during the game, hinted at by the ability to revive 'downed' players, as well as the fact that being the 'lone wolf' often leads to a short life.

Ever get that feeling of déjà vu? You shoot and a portal appears, you shoot again and then there is another one. Magically you now have the ability to run between these objects and propel inanimate objects through them.
I thought this game was a carbon copy of Portal 1 but I wrong for sure. Now, where were we? This simple but complex first person shooter is sure to entertain and generate massive amounts of enjoyment value for the masses. The ability to share this emotional journey with a friend through the co-op campaign was right on target for ensuring that the people coming into this game straight from Portal 1 wouldn't be disappointed with a re-skin and graphics update and actually have a good new game to enjoy. Another thing this game has going for it is it's full language support for almost every country/language available which is a big improvement from Portal 1.
The controls for this game are easy to use and understand as well as having full controller support and being able to get steam trading cards is definitely a plus. The one downside however is the length of the story being a bit of a letdown. It seems that there is definitely room for improvement in this sense which will probably result in Valve making more money from a sequel and potentially a pre-prequel. That being said I will happily open up my steam wallet to indulge in this excellent indie series.
As GLADOS always says, Let's try that again.

Strongly recommend this game to anyone who's a fan of shooters, class-based or not. While you may struggle to pick up the game at first, after the first ten to twenty hours your enjoyment of the game will begin to increase as you'll have familiarized yourself with everything from the mercs to the weapons to the maps. This game features a wide arsenal of weapons, and anyone who has ever played a shooter before will find a loadout card or merc with a weapon or playstyle they're comfortable with. You name it, we have it - Assault Rifles, Sniper Rifles (Bolt action, Semi-auto or the unique Grandeur), Shotguns, Sub-machine guns, Light Machine Guns, Machine Pistols - and that's just for the primaries! We also have Grenade Launchers, REVIVR rifles, Miniguns and abilities like Artillery Salvos, Airstrike Markers, Orbital Lasers, Molotov Grenades, Frag Grenades (affectionately referred to as "pineapples")... the list is endless. Aside from the fact that mercs have to be purchased (save for the first two), the only fault I can find with Dirty Bomb is the ammo system can be a problem for new players who aren't playing a Fire Support (a merc that can dispense ammo) since ammo is sparse and without a Fire Support merc new players are forced run around a map they are very unfamiliar with in order to find ammo supplies.
Also, don't buy Vassili first. Not only will you most likely suck with him, the self-proclaimed "sniperest sniper" in the game, the other mercs (even the other two snipers!) are far more suited for team and aggressive play. Admit it, you'd rather be at the front lines, manning the machine gun on the EV and mowing down the enemy team, calling in an airstrike on the enemy's forward base, slicing and dicing people with a katana or dancing around the enemy shotgunning them than in the back, scoped in and feeding the enemy Phantom free frags.

Extremely enjoyable shooter with a rich story and a somewhat believeable plot. A worthy successor to the legendary Max Payne games. If however, you're opposed to cutscene heavy games it's not for you. The cutscenes are an essential part to the story and by skipping them all you will miss ALOT of the key plot points and twists.
Gameplay in Max Payne 3 is rock solid. Nice physics with incredibly fun and "cinematic" action sequences and ofcourse the notorious bullet time will ensure a very enjoyable 10 to 12 hours of gameplay. Shooting feels great and the "meaty" and gruesome hit detection makes for some brutal combat that will at times make you cover your mouth and go "oooooh, that must have hurt".
I recommend this game to all Max Payne fans. The custcenes really don't take away from the experience. They give context for the shooting segments and move the story forward. What was done with the comic book style story telling in the original Max Payne games, are now done with regular cutscenes.
Replay value is high in my honest opinion, all the collectable gun parts and clues that you might have missed on the first playthrough are more than enough of a reason to start from the beginning and finding all the pieces. I will infact play through Max Payne 3 again just to find all the gun parts and clues.
When it comes to multiplayer, well to be honest multiplayer to me has never been needed in a Max Payne game and I will treat Max Payne 3 as that. A singleplayer game. If you want to find out about the multiplayer aspect of Max Payne 3, there are plenty of sources for you to check it out.

Rather unexpectedly, I've found Wolftenstein: The New Order to be the most engaging and most entertaining first person shooter I've played since the original Bioshock.  Everything about the game feels like it was crafted with care and expertise.  I shouldn't be surprised given that the game was made by much of the same team behind Riddick: EFBB (one of my favorite FPSes of all time).
The story is serious and ridiculous in nearly equal measure and yet somehow they make it work.  I think perhaps because even when it's being silly, it's still self-serious, like *good* 80's action movies.  It creates an experience that has enough gravitas to be a compelling outside of gameplay alone, yet stays just outside the territory of getting too grim to be something you'd call fun.
The gameplay is very well paced with bouts of action perforated by quieter moments of exploration and dialog.  There's a great amount of variety in play for a straight action shooter as well, with some vehicle segments and rewarding, yet entirely optional, stealth opportunities.  The weapon set is relatively limited, but each weapon feels distinct and useful; and the ability to dual-wield everything is a blast.
The graphics are the only area where I have a minor gripe.  The game is rock solid stable and runs quite well for the overall level of visual fidelity.  The idTech5 engine can produce some amazing vistas and uniquely detailed environments at at a distance, but it still has the same weaknesses.  Namely close up texture detail suffers and pop-in, though significantly improved since Rage, is still visible and immersion breaking when turning around in crowded environments. The game also lacks a built-in AA option, when post process (shader-based) AA has really become an easy to implement standard at this point.  Even so, it's still a good looking game.

Extremely enjoyable shooter with a rich story and a somewhat believeable plot. A worthy successor to the legendary Max Payne games. If however, you're opposed to cutscene heavy games it's not for you. The cutscenes are an essential part to the story and by skipping them all you will miss ALOT of the key plot points and twists.
Gameplay in Max Payne 3 is rock solid. Nice physics with incredibly fun and "cinematic" action sequences and ofcourse the notorious bullet time will ensure a very enjoyable 10 to 12 hours of gameplay. Shooting feels great and the "meaty" and gruesome hit detection makes for some brutal combat that will at times make you cover your mouth and go "oooooh, that must have hurt".
I recommend this game to all Max Payne fans. The custcenes really don't take away from the experience. They give context for the shooting segments and move the story forward. What was done with the comic book style story telling in the original Max Payne games, are now done with regular cutscenes.
Replay value is high in my honest opinion, all the collectable gun parts and clues that you might have missed on the first playthrough are more than enough of a reason to start from the beginning and finding all the pieces. I will infact play through Max Payne 3 again just to find all the gun parts and clues.
When it comes to multiplayer, well to be honest multiplayer to me has never been needed in a Max Payne game and I will treat Max Payne 3 as that. A singleplayer game. If you want to find out about the multiplayer aspect of Max Payne 3, there are plenty of sources for you to check it out.

This game is probably one of my favorite shooters I have played in a long time. Full disclosure, I have not played Max Payne 1 or 2, so i cannot comment if they are similar.
The shooting is very tight and accurate, and it makes you feel like you are really in control and that gives you the confidence to jump into a room and try various daring manouvers. This is the great thing about this game, it plays differently and more fun then the generic third person shooter where you hide behind cover until an enemy puts his head above cover.
You are constantly and frantically running around trying to get angles on your enemies. When you have enough meter, you can then slow down time and pick apart your enemies.
When it comes to the story, this game does not skimp out on the cutscenes. They are usually not long, but there are many and they nicely divide up the action. The story is gritty and the noir aspect of Max Payne makes me like it even more. Max is always giving the player his thoughts on the situation and it gives us even more insight into what Max is going through. They really focus on Max and I really appreciate that.
Finally, the amount of detail in the enviroments is just down right impressive. Whether you are running through a cubical laden office building or a run down favela, there is so much detail everywhere you look. The graphics are also very impressive. The first time you have a shoot-out and the enviroment is completely destroyed, you will see how much work they put into this game.
One thing to realize about this game is that it is very gritty and gory. At the end of every shoot-out, the last person you kill triggers a slo-mo moment where the camera zooms in on the enemy and you can see the bullet impacts. You can keep on shooting during these scenes and absolutely decimate the persons body. The story also goes into very dark places, so just be prepared.
This game is a must play.

[wrote this since it's dirt cheap again] My favorite grimaced alcoholic detective returns with nice improvements on the previous 2 games. The tough difficulty is back with more bite, as Max will die from headshots in single-player instantly and enemies are more plentiful and aggressive, making the new cover system a need when you're out of bullettime. The aiming in the game is tight, meaning you will score headshots in bullettime if you've aimed well and fired single shots at a time, something that was absent from the first two games with most weapons, and there may be some difficulty keeping track of the small dot reticule because of this change. There are proper physics in MP3 and the impact of bullets can be felt well, either stumbling an enemy or the player, dependent on the bullet caliber & muzzle energy. Multiplayer is finally in the series and is frustrating from all the seasoned players at first, but rewarding when you get a good feel for the game and have unlocked a few items, given how tight the controls/aiming is. I'd recommend beating the single-player at least once before heading online, though there doesn't seem to be many players around these days.
The game is definitely weak story-wise, and MP3 moves away from the alleyways, warehouses, and abandoned buildings of New Jersey to Rio de Janeiro. MP3 also ditches a lot of the campiness in the first 2 games for more cool & gritty. There are also some glitches but they're avoidable for the most part and aren't too common in my experience. The levels were done with a good amount of detail in mind, even if it's just a flashy nightclub you blaze through in a few minutes, some cramped favelas, or a large party yacht, and are all rendered beautifully, somewhat justifying the 32 gigs of so of HDD space this game takes up. HEALTH, the noise band, did a great job on the score as well, and provides a somber mood but with electronic intensity.
Overall, it's a polished and tight third person shooter for those twitchy, arcadey gamers that just want to feel like a single-man army in a modern action movie, dodging bullets and shooting akimbo while diving through the air, with a hefty amount of challenge to make it feel like more of an accomplishment to beat

This masterpiece is one of the key pillars of PC gaming I would say. Should be everyone's "must-have" game.
First of all, the campaign. The single player story of the game lets us play as "Chell", a test subject of Aperture Science, the company which has made the first Portal Gun. This gun is your tool to complete levels as you advance further and further. The game gives you not one but two characters in the first ten minutes of the game who will narrate through the story.  The whole story is quite long and provides a big variety of puzzles and places to go to.
Your goal is to complete levels by using your brain and solving puzzles to reach the end of the game and stop GLaDOS (main villain of the game, look her up on wiki, has many-many informations the game does not tell you directly). These puzzles are fun to solve and even though they can be quite a challenge they are still relaxating and calm.
The game contains a Co-Op mode with - unlike the first episode of the game - a unique story about two robots. The maps made for this mode do actually require another player and teamwork. The whole mode is so enjoyable, we spent half an hour taunting and jumping around at the starting zone with a friend. The Co-Op campaign provides tons (literally) of maps to play and also a bonus set of levels after finishing the main story.
The achievments are fun and unique and the whole game takes place in the same universe as Half-Life, making sure we got the hype for the sequel. As a true Valve game, Portal 2 contains many and more easter eggs, some of them being reallly hidden (really, just look up the wiki after finishing the story, you'll be amused).
The Workshop also contains awesome fan-made maps and complete co-op campaings (MEL Stories, which has become a mod). After finishing the story it provides even more fun to play the levels the community made. The game is also speedrunnable and there are many challenges too (eg. least portals used).
I will not write Pros/Cons for this game as it basically only has pros the only con being that the community is now dead, but it is forgivable as the game is so old that its usual, old hype has gone now. My rating would be a 10/10, and I recommend playing the first one as well if you did not before, it gives a lot more information about story, and is almost as fun as this one is.

I've finished my Uber run after 15 hours and 56 deaths. I would describe it as possibly the best FPS I've played since Half-Life 2, certainly since the original Modern Warfare.
It has some of the modern sensibilities baked in, like a cover system, and the ability to stealth kill people, but it's very much an FPS in the Half-Life vein. And like Half-Life 2 it's a superb game despite the shooting not actually being that great and the story being by-the-numbers and an excuse for cool set pieces.
You see, where this game excels is in everything else. There is great enemy variety and they all feel distinctive and you handle them in different ways. The guns handle differently and you will use them in different circumstances. And despite the shooting not being great, these elements combine to bring you that great feeling of the classics like Doom and Half-Life, because you will choose the right gun depending on the encounter you're in.
And it works in newer stuff really well. OK, I could live without the cover system, but the perks give you a great incentive to try out different ways of playing, without feeling like a necessary burden. Get lots of throwing knife kills? Here, have an extra knife slot. It's just fun. Stealth provides you one alternative to many encounters, and in addition the game will often provide you another route which you can discover to make life easier. You feel like you have options, and on the top difficulty I felt like I needed to explore them to win. It even has some replayability in that you make an early choice which bumps you into one of two timelines.
Uber difficulty felt just right to me. I could die, but generally it felt like I'd messed up. Maybe a couple of encounters towards the end where I felt I had to play off advance knowledge, but generally I was just deadly enough but a slip up could cost me dearly.
Collectables have been nicely updated. I was doing my best to track them down, but finding them didn't feel like it ruined the pacing. They're not obnoxious to find, yet surprisingly difficulty to spot, but not in an unfair way. Hell, they glow and I still managed to miss some. Never quite figured out what causes them to get marked on my map sometimes and not others though. I thought it was collecting the level map, but apparently not.
But the real jewel in the crown are the characters and the story telling. As I said, the story itself isn't anything to write home about, it's just an excuse for lots of big set pieces. However, this is the first FPS in a long, long time where I have been invested in the people. The game paces it perfectly, you learn about these people, get to know them, and you care about what happens. It's the equal of any Valve game in this respect. And it's all set against this monstrous backdrop of war crimes. In a way it's odd to have this contrast between over-the-top nazi robots and mad scientists, and then these mundane yet horrific crimes and psychopaths. But it works.
There's some niggles I have, but they're not worth getting into because overall this game is just plain good. It leaves itself open for another in the series, and were it developed by MachineGames I'd put down for a pre-order.

Alright so this game was rather unexpected to me. Wolfenstein (Goddammit, I hope I write the name well throughout the whole review) from 2009 didn't sell THAT well and I honestly have no idea about what happened to make Bethesda own the IP rather than Activision. But since Bethesda isn't all about the money (though it has it's greeds and I very much felt that on my own skin...), they are now going a bit more... old-school-y. First: this, now a new DOOM game is coming and sounds promising and I'm already hyping it alot. And we know the Prey 2 project was scrapped and handed over to the bros at Arkane (Devs of DIshonored, Dark Messiah) to make it a true sequel to the cult-classic original from 2006.
Anyways, knowing The New Order would be a return to old-school shooters, excitement grew. But then the E3 Demo was rather poor: they showed the very first level of the game (which is the most linear and cutscene-ish). It was a poor decision that then didn't stop me from paying full retail price for the Special Edition Retail Box (New DOOM Beta, yay! :D). 50€ for this.
It was totally worth it...
Alright so! Lets get on with the graphics: iD Tech 5 Engine - I'm AMD so... was I ♥♥♥♥ed alongside other AMD users?
Nope! Works perfectly on my PC, it's the 2nd game in history (afaik) that uses the iD Tech 5 technology by Carmack and thus: yes, the infamous Mega-Texture system. Sounds scary, doesn't it? Basically a regular texture game (every other game except iD Tech 5 games (I think all) have everything textured by it's own: a box has its own texture quality, the tree has its own texture-work, characters, guns, fooliage, etc. etc. Everything has its own texture-work. Mega Textures aren't like that: with this system, the whole world around you is made of 1 single texture-work. 1 texture for the environments, boxes, gun-models, characters, fooliage, etc. etc. As you can see, it's a huge texture (thus the name) so one thing you can predict quite easily if you think a bit: Lengthy texture loading! Yes! This will result in texture pop-in, especially worse in the PC version of these games, I will then talk about pop-in in The New Order).
It actually shouldn't worry you. Mega-Textures allow the game to look good or very good and also allows players with weaker PC's to run the game well! RAGE was the previous iD Tech 5 game and it was terrible on AMD, I can claim it myself, the pop-in was ridiculous!
Nevertheless, pop-in is pretty much non-existant in Wolfenstein: The New Order (hell! I've been playing Duke Nukem Forever recently again, and the pop-in is worse there!) which is great and unexpected tbh. The game runs really well and looks weird.
Weird because 80% of the game looks good, some parts even excellent. But then others... oh man! Looks 2002...
No, I'm serious! I remember a vent whose walls and it's screws were all like paper drawings, no 3D modelling for the screws or the metal bendings. Just looks kinda ugly.
Despite that, overall graphics are pretty good, not great, the game is quite colourful compared to other shooters, which is nice.
Many people still think how the game is this big. I would bet on the Mega-Textures being the reason, but I'm only assuming. RAGE was the previous Mega-Textured game and it was also really big (Complete Edition is ~24 Gb). Wolfenstein is (don't fall from your chair, please) ~45 Gb. This game is quite heavy on cutscenes so, that should increase the HDD Space count by a lot (games like Alan Wake are like 10 Gb, 6 or 8 Gb of those if I recall correctly were custcene videos!).
It will be a pain to download Mega-textured games, but there you go... it's worth it so... enjoy 5 hours of DL time.
Audio is good... for the most part. Guns sound fantastic, voice acting is probably the best this year. However, sound consistency is weak at best. During gameplay, Blazkowicz (the protagonist) will sometimes speak in a super low whisper, which is hard to listen to at times when the rest of the game sounds great and at a normal volume (gun-fire, nazi screams, cuscene voicing, etc.), thank God for subtitles!
The story, this is the most story focused Wolfenstein game. And it's a very good one at that. I love Alternate History (What If type of stories based on real stuff) and this is probably the best Alt. Hist. Storyline ever.
Nazis are winning the war,  Blazkowicz and other allies organize an attack to a castle (General Deathshead's Lair) to kill the General who is responsible for the huge Nazi upgrade and technology boost. The assault goes south, the Nazi's win and that's all I'm explaining...
A very good layer of characterization is made to Blazkowicz, making him likeable and interesting. During Hub missions we can talk to many resistance members and also characterization is well done there. There's a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥ing and screaming and raging. But that isn't annoying the player. It's just arguments and frustrations of rational people living in a sadly, irrational environment full of hostility.
The ending is very well done, and while some hate it, I found it to be pretty much perfect (and I will not explain why, to avoid spoilers, any curious people just chat with me).
The story behind this game is stronger than 90% of movies and videogames and that's a job well done, Machine Games!
There's no MP. Good, 100% focus on the story and the campaign, which is just excellent! I wish more devs were like this! ♥♥♥♥ing sick of co-op ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t on my games. Everything now has to be online, ugh! Disgusting. Co-Op is dead to me. it's never well done and always tacked on. Good online is CoD and Battlefield. Good Co-Op is Killing Floor and Left 4 Dead. The rest is tacked on♥♥♥♥♥♥(yeah, you too Borderlands!).
Commendable to make an SP only game and have the balls to do it in a AAA title.
Moving on to the gameplay: superb. Guns feel great, the game doesn't take itself too serious (you can eat dog-food to replenish health, you can use car doors and piece of broken robots to replenish your armor).
It's just great! In what game can you dual wield Sniper Rifles and go berserk?! What game has a sniper rifle with a secondary fire mode that is an ironsight mode that fires a laser beam! And guess what? You can dual wield that too!
You can dual wield knives because "Hey, why not?"...
A nice layer of depth is added to gameplay with the perk system: if you pull off a certain achievement (kill 3 enemies while dual wielding without releasing the triggers, kill 100 enemies with assault rifles, stealth kill 20 enemies with throwing knives, etc.) you will unlock some nice passive buffs to your character like moving faster while crouching, receiving health or armor during quick consecutive kills, the ability to carry more grenades, more knives, increased magazine ammo count, etc.
It's a nice way to make the player do certain stuff and vary the gameplay in order to get those buffs.
Every gun is fun to use and this is one of the few games that made me replay it though there's absolutely no reason too! Except to get collectibles. Anyways, I can proudly say I've played this game 2 times and I'm almost done with the 3rd playthrough. I still intend in doing the bonus modes so...yeah...
Level design is overall very good. The first level is linear but once you arrive at the castle, it gets more expansive. You can get to a place usually through 3 or more different paths. I agree it could've been a liiiiittle bit more open, as some places are highly linear but overall the level design excells!
The game also has MANY Collectibles, 150 if I'm not mistaken. There is nazi gold pieces to collect. Enigma codes (once you unlock a whole set of enigma codes and solve the math equation, you will unlock new game modes, which I won't spoil here, but I must admit, some are REALLY fun and interesting and will allow you to keep yourself busy for quite some time!).
(Word limit is very close, gotta wrap up) 14 hours to beat.

This game is so good, I didn`t know what to say about it, so here is a California fish taco. :P
INGREDIENTS
• 2 pounds mahi mahi (skinned, boned and cleaned) cut into 1-ounce strips
• 2 cups all-purpose flour
• 3 eggs, lightly beaten
• 4 tablespoons water
• 2 cups panko bread crumbs
• Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
• Vegetable oil, for frying
• 1/2 head savoy cabbage, finely shredded
• 1 bunch cilantro, leaves picked
• 1 bunch chives, chopped
• 3 limes, cut into wedges for garnish
PINK CHILE MAYONNAISE:
•	1 cup sour cream
•	1 cup mayonnaise
•	3 chipotles in adobo, plus 2 tablespoons of adobo sauce
•	1/2 lemon, juiced
•	Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
MANGO-RADISH SALSA:
•	2 limes
•	2 mangoes, diced
•	4 to 5 red radishes, diced
•	1 red onion, diced
•	1 tablespoon chili powder
•	1/2 bunch fresh cilantro, leaves chopped
•	1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
•	Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
DIRECTIONS
Prepare the fish. Cut the pieces of fish into 1-ounce strips. Set up abreading station of flour, lightly beaten eggs with water, and seasoned panko bread crumbs. Season all with salt and pepper.Dredge the pieces of fish in flour, egg then bread crumbs. Once all the fish is breaded deep-fry in small batches in (375 degrees F) oil.Drain on paper towels and season with salt. Keep warm until ready to serve.
Prepare the pink chile mayonnaise. Put the chipotles in a blenderand puree until smooth. Add the sour cream, mayonnaise, adobo sauce and lemon juice and continue to process until the mixture is consistent and creamy. Season with salt and pepper and refrigerate until ready to use.
Prepare the mango-radish salsa. Remove the peel and pith from the limes and cut between the membranes to remove the segments. Put these "supremes" into a bowl and squeeze over the juice from the membranes. Add the remaining ingredients and mix. Season and refrigerate until ready to use. You can also place all of the ingredients into a food processor and puree for a smoother salsa.
To serve, set up the tacos "family-style". Assemble the fish in a pile on a plate; the pink chile mayonnaise in a bowl; and mango-radish salsa in another. Set a pile of shredded savoy cabbage, cilantro leaves, chopped chives and lime wedges next to the fish. Toast the corn tortillas lightly over an open flame (on your stove top) and serve.

I really enjoy this game. It has a uniqueness to it that makes it stand out from other First Person Shooters. The gameplay is standard FPS, but with a different twist. Each merc has a collection of loadout cards, access to 3 primary weapons, 3 secondaries, and 3 melee weapons for a total of 9 different loadout cards you can get. There are also 3 perks attached to each card after Bronze rarity. There are 5 regular rarities, and several different special ones. Default cards have no perks, Lead has 1 perk, and Iron has 2 perks. Bronze has 3 perks, and everything after Bronze (Silver, Gold, and Cobalt) have nothing different added to them, just shinier bling. Obsidian is a special card that only a few mercs have access too, and is usually given for an event. There are several other special event cards that are equivalent to a Bronze rarity, just have unique skins. So you don't need to have that Cobalt card, but it'll look damn good on your favorite merc.
There are currently 19 mercs at the time of this review, with each being different and seperated into a category.
Fire Support - These guys generally use an assault rifle, and hand out ammo to players, and usually have a good team sweeper ability such as Skyhammer's Airstrike Marker.
Medic - These are, you guessed it, Medics, and heal teammates and revive them as well. Dirty Bomb has an interesting and unique system where if you kill a player, they "go down", which gives medics an oppurtunity to revive them and get them back up on their feet. You can still kill a player with an explosive or headshot so they can't get revived, but more weapons will down them. Quick tip: Use your knife to finish them in one hit if its safe to so so, otherwise you'll waste a half a clip or so killing them with bullets. All medics come with defib units, which is how you revive players. They also come with a healing unit of some sort, such as Aura's Healing Station.
Engineer - These are the guys you ALWAYS want one of, because both game modes that are currently available either require you to plant or defuse C4, or build something, which an Engineer does twice as fast. They are not usually good frontline units, but if you use their abilities right, such as Proxy's mines, they can be used as great frontline support units.
Assault - These mercs are pretty self explanatory, they usually only have one ability, such as Fragger's Frag Grenades, and use hard hitting assault weapons. These are the guys that will always be on the frontlines, and most have a good amount of health to back themselves up with.
Recon - Finally, we have the recon mercs, which mostly use sniper rifles or semi auto rifles of some sort. They are have devices that can pinpoint enemy locations, and than can take them out from long range, such as Vassilli, and his Heart-Beat Sensor, which will mark enemies for you and your allies. They are long range support, as such, they don't have a lot of health, and can be taken out pretty easily. Their recon devices can also almost always be disrupted, either through killing them, or destroying the devices themselves.
The game itself is really fun, and it is free to play, so you should give it a shot! I don't play it nearly as much as I used to mostly because the game doesn't give you enough rewards to play after you complete the missions. And sometimes, you can complete all 3 missions in one Stopwatch match. Other than that, the game is pretty great, so you should try it.

FreeJam ♥♥♥♥ed up a perfectly good game.
1 year ago, this game was great. The game was based on a tier progression system, depending on your robot's ranking which was decided upon the blocks used to build the robot. Starting from tier 1, to 10. That system is now long gone for more than a year. What came after that was CPU matchmaking. Based on CPU consumption on your robot, you would be put with stronger enemies. So that ♥♥♥♥ed up the game. And guess what they did after that. Yeah. You guessed it. They ♥♥♥♥ed it up even more. How? The currency used in the game called RP (along with GC, premium currency) were both eradicated. Instead came a lousy universal currency called Robits. So how do you get Robits? You don't. Max Pine 3 plays nothing like any other shooter. You move like a fat old drunk due to rockstar controls, and because Max Payne is a fat old drunk. So it fits. There's a cover mechanic, but it's not the be all end all feature like in Tears of War or whatever. You get flanked and you get dead. Max Payne 3 is best played like a man with nothing to lose would do it, running into the hail of bullets guns blazing. Except when it's not, and you want to duck and cover instead. It has a unique balance to it!
Max gets killed easily and sometimes almost randomly. It's pretty great, honest. The gameplay is all clumsy and grimy, but it feels more like a gunfight than a lot of other games, where you're staring at your hit points while circle-strafing around people, or sitting behind cover forever, healing your wounds with heavy breathing. Max Payne 3 is organic, chaotic! The bullet time mechanics do not have much in common with the previous games. Bullet time is a more limited resource than before, and it's intended to be used as a sharp-shooting aid, rather than something you turn on to clear the room with ease. The shootdive is more of a desperation move now.
The game does occasionally end up feeling too much like a simple, confined shooting gallery minigame crammed between overlong cutscenes, a lot of which you can't skip because it's a console port.

Well, a couple of days ago I bought Age of Empires II on Steam, because I have so many fond memories of playing it as a kid. The thing that got me worried though was that I wasn't sure whether I would still enjoy it now...
I couldn't have been more wrong!
Man I used to play this game on my crappy old laptop, it was so much fun! I remember making whole maps with oceans and forests, then starting from the dark ages with a few villagers to make it to the imperial age whilst fighting off armies of intruders from the inky blackness of the unexplored regions. It really is a fun game to play and here are some of the reasons why:
1) There are so many customisation possibilities, you can make almost any scenario imaginable (well, as long as they are historical ones). There is a fully customisable map editor, where you can build anything from natural landscapes to villages and cities. In this editor you can also change the game type (conquest, king of the hill etc.) and the enemies you face (including their civilisation, eg. the vikings). There are up to seven AI controlled players to either battle with, or even form alliances and trade.
2) The mixture of building an thriving economy, amassing a formidable army and furthering your civilisation with loads of technologies to research (which differ between civilisations), makes gameplay rewarding and addictive. There is nothing better than watching your civilisation grow and prosper from a tiny group of villagers with a town centre into an amazing city, producing forces to bring your enemies to their knees!
3) There is a great campaign mode that is both fun and challenging. The campaigns are split up into different historical events (for example, the tutorial features the Scottish battles against Edward Longshanks' English forces) and feature figures such as Joan of Arc and Atilla the Hun. It's surprising how much detail has gone into these campaigns when it so easy to make your own games; there are fully voiced introductions to each of the missions, and numerous objectives and optional missions to complete each time.
4) With the introduction of the title onto Steam, there has been a complete revamp of the online features. There is a whole community of players with which to battle and ally yourself with (admittedly I haven't tried the online features yet, but they do look promising). Steam has also introduced achievements and trading cards to the game, which can only make things better right? However one of the best things about moving onto steam though is the fact that there are so many mods available! (right now I have a mod that includes Arnold Schwarzeneggar taunts to my sound list)
My one gripe with the game is something that I believe has been many peoples' concerns since the game was first released back in 1999; the AI can be pretty awkward sometimes. This usually comes through when your army runs off without you noticing to pursue a single enemy scout, only to be slaughtered when they reach the enemy stronghold. Or you build an amazing empire to realise that the enemy hasn't built a single thing... they have just chopped down every tree on the map (why this happened I have no idea).
The one thing I will say about this is that the AI on the new steam version is updated (and so are the graphics, huzzah!) and doesn't seem as silly as before, and there are updates still coming. All in all though, I think that this game is completely worth your time and money, and will keep you entertained for hours, so grab a copy or download it from steam, you won't regret it!

Wallpaper Engine is a fantastic piece of software, which allows you to display 4 types of wallpapers for your desktop, these backgrounds can be as follows:
- Scene : Basic wallpaper, can be animated.
- Video : Video wallpaper, in most cases looped to seem animated, can also have sound.
- Application : Run an application (such as a basic game) as your wallpaper.
- Web Application : Run a web based application as your wallpaper.
Now as many of you may be thinking, a lot of these formats can be fairly intensive on your GPU and CPU, however on my specs (albeit fairly good, check my profile for them) I have not noticed any lag. And performance on my favorite wallpaper which is a looped video of a log fire, only uses 3% CPU and 2% GPU capacity. In any case when you are on your desktop and have nothign significant to run, using up clock cycles to run a nice background isn't going to bother you that much. And if you are worried about the background impacting performance in games, do not worry! There are an array of options within the engine to mean you only really have to open Wallpaper Engine when you want to change wallpaper, the options within this menu allow you to set the wallpaper you choose to launch on computer startup, to pause when not in view to save system resources, change the volume for backgrounds (if it has any sound) and so much more.
Still now convinced? Below is a short list of the Pro's and Con's of Wallpaper Engine.
Pro's:
- Cheap.
- Do not have to buy DLC, can get LOADS of wallpapers from the workshop.
- No noticeable performance impact.
- Lots of settings to reduce system usage, and individual wallpaper settings.
- Developer is extremely active with the community and regularly patches bugs (were a few at launch, but were all patched within first couple of weeks, works perfectly now).
Con's:
- Workshop is now full of anime..
Final rating 10/10, great piece of software with even greater potential.

This is a fantastic addition to the series. The previous iteration by Raven Software was... bad. I have enjoyed the ability to choose whether I Rambo my way through the map dual weilding assault rifles, sneak through a hidden corridor to come up behind a commander and slit his throat, or a combination of the two. The graphics are great and will really shine on Ultra settings, provided you have the GPU to support it. There have been a few instances where the automatic weapons will have a stray shell casing stuck next to the gun, but this was a minor glitch.
One neat little gameplay element that I have enjoyed so far is the way the map is unlocked. Of course as you progress through the level, you reveal the places that you have been, but say you find an emergency exit map on the wall... pick it up and you reveal the entire location. It was a subtle gameplay presentation that I really enjoyed; however, I can see this getting redundant and losing its appeal over time.
In past reviews, other players have reccommended starting on Hard difficulty for experienced FPS players and I agree. I usually start on Normal difficulty on all games just to get a feel for it before I crank it up on a second playthrough. In this case, I started on Hard and have not been disappointed. It definitely presents a challenge, but it is not overbearing so long as you take cover when necessary. The ammo and health are abundant between firefights and I'm often forced to leave bullets behind due to max ammo cap. This, of course, could be due to my playstyle.
Overall, in the crowded genre of FPS, this game does not introduce any gamechanging mechanics. The story is well written, the graphics are great, and the gameplay is solid. The lack of multiplayer may decrease the replay value, but some games just don't need it. While a co-operative campaign would have been a good addition, it would not have fit with the story, and a hastily thrown together adversarial multiplayer would have detracted from the overall experience.

As I first saw the Wolfeinstein on the front page I was turned off by its $60 price tag and the unfamiliarity I had with it. I overlooked it until my friend had praised it and I was thinking about purchasing it, but it wasn't until a sale sold it for half off. Here is why I wasn't dissapointed:
1) Story: While I've heard some call the plot shallow and underwhelming I thorougly enjoyed it. I can honestly say that I always felt driven to go to the next objective. There are plenty of papers and notes you can find that supplement the game with history and you eventually get revenge with your beaten down group of resistance fighters that lead you through an attack on Deathshead's castle, to a nuclear-powered U-boat all the way to the moon. Plus, you get to kill some Nazi's. That's always a plus. Near the end of the game, I was actually felt a need to kill Deathshead. Despite the dozens of times it required me to kill him on Uber.
2) Gameplay: This is not just a generic FPS -- let me tell you that. Starting from the end of the prologue you get a whole new set of weapons (all similiar, but still) where you consistently find new upgrades in the following levels. You find new ways to kill Nazis that allow you to go unseen or with dual-wielded automatic shotguns. I've seen some complaints that some enemies require multiple clips to kill, and I have to say having completed the game on Uber, that's far from true. Uber was a challenge and if you made a simple mistake within seconds you were dead and you had to force yourself to use the evironment to destroy your enemies. During a mission, you enter the final area of the level and you easily dispatch the Nazi soldiers with stealth, and you search for armor upgrades, gold, secret codes, and you go to the objective, and suddenly two huge robots emerge. Now, in the early part of the game you don't have much to kill them with by yourself, especially on Uber, but if you pay attention you see a robot shut off switch right in front of you. You see a metal grate which can be shot through with turrets to net you some much needed armor. You ultimately die a few times, but you manage to shut one of the robots off and destroy the other by nailing it with one of the energy turrets on each side of the area. The struggle and panic I felt during that single fight really got me into the game where it maintains that level of difficulty with stronger enemies, but you're helped by finding stronger weapon upgrades.
In the end, you strap up with your auto shotty, mow down a few Nazis, a few armored dogs, and you're gifted a pretty good story. I only hope the developers make the sequal just as compelling as you end with a cliffhanger that made me want more.

This game has become very user friendly since I first got it about 2 years ago.
This is a lengthy review, so TL;DR Good game 9.8/10
Not only do you get a LOT of in game money in the first 15 levels, which you can use to get whatever you want,
ALL STARTING WEAPONS ARE GOOD
Each weapon in the game is situational, just like how shotguns are ideal for cqc and not sniper rifles.
If you find yourself getting beaten over and over by the same player who has a "cooler" looking gun, It is a result of one of three facts:
- They are better at playing than you. This means they can keep their cursor on you/on/near your head throughout the firefight.
- They have a weapon better suited to the environment you are fighting in. This is not because they paid money to get a better gun - Their gun just simply outclasses yours in the situation. This can be avoided by engaging your targets in situations suited to your weapon
- There may be lag during a fight - A thing called "Client side hit detection" is in the game, meaning if they hit you on their screen, the damage is dealt even if lag means you did not see them. Such situations give the advantage to the defender: simply stay in cover and you should avoid this problem.
There is also a place you can warp to called "VR training" in which you can trail almost any upgrade/weapon in game for free against target dummys. This is a good way to see if buying a weapon/sight will fit your style of play before purchasing it with hard-earned certs
All that said, there are still downsides. Every continent except hossin is very vehicle oriented, ESPECIALLY after the nerf to c4. 2 c4 used to one shot a sunderer, but now it takes 3 bricks. The cost of the second c4 brick was also increased by 100 certs, quite a lot for no real purpose.
Zergs (Large groups of infantry/vehicles with no leader except a driving force to cap bases as a large group) are very annoying to deal with. The only way for expierenced outfit leaders to defeat a large zerg is to backcap, but the only way to deal with these players later is to fight them head on, a very difficult feat against zergs that out number you as much as 3 to one.
Grinding is a big deal in this game. Though the cert gain system has improved dramatically, if you want to pick up this game and play it like cod or battlefield, you are out of luck. Unlocking one thing will mean you cannot unlock another for a VERY long time, unlike cod and battlefield where it is quite easy to get new weapons quicky.
Basically, get this game if you enjoy large scale fights that can go on for quite some time, and are confident with your ability in first person shooters. Not much (if any) replayability as you want to stay on the same account for the entire game, the game has become more "play to win" now than ever. 9.8/10 would reccomend for non-casual players.

As I first saw the Wolfeinstein on the front page I was turned off by its $60 price tag and the unfamiliarity I had with it. I overlooked it until my friend had praised it and I was thinking about purchasing it, but it wasn't until a sale sold it for half off. Here is why I wasn't dissapointed:
1) Story: While I've heard some call the plot shallow and underwhelming I thorougly enjoyed it. I can honestly say that I always felt driven to go to the next objective. There are plenty of papers and notes you can find that supplement the game with history and you eventually get revenge with your beaten down group of resistance fighters that lead you through an attack on Deathshead's castle, to a nuclear-powered U-boat all the way to the moon. Plus, you get to kill some Nazi's. That's always a plus. Near the end of the game, I was actually felt a need to kill Deathshead. Despite the dozens of times it required me to kill him on Uber.
2) Gameplay: This is not just a generic FPS -- let me tell you that. Starting from the end of the prologue you get a whole new set of weapons (all similiar, but still) where you consistently find new upgrades in the following levels. You find new ways to kill Nazis that allow you to go unseen or with dual-wielded automatic shotguns. I've seen some complaints that some enemies require multiple clips to kill, and I have to say having completed the game on Uber, that's far from true. Uber was a challenge and if you made a simple mistake within seconds you were dead and you had to force yourself to use the evironment to destroy your enemies. During a mission, you enter the final area of the level and you easily dispatch the Nazi soldiers with stealth, and you search for armor upgrades, gold, secret codes, and you go to the objective, and suddenly two huge robots emerge. Now, in the early part of the game you don't have much to kill them with by yourself, especially on Uber, but if you pay attention you see a robot shut off switch right in front of you. You see a metal grate which can be shot through with turrets to net you some much needed armor. You ultimately die a few times, but you manage to shut one of the robots off and destroy the other by nailing it with one of the energy turrets on each side of the area. The struggle and panic I felt during that single fight really got me into the game where it maintains that level of difficulty with stronger enemies, but you're helped by finding stronger weapon upgrades.
In the end, you strap up with your auto shotty, mow down a few Nazis, a few armored dogs, and you're gifted a pretty good story. I only hope the developers make the sequal just as compelling as you end with a cliffhanger that made me want more.

I've been playing this game for almost three years now and while it has had its ups and downs it's slowly settling in becoming stable, well-balanced and recieving rather frequent and good updates,
I don't know how to review this game in a coherent way over Steam as the review section is mostly used for one-liners or jokes. But to sum up quickly:
Excellent shooter if you're playing organized with a friend or more, alternatively actively try and find some in-game guys to play with. Playing alone can be tedious, as it puts so much more pressure on your performance and there's no guarantee anyone will be around to help you.
Game also hosts proximity VOIP which adds to spontanous teamplay and local communication alot.
Guns are fairly tightly balanced and getting better all the time, there's no pay-to-win element as the only upgrades that are straight up character upgrades [like carrying more ammo or getting faster shield recharge] cannot be bought for money and all custom weapons are side-grades - default weapons are the default and are solid at all ranges and all tasks but excel in none.
Lots of customization that lets you and your outfit get a distinct look which adds alot to the immersion down the line when you start recognizing friends and enemies in the MMO world.
So; if you're a single-player that doesn't feel like playing organized with others then this game might not be for you. For people who enjoyed the old Battlefield games then this game ought to be a natural step in the right direction.
The new publisher also seems to take the game in a healthy direction with pretty good updates, good amount of communication and no real signs of reducing the steady package that is Planetside 2 into a Warface-P2W cashgrab.

Now I know what you're thinking: "How can this guy have played 600 hours on this game and NOT recommend it???" Well, Let me tell you why.
It's not that it's a bad game, but over the years, the devs have ruined it for the veterans that just started this game. I mean this game used to have tiers, armor class, and even made you have to think about how you were meant to make your bot both strong and good looking. Now it's just "Here, make whatever, we don't care just give us money."
Now, it does have it's pros and cons, which I'll list, and if you're a new player, go ahead, try it out! But if you're a veteran who forgot about this game and is wanting to reinstall it, DON'T. Here's why:
PROS:
Easy to start and get the hang of
Was fun in the good old days, and people seem to enjoy it, I just don't, that's my opinion
Can be creative while at the same time blowing up everyone you see
CONS:
The unlocking system used to be tier based, and to unlock things, you had to get tier tokens, which they cut out, and I enjoyed unlocking things, but now it's just a "Once you get lucky and get it once you can get a sh!t ton of them" kind of thing
Alot of people just use the same bots from the workshop, just because it's good and inexpensive, or just because their favourite youtuber made it, and it makes it so there is almost no diversity in the bots.
No more megabots, like seriously, why put them in to take them out less than a year later?
That's all I got for now, hope it will help some vets steer clear of this. Now if you're a newbie and have never played, I recommend you give it a shot, but just know it used to be alot better.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Almost every major area transiton or end of chapter portion in the game has an unskippable cutscene. Attempting to skip them will prompt you with a "still loading" message at the bottom right; but I am highly suspicious of the message when, while running the game from an SSD, that cutscenes become skippable when they transition from the previous area's closeout to the new area's setup, and never sooner. It seems like the game is torn torn between never showing you a loading screen, but also trying to let you skip its cutscenes, in that it can't let you skip the initial portion as its still using those assets to play the in game cutscenes, and can only do so once it swaps scenes. In the end what you get is a game that will happily force you to watch atleast half of the cutscenes in full again, should you decide to play through the game another time.
Gun play is average, much like all third person shooters they pay too much attention to keeping the weight of your character and their gun's position. While thats great and all for realism's sake, the crosshair on the screen is completely fixed and can give you mis information of where Max is actually pointing his gun. I'd prefer less realism in turn for more responsiveness, as some of the actions feel so shackled by the animations. Tapping A and D rapidly will make Max's animations clip, and he'll shuffle, its quite amusing the first time you do it.
Mechanics wise, the stickiness of the cover in the game just makes that part of it just boring and bad. Enemies will hide behind cover for ages if you do the same, and just play out a slow whack-a-mole shooting gallery. Because of that, I would just avoid using cover whenever I could, save for the parts where the game has gimmicks like a sniper who can rapid fire their weapon at you.
Virtually every cutscene you pop into from one gallery to the next will most likely force Max to pull out his pistol, regardless of how much ammo you have left in it. In others, also regardless of the ammo of the pistol(s), you may also find your rifle discarded. Nothing like waiting for that long cover zoom in, just to aim at the first guy and realize, once again, your spent pistol is out for no reason.
I'd even forgive the game for not having borderless window as a display option if the windowed version wasn't so terrified of the top of my screen; but unfortunately, I can't even anchor it so that it covers the majority of my screen. My attempts at "forcing" borderless window just cause it to crash, fun.

One of the most surprisingly good games I've played in a long time. I wasn't expecting much with this when I originally heard about it given Wolfenstein's lackluster history after Return to Castle Wolfenstein and the tendency of Bethesda published games to be mediocre at best, but I was proven wrong. If there was ever a prime example of the statement "Don't judge a book by its cover" for video games, this is it.
The story is very engaging and somehow manages to make hating Nazis feel new again. The characters on both sides are very well written, and even B.J. still feels compelling as a character outside of brutally murdering Nazis. The main plot is very interesting and solid. Besides maybe a hiccup here and there concerning jumping to different levels, it's very coherent. The overall tone and style of the plot is what I would describe as Bioshock Infinite meets Metro 2033. The entire campaign lasts for around 8-10 hours, and that is without trying to look for all the secrets hidden in each level. Not to mention there are 2 branching paths to choose from.
The visuals are great. Not really eye melting and some textures and effects could be better, but the overall aesthetic is astounding. The annoying visual anomalies present in the only previous idTech 5 game, RAGE, are no longer present for the most part. Maybe some popping in textures every so often, but it's not nearly as jarring as it was with RAGE or some Unreal 3 games.
The sound design and soundtrack are great as well. Weapons are just a joy to use with the sounds they have. The Nazis sound authentic and are in no way cheezy. As for the music, if you're a fan of the new Killer Instinct reboot, you may recognize the stylings of Mick Gordon in the gameplay tracks. The songs range from moody and atmospheric to intense and thrilling. Even though some of my friends jokingly refer to the more intense tracks as "Nazi robot dubstep", it just feels right in this game and I quite enjoy them. There's even some German covers and re-imaginings of famous songs from the time period given a Nazi Germanic spin to them. While you probably won't hear them much throughout the game, it's a nice touch that most game developers wouldn't even consider.
The gameplay is tight and precise as with any idTech shooter. If there's one thing idTech based games always get right, it's player input. As alluded to earlier, the weapons are a joy to use. They feel powerful and weighty without making the game feel like a chore to play. The game is also quite unforgiving on the hardest (Uber) difficulty. Even will all the upgrades you can obtain throughout the game, it always presents you with a challenge.
The only thing I would've liked to see with this game is a multiplayer mode. I can understand it not having one given how immaculate the campaign is, but the mechanics are so solid and fun that it almost seems ridiculous to not have it.
The only negative thing I can say about this game is that I don't think it's worth $60 USD. I know that's more Bethesda's fault than the developers, but I feel this game would be more suited in the $40-$50 price range. Anytime that it's on sale, I wholeheartedly recommend getting it though.
Overall, I very much enjoyed this game, and it's pretty much set to become the GOTY for me in 2014. This game shows that an old concept can be quite reinvigorating and fun if it's just given a little polish here and there.

You know, this was one of those games that I wish they had an inbetween 'thumbs up' and 'thumbs down' symbol for; a flat hand. or a one handed clap prehaps.
Despite all of it's pomp and ceremony, all of it's puffed out chested macho swagger and DX 11 graphics this game only ever managed to strike a middling cord for me.
So, to stop any TL;DR comments from individuals brought up on MTV and free porn leading to 30 seconds of action prior to satisfaction, let's sum it up in a simple pros and cons...
Pros
Fantastic looking game on a decent rig... seriously, awesomely detailed and textured- the shadows and lights are also  immense: this game just looks fantastic.
Well driven single player story mode..It feels like a Hollywood blockbuster in which you get to play the star. It feels, infact, every bit like you are the main protagonist in a Die Hard film; even down to the white vested, chest thumping appearence.
Combat: Accurate and well paced.
Cons: It feels every bit like a Hollywood blockbuster... It's like a square peg being pushed into a round whole:
If I want to watch a narrative driven, explosion strewn extravaganza with shallow characters and pretty pictures then I'll stream any of the 1000s of actions films that are readily available. Film is the perfect medium for this 'brain out' type of experience; big bangs and simple entertainment... and there is absolutely a place for this, which is just as well as this is what this game will give you: simple entertainment.
It's just that this game doesn't utilise the medium of video games to anything like their potential. There is no choice here, there is no player affecting the world; there is no freedom. For me, there is none of what great computer games do: make you the agent of your destiny (or at least give you the illusuion that this is the case). It feels instead like a video game made by the film industry.
If you don't mind this then you'll have a blast, and as long as you understand this when spending your hard earned mulla on this product then I recommend it - just maybe wait until it's on offer again ;-)
